📶 OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) Model — 7 Layers REFERENCE MODEL ▶
Reference Model — OSI / DoD (Department of Defense)
Open Systems Interconnection — 7-Layer Stack & Functions
Divides network communication into 7 abstraction layers. Mnemonic ↑: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away (Phy→App) · Mnemonic ↓: All People Seem To Need Data Processing (App→Phy).
▸ LAYER STACK — PDU (Protocol Data Unit) & PROTOCOLS
7
Application
Data  |  HTTP/S, FTP (File Transfer Protocol), DNS (Domain Name System), SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), SSH (Secure Shell)
6
Presentation
Data  |  TLS/SSL, JPEG (Joint Photographic Experts Group), ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange), MPEG
5
Session
Data  |  NetBIOS (Network Basic Input/Output System), RPC (Remote Procedure Call), SMB (Server Message Block)
4
Transport
Segment/Datagram  |  TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) · UDP (User Datagram Protocol) · SCTP
3
Network
Packet  |  IP (Internet Protocol) · ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) · OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) · BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) · RIP (Routing Information Protocol)
2
Data Link
Frame  |  Ethernet · 802.11 · PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) · ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)
1
Physical
Bits  |  Coax · Fiber · UTP (Unshielded Twisted Pair) · Hubs
▸ LAYER REFERENCE TABLE
# Layer PDU Key Protocols / Devices Function
7 Application Data HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol), HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure), FTP, SMTP, DNS, SNMP, SSH User-facing services, application APIs (Application Programming Interface)
6 Presentation Data TLS/SSL, JPEG, MPEG, ASCII, encryption Encoding, encryption, compression
5 Session Data NetBIOS, RPC, SQL (Structured Query Language) sessions, NFS (Network File System) Establish, manage, terminate sessions
4 Transport Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP) TCP, UDP, TLS (Transport Layer Security) (also L5–L7) End-to-end delivery, flow control, ports
3 Network Packet IP, ICMP, OSPF, BGP, routers Logical addressing, routing between networks
2 Data Link Frame Ethernet, ARP, MAC (Media Access Control), switches, bridges Physical addressing (MAC), error detection
1 Physical Bits CAT5/6, fiber, hubs, repeaters, RJ45 (Registered Jack 45) Raw bit transmission over physical medium

DoD Layer OSI Layers Protocols
Application 5, 6, 7 HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS, SNMP, SSH, Telnet
Transport 4 TCP, UDP

🤝 TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) vs UDP (User Datagram Protocol) — Transport Layer NETWORK+ ▶
Reference — RFC (Request for Comments) 793 (TCP) · RFC 768 (UDP)
Connection Types · 3-Way Handshake · Flags · Use Cases
TCP — connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, error-checked. UDP — connectionless, low-overhead, best-effort. Choose based on need for reliability vs speed.
▸ COMPARISON
Feature TCP UDP
Connection 3-way handshake (SYN→SYN-ACK→ACK) None — send and forget
Reliability ACK, retransmission, ordering No guarantees
Speed Slower (overhead) Faster (low overhead)
Header size 20–60 bytes 8 bytes
Flow control Yes (sliding window) No
Use cases HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol), HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure), FTP (File Transfer Protocol), SSH (Secure Shell), SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), databases DNS (Domain Name System), VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol), video streaming, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), gaming
▸ TCP 3-WAY HANDSHAKE & FLAGS
# 3-Way Handshake (connection establishment) Client → Server SYN seq=100 Server → Client SYN-ACK seq=200, ack=101 Client → Server ACK seq=101, ack=201 # Connection established ────────────────────────────── # 4-Way Teardown (graceful close) Client → Server FIN Server → Client ACK Server → Client FIN Client → Server ACK # TIME_WAIT state follows # TCP Flags (URG ACK PSH RST SYN FIN) SYN - Synchronize (start connection) ACK - Acknowledge FIN - Finish (graceful close) RST - Reset (abrupt close / port closed) PSH - Push (flush buffer immediately) URG - Urgent pointer valid ECE - ECN echo (congestion notification) CWR - Congestion window reduced # SYN scan (Nmap -sS) — half-open, sends SYN, reads SYN-ACK/RST # SYN-ACK = open port; RST = closed; no reply = filtered
🗺️ Network Topologies VISUAL MODELS ▶
Diagram
Physical & Logical Topology Types
Star
Central switch. Easy isolation. SPF at hub.
Bus
Shared backbone. Single failure = full outage.
Ring
Token passing. One break = outage (unless dual-ring).
Full Mesh
All-to-all. Max redundancy. n(n-1)/2 links.
Hybrid
Mixed types (star-bus). Most enterprise nets.
🔢 Subnetting & CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) NETWORK+ · A+ ▶
Reference — IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) Subnetting & CIDR Notation
CIDR Table · Private Ranges · Subnet Math · IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) Basics
CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) expresses a subnet as address/prefix where prefix = number of network bits. Hosts per subnet = 2^(32−prefix) − 2 (subtract network + broadcast addresses).
▸ CIDR QUICK REFERENCE
CIDR Subnet Mask Hosts Subnets from /24 Common Use
/8 255.0.0.0 16,777,214 — Class A (10.0.0.0/8)
/16 255.255.0.0 65,534 — Class B (172.16.0.0/16)
/24 255.255.255.0 254 1 Common LAN (Local Area Network) segment
/25 255.255.255.128 126 2 Split /24 in half
/26 255.255.255.192 62 4 Smaller segments
/27 255.255.255.224 30 8 Point-to-point + small
/28 255.255.255.240 14 16 Small DMZ (Demilitarized Zone)
/29 255.255.255.248 6 32 Point-to-point links
/30 255.255.255.252 2 64 WAN (Wide Area Network) point-to-point
/31 255.255.255.254 2* 128 P2P no broadcast (RFC 3021)
/32 255.255.255.255 1 (host) — Single host route / loopback
▸ PRIVATE & SPECIAL RANGES (RFC 1918 / RFC 5735)
Range CIDR Class Use
10.0.0.0–10.255.255.255 /8 A Private (large enterprise)
172.16.0.0–172.31.255.255 /12 B Private (medium enterprise)
192.168.0.0–192.168.255.255 /16 C Private (home / small office)
127.0.0.0–127.255.255.255 /8 — Loopback (localhost)
169.254.0.0–169.254.255.255 /16 — APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) / link-local (no DHCP)
100.64.0.0–100.127.255.255 /10 — Shared address space (ISP NAT)
0.0.0.0 /32 — Default route / unspecified
255.255.255.255 /32 — Broadcast (all hosts)
▸ SUBNET MATH
# Given: 192.168.10.200/26 — find network, broadcast, range Prefix = /26 → 26 network bits, 6 host bits Hosts = 2^6 − 2 = 62 Block size = 2^6 = 64 (256 − 192 = 64) Subnets = 2^2 = 4 (26 − 24 borrowed bits) # Blocks: .0, .64, .128, .192 # .200 falls in block .192 Network = 192.168.10.192 Broadcast = 192.168.10.255 Host range = 192.168.10.193 – 192.168.10.254 # Subnet mask from CIDR /26 = 11111111.11111111.11111111.11000000 = 255.255.255.192
▸ IPv6 ESSENTIALS
Feature Detail
Address length 128-bit, written as 8 groups of 4 hex digits: 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334
Abbreviation Leading zeros dropped per group; consecutive zero groups → :: (once only)
::1 Loopback (≡ 127.0.0.1)
fe80::/10 Link-local (auto-configured; not routable)
fc00::/7 Unique-local (≡ RFC 1918 private)
ff00::/8 Multicast (replaces IPv4 broadcast)
2000::/3 Global unicast (public internet)
NDP Neighbor Discovery Protocol — replaces ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)
SLAAC Stateless Address Autoconfiguration — no DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) needed
🗺️ Routing, VLANs (Virtual Local Area Network) & Network Devices NETWORK+ ▶
Reference — Routing Protocols · Switching · Network Hardware
Dynamic Routing · VLANs · Spanning Tree · Device Comparison
Routing operates at L3 (IP). Routers select paths using routing tables. Dynamic protocols automate table updates. VLANs segment a single physical switch into logical L2 networks.
▸ ROUTING PROTOCOLS
Protocol Type Metric Scope Notes
RIP (Routing Information Protocol) v2 Distance vector Hop count (max 15) IGP (Interior Gateway Protocol) Legacy; slow convergence
OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) Link-state Cost (bandwidth) IGP Dijkstra SPF; fast convergence; enterprise standard
EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) Hybrid Bandwidth + delay IGP Cisco proprietary; DUAL algorithm
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) Path vector AS path, policy EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol) Internet backbone; connects ASes; complex policy
IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) Link-state Cost IGP Used by ISPs (Internet Service Provider); similar to OSPF
Static route Manual Admin distance 1 Any Predictable; no overhead; no failover
▸ VLANS & TRUNKING
# VLAN — logical L2 segmentation on a switch # Access port — carries 1 VLAN (end devices) # Trunk port — carries multiple VLANs (switch-to-switch, switch-to-router) # 802.1Q tag — 4-byte VLAN tag added to Ethernet frame on trunk links # Common VLAN design VLAN 1 = Default (avoid using for production) VLAN 10 = Data / Users VLAN 20 = Voice (VoIP — QoS priority) VLAN 30 = Management (network devices) VLAN 40 = DMZ / Guest VLAN 99 = Native VLAN (untagged traffic on trunk) # Inter-VLAN routing: "router-on-a-stick" OR L3 switch SVIs # Spanning Tree Protocol (STP 802.1D) — prevents L2 loops # RSTP (802.1w) — rapid convergence (<1s vs 30-50s STP)
▸ NETWORK DEVICE COMPARISON
Device OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) Layer Function Forwards by
Hub L1 Repeats signal to all ports — collision domain Broadcasts bits
Bridge L2 Connects two segments; learns MACs (Media Access Control) MAC address
Switch L2 (L3 if managed) Learns MACs; forwards frames to correct port only MAC address
Router L3 Routes packets between networks; enforces ACLs (Access Control List) IP (Internet Protocol) address
Firewall L3–L7 Inspects and filters traffic by rule set IP/port/state/DPI
WAP L1–L2 Wireless access point; bridges Wi-Fi to wired LAN (Local Area Network) MAC / radio
Proxy L7 Intermediary for client requests; caching, filtering Application data
Load Balancer L4 / L7 Distributes traffic across servers Port / content
📡 Wireless — 802.11 Standards & Security NETWORK+ · SECURITY+ ▶
Reference — IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.11 Family
Wi-Fi Standards · Frequency Bands · Authentication · Attack Vectors
Wi-Fi generations use IEEE 802.11 standards. Frequency band affects range vs speed: 2.4 GHz = longer range, more interference; 5 GHz = shorter range, faster throughput; 6 GHz = Wi-Fi 6E/7, minimal interference.

Standard Wi-Fi Gen Max Speed Band(s) Year
802.11b Wi-Fi 1 11 Mbps 2.4 GHz 1999
802.11a Wi-Fi 2 54 Mbps 5 GHz 1999
802.11g Wi-Fi 3 54 Mbps 2.4 GHz 2003
802.11n Wi-Fi 4 600 Mbps 2.4 / 5 GHz 2009
802.11ac Wi-Fi 5 3.5 Gbps 5 GHz 2013
802.11ax Wi-Fi 6/6E 9.6 Gbps 2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz 2019
802.11be Wi-Fi 7 46 Gbps 2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz 2024
▸ WIRELESS SECURITY PROTOCOLS
Protocol Encryption Auth Status
WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) RC4 (40/104-bit) Shared key Broken — do not use
WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) (RC4) PSK / 802.1X Deprecated
WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) AES-CCMP PSK / 802.1X Current standard — use AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) mode
WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) AES-GCMP-256 SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) / 802.1X Recommended; SAE replaces PSK handshake
802.1X EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) variants RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) + certs Enterprise auth; required for WPA2/3-Enterprise
📡 DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) — DORA (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) Process 4-STEP SEQUENCE ▶
Sequence
Dynamic Host Configuration — Discover · Offer · Request · Acknowledge
DHCP assigns IP (Internet Protocol) addresses automatically. All 4 messages use UDP (User Datagram Protocol) (client port 68, server port 67). Client uses broadcast because it has no IP yet. Relay agents (ip helper-address) forward DHCP across subnets.
D
Discover
Broadcast — find DHCP servers
→
O
Offer
Server offers available IP
→
R
Request
Client requests offered IP
→
A
Acknowledge
Server confirms lease
APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) fallback: 169.254.x.x · Lease renewal at 50% & 87.5% of lease time · DHCP snooping prevents rogue servers
🔌 Common Ports — Protocol Reference REFERENCE TABLE ▶
Well-Known Ports 0–1023 · Registered 1024–49151
TCP/UDP Port Numbers — Services, Protocols & Security Notes
Well-known ports (0–1023) require root/admin to bind. Memorize all ports below for CompTIA (Computing Technology Industry Association) exams — they appear across A+, Net+, Sec+, CySA+.
Port(s) Protocol Transport Security Notes
20 / 21 FTP (File Transfer Protocol) (data/control) TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) Cleartext — use SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) (22) or FTPS (File Transfer Protocol Secure) (990)
22 SSH (Secure Shell) / SFTP / SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) TCP Encrypted; replaces Telnet (23)
23 Telnet TCP Cleartext — avoid; legacy only
25 SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) (send email) TCP Cleartext; SMTPS (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure) = 465, SMTP+STARTTLS = 587
53 DNS (Domain Name System) UDP (User Datagram Protocol) (queries) / TCP (zone transfers) Zone transfers (TCP 53) must be restricted
67 / 68 DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) (server/client) UDP DHCP snooping prevents rogue servers
69 TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) UDP No auth, no encryption — internal only
80 HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) TCP Cleartext — prefer HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) (443)
110 POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) TCP Email retrieval; POP3S = 995
119 NNTP (Network News Transfer Protocol) (Usenet) TCP Legacy; rarely used
123 NTP (Network Time Protocol) UDP Time sync; NTP amplification DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) vector
135 RPC (Remote Procedure Call) / MSRPC TCP Windows; block at perimeter
137–139 NetBIOS (Network Basic Input/Output System) TCP/UDP Legacy Windows; block externally
143 IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) TCP Email; IMAPS = 993
161 / 162 SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) (poll/trap) UDP v1/v2 cleartext; use SNMPv3
389 LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) TCP Directory; LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over SSL) = 636
443 HTTPS / TLS (Transport Layer Security) TCP Encrypted HTTP; standard secure web
445 SMB (Server Message Block) / CIFS (Common Internet File System) TCP Windows file shares; EternalBlue target
465 / 587 SMTPS / Submission TCP 587 = authenticated submission (preferred)
514 Syslog UDP UDP — no delivery guarantee; TCP syslog = 6514
636 LDAPS TCP LDAP over TLS
993 / 995 IMAPS / POP3S TCP Encrypted email retrieval
1433 MS SQL (Structured Query Language) Server TCP Block external access; requires auth
1521 Oracle DB TCP Block external; strong auth required
3306 MySQL / MariaDB TCP Bind to localhost; use SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) in transit
3389 RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) TCP Brute-force target; restrict with NLA + MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication)
5060 / 5061 SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) (VoIP) UDP/TCP 5061 = TLS-encrypted SIP
5432 PostgreSQL TCP Bind to localhost; SSL in transit
6514 Syslog TLS TCP Reliable, encrypted log transport
8080 / 8443 HTTP-alt / HTTPS-alt TCP Dev/proxy; same risks as 80/443
🌐 DNS (Domain Name System) Record Types REFERENCE TABLE ▶
Reference — Source: CEH (Certified Ethical Hacker) + Net+
DNS Record Types & Zone Transfer
DNS uses UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 53 for queries and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 53 for zone transfers >512 bytes. Tools: nslookup, dig, whois.
Record Full Name Purpose
A Address Maps hostname → IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) address (forward DNS lookup)
AAAA (IPv6 Address Record) IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) Address Maps hostname → IPv6 address
CNAME Canonical Name Alias pointing to another hostname (e.g., www → host)
MX Mail Exchange Mail servers for the domain; has priority value
PTR (Pointer Record) Pointer Maps IP (Internet Protocol) → hostname (reverse DNS lookup)
NS Name Server Authoritative name servers for the domain
SOA Start of Authority Primary name server + zone metadata (serial, TTL)
SRV Service Hostname and port number of services (SIP, XMPP, LDAP)
TXT (Text Record) Text Arbitrary text; used for SPF, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail), DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) email auth
DNS FOOTPRINTING COMMANDS
# Forward lookup nslookup example.com dig example.com A # Reverse lookup (PTR record) dig -x 93.184.216.34 # Zone transfer attempt (TCP 53) — reveals all records dig axfr @ns1.example.com example.com # All record types dig example.com ANY # Domain/IP ownership whois example.com

🔭 NMAP Scan Types Reference PENTEST TOOL ▶
Reference — Source: CEH (Certified Ethical Hacker) Cheat Sheet
NMAP — Scan Flags, Responses & Common Options
Nmap is the de-facto tool for network discovery and port scanning. Use nmap <SCAN> <TARGET> syntax. Requires root/administrator for raw socket scans (SYN, FIN, XMAS, etc.).
▸ SCAN TYPES
Flag Scan Type Open Response Closed Response Notes
-sT TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) Connect SYN/ACK RST/ACK Full 3-way handshake; logged by target
-sS SYN (Synchronize) stealth scan SYN/ACK RST/ACK Half-open; doesn't complete handshake; less logged
-sF FIN No response RST Works on Linux/Unix; bypasses some firewalls
-sX XMAS Tree No response RST Sets FIN+URG+PSH flags; binary 00101001
-sN NULL No response Varies by OS (Operating System) No flags set; designed for Linux/Unix
-sA ACK RST No response Maps firewall rules; determines filtered/unfiltered
-sI IDLE (Zombie) SYN/ACK RST/ACK Uses spoofed IP (Internet Protocol); maximum stealth scan
-sU UDP (User Datagram Protocol) UDP response ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) unreachable Slower; needed for DNS/DHCP/SNMP discovery
-sn Ping Sweep — — Host discovery only; no port scan
▸ USEFUL NMAP OPTIONS
# Speed / Timing: -T0 (paranoid) → -T5 (insane) nmap -T4 -A 10.5.23.0/24 # Aggressive: OS detect + version + scripts nmap -sS -p 22,80,443 10.5.23.1 # SYN scan specific ports nmap -sV --top-ports 100 target # Version detection on top 100 ports nmap -sC -sV target # Default scripts + version detection nmap -n -Pn -p- target # All 65535 ports, skip DNS/ping nmap --script vuln target # Run vulnerability scripts nmap --script "vuln and safe" target # Safe vuln scripts only nmap -oX scan.xml target # XML output for import to tools nmap -oN scan.txt target # Normal text output nmap -6 target # IPv6 scan

📡 TCPDump — Packet Capture Reference COMPLETE REFERENCE ▶
Reference — Source: TCPDump Cheat Sheet
Capture · Filter · Display · Output — Full Command Reference
TCPDump is the standard CLI (Command Line Interface) packet analyzer on Linux/Unix. Requires root or CAP_NET_RAW. Use which tcpdump to locate. Write to .pcap files to open in Wireshark.
CAPTURE FLAGS
tcpdump -i any # Capture on ALL interfaces (needs root) tcpdump -i eth0 # Capture on specific interface tcpdump -i eth0 -c 100 # Stop after 100 packets tcpdump -i eth0 tcp # TCP packets only tcpdump -i eth0 udp # UDP packets only tcpdump -i eth0 icmp # ICMP only (ping traffic) tcpdump -i eth0 arp # ARP packets only tcpdump -I eth0 # Monitor mode (Wi-Fi sniffing) tcpdump -r capture.pcap # Read & analyze saved capture file
FILTER EXPRESSIONS
# Host filters tcpdump host 192.168.1.1 # Any traffic to/from IP tcpdump src host 10.0.0.5 # Source IP only tcpdump dst host 10.0.0.5 # Destination IP only tcpdump net 192.168.0.0/24 # Entire subnet # Port filters tcpdump port 443 # Any traffic on port 443 tcpdump src port 80 # Source port 80 tcpdump portrange 1000-2000 # Port range tcpdump tcp dst port 22 # TCP to port 22 (SSH) # MAC/Layer 2 filters tcpdump ether host 00:11:22:33:44:55 tcpdump ether broadcast # Ethernet broadcast frames # Logical operators tcpdump src 10.0.0.1 and port 443 # AND tcpdump dst 10.0.0.1 or src port 22 # OR tcpdump port 80 and not host 192.168.1.5 # NOT tcpdump dst host 10.0.0.1 and greater 128 # Packet > 128 bytes
DISPLAY & OUTPUT FLAGS
tcpdump -n # Don't resolve IPs to hostnames (faster) tcpdump -nn # Also don't resolve port names tcpdump -v # Verbose output (TTL, checksum, etc.) tcpdump -vv # More verbose tcpdump -A # Print payload in ASCII (HTTP inspection) tcpdump -X # Print payload in hex + ASCII tcpdump -XX # Include link-layer header in hex tcpdump -e # Print link-layer header (MAC addresses) tcpdump -q # Quick/quiet — shorter output lines tcpdump -t # Suppress timestamp tcpdump -tttt # Full date+time timestamp # Write/read pcap files tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap # Write to file (for Wireshark) tcpdump -i eth0 -U -w capture.pcap # -U: write packets immediately (no buffer) tcpdump -r capture.pcap port 443 # Read file with filter
PRACTICAL EXAMPLES
# Capture all HTTP traffic (show payload in ASCII) tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 80 # Capture SSH attempts to this host (no DNS resolution) tcpdump -nn -i eth0 tcp dst port 22 # Capture all traffic EXCEPT SSH (avoid capturing your own session) tcpdump -i eth0 not port 22 # Save 30 large packets to file, no DNS resolution tcpdump -i eth0 -n greater 32 -w out.pcap -c 30 # Pipe remote traffic to local Wireshark in real time ssh user@router "tcpdump -U -s 65535 -w - 'not port 22'" | wireshark -k -i - # Find all HTTP GET requests (show source IP + URL) tcpdump -i eth0 -A 'tcp port 80 and (tcp[((tcp[12:1] & 0xf0) >> 2):4] = 0x47455420)'
🧒Networking for Absolute BeginnersNet+ • Start Here▶
BIG IDEA
What Is a Network?
A network is just two or more computers that can talk to each other. Your home Wi-Fi is a small network; the Internet is the giant network that connects all the small ones together. If computers are houses, the network is the system of roads between them.
ANALOGY
IP (Internet Protocol) Address = Mailing Address
Every device on a network has an IP address (e.g., 192.168.1.10) so data knows where to go — exactly like a street address tells the mail carrier which house. No address, no delivery.
ANALOGY
Packets = Envelopes
Big files are chopped into small chunks called packets. Each packet is an envelope with a from-address, a to-address, and a piece of the message. They travel separately and get reassembled at the other end.
ANALOGY
Ports = Apartment Numbers
One device (one IP) runs many programs at once. A port number says which program the data is for — like an apartment number after the street address. Web pages use port 80/443, email and other services use their own.
ROLES
Client vs. Server
The client asks (your phone opening a website); the server answers (the computer that stores that website). Most of what you do online is a polite back-and-forth of requests and responses.
HARDWARE
Router vs. Switch
A switch connects devices inside one network (like hallways in a building). A router connects different networks together and finds the path between them (like roads between cities). Your home box is usually both in one.
ANALOGY
DNS (Domain Name System) = The Phonebook
Humans remember names (google.com); computers need numbers (an IP). DNS is the phonebook that looks up the name and returns the number, automatically, every time you click a link.
Beginner TermPlain-English Meaning
BandwidthHow wide the pipe is — how much data fits per second
LatencyHow long one trip takes — the delay / 'lag'
LAN (Local Area Network)Local network — your home or office
WAN (Wide Area Network)Wide network — connects distant sites; the Internet is the biggest
Wi-FiA network with no cables — radio instead of wires
FirewallA guard that decides which traffic is allowed in or out
🔢IP (Internet Protocol) Addresses & Subnets (Gently)Net+ • Start Here▶
READ IT
What an IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) Address Looks Like
IPv4 is four numbers 0–255 separated by dots, like 192.168.1.50. Each device on a network needs one. We’re slowly running out of them, which is why IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) (much longer, with letters) was invented.
TWO WORLDS
Public vs. Private
Private addresses (like 192.168.x.x and 10.x.x.x) are reused inside homes and offices — like apartment numbers that only mean something in your building. Public addresses are unique on the whole Internet, like a full street address.
NEIGHBORHOODS
What a Subnet Is
A subnet groups nearby addresses into one neighborhood so traffic stays local and organized. The subnet mask (e.g., 255.255.255.0) is just the line that says “these addresses are neighbors; everything else is out of town.”
TermPlain-English Meaning
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)Hands out IP addresses automatically so you don’t have to
Default gatewayThe exit door to other networks / the Internet
Subnet maskMarks which part of the address is the neighborhood
IPv6The newer, much larger address system
NAT (Network Address Translation)Lets many private devices share one public address
📖 DNS (Domain Name System) — The Internet's Phone Book NET • Start Here ▶
THE PROBLEM DNS SOLVES
Humans Hate Numbers
Computers talk to each other using IP (Internet Protocol) addresses like 142.250.80.46. Humans want to type google.com. DNS (Domain Name System) translates names into numbers — like a phone book that covers the whole internet.
THE DNS LOOKUP JOURNEY
8 Steps From Name to IP
1. You type google.com in your browser.
2. Browser checks its own cache. If found → done.
3. OS (Operating System) checks its cache. If found → done.
4. OS asks your recursive resolver (your ISP or 8.8.8.8).
5. Resolver asks a root nameserver (13 clusters worldwide) — "who handles .com?"
6. Root points to the .com TLD nameserver (Verisign).
7. TLD server points to Google's authoritative nameserver.
8. Authoritative server returns the IP. Resolver caches it and gives it to you.
DNS Record TypePurposeExample
ADomain → IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) addressgoogle.com → 142.250.80.46
AAAADomain → IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) addressgoogle.com → 2607:f8b0:…
CNAME (Canonical Name)Alias → another domainwww.example.com → example.com
MXMail server for domainexample.com → mail.example.com
TXT (Text Record)Arbitrary text (SPF, DKIM, verification)v=spf1 include:… ~all
NSNameservers for domainns1.google.com
PTR (Pointer Record)Reverse lookup: IP → domain46.80.250.142.in-addr.arpa → google.com
SOAStart of Authority; zone metadataSerial, refresh, retry, expire
USEFUL DNS TOOLS
Dig, nslookup, host
# Query A record for a domain dig google.com A # Query MX records (mail servers) dig google.com MX # Reverse lookup dig -x 142.250.80.46 # Use a specific resolver (8.8.8.8 = Google DNS) dig @8.8.8.8 google.com # Windows equivalent nslookup google.com nslookup -type=MX google.com
TTL
Time to Live — DNS Caching Timer
Every DNS record has a TTL (Time To Live) in seconds. After TTL expires, resolvers re-query for fresh results. Low TTL = fast changes but more queries. High TTL = slow propagation but less load. When migrating a website, lower the TTL 24 hours before the switch.
🔢 DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) — How Devices Get Their IP (Internet Protocol) Address NET • Foundation ▶
DORA PROCESS
Discover → Offer → Request → Acknowledge
Discover — new device broadcasts "I need an IP!" to 255.255.255.255.
Offer — DHCP server says "How about 192.168.1.25? Here's a lease offer."
Request — client says "Yes, I'll take 192.168.1.25" (broadcast, so other servers know).
Acknowledge — server confirms: "192.168.1.25 is yours for 24 hours. Here's gateway and DNS (Domain Name System) too."
WHAT DHCP HANDS OUT
More Than Just an IP
A DHCP lease typically includes:
• IP address — unique on the local network
• Subnet mask — defines network boundary (e.g., 255.255.255.0)
• Default gateway — the router's IP (traffic leaving the network goes here)
• DNS server(s) — where to resolve names
• Lease duration — how long before re-requesting
STATIC vs DYNAMIC
Manual vs Automatic Assignment
Dynamic — DHCP assigns from a pool; good for laptops and phones. IP may change on reconnect.
Static — manually set; never changes. Required for servers, printers, network gear (you don't want DNS records breaking because the server got a new IP).
DHCP Reservation — best of both worlds: DHCP assigns based on MAC (Media Access Control) address, so the device always gets the same IP automatically.
TROUBLESHOOTING
When DHCP Fails — APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing)
If a device can't reach a DHCP server, Windows auto-assigns an APIPA address: 169.254.x.x. This is a red flag — the device only has link-local connectivity and cannot reach the internet. Check: cable unplugged? DHCP server down? VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) misconfigured?
📡 Wi-Fi Basics — 802.11, Bands, and Security NET • Practical ▶
802.11 STANDARDS
The Evolution of Wi-Fi
The 802.11 family are the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) wireless LAN (Local Area Network) standards. Each letter suffix means a different generation:
StandardWi-Fi NameMax SpeedBandYear
802.11b—11 Mbps2.4 GHz1999
802.11g—54 Mbps2.4 GHz2003
802.11nWi-Fi 4600 Mbps2.4/5 GHz2009
802.11acWi-Fi 53.5 Gbps5 GHz2013
802.11axWi-Fi 6/6E9.6 Gbps2.4/5/6 GHz2019
802.11beWi-Fi 746 Gbps2.4/5/6 GHz2024
2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz
Range vs Speed Trade-off
2.4 GHz — longer range, penetrates walls better, more congestion (microwaves, Bluetooth, neighbors all compete), slower. Good for: IoT (Internet of Things) devices, devices far from router.
5 GHz — shorter range, struggles through walls, less congested, faster. Good for: laptops and phones close to router, streaming, gaming.
6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E) — even faster, very short range, nearly empty spectrum. Best for: dense environments (offices, stadiums).
WIRELESS SECURITY
WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) → WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) → WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) → WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3)
WEP — broken in minutes; do not use.
WPA — better but still has vulnerabilities; phase out.
WPA2-Personal (PSK) — current standard for home; uses AES-CCMP; strong if you use a long passphrase.
WPA2-Enterprise — uses RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) authentication; each user has their own credentials. Used in corporate environments.
WPA3 — latest; uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) instead of PSK (Pre-Shared Key) handshake; resistant to offline dictionary attacks.
🔀 Switching & VLANs (Virtual Local Area Network) — Dividing Your Network Logically NET • Foundation ▶
SWITCH vs HUB vs ROUTER
Three Different Devices, Three Layers
Hub — Layer 1; dumb repeater. Sends every frame to every port. Creates collisions. Legacy/obsolete.
Switch — Layer 2; intelligent. Learns which MAC (Media Access Control) addresses are on which ports using a MAC address table. Sends frames only to the correct port. Creates collision domains per port.
Router — Layer 3; connects different networks. Uses IP (Internet Protocol) addresses and routing tables to forward packets between subnets and out to the internet.
HOW A SWITCH WORKS
MAC Address Table Learning
1. Frame arrives with source MAC AA:BB on port 1 → switch records AA:BB → Port 1 in table.
2. Destination MAC CC:DD — not in table yet → switch floods to all ports except source.
3. Device CC:DD responds → its MAC gets recorded.
4. Next frame to CC:DD → switch delivers it only to the correct port.
This is why switches are efficient — after learning, minimal unnecessary traffic.
VLANS
Virtual LANs (Local Area Network) — Logical Network Segmentation
A VLAN divides one physical switch into multiple logical networks. Devices in different VLANs cannot communicate directly even if they're plugged into the same switch — they need a router (Layer 3) to cross VLAN boundaries. Benefits:
• Security: production servers on VLAN 10, guest WiFi on VLAN 99 — guests can't see servers
• Performance: reduce broadcast domain size
• Organization: group devices by function, not location
TRUNK vs ACCESS PORTS
Single VLAN vs Multiple VLANs
Access port — carries traffic for exactly ONE VLAN. Used for end devices (PCs, printers). Device doesn't know it's on a VLAN.
Trunk port — carries traffic for MULTIPLE VLANs simultaneously. Used between switches, or switch-to-router. Uses 802.1Q tags to label which VLAN each frame belongs to.
FeatureAccess PortTrunk Port
VLANs carriedOneMultiple
802.1Q tagNo (stripped)Yes (tagged)
Connected toEnd devicesSwitches, routers, uplinks
Native VLANN/AUntagged VLAN (usually VLAN 1)
🗺️ Routing Protocols — How Routers Find the Best Path NET • Intermediate ▶
STATIC vs DYNAMIC ROUTING
Manual Routes vs Self-Learning
Static routes — an admin manually configures each route. Simple, predictable, no overhead. Works for small networks. Fails when the network changes (adding a link, a failure) because you have to manually update every router.
Dynamic routing protocols — routers talk to each other and automatically discover routes. Self-healing when links fail. Required for large networks.
ProtocolTypeAlgorithmUse Case
RIP (Routing Information Protocol)Distance VectorHop count (max 15)Legacy / tiny networks
OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)Link StateDijkstra (cost)Enterprise interior routing
EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol)Hybrid (Cisco)Bandwidth + delayCisco enterprise networks
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)Path VectorPolicy-basedInternet backbone; ISP (Internet Service Provider) routing
BGP
The Protocol That Runs the Internet
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is used between ISPs and large organizations to exchange routing information across the internet. Every major network has an ASN (Autonomous System Number). BGP is policy-driven — companies can influence which paths their traffic takes. A BGP misconfiguration can accidentally route the internet's traffic through your network (BGP hijacking).
DEFAULT ROUTE
The Fallback Route (0.0.0.0/0)
The default route (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0) matches ANY destination. It's the "if nothing else matches, send it here" rule — usually pointing to the upstream router or internet gateway. Every end device has a default gateway for this reason.
🧱 Firewalls — The Network's Bouncer NET • Foundation ▶
WHAT A FIREWALL DOES
Permit or Deny Based on Rules
A firewall inspects network traffic and decides whether to allow or block it based on rules. Think of it as a bouncer with a list: traffic that matches an allow rule gets in; everything else is dropped or rejected. The implicit deny rule: if nothing matches, deny.
FIREWALL TYPES
Packet Filter → Stateful → NGFW (Next-Generation Firewall)
Packet filter (L3/L4) — examines individual packets: source/dest IP (Internet Protocol), port, protocol. No context (doesn't know if it's a new connection or response). Fast but dumb.
Stateful inspection — tracks connection state. Knows if a packet is part of an established session. Much smarter — allows response traffic automatically.
NGFW (Next-Gen Firewall) — adds application awareness (block YouTube regardless of port), IPS (Intrusion Prevention System), deep packet inspection, user identity, SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) inspection. Most enterprise firewalls today.
IPTABLES BASICS
Linux Built-In Firewall
# View current rules sudo iptables -L -v -n # Allow established connections (critical — add first) sudo iptables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT # Allow SSH (before blocking everything else!) sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT # Allow web traffic sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT # Drop everything else sudo iptables -A INPUT -j DROP # Modern replacement: nftables / ufw sudo ufw enable sudo ufw allow 22/tcp sudo ufw allow 443/tcp sudo ufw status verbose
DMZ (Demilitarized Zone)
De-Militarized Zone — Public-Facing Servers
A DMZ is a network segment between the internet and your internal network. Public-facing servers (web servers, mail servers) go in the DMZ. If they're compromised, the attacker is in the DMZ — not directly on your internal network. Two firewalls: one between internet and DMZ, another between DMZ and internal. Defense in depth.
⚖️ Load Balancers & High Availability — Never Go Down NET • Intermediate ▶
THE PROBLEM
One Server = Single Point of Failure
If your entire service runs on one server and it crashes, everyone is down. High availability (HA) architectures spread load across multiple servers so that if one fails, others continue serving traffic seamlessly. HA goal: no single component failure takes down the service.
LOAD BALANCER
Distributes Traffic Across Backend Servers
A load balancer sits in front of your servers and routes each incoming request to one of the backends. Algorithms:
Round-robin — server 1, server 2, server 3, server 1… Even distribution.
Least connections — sends to whichever server has the fewest active connections.
IP (Internet Protocol) hash — same client IP always goes to the same server (sticky sessions).
Weighted — big server gets more traffic than small server.
HEALTH CHECKS
Automatically Remove Failing Servers
A load balancer periodically pings each backend (HTTP GET /health, TCP connect, etc.). If a backend fails N consecutive checks, it's removed from the pool. No human intervention needed — traffic automatically shifts to healthy servers. When it recovers, it re-enters the pool.
ConceptMeaningCommon SLA (Service Level Agreement)
High Availability (HA)System stays up despite component failures99.9% = 8.7 hrs/yr downtime
99.99% ("four nines")Enterprise HA target52 min/yr downtime
99.999% ("five nines")Telco/critical systems5.25 min/yr downtime
RTORecovery Time Objective — max acceptable downtimeDefined in DR plan
RPORecovery Point Objective — max acceptable data lossDefined in DR plan
☁️ Cloud Networking — VPC (Virtual Private Cloud), Subnets & CDNs (Content Delivery Network) NET • Cloud ▶
CLOUD MODELS
IaaS · PaaS (Platform as a Service) · SaaS (Software as a Service)
IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) — rent VMs (Virtual Machine), storage, networking. You manage OS (Operating System) and above. Examples: AWS (Amazon Web Services) EC2, Azure VMs, Google Compute Engine. Most control, most responsibility.
PaaS (Platform as a Service) — deploy your app code; provider manages OS, runtime, scaling. Examples: Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Google App Engine.
SaaS (Software as a Service) — use the finished product. Salesforce, Office 365, Gmail. No infrastructure concern at all.
VPC
Virtual Private Cloud — Your Private Network in the Cloud
A VPC is a logically isolated section of the cloud where you launch resources in a network you define. You control IP (Internet Protocol) ranges, subnets, routing tables, and gateways — just like a physical data center, but virtualized.
ComponentPurpose
VPC CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing)IP range for the entire VPC (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16)
SubnetSub-range within VPC; public (internet) or private
Internet GatewayAllows public subnets to reach the internet
NAT (Network Address Translation) GatewayLets private subnets initiate outbound internet; no inbound
Route TableDefines where traffic goes (0.0.0.0/0 → IGW for public)
Security GroupStateful firewall at instance level
NACL (Network Access Control List)Stateless firewall at subnet level
CDN
Content Delivery Network — Cache at the Edge
A CDN stores copies of your static content (images, JS, CSS, videos) at servers (PoPs — Points of Presence) close to users worldwide. When a user in Tokyo requests your image, it comes from a Tokyo edge node, not your origin server in Virginia. Result: dramatically lower latency and reduced origin server load. Examples: Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Fastly, Akamai.
SHARED RESPONSIBILITY MODEL
Who Is Responsible for What in Cloud?
AWS/Azure/GCP secure the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, network). You secure in the cloud (your VMs, data, IAM config, encryption, application code). Misconfigurations (public S3 buckets, overly permissive security groups, no encryption) are YOUR responsibility, not the cloud provider's. This is the source of most cloud breaches.
🔍 Network Troubleshooting — A Systematic Approach NET • Practical ▶
OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) TROUBLESHOOTING
Bottom-Up or Top-Down
Two strategies for network problems:
Bottom-up (most common for no-connectivity): Physical (cable/light?) → Data Link (ARP, MAC?) → Network (ping, IP?) → Transport (port open?) → Application (service running?).
Top-down: Start at the application ("the web page is slow") and work down to find where the degradation is.
THE DIAGNOSTIC TOOLKIT
Commands Every Network Person Uses
# Layer 1-2: Physical / Link ip link show # interface status, MAC ethtool eth0 # speed, duplex, link detected # Layer 3: IP connectivity ip addr show # IP addresses ip route show # routing table ping 8.8.8.8 # basic reachability ping -c 4 google.com # DNS + ICMP check # Path tracing traceroute 8.8.8.8 # hops to destination mtr google.com # live traceroute with packet loss # Layer 4: Transport / Ports ss -tlnp # listening TCP ports ss -ulnp # listening UDP ports nc -zv 192.168.1.1 22 # test TCP port connectivity telnet 192.168.1.1 80 # old-school port test # DNS dig google.com # DNS lookup nslookup google.com # Windows/Linux resolvectl query google.com # systemd-resolved
PACKET CAPTURE
See What's Actually on the Wire
# Capture on interface eth0 sudo tcpdump -i eth0 # Capture HTTP traffic sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 80 -w capture.pcap # Capture DNS queries sudo tcpdump -i any port 53 -n # Show packet contents in ASCII sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A # Read saved capture tcpdump -r capture.pcap
Open .pcap files in Wireshark for graphical analysis. Wireshark's "Follow TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) Stream" shows entire conversations. Filter: http.request, tcp.flags.syn==1, dns, ip.addr==192.168.1.5
COMMON SYMPTOMS
Problem → Most Likely Cause
SymptomCheck First
No connectivity at allIP (Internet Protocol) address assigned? (169.254.x.x = DHCP failed)
Can ping IP, not hostnameDNS (Domain Name System) — wrong resolver, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) giving bad DNS
Can ping gateway, not internetISP (Internet Service Provider) issue, default route, firewall blocking outbound
Intermittent packet lossBad cable, duplex mismatch, overloaded link
High latency only to one siteRouting issue, CDN (Content Delivery Network) problem, that site's servers
App works internally, not externallyFirewall port not open, NAT (Network Address Translation) not configured
🌐 IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) — The Internet's Upgrade NET • Essential ▶
WHY IPv6
IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) Ran Out of Addresses
IPv4 has 4.3 billion addresses. That sounds like a lot — until you realize there are 8 billion people, each with multiple devices, plus billions of IoT (Internet of Things) gadgets. IPv4 officially ran out in 2011. IPv6 solves this with 340 undecillion addresses (3.4 × 10³⁸) — roughly one address per atom on Earth's surface. You'll encounter IPv6 constantly in modern networks.
ADDRESS FORMAT
Reading and Writing IPv6 Addresses
IPv6 addresses are 128 bits written as 8 groups of 4 hex digits separated by colons. Two simplification rules reduce the ugliness.
# Full form — 8 groups of 4 hex digits 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329 # Rule 1: Drop leading zeros in each group 2001:db8:0:0:0:ff00:42:8329 # Rule 2: Replace ONE run of consecutive all-zero groups with :: 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329 # :: replaces :0:0:0: # Loopback (equivalent to 127.0.0.1) ::1 # Unspecified address (equivalent to 0.0.0.0) :: # IPv6 in URLs — brackets required to avoid port confusion http://[2001:db8::1]:8080/path
ADDRESS TYPES
IPv6 Address Categories
TypePrefixScopeIPv4 Equivalent
Global Unicast2000::/3Public internet-routablePublic IP (Internet Protocol)
Link-Localfe80::/10This link only (not routed)169.254.x.x (APIPA)
Unique Localfc00::/7Private org networkRFC (Request for Comments) 1918 (10.x, 172.16.x, 192.168.x)
Loopback::1/128This device only127.0.0.1
Multicastff00::/8Group of devices224.0.0.0/4
AnycastFrom unicast rangeNearest of a groupNo direct equivalent
KEY DIFFERENCES
IPv6 vs IPv4 — What Changed
FeatureIPv4IPv6
Address size32 bits (~4.3B addresses)128 bits (340 undecillion)
NAT (Network Address Translation) required?Yes (address exhaustion)No (enough for all devices)
Header sizeVariable (20-60 bytes)Fixed (40 bytes) — faster routing
BroadcastYes (network noise)No — replaced by multicast
Auto-configurationNeeds DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) (stateless, no server needed)
IPsec (Internet Protocol Security)OptionalBuilt into spec
FragmentationRouters can fragmentEnd hosts only (routers don't)
DUAL-STACK & TRANSITION
Running IPv4 and IPv6 Together
Most networks today run dual-stack — both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously. When a client connects, it prefers IPv6 (via "Happy Eyeballs" algorithm). This lets networks migrate gradually without a hard cutover.
# Check your IPv6 addresses (Linux) ip -6 addr show # Ping using IPv6 ping6 ::1 # loopback ping6 -I eth0 fe80::1%eth0 # link-local requires interface # Traceroute IPv6 traceroute6 2001:4860:4860::8888 # Google's IPv6 DNS # Check if site has IPv6 (AAAA record) dig AAAA google.com nslookup -type=AAAA google.com # Curl over IPv6 curl -6 https://ipv6.google.com
🔌 Common Protocols — What's Actually Happening on the Wire NET • Reference ▶
APPLICATION LAYER PROTOCOLS
Protocols You'll Use Every Day
ProtocolPortPurposeSecure Version
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)80/tcpWeb trafficHTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) (443)
HTTPS443/tcpEncrypted webAlready secure
DNS (Domain Name System)53/udp+tcpName resolutionDoH (DNS over HTTPS) (443), DoT (DNS over TLS) (853)
SSH22/tcpEncrypted remote shellAlready secure
FTP (File Transfer Protocol)21/tcpFile transfer (insecure)SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) (22), FTPS (File Transfer Protocol Secure) (990)
SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol)25/tcpSend email (server-to-server)SMTPS (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure) (465/587)
IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol)143/tcpRead email (syncs)IMAPS (993)
POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3)110/tcpRead email (downloads)POP3S (995)
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol)161/udpNetwork device managementSNMPv3
NTP (Network Time Protocol)123/udpTime synchronizationNTPsec
RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol)3389/tcpWindows remote desktopTLS-wrapped RDP
LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol)389/tcpDirectory services (AD)LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over SSL) (636)
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) VS UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
Choosing the Right Transport Protocol
FeatureTCPUDP
ConnectionConnection-oriented (3-way handshake)Connectionless — fire and forget
ReliabilityGuaranteed delivery, retransmits lost packetsNo guarantee — packets can be lost
OrderingDelivers in orderOut-of-order possible
SpeedSlower (overhead)Faster (minimal overhead)
Use caseHTTP, SSH, email, file transferDNS, video streaming, VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol), gaming
Header size20+ bytes8 bytes
🔐 VPNs (Virtual Private Network) & Tunneling — Secure Connections Over Untrusted Networks NET • Essential ▶
WHAT A VPN ACTUALLY DOES
An Encrypted Tunnel Through a Hostile Network
A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and a VPN server. Everything inside the tunnel is encrypted, so even on untrusted networks (coffee shop Wi-Fi), nobody can read your traffic. There are two distinct use cases that people confuse:
TypePurposeExample
Remote Access VPNConnect a remote user to a private corporate networkWorking from home, accessing internal apps
Site-to-Site VPNConnect two networks (offices) over the internetBranch office ↔ HQ network
Commercial VPNPrivacy/geo-unblocking for consumersNordVPN, hiding traffic from ISP (Internet Service Provider)
VPN PROTOCOLS
How the Tunnel Is Built
ProtocolNotes
WireGuardModern, fast, simple, ~4000 lines of code. Increasingly the default.
OpenVPNMature, flexible, widely supported. SSL/TLS-based.
IPsec/IKEv2Built into most OSes, great for mobile (reconnects fast). Common for site-to-site.
L2TP/IPsecOlder; L2TP (Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol) provides tunnel, IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) provides encryption.
PPTP (Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol)Obsolete — broken encryption. Never use.
PROXIES VS VPNs
Related But Different
FeatureProxyVPN
ScopePer-application (e.g., just the browser)Entire device (all traffic)
EncryptionOften none (just relays)Always encrypted
LayerApplication layer (L7)Network layer (L3)
Common useWeb filtering, caching, hiding origin IP (Internet Protocol)Secure remote access, privacy
A forward proxy sits between users and the internet (corporate web filtering). A reverse proxy sits in front of servers (load balancing, TLS termination, hiding backend — e.g., nginx, Cloudflare).
SSH (Secure Shell) TUNNELING
The Poor Man's VPN
SSH can forward ports through its encrypted connection — a quick way to securely reach services without a full VPN. Essential for accessing internal services through a jump host.
# Local port forward — reach a remote DB through SSH # "Make my localhost:5432 → db.internal:5432 via jumphost" ssh -L 5432:db.internal:5432 user@jumphost # Now connect to localhost:5432 → actually hits db.internal # Remote port forward — expose YOUR local service to remote ssh -R 8080:localhost:3000 user@remote # remote's :8080 → your local :3000 # Dynamic forward — SOCKS proxy (route browser through SSH) ssh -D 1080 user@jumphost # Set browser SOCKS proxy to localhost:1080 # Jump through a bastion to reach an internal host ssh -J bastion.example.com user@internal-host
ZERO TRUST NETWORK ACCESS
The VPN Replacement
Traditional VPNs give you access to the whole network once connected (overly trusting). Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) flips this: "never trust, always verify." Every request is authenticated and authorized individually, granting access only to specific applications — not the whole network. Tools like Cloudflare Access, Tailscale, and Zscaler implement this. Increasingly replacing legacy VPNs.
🧮 Subnetting — The Math That Scares Beginners (It Shouldn't) NET • Foundation ▶
WHAT IS SUBNETTING
Dividing a Network Into Smaller Networks
An IP (Internet Protocol) address has two parts: a network portion (which network you're on) and a host portion (which specific device). Subnetting is the art of deciding where to draw that line — splitting a big address block into smaller, organized chunks. Why? Security (isolate departments), efficiency (reduce broadcast traffic), and organization. It intimidates beginners, but it's just binary math you can learn in an afternoon.
CIDR NOTATION
The /24 Explained
An IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) address is 32 bits. CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) notation like 192.168.1.0/24 means "the first 24 bits are the network portion." The remaining bits (32 − 24 = 8) are for hosts. More network bits = smaller subnet = fewer hosts.
# 192.168.1.0/24 in binary 192.168.1.0 11000000.10101000.00000001.00000000 └──────── 24 network bits ────────┘└8 host┘ # The /24 tells you the subnet mask /24 = 255.255.255.0 # (24 ones, then 8 zeros) 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000
THE KEY FORMULAS
Hosts and Subnets — Memorize These
# Number of usable hosts per subnet usable hosts = 2^(host bits) − 2 # (subtract 2: network address + broadcast address) # Example: /24 has 8 host bits 2^8 − 2 = 256 − 2 = 254 usable hosts # Example: /26 has 6 host bits 2^6 − 2 = 64 − 2 = 62 usable hosts # Number of subnets when you "borrow" bits subnets = 2^(borrowed bits)
CIDR CHEAT SHEET
Common Prefixes at a Glance
CIDRSubnet MaskHost BitsUsable HostsBlock Size
/30255.255.255.252224 (point-to-point links)
/29255.255.255.248368
/28255.255.255.24041416
/27255.255.255.22453032
/26255.255.255.19266264
/25255.255.255.1287126128
/24255.255.255.08254256
/23255.255.254.09510512
/16255.255.0.01665,53465,536
WORKED EXAMPLE
Finding Network, Broadcast, and Range
Given an IP and CIDR, here's how to find the key addresses. This is the most common subnetting question on exams and the job.
# Given: 192.168.1.100/26 — what subnet is it in? # Step 1: /26 → block size. Host bits = 32-26 = 6. Block = 2^6 = 64 # Step 2: subnets start at multiples of the block size (64): # 192.168.1.0, .64, .128, .192 # Step 3: .100 falls between .64 and .128 → subnet is .64 Network address: 192.168.1.64 # first address (not usable) First usable host: 192.168.1.65 Last usable host: 192.168.1.126 Broadcast address: 192.168.1.127 # last address (not usable) Next subnet: 192.168.1.128 # Shortcut: "block size" trick — count by 64s. Done.
LET THE COMPUTER DO IT
Tools That Calculate Subnets For You
# Linux: ipcalc shows everything ipcalc 192.168.1.100/26 # Address, Netmask, Network, Broadcast, HostMin, HostMax, Hosts/Net # sipcalc (more detailed) sipcalc 10.0.0.0/22 # Python — the ipaddress module is built in python3 -c "import ipaddress; n=ipaddress.ip_network('192.168.1.0/26'); \ print(n.network_address, n.broadcast_address, n.num_addresses)" # Python interactive — useful for automation import ipaddress net = ipaddress.ip_network('192.168.1.0/26') print(net.netmask) # 255.255.255.192 print(list(net.hosts())[0]) # first usable host print(net.num_addresses) # 64
🗺️ Network Design — How Networks Are Structured NET • Foundation ▶
TOPOLOGIES
The Shapes Networks Take
TopologyStructurePros / Cons
StarAll devices connect to a central switch+ Easy to manage; − central point of failure (most common LAN)
MeshDevices interconnect (full or partial)+ Highly redundant; − expensive, complex (used in WANs, Wi-Fi mesh)
BusAll on a single backbone cable− Obsolete; one break kills all
RingEach device connects to two neighborsUsed in some fiber/MAN setups (with redundant ring)
HybridCombination (e.g., star-of-stars)Real-world networks are hybrids
THE THREE-TIER MODEL
How Enterprise Networks Are Layered
Classic enterprise network design uses three hierarchical layers. This separation makes networks scalable, manageable, and resilient.
LayerRoleDevices
AccessWhere end devices connect (PCs, phones, APs)Access switches, wall ports
DistributionAggregates access layer; policy, routing between VLANs (Virtual Local Area Network)L3 switches, routers
CoreHigh-speed backbone; moves traffic fastHigh-capacity core switches/routers
In modern data centers, this is often replaced by a spine-leaf architecture: every leaf (access) switch connects to every spine switch, giving predictable low latency and easy horizontal scaling — ideal for east-west (server-to-server) traffic.
DESIGNING FOR RESILIENCE
No Single Point of Failure
TechniqueWhat It Provides
Redundant links + STPBackup paths; Spanning Tree Protocol prevents loops
Link aggregation (LACP)Bundle multiple links for bandwidth + failover
Redundant gateways (HSRP/VRRP)Two routers share a virtual IP; one takes over if the other fails
Dual power supplies / UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply)Survive power failures
Multiple ISPs (Internet Service Provider) (multihoming)Survive an internet provider outage
Out-of-band managementManage gear even when the production network is down
QUALITY OF SERVICE
QoS — Not All Traffic Is Equal
When the network is congested, QoS decides what gets priority. A dropped video-call packet is far worse than a delayed email — voice and video are real-time and sensitive to latency/jitter, while file downloads can wait. QoS classifies and prioritizes traffic so critical, time-sensitive flows (VoIP, video conferencing) get served first. Without it, a big backup job could ruin everyone's video calls.
🌍 DNS (Domain Name System) Deep Dive — Records, Resolution & Security NET • Essential ▶
RECORD TYPES
The DNS Records You'll Actually Touch
RecordMapsExample / Use
AName → IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4)example.com → 93.184.216.34
AAAA (IPv6 Address Record)Name → IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6)example.com → 2606:2800:...
CNAME (Canonical Name)Name → another name (alias)www → example.com
MXMail servers for a domainRoutes email; has priority values
TXT (Text Record)Arbitrary textSPF, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail), domain verification
NSAuthoritative nameserversWho's in charge of this zone
SOAZone metadataSerial, refresh, TTL (Time To Live) defaults
PTR (Pointer Record)IP (Internet Protocol) → name (reverse DNS)Mail server reputation, logging
SRVService location (host+port)SIP (Session Initiation Protocol), LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), Microsoft AD (Active Directory)
CAAWhich CAs (Certificate Authority) may issue certsPrevents rogue certificate issuance
DIG — THE DNS SWISS ARMY KNIFE
Query DNS Like a Pro
dig example.com # A record (default) dig example.com +short # just the answer dig AAAA example.com # IPv6 dig MX example.com # mail servers dig TXT example.com # SPF/DKIM/verification dig NS example.com # nameservers dig +trace example.com # follow the full resolution path dig @8.8.8.8 example.com # query a specific resolver dig -x 93.184.216.34 # reverse lookup (PTR) dig example.com ANY # all records (often restricted) # Troubleshooting: is it a DNS problem or not? # If dig resolves but the app fails → not DNS # If dig fails → check resolver (/etc/resolv.conf)
DNS SECURITY
DNS Was Not Built Securely
Classic DNS is unauthenticated and unencrypted — attackers can forge responses (cache poisoning, spoofing) or snoop on your lookups. Several technologies address this:
TechProtectsHow
DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions)Integrity / authenticityCryptographically signs records — detects forgery (doesn't encrypt)
DoH (DNS over HTTPS)PrivacyEncrypts queries inside HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) (port 443)
DoT (DNS over TLS)PrivacyEncrypts DNS in TLS (Transport Layer Security) (port 853)
DNS filteringBlockingResolver blocks malicious/known-bad domains (e.g., Pi-hole, Quad9)
DNS-BASED ATTACKS
Why Defenders Watch DNS Closely
AttackWhat It Does
Cache poisoningInject false records so victims go to attacker's site
DNS tunnelingSmuggle data/C2 traffic inside DNS queries (evades firewalls)
Domain hijackingTake over a domain's registration or nameservers
Fast fluxRapidly rotate IPs to keep malicious infra alive
TyposquattingRegister lookalike domains (gooogle.com) for phishing
DNS logs are gold for threat hunting — unusual domains, high-entropy subdomains (tunneling), and newly-registered domains are strong indicators of compromise.
🔀 NAT (Network Address Translation) & Port Forwarding — How Private Networks Reach the Internet NET • Essential ▶
WHY NAT EXISTS
Many Private Devices, One Public IP (Internet Protocol)
There aren't enough IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) addresses for every device. NAT (Network Address Translation) lets a whole network of devices with private IPs (192.168.x.x) share a single public IP. Your home router does this: it translates internal addresses to its one public address on the way out, and remembers which internal device each connection belongs to so replies come back correctly.
TYPES OF NAT
Static, Dynamic, and PAT (Port Address Translation)
TypeHow It WorksUse
Static NATOne private IP ↔ one public IP (fixed)Exposing a specific internal server
Dynamic NATPrivate IPs map to a pool of public IPsLess common; needs many public IPs
PAT / NAT overloadMany private IPs → one public IP, distinguished by portThe home router model — by far the most common
PAT (Port Address Translation) is what "NAT" almost always means in practice. The router tracks connections by (internal IP:port ↔ public IP:port) so dozens of devices share one address.
PORT FORWARDING
Letting the Outside Reach In
By default, NAT blocks unsolicited inbound connections (a nice side-effect: a basic firewall). But sometimes you WANT external access to an internal service — a game server, a web server, SSH (Secure Shell) to your home lab. Port forwarding tells the router: "traffic arriving on public port X → send to internal host:port Y."
# Example port-forward rules on a router Public :443 → 192.168.1.10:443 # web server Public :2222 → 192.168.1.20:22 # SSH to lab box # ⚠️ Security: every forwarded port is exposed to the internet. # Forward only what you must; prefer a VPN for remote access. # Linux iptables DNAT (what routers do under the hood) iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 443 \ -j DNAT --to-destination 192.168.1.10:443
NAT CHALLENGES
Why Some Apps Struggle Behind NAT
IssueSolution
Two peers both behind NAT (VoIP, P2P, gaming)STUN/TURN/ICE — NAT traversal protocols
App needs a stable inbound portPort forwarding or UPnP (Universal Plug and Play) (convenient but risky)
Tracking which device did what (logging)CGNAT (Carrier-Grade Network Address Translation) complicates attribution at ISP (Internet Service Provider) scale
Reaching home services remotelyVPN (Virtual Private Network), reverse tunnel, or ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) (Tailscale/Cloudflare)
Note: IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) largely removes the need for NAT — there are enough addresses for every device to have a public one (with firewalls, not NAT, providing the security boundary).
🚪 802.1X & NAC (Network Access Control) — Who Gets On the Network? NET • Enterprise ▶
THE PROBLEM
An Open Network Port Is an Open Door
In a basic network, anyone who plugs into a wall jack or knows the Wi-Fi password is on the network. In an enterprise, that's a serious risk — an attacker in the lobby, a rogue device, a compromised laptop. 802.1X and NAC enforce authentication before access: prove who/what you are before the network lets you communicate.
802.1X
Port-Based Authentication
802.1X authenticates a device at the port level before granting network access. It involves three roles working together via the EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) protocol.
RoleWhoJob
SupplicantThe device wanting access (laptop)Provides credentials/certificate
AuthenticatorThe switch or wireless APGatekeeper — blocks traffic until authorized
Authentication ServerRADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) serverVerifies credentials, says yes/no
Until authentication succeeds, the port only passes authentication traffic — everything else is blocked. Enterprise Wi-Fi (WPA2/3-Enterprise) uses exactly this model, which is why you log in with your own username/password instead of a shared Wi-Fi key.
NAC
Network Access Control — Beyond Just Identity
NAC extends the idea: it doesn't just check who you are, but whether your device is healthy and compliant before allowing full access — and what it's allowed to reach.
NAC CapabilityExample
Posture assessmentIs AV running? OS (Operating System) patched? Disk encrypted?
Quarantine / remediationNon-compliant device → restricted VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) to fix itself
Role-based accessGuest → internet only; employee → full; IoT (Internet of Things) → isolated
Dynamic VLAN assignmentPut devices on the right segment automatically
Guest onboardingCaptive portal, sponsored access
RADIUS
The AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) Workhorse
RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is the protocol behind most network authentication. It provides AAA: Authentication (who are you?), Authorization (what may you do?), and Accounting (what did you do? — logging/billing). It centralizes credentials so every switch and AP checks against one source (often tied to Active Directory). TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) is a Cisco-oriented alternative more focused on device administration.
🌐 HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) — The Protocol That Runs the Web NET • Essential ▶
ANATOMY OF A REQUEST
What Actually Goes Over the Wire
# An HTTP request is plain text (in HTTP/1.1) GET /api/users?page=2 HTTP/1.1 # method, path, version Host: example.com # required header User-Agent: curl/8.0 Accept: application/json Authorization: Bearer eyJ... # blank line = end of headers # (body goes here for POST/PUT) # The response HTTP/1.1 200 OK # version, status code, reason Content-Type: application/json Content-Length: 142 {"users": [...]} # body
METHODS (VERBS)
What You Want to Do
MethodPurposeSafe?Idempotent?
GETRetrieve dataYes (no change)Yes
POSTCreate / submitNoNo (repeats create dups)
PUTReplace entirelyNoYes
PATCHPartial updateNoUsually no
DELETERemoveNoYes
HEADLike GET, headers onlyYesYes
OPTIONSAsk what's allowed (CORS preflight)YesYes
Idempotent = doing it twice has the same effect as once. Matters for retries: safely retry a PUT/DELETE, but a retried POST might create duplicates.
STATUS CODES
The Server's Answer, by Category
RangeMeaningCommon Examples
1xxInformational100 Continue, 101 Switching Protocols
2xxSuccess200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
3xxRedirection301 Moved, 304 Not Modified, 307 Temp Redirect
4xxClient error (YOUR fault)400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests
5xxServer error (THEIR fault)500 Internal Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Unavailable, 504 Timeout
Quick memory aid: 4xx = you messed up (bad request, not allowed); 5xx = the server messed up. 401 = "who are you?" (not authenticated); 403 = "I know who you are, but no" (not authorized).
HTTP VERSIONS
1.1 → 2 → 3
VersionKey ChangeBenefit
HTTP/1.1Text-based, one request at a time per connectionSimple; suffers head-of-line blocking
HTTP/2 (HyperText Transfer Protocol version 2)Binary, multiplexed streams over one connectionMany parallel requests, header compression — faster
HTTP/3 (HyperText Transfer Protocol version 3)Runs over QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) (UDP) instead of TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)No TCP head-of-line blocking; faster on lossy/mobile networks
Statelessness: HTTP itself is stateless — each request is independent. "Sessions" are layered on top via cookies/tokens, because the protocol doesn't remember you between requests.
📡 Network Monitoring — Seeing What Flows Through NET • Operations ▶
WHY MONITOR
You Can't Manage What You Can't See
Network monitoring tells you device health, bandwidth use, errors, and unusual traffic — essential for both operations (is the link saturated? is a switch down?) and security (is data being exfiltrated? is there C2 traffic?). Different techniques answer different questions, from device health to per-flow detail.
SNMP
Polling Device Health
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) lets a monitoring system query devices (switches, routers, servers, printers) for metrics — interface status, CPU (Central Processing Unit), temperature, traffic counters. Devices expose values in a hierarchical database (MIB) addressed by OIDs. Tools like Zabbix, LibreNMS, and PRTG poll via SNMP and graph/alert on the results.
VersionNote
SNMPv1 / v2cUses a plaintext "community string" — insecure; avoid on untrusted networks
SNMPv3Adds authentication + encryption — use this
FLOW DATA
NetFlow / IPFIX / sFlow — Who Talked to Whom
Flow data records metadata about conversations (source/dest IP, ports, protocol, bytes) without capturing full packet contents. It answers "who is talking to whom, how much?" — invaluable for capacity planning, billing, and security (spotting exfiltration, scanning, or C2 beaconing) at scale, far more cheaply than full packet capture.
TechOriginNote
NetFlowCiscoThe original; widely supported
IPFIXIETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) standardVendor-neutral "NetFlow v10"
sFlowMulti-vendorPacket sampling, lower overhead
PACKET CAPTURE
The Full Truth on the Wire
When you need to see exactly what was sent — debugging an app, analyzing an attack — capture full packets. tcpdump on the CLI (Command Line Interface), Wireshark for deep GUI (Graphical User Interface) analysis. The most detailed (and storage-heavy) option; usually targeted at a specific problem, not always-on.
# tcpdump basics sudo tcpdump -i eth0 # live capture sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 443 # filter by port sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.0.0.5 # filter by host sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap # save to file sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' # SYN packets # Then open capture.pcap in Wireshark for deep analysis # Wireshark display filters: http, dns, ip.addr==10.0.0.5, tcp.port==22
Beginner Active Directory & LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) – Enterprise Identity 101
Core Concept
What Is Active Directory?
Active Directory (AD) is Microsoft's directory service — the central phonebook of every Windows enterprise. It stores users, computers, groups, and policies in a tree of Organizational Units (OUs). When you log in at work, your laptop asks a Domain Controller (DC) to verify your password.

Key vocabulary:
• Domain – a boundary of administration (e.g. corp.example.com).
• Forest – one or more domains that trust each other.
• OU – a folder inside AD used to organise objects.
• GPO – Group Policy Object; rules pushed to computers/users.
• DC – Domain Controller; the server that runs AD.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — if you are not the AD admin, do not make changes in AD. Escalate to the team that owns it.
Protocol
LDAP – How Applications Talk to AD
LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is the language software uses to query AD. Every object has a Distinguished Name (DN) — a path like a file system path:
CN=Alice Smith,OU=Finance,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com

Common LDAP operations:
• Bind – authenticate (log in) to the directory.
• Search – find objects matching a filter.
• Add / Modify / Delete – manage objects (admin only).

Port 389 = plain LDAP  |  Port 636 = LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over SSL) (TLS encrypted — always prefer this).
# Query AD with Python ldap3 (read-only example) from ldap3 import Server, Connection, ALL, SUBTREE server = Server('ldaps://dc01.corp.example.com', get_info=ALL) conn = Connection(server, user='corp\svc_readonly', password='S3cur3P@ss!', auto_bind=True) # Find all users in the Finance OU conn.search( search_base='OU=Finance,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com', search_filter='(&(objectClass=user)(!(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=2)))', search_scope=SUBTREE, attributes=['cn', 'mail', 'department'] ) for entry in conn.entries: print(entry.cn, entry.mail) conn.unbind() # The filter above: objectClass=user AND NOT disabled (bit 2 of UAC)
Authentication
Kerberos in Plain English
Kerberos is the default authentication protocol for AD domains. Think of it as a theme-park wristband system:

1. You show your password once to the Key Distribution Center (KDC) on the DC.
2. The KDC gives you a Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT) — your all-day wristband.
3. When you access a resource (file share, web app), you show the TGT to get a Service Ticket — a ride ticket for that specific attraction.
4. The resource trusts the service ticket without ever seeing your password again.

Why this matters for beginners: you never type your password again during the work day — Single Sign-On (SSO). Kerberos tickets expire (default 10 hours), so you may be prompted again next day.
Best Practice
Principle of Least Privilege in AD
"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume a user needs more permissions than their job requires. In AD:

• Give users standard accounts for daily work.
• Admins use a separate admin account (e.g. a-alice) only when elevated tasks are needed.
• Service accounts get only the groups they need.
• Review group memberships quarterly — "account creep" is real.

The Domain Admins group is the most powerful group in the domain. Its membership list should be tiny and audited constantly.
Beginner Cloud Networking – VPC (Virtual Private Cloud), Subnets & Security Groups
Core Concept
What Is a VPC?
A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is your own private network inside a cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP). Think of it as renting a section of a data centre and installing your own private network switches — except it's all software.

Key building blocks:
• VPC – the outer boundary; you choose the IP (Internet Protocol) range (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16 = ~65 000 addresses).
• Subnet – a slice of the VPC in one availability zone. Public subnets reach the internet; private subnets do not.
• Internet Gateway (IGW) – the door between your VPC and the public internet.
• NAT (Network Address Translation) Gateway – lets private-subnet resources make outbound internet calls without being reachable from outside.
• Route Table – rules that decide where packets go (like a router's routing table).
• Security Group – a stateful firewall attached to an individual resource (VM, load balancer).

"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume a cloud resource is private just because it's in a VPC. Check security groups AND network ACLs (Access Control List); both must permit the traffic.
AWS (Amazon Web Services) Example
Building a VPC with AWS CLI (Command Line Interface)
AWS CLI lets you build the entire network from the command line. This is the same thing the console does behind the scenes.
# Create a VPC aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 --query Vpc.VpcId --output text # Output: vpc-0abc1234def567890 # Create a public subnet (AZ us-east-1a) aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-0abc1234def567890 --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a # Create a private subnet aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-0abc1234def567890 --cidr-block 10.0.2.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a # Attach an internet gateway aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --query InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --internet-gateway-id igw-0xyz --vpc-id vpc-0abc1234def567890 # Security group: allow SSH from your IP only aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name web-sg --description "Web server SG" --vpc-id vpc-0abc1234def567890 aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0xyz --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 203.0.113.5/32 # your IP only!
Best Practice
The Shared Responsibility Model
Cloud providers operate a Shared Responsibility Model: the provider secures the infrastructure of the cloud; you secure everything in the cloud.

AWS/Azure/GCP handles: Physical data centres, hypervisor security, global network, managed service patches.

You handle: VM (Virtual Machine) OS (Operating System) patches, security group rules, S3 (Simple Storage Service) bucket permissions, IAM (Identity and Access Management) roles, encryption of your data, application code security.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" only applies to the provider's layer. Misconfigured S3 buckets, open security groups, and leaked IAM keys are 100 % your responsibility. Most cloud breaches are misconfiguration, not a failure by the provider.
Beginner DNS (Domain Name System) Deep-Dive – How Domain Names Actually Work
Core Concept
The DNS Resolution Walk
When you type www.example.com in a browser, this is what happens before the first byte of the page arrives:

1. Browser checks its local cache — did we look this up recently?
2. OS (Operating System) checks /etc/hosts (or Windows Hosts file) — manual overrides.
3. OS asks the Recursive Resolver (usually your router or ISP, or 8.8.8.8/1.1.1.1).
4. Resolver asks a Root Name Server (.): "Who handles .com?"
5. Root refers to the .com TLD server: "Ask ns1.example.com."
6. Resolver asks ns1.example.com: "What's the IP (Internet Protocol) for www?"
7. Authoritative answer returned: 93.184.216.34.
8. Resolver caches the result for the TTL (Time To Live); returns it to your browser.

Total time: usually 10–100 ms. Cached lookups: <1 ms.
Record Types
DNS Record Types You Must Know
DNS stores different information in different record types:
Record Purpose Example A IPv4 address www A 93.184.216.34 AAAA IPv6 address www AAAA 2606:2800::1 CNAME Alias to another name blog CNAME myapp.netlify.app. MX Mail server (+ priority) @ MX 10 mail.example.com. TXT Arbitrary text (SPF, DKIM) @ TXT "v=spf1 include:..." NS Authoritative name servers @ NS ns1.example.com. PTR Reverse lookup (IP → name) 34.216.184.93.in-addr.arpa PTR www.example.com. SOA Zone metadata (serial, TTL) Start of Authority record SRV Service location _sip._tcp SRV 10 5 5060 sip.example.com. # Query DNS with dig dig www.example.com A # IPv4 dig www.example.com AAAA # IPv6 dig example.com MX # mail servers dig example.com TXT # SPF / DKIM / verification tokens dig -x 93.184.216.34 # reverse lookup (PTR) dig @8.8.8.8 www.example.com # use Google's resolver dig +trace www.example.com # walk the full resolution chain
Security
DNS Security – DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions), DoH (DNS over HTTPS), DNS Attacks
DNS was designed in the 1980s with no security. Several attacks exploit this:

DNS Cache Poisoning — attacker injects a false record into a resolver's cache so users get sent to the wrong IP.
Fix: DNSSEC — cryptographic signatures on DNS records.

DNS Hijacking — malware or rogue ISP (Internet Service Provider) changes the resolver you use.
Fix: DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) or DNS-over-TLS (DoT) — encrypts queries so no one can tamper in transit.

DNS Tunnelling — attacker encodes data inside DNS queries to exfiltrate data or establish C2 (Command and Control) (bypasses firewalls).
Fix: Monitor for unusually long query names, high query volume per host, rare TLDs.

"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume DNS responses are authentic unless DNSSEC is validated end-to-end.
# Check if a domain has DNSSEC enabled dig example.com DNSKEY +short dig example.com DS +short # Test DNS-over-HTTPS (Cloudflare DoH) curl -sH "accept: application/dns-json" "https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?name=example.com&type=A" | python3 -m json.tool # Detect suspicious long DNS names (potential tunnelling) # In tcpdump: capture DNS on port 53 sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w dns.pcap port 53 # Then grep for names longer than 50 chars tshark -r dns.pcap -T fields -e dns.qry.name | awk 'length > 50' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Operations
Managing DNS Zones
Whether you use Route 53, Cloudflare, or BIND on-prem, the concepts are the same. Best practices:

• Set low TTLs (e.g. 300 s) before planned changes; restore high TTLs (3600+) after.
• Always have at least two NS servers in different locations for redundancy.
• Use split-horizon DNS — internal names resolve to private IPs; external names resolve to public IPs.
• Add SPF, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail), DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) TXT (Text Record) records for every domain that sends email to prevent spoofing.
• You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — when a TTL-expired stale record sends users to a dead IP, reduce TTL proactively next time.
Beginner Wireless Security – 802.11 Standards & Wi-Fi Hardening
Core Concept
Wi-Fi Security Evolution: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) → WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3)
Wi-Fi security has gone through several generations. Knowing the history helps you understand why old protocols are dangerous:

ProtocolYearEncryptionStatus
WEP1997RC4 (broken)Never use
WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) (TKIP)2003RC4 improvedAvoid
WPA2-Personal2004AES-CCMPOK with strong passphrase
WPA2-Enterprise2004AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) + 802.1X/RADIUSRecommended for orgs
WPA3-Personal2018AES + SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals)Best for home/small biz
WPA3-Enterprise2018AES-256 + SAEBest for enterprise

WPA2-Personal weakness: offline dictionary attacks against the 4-way handshake. A weak passphrase = cracked in hours.
WPA3 fix: SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) prevents offline cracking — each authentication is unique.
Enterprise Wi-Fi
WPA2-Enterprise with RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service)
In corporate environments, each user authenticates with their own AD (Active Directory) credentials rather than a shared passphrase. This uses 802.1X and a RADIUS server (FreeRADIUS or Windows NPS).

Benefits:
• No shared secret to leak — each user has unique creds.
• Revoke a single user's access without changing the Wi-Fi password for everyone.
• Full audit trail of who connected when.
• Mutual authentication via certificates prevents evil-twin attacks.
