Framework
Tactics · Techniques · Procedures (TTPs)
A globally-accessible knowledge base of adversary behavior. Tactics = the why (goal). Techniques = the how. Sub-techniques = specific implementations. Referenced by SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) rules, threat intel reports, and IR (Incident Response) playbooks.
Reconnaissance
Active/passive info gathering before attack
Resource Dev.
Infrastructure, accounts, tools acquisition

Maintain foothold: registry, cron, boot scripts

Discovery

Collection
Stage data: screen capture, clipboard, email
C2 (Command and Control)
Maintain comms: HTTP/S, DNS (Domain Name System), encrypted channels
Exfiltration
Transfer data out: compressed, encrypted, chunked
Impact
Encrypt, wipe, deface, DoS (Denial of Service), manipulate data

Human-Based · Computer-Based · SE Attack Types
Social engineering exploits human psychology rather than technical vulnerabilities. It is the leading initial access vector. Awareness training is the primary defense.

Technique Description Target
Phishing Mass deceptive email appearing legitimate; harvest credentials General employees

Technique Description

Tailgating / Piggybacking Follow authorized person through a secure door without badge-in

Type Description Key Characteristic

Subtype Description
Boot Sector Moves/overwrites MBR (Master Boot Record); loads before OS; almost impossible to remove without reimaging

🧒Threats Explained SimplySec+ • Start Here▶
BIG IDEA
Malware = Digital Germs
Malware is any software built to harm or steal. Like germs, some spreads on its own, some needs you to 'touch' it (open a file), and good hygiene (updates, caution, antivirus) prevents most infections.
FIELD GUIDE
Virus vs. Worm vs. Trojan
A virus attaches to a file and spreads when you run it. A worm copies itself across the network with no help. A trojan pretends to be something good (a free game) but smuggles in something bad — named after the wooden horse.
ANALOGY
Vulnerability → Exploit → Threat
The unlocked window is the vulnerability. Climbing through it is the exploit. The burglar who does it is the threat actor. Fixing the lock (patching) removes the opportunity.
HUMAN HACKING
Social Engineering
The easiest way past a strong lock is to trick someone into opening it. Social engineering hacks people, not machines — impersonation, fake urgency, flattery, or pretending to be IT support. Skepticism is a control.
MODERN THREAT
Ransomware
Ransomware locks your files with encryption and demands payment for the key. The best defense isn't paying — it's good, tested backups kept offline, so you can restore and walk away.
TrickHow to Not Fall for It
Phishing emailCheck the sender; hover links; never rush
TailgatingDon't hold secure doors for strangers
PretextingVerify identity before sharing info
Baiting (free USB)Never plug in found devices
Pop-up 'virus' alertClose it; real AV doesn't cold-call you
🔗Anatomy of an Attack (Step by Step)Sec+ • Start Here▶
BIG IDEA
Attacks Happen in Stages
Real attacks aren’t one magic click — they’re a chain of steps, each depending on the last. The good news: break any link and you stop the whole attack. Defenders aim to catch it as early as possible.
WALKTHROUGH
The Cyber Kill Chain, Plainly
First the attacker studies you (recon), then sends the bait (delivery), tricks a weakness (exploitation), drops their tool (installation), phones home for orders (command & control), and finally acts — steals, encrypts, or spies (actions on objectives).
StageWhat the Attacker DoesA Defense
ReconResearch the targetLimit public info
DeliverySend phishing / malwareEmail filtering, training
ExploitationTrigger the weaknessPatch & harden
InstallationPlant their footholdEndpoint protection (EDR)
Command & ControlRemote-control itMonitor outbound traffic
ActionsSteal / encrypt / spyLeast privilege, backups
🎯 How Attacks Actually Work — The Attacker's Mindset THREAT • Start Here ▶
THE CYBER KILL CHAIN
Lockheed Martin's 7-Phase Attack Model
Attacks almost never happen in a single step. They follow a pattern — and defenders can stop the attack at any phase.
#PhaseWhat the Attacker DoesDefender's Job
1ReconnaissanceResearch target: LinkedIn, DNS (Domain Name System), Shodan scansMinimize public attack surface
2WeaponizationBuild exploit + payload (malware, phishing doc)Threat intelligence
3DeliverySend the payload (email, USB, watering hole)Email filtering, web proxy
4ExploitationTrigger the vulnerability, execute codePatching, endpoint protection
5InstallationInstall backdoor / malware for persistenceApplication whitelisting, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response)
6C2 (Command & Control)Phone home; receive instructions from attackerNetwork monitoring, DNS filtering
7Actions on ObjectivesSteal data, encrypt for ransom, pivot laterallyDLP (Data Loss Prevention), data segmentation, SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) alerts
MITRE ATT&CK
A Library of Real Attacker Techniques
MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) is a free, publicly maintained matrix of Tactics (why), Techniques (how), and Sub-techniques (specific implementation) that real adversaries actually use. It's based on observed incidents, not theory.
Tactics: Initial Access → Execution → Persistence → Privilege Escalation → Defense Evasion → Credential Access → Discovery → Lateral Movement → Collection → Exfiltration → Impact
Use it to: map what an attacker could do, identify detection gaps, communicate about threats in a standard language.
INDICATORS
IOC vs IOA vs TTP (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures)
IOC (Indicator of Compromise) — forensic evidence that an attack occurred: malicious IP (Internet Protocol), hash of known malware, C2 domain. Reactive — tells you it already happened.
IOA (Indicator of Attack) — behavior suggesting an attack is in progress: port scan, privilege escalation, unusual process. Proactive — catch it as it happens.
TTP (Tactics, Techniques, Procedures) — the attacker's playbook. Hardest to change. Even if they change their malware hash, TTPs stay constant. Best for long-term defense.
COMMON MALWARE TYPES
Virus · Worm · Trojan · Ransomware · Rootkit · Spyware
Virus — attaches to legitimate files; needs user action to spread.
Worm — self-replicating; spreads over networks without human action (WannaCry, Slammer).
Trojan — looks legitimate; hides malicious payload (fake crack, infected installer).
Ransomware — encrypts your files; demands payment for the key.
Rootkit — hides malware from the OS (Operating System) itself; persistence at the kernel level.
Spyware/Keylogger — silently records keystrokes, screenshots, credentials.
Botnet agent — your machine becomes a "zombie" that attackers remotely control.
🎭 Social Engineering — People Are the Attack Surface THREAT • Practical ▶
SIX INFLUENCE PRINCIPLES
Cialdini's Weapons Attackers Exploit
Reciprocity — do something for someone, they feel obligated to return the favor.
Commitment & Consistency — once someone agrees to a small ask, they're likely to agree to bigger asks.
Social Proof — "Everyone on your team already approved this."
Authority — "This is the CTO (Chief Technology Officer)" / "Microsoft support calling."
Liking — you comply more with people you like or who seem like you.
Scarcity/Urgency — "This needs to happen in the next 30 minutes or the system goes down."
PRETEXTING
Creating a False Identity or Scenario
The attacker creates a believable story — "I'm from IT, we're doing an audit," or "I'm a new vendor, I need temporary access." They do research first (LinkedIn, OSINT) to make it convincing. The pretext gives the victim a reason to comply that doesn't trigger suspicion.
DEFENSE
Out-of-Band Verification Is the Key
When someone asks for access, credentials, or data:
1. Slow down — urgency is a manipulation tool. Real emergencies have procedures.
2. Verify independently — don't call the number they gave you; look it up yourself.
3. Follow the process — the process exists exactly for these moments.
4. It's okay to say no — "Let me verify this request through proper channels first." A real insider won't mind.
🩹 Vulnerability Management — Finding and Fixing Weaknesses THREAT • Foundation ▶
VULNERABILITY LIFECYCLE
Identify → Assess → Prioritize → Remediate → Verify
Vulnerability management is a continuous cycle, not a one-time scan. Networks change daily — new systems appear, software updates fail, configurations drift. The cycle never ends.
CVE & CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System)
Common Vulnerabilities and Their Severity
CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) — a unique identifier for each publicly known vulnerability. Format: CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell). The year and a serial number. Lookup: cve.mitre.org or nvd.nist.gov.
CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) — a 0-10 score for severity:
9.0-10.0 = Critical: patch immediately
7.0-8.9 = High: patch this week
4.0-6.9 = Medium: patch this month
0.1-3.9 = Low: scheduled patching
0.0 = None: not a security issue
SCANNING TOOLS
Identify What's Exposed
Nessus (Tenable) — industry standard enterprise vuln scanner. Identifies unpatched software, misconfigurations, weak credentials.
OpenVAS — open-source alternative.
Qualys — cloud-based; no agent required for network scans.
Trivy — open-source container image scanner; finds vulnerable packages in Docker images.
OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) ZAP — web application scanner; finds XSS (Cross-Site Scripting), SQLi (SQL Injection), CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery), etc.
PATCH STRATEGY
Risk-Based Prioritization
You'll never patch everything immediately — there are always too many vulnerabilities. Prioritize based on:
1. CVSS score — base severity
2. Exploitability — is it being actively exploited? Check CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency)'s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.
3. Asset criticality — a critical vuln on an internet-facing production server beats the same vuln on an air-gapped test system.
4. Compensating controls — if a WAF (Web Application Firewall) blocks the exploit vector, urgency is lower until you can patch.
ZERO DAY
The Patch Doesn't Exist Yet
A zero-day vulnerability is one that has no patch yet — vendors have had "zero days" to fix it. Zero-days in the wild (actively being exploited) are the most dangerous. Defenses: defense-in-depth (don't rely on patches alone), network segmentation to limit blast radius, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) to detect exploitation behavior, and monitoring for indicators.
🏹 Threat Hunting — Proactively Finding What Slipped Through THREAT • Advanced ▶
WHAT IS THREAT HUNTING
The Difference Between Hunting and Alerting
Reactive security waits for alerts — SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) detects something, you investigate. Threat hunting flips this: you assume the adversary is already in your network (a reasonable assumption for mature organizations), then proactively search for evidence of compromise. It requires no alert to trigger; you drive the investigation.
ConceptAlert-Based (Reactive)Threat Hunting (Proactive)
TriggerSIEM rule firesHunter's hypothesis
Starting pointAlert tells you where to lookYou decide where to look
OutcomeConfirm or dismiss alertFind what rules missed; improve detection
Skill requiredTriage / analysisDeep knowledge of attacker TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures)
Maturity levelAll orgsMature orgs (assume breach mindset)
THE HUNT PROCESS
Hypothesis-Driven Hunting
Good threat hunting starts with a hypothesis based on threat intelligence, ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) techniques, or recent threat reports — not just "look for bad stuff." A structured hunt has a clear scope and produces either a confirmed finding or improved detection logic.
StepActivityExample
1. HypothesisDefine what attacker behavior you're looking for"Living-off-the-land — attacker using built-in Windows tools (T1218)"
2. Data collectionIdentify relevant log sourcesWindows Event Logs, Sysmon, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) telemetry
3. InvestigationQuery, filter, and analyze dataSearch for mshta.exe, regsvr32.exe, certutil.exe with unusual parent processes
4. TriageSeparate normal from abnormalBaseline normal use, flag deviations
5. ResponseEscalate findings, or...Confirm incident → IR team
6. Improve detectionWrite new SIEM rulesCreate alert for technique if no existing detection
LIVING OFF THE LAND
LOLBins (Living Off the Land Binary) — Attackers Using Your Own Tools Against You
Modern attackers rarely drop custom malware immediately. Instead they abuse legitimate OS (Operating System) tools that are already present and trusted — harder to detect than malware. These are called LOLBins (Living Off the Land Binaries). Knowing which tools are commonly abused helps focus your hunts.
ToolLegitimate UseAttacker Abuse
powershell.exeScripting, administrationDownload + execute malware, encoded commands
certutil.exeCertificate managementDownload files, decode base64 payloads
mshta.exeRun HTA applicationsExecute malicious scripts from remote URLs (Uniform Resource Locator)
regsvr32.exeRegister DLLs (Dynamic Link Library)Execute malicious scripts (Squiblydoo)
wscript/cscriptRun VBS/JS scriptsMalicious scripts, fileless malware
msiexec.exeInstall MSI (Microsoft Installer) packagesRemote payload delivery
curl/wget (Linux)HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) requestsPull down next-stage payloads
THREAT INTEL FEEDS
Fueling Your Hunts with Intelligence
SourceTypeFree?Best For
MITRE ATT&CKTTP frameworkYesHunt hypotheses, detection mapping
AlienVault OTXIOC (Indicator of Compromise) feeds (IPs, hashes, domains)YesBlocking bad IPs (Internet Protocol), checking IOCs
VirusTotalFile/URL/IP reputationYes (limited)Checking suspicious files and URLs
Abuse.ch (MalwareBazaar, URLhaus)Malware samples, malicious URLsYesIOC lookup, firewall block lists
CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) KEVKnown Exploited VulnerabilitiesYesPatch prioritization — these are being exploited NOW
Recorded Future / MandiantPremium threat intelNoEnterprise threat landscape, APT (Advanced Persistent Threat) tracking
🔬 Digital Forensics — Reconstructing What Happened THREAT • Investigation ▶
WHAT IS DFIR
Digital Forensics & Incident Response
When something bad happens — a breach, insider theft, malware — digital forensics is the discipline of collecting, preserving, and analyzing evidence to answer: what happened, when, how, and who. Forensics must be done carefully because the findings may end up in court, or drive critical business decisions. The cardinal rule: preserve the original, work on copies.
ORDER OF VOLATILITY
Collect the Most Fragile Evidence First
Some evidence disappears fast (RAM vanishes on shutdown); some persists (disk). When collecting evidence, work from most volatile to least — RFC (Request for Comments) 3227's order of volatility — or you'll lose the fragile stuff forever.
OrderSourceLifetime
1 (most volatile)CPU (Central Processing Unit) registers, cacheNanoseconds
2RAM (Random Access Memory) (running processes, network connections, encryption keys)Until power off
3Network state, routing tables, ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cacheSeconds to minutes
4Running processes, temp filesUntil reboot
5Disk (files, logs, deleted-but-recoverable data)Persistent
6 (least volatile)Backups, archived logs, printoutsLong-term
CHAIN OF CUSTODY
Proving the Evidence Wasn't Tampered With
Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken trail showing who handled evidence, when, why, and how — from collection to courtroom. If you can't prove the evidence wasn't altered, it's worthless. Two technical pillars support this:
TechniquePurpose
Hashing (SHA-256)Hash the evidence at collection. Any change = different hash = tampering detected.
Write blockersHardware/software that allows reading a drive but prevents any writes to it
Forensic imagingBit-for-bit copy (dd, FTK Imager). Analyze the image, never the original.
DocumentationLog every transfer: who, what, when, where, why — signed
# Create a forensic disk image and hash it (Linux) sudo dd if=/dev/sdb of=evidence.img bs=4M status=progress # Hash BEFORE and AFTER to prove integrity sha256sum /dev/sdb # hash of original sha256sum evidence.img # must match — proves a faithful copy # Better: use a tool that images AND hashes in one step # dc3dd, ewfacquire (E01 format), or FTK Imager
ARTIFACTS TO EXAMINE
Where the Evidence Lives
ArtifactWhat It Reveals
Memory dumpRunning malware, decryption keys, network connections, injected code
Windows Event LogsLogons, process creation, service installs, account changes
RegistryPersistence mechanisms, USB (Universal Serial Bus) history, recently run programs
Browser history/cacheDownloaded files, visited sites, exfil destinations
Prefetch / Shimcache / AmcacheEvidence of program execution (even if deleted)
File system timestamps (MACB)Modified, Accessed, Created, Birth — timeline reconstruction
Network captures (PCAP)C2 (Command and Control) traffic, data exfiltration, lateral movement
🔒 Ransomware — The Defining Threat of the Era THREAT • Critical ▶
HOW IT WORKS
The Ransomware Attack Lifecycle
Ransomware encrypts your files and demands payment for the decryption key. But modern ransomware is rarely a single event — it's the final stage of a longer intrusion. Understanding the full lifecycle reveals many points where defenders can intervene before the encryption ever happens.
StageWhat HappensDefense Opportunity
1. Initial accessPhishing, exposed RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol), exploited VPN/vulnMFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), patching, email filtering, awareness
2. Establish footholdInstall backdoor, C2 (Command and Control) channelEDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) detection, egress filtering
3. Privilege escalationGet domain adminLeast privilege, tiered admin, patching
4. Lateral movementSpread across the networkNetwork segmentation, monitoring
5. ExfiltrationSteal data for double extortionDLP (Data Loss Prevention), egress monitoring
6. EncryptionDeploy ransomware everywhere at onceImmutable backups, EDR behavioral blocking
7. ExtortionDemand payment; threaten to leak dataIR (Incident Response) plan, backups, legal/comms ready
MODERN TACTICS
Why It Got So Much Worse
TacticWhat It Means
Double extortionSteal data BEFORE encrypting — "pay or we leak it publicly." Backups alone no longer save you.
Triple extortionAlso threaten customers, DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service), or regulators
RaaS (Ransomware-as-a-Service)Developers rent ransomware to "affiliates" for a cut — lowers the skill barrier dramatically
Big game huntingTargeting large orgs for massive payouts rather than spray-and-pray
Living off the landUsing built-in tools (PsExec, PowerShell) to evade detection
DEFENSE & RESPONSE
Should You Pay? (Generally, No)
Authorities (FBI, CISA) discourage paying: it funds crime, marks you as a target, and offers no guarantee of recovery (decryptors are often buggy or incomplete). The best defense is preparation: immutable, offline backups (can't be encrypted), tested recovery, network segmentation, MFA everywhere, and a rehearsed incident response plan. The organizations that recover fastest are the ones that prepared before the attack.
🎭 Threat Actors — Know Your Adversary THREAT • Foundation ▶
WHO ATTACKS AND WHY
The Threat Actor Spectrum
Different attackers have different motivations, resources, and skill — which shapes how they attack and how you defend. Understanding who might target you (your "threat model") helps prioritize defenses.
ActorMotivationSophisticationExample
Script kiddieBragging rights, curiosityLow — uses others' toolsRunning downloaded exploits
HacktivistIdeology, political messageLow-mediumAnonymous, website defacement, DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service)
CybercriminalMoneyMedium-highRansomware gangs, banking trojans, fraud
Insider threatRevenge, money, negligenceVaries (has legit access)Disgruntled employee stealing data
Nation-state (APT)Espionage, sabotage, strategicVery high, well-funded, patientStuxnet, SolarWinds
Terrorist / cyberterrorFear, disruptionVariesAttacks on critical infrastructure
APTs
Advanced Persistent Threats
An APT is a sophisticated, well-resourced (usually nation-state) attacker that gains access and stays hidden for a long time — months or years — pursuing strategic goals like espionage. The name breaks down: Advanced (custom tools, zero-days), Persistent (long-term, patient, re-establishes access), Threat (organized, funded, goal-driven). They're given names/numbers by researchers: APT28 (Fancy Bear), APT29 (Cozy Bear), Lazarus Group. Defending against APTs requires assuming breach, deep monitoring, and threat hunting — you won't stop them at the door.
📧 Email Authentication — SPF, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail), DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) THREAT • Essential ▶
THE PROBLEM
Email Was Built With No Identity Checks
The original email protocol (SMTP) lets anyone claim to be anyone — you can trivially forge the "From" address. This is why phishing and spoofing are so easy. Three layered DNS-based standards were bolted on to fix this: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. Together they let receiving servers verify that an email genuinely came from the domain it claims. Every email/security admin must understand these.
THE THREE STANDARDS
How They Work Together
StandardQuestion It AnswersHow
SPF
Sender Policy Framework		"Is this server allowed to send for this domain?"DNS (Domain Name System) TXT (Text Record) record lists authorized sending IPs (Internet Protocol)
DKIM
DomainKeys Identified Mail		"Was this message altered? Is the signature valid?"Server signs mail with a private key; public key in DNS verifies it
DMARC
Domain-based Message Auth		"What do I do if SPF/DKIM fail?"DNS policy: none / quarantine / reject + reporting
# Example DNS records # SPF — only these may send for example.com example.com TXT "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ip4:203.0.113.5 -all" # DMARC — reject failures, send reports _dmarc.example.com TXT "v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com" # Check a domain's records dig TXT example.com +short dig TXT _dmarc.example.com +short
DMARC POLICIES
From Monitoring to Enforcement
Policy (p=)EffectWhen to Use
noneTake no action, just reportInitial monitoring — see who sends as you
quarantineSend failures to spam/junkAfter verifying legit senders pass
rejectBlock failing mail outrightFull enforcement — the goal
Best practice: roll out gradually — start at p=none, read the reports to find all legitimate senders, fix their SPF/DKIM, then tighten to quarantine, then reject. Going straight to reject risks blocking your own legitimate mail.
BUSINESS EMAIL COMPROMISE
BEC — The Most Costly Email Attack
BEC is a sophisticated scam where attackers impersonate executives, vendors, or partners to trick employees into wiring money or sending data. By dollar losses, the FBI ranks it as one of the most damaging cybercrimes — far more than ransomware in some years. It often uses no malware at all — just social engineering and a convincing email.
BEC TacticDefense
"CEO" urgently requests a wire transferOut-of-band verification (call a known number)
Vendor sends "updated banking details"Verify changes via a previously-known contact
Lookalike domain (rn vs m, .co vs .com)Scrutinize sender domains; DMARC enforcement
Compromised real account (no forgery)MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), anomaly detection, dual approval for payments
🛰️ OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) for Defenders — See Yourself as Attackers Do THREAT • Recon ▶
WHAT IS OSINT
Open-Source Intelligence
OSINT is intelligence gathered from publicly available sources — no hacking required. Attackers use it to map your organization before striking; defenders use the same techniques to find their own exposure before attackers do. Reducing your "attack surface" starts with knowing what's actually out there with your name on it. It's legal, passive, and one of the highest-value defensive exercises.
WHAT LEAKS OUT
Your Public Footprint
ExposureWhere Attackers Find It
Forgotten internet-facing serversShodan, Censys (search by org/IP range)
Subdomains & shadow ITcrt.sh (cert transparency), subdomain enumeration
Employee emails & namesLinkedIn, Hunter.io, theHarvester
Leaked credentialsHaveIBeenPwned, breach databases
Tech stack & versionsJob postings, BuiltWith, HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) headers
Secrets in codePublic GitHub repos, gists
Sensitive documentsGoogle dorks (site: filetype:)
GOOGLE DORKING
Advanced Search Operators
# Find exposed files on your own domain site:example.com filetype:pdf site:example.com filetype:xlsx site:example.com ext:sql | ext:env | ext:log # Find login portals / admin pages site:example.com inurl:admin | inurl:login # Find directory listings (often unintended exposure) site:example.com intitle:"index of" # Find exposed config / git site:example.com inurl:.git # Do this against YOUR OWN org to find leaks before attackers
DEFENSIVE ACTIONS
Turning OSINT Into Defense
FindingAction
Unknown internet-facing hostAdd to inventory, assess, patch or decommission
Leaked employee credentialsForce reset, enable MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), monitor the account
Secrets in a public repoRotate the secret immediately, scrub history
Excessive info in job postsGeneralize tech details in future postings
Exposed sensitive documentRemove it, check access logs, review process
Continuous, not one-time: your attack surface changes constantly as people spin up servers and post online. Many orgs use Attack Surface Management (ASM) tools to monitor this automatically.
🔬 Malware Analysis — Understanding What the Bad Code Does THREAT • Investigation ▶
⚠️ SAFETY FIRST
Analyze Only in an Isolated Lab
Live malware can spread, exfiltrate, or destroy. Analyze it only in an isolated environment: an air-gapped or snapshot-able VM (Virtual Machine), no shared folders, no network (or a controlled fake network). Never run a sample on your real machine or corporate network. Take a VM snapshot before, revert after.
STATIC VS DYNAMIC
Two Complementary Approaches
ApproachWhat It IsRiskReveals
Static analysisExamine the file WITHOUT running itLow (not executed)Strings, imports, structure, indicators
Dynamic analysisRUN it in a sandbox and observe behaviorHigher (it executes)Actual network calls, file/registry changes, persistence
Real analysts use both: static to form hypotheses safely, dynamic to confirm what it actually does. Advanced malware detects sandboxes and hides — so neither alone is complete.
STATIC ANALYSIS TOOLKIT
First Look at a Sample
# Hash it (identify + look up reputation — never UPLOAD if sensitive) sha256sum sample.exe # Check the hash on VirusTotal (hash lookup, not file upload) # Extract readable strings — URLs, IPs, commands often hide here strings -n 8 sample.exe | grep -iE "http|\.exe|cmd|powershell" # File type and metadata file sample.exe # PE analysis (Windows executables) — imports reveal capabilities # e.g., imports of WinHTTP = network; CryptEncrypt = ransomware? # Tools: PEStudio, pefile (Python), CFF Explorer # Detect packing/obfuscation (high entropy = likely packed) # Tools: DIE (Detect It Easy)
DYNAMIC ANALYSIS
Watch It Misbehave Safely
What to WatchTool / Method
Processes spawnedProcess Monitor / Process Explorer (Windows)
File & registry changesProcmon, Regshot (before/after diff)
Network connections (C2)Wireshark, fakedns, INetSim (fake internet)
Persistence mechanismsAutoruns — what it set to survive reboot
Automated sandboxCuckoo, Any.Run, Joe Sandbox — full report
The goal is to extract IOCs (Indicators of Compromise) — hashes, C2 (Command and Control) domains/IPs, file paths, registry keys — that you can then hunt for across your environment to find other infected hosts.
🧭 Threat Intelligence — Turning Data Into Decisions THREAT • Strategic ▶
WHAT IT IS
Knowing Your Enemy
Threat intelligence (CTI) is evidence-based knowledge about threats — who's attacking, how, and why — used to make better security decisions. It's the difference between reacting blindly and defending with foresight. Good intel is actionable: it tells you what to do, not just interesting facts. There are three levels, serving different audiences.
LevelAudienceExample
StrategicExecutives"Ransomware groups are targeting our industry" — informs budget/risk
OperationalSOC (Security Operations Center) managers, hunters"This group uses spear-phishing then RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol)" — TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures), campaigns
TacticalAnalysts, toolsSpecific IOCs (Indicator of Compromise): bad IPs (Internet Protocol), hashes, domains to block
THE INTEL LIFECYCLE
From Requirement to Action
PhaseWhat Happens
1. DirectionDefine what you need to know (intelligence requirements)
2. CollectionGather data (feeds, OSINT, internal logs, dark web)
3. ProcessingNormalize, deduplicate, translate, structure
4. AnalysisTurn data into meaning — context, assessment
5. DisseminationGet it to the right people in a usable form
6. FeedbackWas it useful? Refine requirements — loop
Standards like STIX (structured threat data) and TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information) (the transport for sharing it) let organizations exchange intel automatically — for example via an ISAC (Information Sharing and Analysis Center) for your industry.
INSIDER THREATS
The Danger From Within
Not all threats come from outside. Insiders — employees, contractors — already have access and trust, making them especially dangerous and hard to detect. They aren't always malicious.
TypeMotivationExample
Malicious insiderRevenge, money, espionageDisgruntled admin steals/sabotages data
Negligent insiderCarelessnessClicks phishing, misconfigures a bucket
Compromised insiderAccount taken overAttacker uses a real employee's credentials
UEBA
User & Entity Behavior Analytics
UEBA builds a baseline of normal behavior for each user/device, then flags anomalies — the technical core of insider-threat and compromised-account detection. Examples: a user suddenly downloading gigabytes at 3am, accessing systems they never touch, or logging in from two countries an hour apart ("impossible travel"). Because it's behavior-based, UEBA catches threats that signature rules miss — including insiders using legitimate access in illegitimate ways.
Beginner Threat Hunting – Finding What Detection Missed
Core Concept
What Is Threat Hunting?
Threat hunting is the proactive, hypothesis-driven search for threats that automated detection has missed. A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) fires alerts when rules match — but sophisticated attackers live below the alert threshold (low-and-slow attacks, living-off-the-land).

Reactive (SIEM): Wait for an alert → investigate.
Proactive (Hunting): Form a hypothesis → search for evidence → prove or disprove it.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — threat hunting is a specialised skill, but junior analysts can learn the mindset: always ask "what would an attacker do that looks normal?"
Process
The Hunt Loop
Every hunt follows the same loop:
1. FORM HYPOTHESIS "Attackers using PowerShell for lateral movement would show powershell.exe spawned by a non-interactive parent process (e.g. wsmprovhost, mmc, svchost) running encoded commands." 2. COLLECT RELEVANT DATA Pull process creation events (Event ID 4688 or Sysmon Event 1) Filter: ParentImage ends with wsmprovhost.exe OR mmc.exe AND CommandLine contains -EncodedCommand OR -Enc 3. ANALYSE Cluster results by user, host, time Look for outliers — rare parents, unusual times, unexpected users 4. INVESTIGATE ANOMALIES Pivot: what did the process do next? (child processes, network, files) Corroborate: does EDR show the same activity? 5. OUTCOME TRUE POSITIVE → Incident response FALSE POSITIVE → Document; tune detection rules INCONCLUSIVE → Expand data sources; reformulate hypothesis 6. CREATE DETECTION RULE Turn confirmed attacker behaviour into an automated SIEM rule so the hunt never needs to be repeated manually
MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge)
Using ATT&CK as a Hunting Framework
MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world attacks. It gives hunters a menu of hypotheses:

• Tactics = why (Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Lateral Movement, Exfiltration…)
• Techniques = how (T1059 – Command and Scripting Interpreter, T1078 – Valid Accounts…)
• Sub-techniques = specific implementations

Workflow:
1. Pick a tactic (e.g. Persistence).
2. List techniques relevant to your environment.
3. Form a hypothesis for each technique.
4. Hunt.
5. Document coverage on your ATT&CK matrix.
# Splunk hunt: T1053.005 – Scheduled Task/Job (Windows) index=windows (EventCode=4698 OR EventCode=4702) | eval suspicious=if(like(TaskContent,"%powershell%") OR like(TaskContent,"%cmd.exe%") OR like(TaskContent,"%wscript%"),"YES","NO") | where suspicious="YES" | stats count by ComputerName, SubjectUserName, TaskName # Linux hunt: T1136.001 – Create Local Account grep "new user" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $1,$2,$3,$NF}' | sort # Hunt for DNS tunnelling: unusually long hostnames # Splunk SPL: index=dns | eval qlen=len(query) | where qlen > 50 | stats count, values(query) by src_ip | sort -count
Tools
Essential Threat Hunting Tools
• Sysmon (Windows) — enriches Windows event logs with process GUID (Globally Unique Identifier), parent-child relationships, network connections, and file hashes. Free from Microsoft Sysinternals.
• Velociraptor — open-source agent for rapid endpoint forensics and hunting at scale.
• osquery (Operating System Query) — SQL (Structured Query Language) interface to OS (Operating System) internals; ask "SELECT name, pid FROM processes WHERE name LIKE '%powershell%'."
• SIGMA (Generic Signature Format for SIEM Systems) — generic detection rule format that converts to Splunk, Elastic, QRadar queries. Hunters write SIGMA rules to share TTP (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) detection across SIEM platforms.
# osquery – live process inspection (runs on Windows/Linux/macOS) osqueryi SELECT name, pid, parent, cmdline FROM processes WHERE name LIKE '%powershell%' OR cmdline LIKE '%-EncodedCommand%'; # Find all network connections to suspicious ports SELECT p.name, p.pid, n.local_port, n.remote_address, n.remote_port, n.state FROM process_open_sockets n JOIN processes p ON p.pid = n.pid WHERE n.remote_port NOT IN (80, 443, 53, 123) AND n.state = 'ESTABLISHED';
Beginner Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) – What to Look For
Concept

An IOC is a clue, not a verdict

An Indicator of Compromise is a piece of forensic evidence that suggests a system may have been breached — a suspicious file hash, an unusual outbound connection, a registry key that shouldn't exist. The word "indicator" matters: a single IOC rarely proves an intrusion on its own. It's a thread to pull, and pulling it carefully — rather than jumping straight to "we've been hacked, shut everything down" — is what keeps a real incident from turning into a self-inflicted outage.

Concept

Common IOC categories, from easy to spoof to hard to spoof

CategoryExampleWhy it's useful / limited
File hashes (MD5/SHA256)A known-malware binary's exact fingerprintPrecise, but trivially defeated by changing one byte of the file
IP (Internet Protocol) addresses / domainsCommand-and-control server addressesUseful for blocking, but attackers rotate infrastructure constantly
File paths / registry keysC:\Windows\Temp\svch0st.exe (note the zero)Reveals attacker tradecraft, but easy to rename next time
Behavioral patterns"Word spawning PowerShell spawning a reverse shell"Hardest to fake — the attacker has to actually do something different to evade it

This is why mature security teams talk about moving "up the Pyramid of Pain" — from easily-changed atomic indicators (hashes, IPs) toward TTPs (tactics, techniques, and procedures) that describe how an attacker operates, which is far more expensive for them to change.

Hands-on

Checking a suspicious file or hash yourself

# Generate a hash for a file you want to check
sha256sum suspicious_attachment.pdf

# Search running processes for anything spawned from an unusual path
ps aux | grep -E "/tmp/|/dev/shm/|AppData\\Local\\Temp"

# List recently modified files in sensitive directories — a common
# sign of tampering or dropped tooling
find /etc /usr/bin /usr/local/bin -mtime -2 -type f 2>/dev/null

# Check outbound connections for anything talking to unfamiliar hosts
ss -tunap | grep ESTAB

Before you act on a hash match from a public threat-intel feed, paste it into a malware analysis service or sandbox to see what others have already learned about it — community context turns a bare indicator into something you can actually act on with confidence.

Mindset

Not my circus, not my monkey — except when it is

If you spot an IOC on a system outside your scope of responsibility, resist the urge to dig in yourself — that's how evidence gets contaminated and chains of custody get broken. Report it through the proper channel to the team that owns it. But on systems that are yours to protect, that same phrase becomes a trap: "probably nothing" is exactly the thought that lets small indicators grow into large incidents. Knowing which circus is yours is half the job.

Beginner The Cyber Kill Chain – Thinking Like the Attacker, Stage by Stage
Concept

An attack isn't one event — it's a sequence

The Cyber Kill Chain (developed by Lockheed Martin) is a model that breaks an intrusion down into a sequence of stages an attacker has to move through, in order, to succeed. Its real value for a defender isn't memorizing the stage names — it's the realization that every stage is a chance to stop the attack. You don't need to catch every intrusion at the front door; catching it at any single stage breaks the whole chain.

Concept

The seven stages, and where defenders can intervene

StageWhat the attacker is doingA defense that fits here
1. ReconnaissanceResearching the target — employee names on LinkedIn, exposed services, leaked credentialsLimiting public information exposure; monitoring for scanning activity
2. WeaponizationBuilding or obtaining a malicious payload (often off-the-shelf)Threat intelligence feeds that flag known tooling and infrastructure
3. DeliveryGetting the payload to the target — phishing email, infected USB (Universal Serial Bus), compromised websiteEmail filtering, web proxies, user awareness training
4. ExploitationTriggering the payload — a user opens the attachment, a vulnerable service is hitPatch management, application allow-listing, endpoint protection
5. InstallationEstablishing persistence — a backdoor, scheduled task, or new serviceEDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) tools that flag unusual process trees and new persistence mechanisms
6. Command & Control (C2)Calling home to an attacker-controlled server for further instructionsNetwork monitoring for unusual outbound connections; DNS (Domain Name System) filtering
7. Actions on ObjectivesThe actual goal — data theft, ransomware deployment, sabotageData loss prevention, network segmentation, offline backups
Hands-on

Mapping a real incident to the chain

# A simplified, anonymized incident timeline mapped to kill-chain stages —
# this is the kind of analysis that goes into a post-incident report

Day 1   - Attacker scrapes employee names from the company website
          [STAGE 1: Reconnaissance]

Day 3   - Crafted phishing email sent to 40 employees, spoofing IT support
          [STAGE 3: Delivery — using a generic, purchased phishing kit, STAGE 2]

Day 3   - One employee clicks the link and enters their credentials
          on a cloned login page
          [STAGE 4: Exploitation]

Day 4   - Attacker logs in with stolen credentials, installs a
          scheduled task that re-establishes a connection on reboot
          [STAGE 5: Installation]

Day 4-9 - Compromised account quietly contacts an external server
          every few hours; goes unnoticed amid normal traffic
          [STAGE 6: Command & Control]

Day 10  - Attacker begins exporting files from a shared drive
          — DLP tooling flags the unusual transfer volume and
          the SOC cuts off network access within 12 minutes
          [STAGE 7: Actions on Objectives — INTERRUPTED HERE]

Notice that the chain was broken at stage 7 — late, but not too late. A faster catch at stage 6 (alerting on the unusual outbound C2 traffic over six days) would have prevented the data exfiltration entirely. Every stage that gets caught earlier shrinks the blast radius of everything that follows.

Mindset

You can't make someone make the right choice...

...yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards. No amount of training guarantees that nobody will ever click a phishing link — humans are the part of the chain you can influence but never fully control. That's exactly why mature security programs don't rely on stage 3/4 prevention alone. They build detection and response capability for stages 5 through 7 too — because when, not if, someone clicks, the chain still has several more links where you can catch it.

Beginner Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) – What's Already Public About You
Concept

OSINT is intelligence gathered from things that are already public

Open-Source Intelligence means collecting and analyzing information from publicly available sources — social media, company websites, public records, code repositories, even old cached pages — to build a picture of a person or organization. It requires no hacking and breaks no laws on its own; the "open" in the name is the whole point. Understanding OSINT matters for two very different reasons: attackers use it during the reconnaissance phase of an intrusion (recall the Cyber Kill Chain's first stage), and defenders use the exact same techniques to find out what an attacker could learn about their own organization before someone else does.

Concept

What attackers commonly piece together — and from where

InformationCommon public sourcesHow it gets used
Employee names & rolesLinkedIn, company "About Us" pages, conference speaker listsCrafting believable spear-phishing emails ("Hi, this is Dana from IT...")
Technology stackJob postings ("must know AWS, Kubernetes, Salesforce"), public code reposTargeting known vulnerabilities in the specific tools an org uses
Email address formatPress releases, public filings, "contact us" pagesGuessing other employees' addresses (firstname.lastname@company.com)
Physical & schedule detailsSocial media check-ins, out-of-office replies, event listingsTiming attacks for when key personnel are away or distracted
Hands-on (lab/personal use only)

Running your own OSINT check on yourself or your org

# See what Google has indexed about a domain — often more than expected
site:example.com filetype:pdf
site:example.com "confidential"

# Check what WHOIS records reveal about a domain's registration
whois example.com | grep -iE "registrant|admin|tech"

# Look up historical versions of a public page — sometimes old,
# supposedly-removed information is still archived
# https://web.archive.org/web/*/example.com

# Search for exposed credentials tied to a domain (read-only check —
# this is the same database breach-notification services use)
# https://haveibeenpwned.com/DomainSearch (requires domain verification)

# Review what a public GitHub org has accidentally exposed —
# old commits sometimes contain credentials that were later "removed"
# but remain in the git history forever
git log -p --all | grep -iE "password|secret|api[_-]?key"

That last command is worth sitting with — deleting a sensitive line from the latest commit does not remove it from history. Anyone who clones the repository can still find it with a simple search. This is one of the most common, entirely preventable ways organizations leak credentials.

Mindset

Not my circus, not my monkey — except your digital footprint is always yours

It's easy to assume "I'm not important enough to be a target" — but OSINT-driven attacks rarely target individuals for who they are; they target whoever happens to be reachable and useful as a stepping stone toward something bigger (a company network, a family member, a connected account). Periodically searching your own name, checking what your old social media posts reveal, and reviewing what your employer has published about you isn't paranoia — it's the same "know what's exposed before someone else finds it" thinking that professional security teams apply to entire organizations, just scaled down to one person.

Beginner Ransomware – How It Spreads, and Why Backups Aren't the Whole Story
Concept

Ransomware in one sentence

Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts a victim's files (or locks them out of their systems entirely) and demands payment — usually in cryptocurrency — for the key to restore access. Modern ransomware operations have evolved well past "encrypt and demand money": many now also steal data first and threaten to publish it, a tactic called double extortion that defeats the old assumption "we have backups, so we're fine."

Concept

A typical attack chain — and where it can be stopped

StageWhat happensA defense that fits here
1. Initial accessPhishing email, exposed RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol), or a vulnerable internet-facing serviceEmail filtering, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), patching, closing unnecessary exposed ports
2. Spread / escalateThe attacker moves laterally through the network, gathering higher privilegesNetwork segmentation, least-privilege access, monitoring for unusual internal traffic
3. Data theft (often skipped by less sophisticated groups)Sensitive files are quietly exfiltrated before anything is encryptedData loss prevention, monitoring for unusual outbound transfer volumes
4. DetonationFiles across the network are encrypted, often during off-hours to maximize damage before detectionEndpoint detection that flags mass file-modification behavior in real time
5. ExtortionA ransom note appears; the attacker may also threaten to leak stolen dataIncident response plan, legal counsel, law enforcement contact — decided BEFORE this moment, not during it

Notice how much happens before stage 4 — the part most people picture when they hear "ransomware attack." By the time files start encrypting, the attacker has often already been inside the network for days or weeks. That's both bad news (damage may already be done) and good news (there were many earlier chances to catch it).

Hands-on

Verifying your backups are actually a safety net (not just a checkbox)

# A backup that ransomware can also encrypt or delete isn't a backup —
# it's just another file the attacker controls. Ask these questions:

# 1. Are backups stored OFFLINE or in a way ransomware can't reach?
#    (immutable cloud storage, air-gapped tape, write-once media —
#    NOT just another network drive with the same credentials)

# 2. Have you actually TESTED a full restore recently — not just
#    confirmed the backup job "completed successfully"?
#    A backup nobody has ever restored from is a THEORY, not a plan.

# 3. How far back do your retention policies go? If an attacker
#    was quietly inside for six weeks before detonating, and your
#    backups only go back two, you may be restoring already-compromised data

# 4. Who has the credentials to delete or modify backups —
#    and is that access separated from everyday admin accounts?

The 3-2-1 rule is a useful baseline to test your setup against: at least 3 copies of your data, on 2 different types of media, with 1 copy stored offsite (and ideally offline). Many organizations that "had backups" still paid ransoms — because their backups were reachable from the same compromised network as everything else.

Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me — "we have backups" is not a plan

"We're covered, we have backups" is one of the most common — and most dangerous — assumptions in incident preparedness, precisely because it sounds like due diligence without requiring anyone to verify it actually works. A real plan answers harder questions: how long would a full restore actually take (hours? days? weeks?), what would you tell customers during that gap, and who makes the call about whether to involve law enforcement? Untested assumptions don't reveal themselves until the worst possible moment to discover them.

🔬 Reverse Engineering & Binary Analysis — Reading Code You Don't Have Source For Malware • SecurityX ▶
Where It Fits
The Third Tier of Malware Analysis
Malware Analysis — Understanding What the Bad Code Does covers the first two tiers: static triage (strings, hashes, imports) and dynamic detonation in a sandbox. Reverse engineering is what you do when both come back thin — the sample is packed, it refuses to run, or you need the exact decryption routine rather than a behavioural summary. It is slow, expensive, and the only way to answer questions like "what is the C2 (Command and Control) protocol" or "can we recover the files without paying."
The Toolchain
Disassembly, Decompilation, Debugging
A disassembler turns machine code into assembly — faithful, and hard going. A decompiler guesses C-like source from that assembly — readable, and sometimes wrong, which is the trade you are making every time you read its output. A debugger runs the sample under your control so you can watch a value that only exists at runtime, like a key decrypted in memory.
ToolRole
GhidraFree NSA-released disassembler and decompiler; the usual starting point
IDA Pro / Binary NinjaCommercial equivalents; strong analysis and scripting
x64dbg / GDBUser-mode debuggers for Windows / Linux
radare2 / rizinScriptable command-line reversing framework
PE-bear, readelf, objdumpHeader, section and import inspection before you open anything bigger
Method
Anchor First, Then Read Outward
Nobody reads a binary from the entry point down. You find an anchor — an interesting imported API (Application Programming Interface), a suspicious string, a network call — and work outward from its cross-references until the function's purpose is obvious. Then rename it, and repeat. A reversing session is mostly the steady accumulation of names. 
# Triage before the disassembler: what does it even want?
file sample.bin                    # architecture, format, stripped?
readelf -d sample.bin              # ELF: dynamic imports
objdump -d sample.bin | head -50   # a first look at the code

# Entropy near 8.0 across a section means packed or encrypted —
# stop and unpack before wasting hours reading noise.
Imports are the cheapest signal in the file. CryptEncrypt plus directory enumeration says ransomware; SetWindowsHookEx says keylogger; a near-empty import table says the real ones are resolved at runtime, which is itself a finding.
Legal & Ethical
Know Your Authorization
Reversing malware you were sent as a defender is routine. Reversing licensed commercial software is a different question, and the answer depends on your jurisdiction, the licence, and what you do with the result — interoperability and security research carve-outs exist in some places and not others. Work samples in an isolated lab, keep custody records if the artefact might become evidence, and get the authorization question answered before you start rather than after.
🎭 Anti-Analysis Techniques — How Malware Hides, and How Analysts Win Anyway Malware • CySA+ ▶
Core Concept
The Sample Is Trying to Detect You
Modern malware assumes it will land in a sandbox before it lands on a victim, so it spends its first moments deciding which one it is in. If it concludes it is being watched, it does nothing interesting — exits quietly, or runs a decoy routine. A clean sandbox report is therefore not evidence the file is safe; it is equally consistent with a sample that recognized the sandbox.
CategoryTechniqueDefeat
Anti-VMChecks MAC (Media Access Control) prefixes, disk size, driver names, CPU (Central Processing Unit) featuresHarden the VM (Virtual Machine); use bare-metal detonation for stubborn samples
Anti-debugIsDebuggerPresent, timing checks, exception tricks, self-checksumsDebugger hiding plugins; patch the check; breakpoint after it
Anti-sandboxLong sleeps, waits for mouse movement, demands a domain-joined hostSleep-patching, simulated user activity, longer detonation
PackingCompressed or encrypted payload unpacked in memory at run timeRun to the OEP and dump memory; a static-only look is worthless
ObfuscationString encryption, control-flow flattening, junk instructions, API (Application Programming Interface) hashingEmulation, deobfuscation scripts, resolving hashes against known API lists
Environmental keyingPayload decrypts only with a key derived from the target's own environmentOften unbeatable without the victim host — say so rather than guessing
Detection Angle
Evasion Is Itself an Indicator
A defender does not need to defeat every trick. Legitimate software rarely checks whether it is being debugged, and almost never sleeps for ten minutes before doing anything. High section entropy, a stub import table, timing checks around the entry point — these are behaviours to hunt for, not just obstacles to overcome. YARA (Yet Another Recursive Acronym) rules that match packer stubs and evasion patterns catch families whose payloads change weekly.
The reporting discipline: write "the sample did not execute its payload under analysis" rather than "the sample is inert." The first is what you observed; the second is a conclusion the evidence does not support, and it is the sentence that gets a sample cleared.
📦 Supply-Chain Attacks — Compromise One, Reach Thousands Threat • SecurityX ▶
Core Concept
Attacking the Thing Your Target Already Trusts
Perimeter defences assume attackers come from outside. A supply-chain attack arrives through the front door, signed, inside an update the victim installed on purpose. The economics are brutal in the attacker's favour: one compromised build server or one popular dependency reaches every downstream consumer at once, and every consumer's own controls are aimed at the wrong direction. The defensive answer lives in Software Supply Chain Security — SBOM, SLSA & Sigstore; this card is the attack side.
VectorHow it works
Build-system compromiseInject into the pipeline so the malicious artefact is legitimately signed
Dependency poisoningTake over or compromise a package many projects already depend on
TyposquattingPublish a package one keystroke from a popular name and wait
Dependency confusionPublish a public package matching an internal name; resolvers may prefer the higher version
Maintainer takeoverPhish or socially engineer commit rights, sometimes over months of "helpful" contributions
Update-channel abuseCompromise the distribution or signing infrastructure rather than the code
Hardware & firmwareInterdiction or implant before the device ever reaches the buyer
Case Pattern
What the Big Ones Taught
The headline incidents rhyme. A trusted update mechanism was subverted and the malicious code was properly signed, so signature verification passed. Detection came from behaviour — unexpected outbound traffic, a process doing something out of character — not from the artefact. And discovery took months, in at least one case only because someone investigated a performance anomaly that had nothing to do with security.
LessonWhat it means operationally
Signed is not safeSignatures prove origin, never intent; validate behaviour too
You need an inventoryAn SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) is how you answer "are we affected" in hours instead of weeks
Egress control pays offBeaconing from a build server should never have reached the internet
Pin and verifyLockfiles, hash pinning, and scoped internal registries close the confusion vector
Volunteer maintainers are infrastructureCritical dependencies are often one exhausted person; treat that as a risk you own
💱 The Criminal Economy — Access Brokers, Affiliates & How Breaches Get Sold Threat Intel ▶
Core Concept
Cybercrime Specialized, and That Changed the Threat
The lone attacker who breaks in, moves laterally, and deploys their own ransomware is mostly a training scenario. The real ecosystem is a supply chain of specialists: one crew harvests credentials, another sells the access, a third operates inside the network, and the ransomware itself is rented software with a support portal. This matters defensively because it decouples who got in from what eventually happened — and it explains the gap, often weeks or months, between the initial compromise and the encryption event.
RoleWhat they sell
Infostealer operatorsBulk credential and session-cookie logs from infected consumer machines
Initial access brokersVerified footholds — VPN (Virtual Private Network) accounts, RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol), web shells — priced by victim revenue
RaaS developersThe encryptor, the leak site and the negotiation portal, for a cut of proceeds
AffiliatesThe intrusion labour; they buy access and run the operation
Bulletproof hosting & proxiesInfrastructure that ignores abuse complaints; residential proxy networks
LaunderersMixers, chain-hopping and cash-out; frequently the arrest point
Defender's Read
What the Market Structure Tells You
Attribution gets harder and matters less: the same access can be resold to different operators, so today's actor may have nothing to do with the intrusion. Meanwhile stolen session cookies bypass password resets and often MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), which is why an infostealer infection on a personal laptop is a corporate incident. Double extortion — encrypt and leak — exists precisely because good backups killed the original business model, so "we have backups" is now a recovery plan, not a negotiation position. See Ransomware — The Defining Threat of the Era for the incident side.
SignalWhy it is worth monitoring
Your domains in stealer logsCredentials and live sessions already for sale
Access-broker listingsA description matching your sector, size and revenue band
Leak-site postingsYour vendors appearing there is your incident too
Affiliate tradecraft shiftsThe tooling changes far faster than the underlying playbook
📐 Threat Modeling Methodologies — STRIDE vs PASTA vs Attack Trees SecurityX • CISSP ▶
Where It Fits
Choosing the Method, Not Just Doing the Exercise
Threat Modeling — Finding Flaws Before You Build Them covers the practice: draw the system, find the threats, decide what to do. This card is the level above — the named methodologies differ in what they optimize for, and picking the wrong one is how a threat-modeling programme dies of paperwork in its second quarter.
MethodAnchored onBest when
STRIDESix threat categories per componentDeveloper-facing design review; fast, teachable, broad coverage
PASTASeven risk-centric stages, business impact firstYou must justify spend to executives in money terms
Attack treesOne goal, decomposed into pathsDeep analysis of a single critical asset or scenario
LINDDUNPrivacy threat categoriesPersonal data is the asset; pairs with a DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment)
Kill chain / ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) mappingReal adversary behaviourYou want threats grounded in what actually happens, not imagination
Reference
STRIDE, and Its Property Mapping
STRIDE's durable value is that each category is the violation of one security property — which turns "think of threats" into six concrete questions you ask of every data flow and every trust boundary.
ThreatViolatesTypical control
SpoofingAuthenticationStrong identity, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), mutual TLS (Transport Layer Security)
TamperingIntegritySigning, hashing, input validation
RepudiationNon-repudiationTamper-evident audit logging
Information disclosureConfidentialityEncryption, access control, minimization
Denial of serviceAvailabilityRate limits, quotas, capacity planning
Elevation of privilegeAuthorizationLeast privilege, sandboxing, authorization checks
Pitfall
The Model Nobody Reads Again
The common failure is not a wrong methodology — it is a beautiful diagram produced once, filed, and never revisited while the system changes underneath it. Model the thing you are actually building this quarter, cap the session at an hour, and end with tracked issues rather than a document. A threat model whose output is a to-do list survives; one whose output is a PDF (Portable Document Format) does not.
🛡️ MITRE D3FEND (Detection, Denial and Disruption Framework Empowering Network Defense) & Engage — Mapping Defenses and Deception to ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) Threat Intel • Blue ▶
Core Concept
Three Matrices, Three Questions
ATT&CK catalogues what adversaries do. It is deliberately silent on what you should do about it, which is why coverage conversations stall at "we have 340 techniques and no idea which controls address them." MITRE's companion knowledge bases fill the other two sides.
Knowledge baseAnswersUnit
ATT&CKWhat does the adversary do?Tactic → technique → sub-technique
D3FENDWhat countermeasure addresses it, and how?Defensive technique, tied to a digital artifact
EngageHow do I deny, direct or deceive them on purpose?Adversary-engagement activity
D3FEND
Countermeasures Tied to Artifacts, Not Vendors
D3FEND's structure is what makes it useful: defensive techniques are linked to the concrete digital artifacts they operate on — a process, a file, a network session, a credential. That gives you a vendor-neutral vocabulary for what a control actually does, and turns "we bought an EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response)" into a specific claim about which techniques are covered by which capability. Its verbs — harden, detect, isolate, deceive, evict — are also a sanity check on a portfolio that has quietly become all detection and no isolation.
Engage
Deception, With the Adults in the Room
Engage reframes deception as a planned operation with goals rather than a honeypot someone stood up for fun. You decide first what you want — deny access, waste the adversary's time, or collect intelligence on their tooling — because those aims conflict. Collecting intelligence means letting them stay, which is a decision for the business and legal, not the SOC (Security Operations Center).
ApproachGoalCost
HoneytokensHigh-fidelity alert when something touches a fake credential or fileVery low — the best value in the category
Decoy hostsWaste time; observe tradecraftModerate; needs realism and upkeep
Full deception environmentSustained intelligence collectionHigh; needs legal sign-off and staff attention
Do not improvise this. Leaving an adversary in place to watch them has regulatory, contractual and disclosure consequences, and the decision belongs to counsel and leadership — recorded in advance, not made at 2 a.m. by whoever is on call.

⚠️ Risk Management Lifecycle 5-STEP CYCLE ▶
Lifecycle
Identify → Analyze → Prioritize → Treat → Monitor
A continuous cycle. Risk = Likelihood × Impact. ALE = ARO × SLE (Annualized Loss Expectancy = Annual Rate of Occurrence × Single Loss Expectancy).
1
Identify Risks
Asset inventory, threat modeling, vulnerability identification, Business Impact Analysis (BIA)
2
Analyze Risks
Qualitative (probability/impact ratings) vs Quantitative (ALE = ARO × SLE). Inherent vs residual risk
3
Prioritize
Risk register · Risk appetite vs tolerance · Heat maps · Residual risk after controls
4
Treat (4 T's)
Transfer (insurance/3rd party) · Avoid (stop activity) · Mitigate (implement controls) · Accept (acknowledge residual risk)
5
Monitor & Review
Continuous monitoring, KRI (Key Risk Indicator) dashboards, reassess after control changes, audit findings, repeat

LOW Impact MED Impact HIGH Impact CRITICAL Impact
HIGH Likelihood MEDIUM HIGH CRITICAL CRITICAL
MED Likelihood LOW MEDIUM HIGH CRITICAL
LOW Likelihood LOW LOW MEDIUM HIGH

🧒Risk & Rules in Plain EnglishGRC • Start Here▶
BIG IDEA
What Is Risk?
Risk = how likely something bad is × how badly it would hurt. Crossing a quiet street is low risk; crossing a highway blindfolded is high. Security work is mostly about lowering one or both of those numbers.
THE FOUR CHOICES
How to Handle Risk
You can Accept it (live with a small chance), Avoid it (don't do the risky thing), Transfer it (buy insurance so someone else pays), or Mitigate it (add controls to shrink it). Everyday life uses all four.
ANALOGY
Policy vs. Standard vs. Procedure
A policy is the rule ('we drive safely'). A standard is the specific requirement ('wear seatbelts'). A procedure is the step-by-step ('click, pull, buckle'). Together they turn good intentions into repeatable action.
WHY IT EXISTS
Compliance Isn't Just Paperwork
Compliance means following laws and standards (like HIPAA for health data). It feels like red tape, but the rules usually exist because someone got hurt before they existed. 'Compliant' is the floor, not the ceiling, of security.
TermPlain-English Meaning
GovernanceWho decides the rules and makes sure they're followed
AssetAnything worth protecting (data, devices, people)
ControlA safeguard that lowers risk (a lock, a backup, a policy)
AuditAn outside check that you actually do what you say
Defense-in-depthMany layers, so one failure isn't game over
📋Frameworks Without the JargonGRC • Start Here▶
WHAT
A Framework Is a Good-Practice Checklist
You don’t have to invent security from scratch — experts already wrote down what works. A framework is that shared checklist, so organizations aim at a known-good target instead of guessing.
THE BIG ONE
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF in Five Words
The popular NIST Cybersecurity Framework boils down to five plain verbs: Identify what you have, Protect it, Detect trouble, Respond when it happens, and Recover afterward. (A newer sixth, Govern, wraps leadership around it.)
WHY
Common Language, Fewer Gaps
Frameworks let a whole team — and auditors, and vendors — speak the same language and spot what’s missing. ‘We’re weak on Detect’ is a clear, actionable sentence everyone understands.
NIST CSF FunctionThe Question It Answers
IdentifyWhat do we have and what’s at risk?
ProtectHow do we safeguard it?
DetectHow will we notice an attack?
RespondWhat do we do when it happens?
RecoverHow do we get back to normal?

THREE CORE TERMS
Threat · Vulnerability · Risk
Threat — something that COULD cause harm (fire, hacker, disgruntled employee). Threats are mostly out of your control.
Vulnerability — a weakness that a threat can exploit (unpatched software, unlocked door, weak password). These are in your control.
Risk — the likelihood × impact of a threat exploiting a vulnerability. Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact.
RISK RESPONSES
Accept · Avoid · Transfer · Mitigate
Avoid — stop doing the risky thing entirely (don't store data you don't need).
Mitigate — reduce likelihood or impact (patch the vulnerability, add MFA).
Transfer — shift the financial impact to someone else (buy cyber insurance, outsource to an MSSP).
Accept — acknowledge the risk but do nothing (when cost of mitigation > expected loss). Always document accepted risks.
QUALITATIVE vs QUANTITATIVE
High/Medium/Low vs Actual Dollars
Qualitative — ranks risks as High/Medium/Low using judgment. Fast, good for prioritization, but subjective.
Quantitative — assigns dollar values. Uses:
AV (Asset Value) — what the asset is worth
EF (Exposure Factor) — % of asset lost if threat occurs
SLE = AV × EF — Single Loss Expectancy
ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) (Annual Rate of Occurrence) — how often per year
ALE = SLE × ARO — Annual Loss Expectancy
AcronymMeaningExample ($1M server, fire burns 30%, happens 0.1/yr)
AVAsset Value$1,000,000
EFExposure Factor30% = 0.30
SLESingle Loss Expectancy (AV × EF)$300,000
AROAnnual Rate of Occurrence0.1 (once per 10 years)
ALEAnnual Loss Expectancy (SLE × ARO)$30,000
RESIDUAL RISK
What's Left After Controls
No control eliminates 100% of risk. After applying safeguards, you have residual risk — what you accept as the remaining exposure. Risk appetite is how much residual risk an organization is willing to tolerate. Risk tolerance is the acceptable variance around that.
📋 Compliance Frameworks — Playing by the Rules GRC • Foundation ▶
WHY FRAMEWORKS EXIST
Baselines, Audits, and Legal Requirements
Companies face legal, contractual, or industry requirements to prove they handle data and systems securely. Frameworks provide a common language and a checklist so everyone knows what "secure enough" means. Being compliant ≠ being secure, but it's a starting floor.
FrameworkWho It's ForFocus
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework)Any org, especially US federalIdentify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 27001Any org worldwideInformation Security Management System (ISMS)
PCI-DSSAnyone taking credit cardsCardholder data security; 12 requirements
HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act)US healthcare providersProtected Health Information (PHI) privacy
SOC 2 (Service Organization Control 2)SaaS (Software as a Service) / cloud service providersTrust Service Criteria: Security, Availability, etc.
GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation)Any org with EU user dataData privacy, user rights, breach notification
CMMCUS defense contractorsCybersecurity Maturity Model; tiered levels
CIS (Center for Internet Security) ControlsAny org18 prioritized security actions
AUDIT TYPES
Internal, External, Third-Party
Internal audit — done by your own staff or internal audit team. Finds issues before outsiders do. Not independent, but faster and cheaper.
External audit — done by a third-party firm. Required for SOC 2, ISO 27001 certification, PCI-DSS. Independent opinion carries more weight.
Penetration test — adversarial: ethical hackers try to break in. Reveals what a real attacker would find. Required by PCI-DSS annually.
POLICY HIERARCHY
Policy → Standard → Procedure → Guideline
Policy — high-level statement of intent. "All data must be encrypted at rest." Non-negotiable.
Standard — specific requirements to meet the policy. "Use AES-256."
Procedure — step-by-step how to implement. "Run this script, configure this setting."
Guideline — recommended but not mandatory best practices. "Consider using a VPN (Virtual Private Network) on public Wi-Fi."
🔄 Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery — Keeping the Lights On GRC • Essential ▶
BC VS DR
Business Continuity vs Disaster Recovery
These terms are related but distinct. People often use them interchangeably — they are not the same thing.
ConceptFocusScopeQuestion It Answers
Business Continuity (BC)Keeping operations running during a disruptionEntire organization (people, process, tech)"How do we keep doing business?"
Disaster Recovery (DR)Restoring IT systems after a disasterIT infrastructure, data, applications"How do we restore our systems?"
BCPBusiness Continuity Plan — the documentStrategic plan covering all scenarios"What's the written playbook?"
DRPDisaster Recovery Plan — the documentIT recovery procedures, step-by-step"What's the IT recovery script?"
KEY METRICS
RTO (Recovery Time Objective) and RPO (Recovery Point Objective) — The Two Numbers That Matter
Every system should have defined RTO and RPO. These drive architecture decisions: lower values require more expensive solutions (hot standby, synchronous replication). Setting them is a business decision, not a technical one — it depends on what downtime costs.
MetricFull NameDefinitionExample
RTORecovery Time ObjectiveMaximum acceptable downtime — how long before systems MUST be back up"We can tolerate 4 hours of outage"
RPORecovery Point ObjectiveMaximum acceptable data loss — how old can the restored data be?"We can lose at most 1 hour of transactions"
MTTR (Mean Time To Repair)Mean Time to RecoverAverage time to restore service after failureHistorical metric from past incidents
MTBFMean Time Between FailuresAverage time between system failuresMeasure of reliability

Warm SiteSystems and infra present, data partially synced. Needs some setup.HoursModerate

Cloud DRReplicate to cloud, spin up on demand. Modern favorite.Minutes to hoursPay-per-use (low idle cost)

Test TypeWhat HappensRiskValidates

🏷️ Data Classification — Knowing What Needs Protecting GRC • Foundation ▶
WHY CLASSIFY
Not All Data Needs the Same Protection
Treating a public press release the same as a Social Security number is wasteful — and treating a Social Security number like a press release is negligent. Data classification is the foundation of a proportionate security program: protect data based on its value and sensitivity, not uniformly.
GOVERNMENT CLASSIFICATION
Military/Government Levels

Secret (S)Sensitive national security informationCause serious damage to national security

Data Categories with Legal Protection

🤝 Third-Party Risk — Your Security Is Only as Strong as Your Vendors GRC • Essential ▶
WHY IT MATTERS
You Outsource the Work, Not the Risk
Modern organizations rely on dozens or hundreds of third parties: cloud providers, SaaS (Software as a Service) apps, payment processors, contractors, managed service providers. Each one is a potential entry point. Some of the biggest breaches in history came through third parties — Target (2013) was breached via an HVAC vendor's credentials. You can outsource a function, but you cannot outsource accountability for the risk.
THE VENDOR RISK LIFECYCLE
Managing Risk Across the Relationship
PhaseActivity
1. Due diligenceBefore signing: assess the vendor's security posture (questionnaires, certifications)
2. ContractingBake security requirements into the contract: SLAs (Service Level Agreement), breach notification, right to audit, data handling
3. OnboardingGrant least-privilege access; integrate securely
4. Ongoing monitoringPeriodic reassessment; watch for the vendor's own breaches
5. OffboardingRevoke all access, retrieve/destroy data, confirm in writing
ASSESSMENT TOOLS
How You Actually Evaluate a Vendor
ToolWhat It IsStrength
SOC 2 (Service Organization Control 2) Type II reportIndependent audit of a vendor's controls over a time periodGold standard — verified by a third party
ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 27001 certificateProof of a certified information security management systemInternationally recognized
Security questionnaire (SIG, CAIQ)Standardized list of security questionsBroad coverage, but self-reported
Penetration test reportEvidence the vendor tests their own securityShows real-world testing
Security ratings (BitSight, SecurityScorecard)External scan-based scoringContinuous, outside-in view
FOURTH-PARTY RISK
Your Vendors Have Vendors Too
It goes deeper. Your SaaS vendor relies on AWS (Amazon Web Services), which relies on... a chain of dependencies. A "fourth party" is your vendor's vendor. The 2020 SolarWinds attack and the 2023 MOVEit breach showed how a single compromised supplier can cascade through thousands of downstream organizations. This is why understanding your full supply chain — and concentration risk (everyone depending on the same provider) — matters.
📣 Security Awareness — Turning People Into a Defense Layer GRC • Human Factor ▶
THE HUMAN FIREWALL
People Are the Most Targeted Attack Surface
The vast majority of breaches involve a human element — clicking a phishing link, weak passwords, misconfiguration, falling for social engineering. You can buy the best technical controls in the world, but a single tricked employee can bypass all of them. Security awareness training turns employees from the weakest link into an active layer of defense — the "human firewall."
WHAT GOOD TRAINING LOOKS LIKE
Beyond the Annual Boring Video
ElementWhy It Works
Phishing simulationsSafe practice — send fake phish, coach those who click (don't punish)
Bite-sized + frequentShort, regular nudges beat one long annual session
Role-specificFinance gets BEC (Business Email Compromise) training; devs get secure coding
Real examplesShow actual attacks the org has seen — relevance drives retention
Easy reportingOne-click "report phish" button — make doing the right thing frictionless
Positive cultureReward reporting; never shame mistakes — fear makes people hide incidents
🏛️ NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF — The Common Language of Cybersecurity GRC • Framework ▶
WHAT IT IS
A Framework to Organize a Security Program
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) is a widely-adopted, voluntary framework that organizes cybersecurity work into a handful of high-level Functions. Its power is providing a common language — executives, engineers, and auditors can all talk about security using the same structure. CSF 2.0 (2024) added "Govern" as a sixth function wrapping the others.
FunctionQuestionExamples
GovernHow do we oversee and prioritize?Risk strategy, roles, policy, supply chain
IdentifyWhat do we have and what's at risk?Asset inventory, risk assessment
ProtectHow do we safeguard it?Access control, training, encryption, patching
DetectHow do we spot incidents?Monitoring, SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), anomaly detection
RespondWhat do we do when attacked?IR (Incident Response) plan, containment, communications
RecoverHow do we restore and learn?Backups, DR, post-incident improvement
POLICY HIERARCHY
Policy vs Standard vs Procedure vs Guideline
These four words are used loosely in conversation but mean specific, different things in governance. Knowing the difference is fundamental GRC (Governance, Risk, and Compliance) literacy.
DocumentDefinesMandatory?Example
PolicyHigh-level intent and rules (the "what" and "why")Yes"All data must be encrypted in transit"
StandardSpecific mandatory requirementsYes"Use TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.2 or higher"
ProcedureStep-by-step instructions (the "how")Yes"To enable TLS: 1. edit config... 2. ..."
GuidelineRecommended best practiceNo (advisory)"Consider using HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) preloading"
THE RISK REGISTER
Where Risks Are Tracked and Owned
A risk register is the living document that records identified risks, their severity, and what's being done about them. It turns vague worry into a managed list with owners and deadlines. Every mature GRC program maintains one.
ColumnWhat Goes There
Risk ID / description"R-014: Unpatched VPN (Virtual Private Network) appliance"
Likelihood × ImpactScored (e.g., High × High = Critical)
Risk responseAccept / Mitigate / Transfer / Avoid
OwnerThe person accountable
Status / due dateOpen, in progress, closed; target date
Residual riskRisk remaining after controls applied
🔍 The Audit Process — Proving Controls Actually Work GRC • Process ▶
WHY AUDITS EXIST
Trust, but Verify — With Evidence
Saying "we're secure" means nothing without proof. An audit is an independent examination that verifies controls exist and actually work — providing assurance to customers, regulators, and leadership. For IT staff, audits can feel like an interruption, but understanding the process makes them far smoother: auditors need evidence, and the better you prepare it, the faster it goes.
AUDIT TYPES
Who's Doing the Auditing?
TypeWhoPurpose
1st party (internal)Your own audit teamSelf-check before external audits; continuous improvement
2nd partyA customer/partner audits youVendor assurance ("can we trust this supplier?")
3rd party (external)Independent firm (e.g., for SOC 2, ISO)Certification, regulatory, customer-facing assurance
THE PHASES
How an Audit Flows
PhaseWhat Happens
1. Planning & scopingDefine what's in scope, which controls, time period
2. FieldworkAuditor requests evidence, interviews staff, tests controls
3. TestingSample-based or full testing of whether controls operate effectively
4. FindingsDocument gaps/exceptions (deficiencies)
