  cache.set(`user:${id}`, u, { ttl: 300 }); // store 5 min
  return u;
}
Invalidation
Keeping Copies Honest
TechniqueWhat It Does
TTL (Time To Live) (expiry)Data auto-expires after N seconds. Simple; tolerates brief staleness.
Explicit purgeDelete the key when the source changes. Precise; needs write-path hooks.
Versioned keysBake a version/hash into the key (user:42:v3); old keys just age out.
Cache-Control headersFor HTTP/CDN: max-age, no-store, ETag for revalidation.
Watch for the thundering herd / stampede: when a hot key expires, thousands of requests miss at once and hammer the DB. Mitigate with a short lock, request coalescing, or staggered TTLs.
☁️ Serverless & FaaS (Function as a Service) — Code Without Managing Servers Cloud ▶
Concept
There Are Still Servers — You Just Don't Touch Them
Serverless means you deploy code and the cloud runs it on demand — provisioning, scaling, patching, and capacity are the provider's problem. The flagship form is Functions as a Service (FaaS): you upload a single function that runs in response to an event (an HTTP request, a file upload, a queue message) and you're billed only for the milliseconds it executes. Idle costs nothing. It's the far end of the "managed" spectrum beyond containers.
Example
A Function That Runs on an Event
AN HTTP-TRIGGERED FUNCTION (NODE)
// The cloud invokes this on each request; no server to run
export async function handler(event) {
  const name = event.queryStringParameters?.name ?? "world";
  return {
    statusCode: 200,
    body: JSON.stringify({ message: `Hello, ${name}` }),
  };
}
Deploy it, wire a trigger (API Gateway, a bucket event, a cron schedule), and it scales from zero to thousands of concurrent invocations automatically — each request gets its own isolated run.
Reference
Providers & the Compute Spectrum
▸ THE BIG FaaS PLATFORMS
ProviderService
AWS (Amazon Web Services)Lambda
AzureFunctions
Google CloudCloud Functions / Cloud Run
EdgeCloudflare Workers, Netlify/Vercel Functions
▸ HOW MUCH DO YOU MANAGE?
ModelYou Manage
On-premEverything — hardware to app
IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) (VMs)OS (Operating System) + runtime + app
ContainersThe image + app
Serverless / FaaSJust the code
Trade-offs
Where Serverless Shines — and Bites
Detail
Scale to zeroNo traffic = no cost. Great for spiky or unpredictable load.
No opsNo servers to patch or capacity-plan; ship features faster.
Cold startsAn idle function takes extra time to spin up on the first request — latency-sensitive paths feel it.
Stateless & time-limitedFunctions keep no memory between runs and have a max duration — long jobs and in-memory state don't fit.
Vendor lock-inTriggers and runtimes are provider-specific; portability takes effort.
Harder local debuggingThe event-driven, managed environment is tricky to reproduce on your laptop.
🪣 Object Storage — S3 (Simple Storage Service) & the Cloud Storage Model Cloud ▶
Concept
A Different Way to Store Data
Traditional storage is files (a tree of folders) or blocks (raw disk a filesystem sits on). Object storage is a third model: every piece of data is an object — the bytes plus metadata plus a unique key — living in a flat bucket, retrieved over HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol). There are no real folders (the "path" in a key is just a naming convention), and you can't edit part of an object — you replace the whole thing. Amazon S3 defined the model; Azure Blob, Google Cloud Storage, and MinIO all speak a similar API (Application Programming Interface).
Comparison
Object vs File vs Block
ObjectFileBlock
UnitObject + keyFile in foldersRaw blocks
AccessHTTP APINFS/SMBAttached disk
Edit in placeNo — replace wholeYesYes
Scales toEffectively unlimitedLimitedLimited
Best forMedia, backups, data lakes, static sitesShared docsDatabases, VMs (Virtual Machine)
Reference
Key Features You'll Use
FeatureWhat It Does
Storage classesTrade price for access speed: hot (Standard) → cool → cold archive (Glacier). Cheaper to store, pricier/slower to retrieve.
Lifecycle rulesAuto-move objects to colder tiers or delete them after N days.
VersioningKeep old copies so an overwrite/delete is recoverable.
Presigned URLs (Uniform Resource Locator)A time-limited link that grants temporary access to one object without exposing credentials.
Static website hostingServe a bucket of HTML/JS directly — often fronted by a CDN (Content Delivery Network).
DurabilityProviders replicate objects across facilities — S3 advertises 99.999999999% ("11 nines") durability.
Commands
Working With a Bucket (AWS CLI)
aws s3 mb s3://my-bucket                 # make bucket
aws s3 cp report.pdf s3://my-bucket/       # upload an object
aws s3 ls s3://my-bucket/                  # list objects
aws s3 sync ./site s3://my-bucket/         # upload a whole folder
aws s3 presign s3://my-bucket/report.pdf   # temp shareable URL
Security note: the classic cloud breach is a bucket left public. Keep buckets private by default, use IAM (Identity and Access Management) policies for access, and reach for presigned URLs when you need to share a single object.
🎚️ Deployment Strategies — Blue-Green, Canary & Rolling Reliability ▶
Concept
Shipping New Code Without Taking the Site Down
The naive deploy — stop the app, swap the code, start it — means downtime and a scary all-or-nothing cutover. Modern strategies release new versions gradually and reversibly, so you can catch a bad release before it reaches everyone and roll back in seconds instead of scrambling. The common thread: never bet all your traffic on an unproven version at once.
Reference
The Main Strategies
StrategyHow It Works
RollingReplace instances a few at a time until all run the new version. No extra capacity needed; rollback is slow (roll the other way).
Blue-GreenRun two full environments. Blue serves live; deploy to idle Green, test it, then flip all traffic. Instant rollback = flip back. Costs 2× capacity during the switch.
CanarySend a small % of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, then ramp up. Limits blast radius; needs good monitoring.
Feature flagsShip code dark, then toggle it on for cohorts at runtime — decouples deploy from release.
Trade-offs
Choosing One
If you want…Use
Instant rollback, simple cutoverBlue-Green
To catch bad releases with real trafficCanary
Zero extra infrastructure costRolling
To release to specific users / A-B testFeature flags
They combine: canary-deploy behind a feature flag on rolling infrastructure. Kubernetes and load balancers make traffic-splitting easy, which is why these went mainstream.
Prerequisites
What Makes Safe Deploys Possible
RequirementWhy
Backward-compatible changesOld and new versions run at once — the DB schema and APIs (Application Programming Interface) must serve both. Use expand-then-contract migrations.
Health checksThe orchestrator must know a new instance is actually ready before sending it traffic.
Good metrics/alertsCanary is blind without error-rate and latency dashboards to compare versions.
Automated rollbackA deploy that can't auto-revert on failing metrics isn't really safe.
🔺 CAP Theorem & Consistency Models Architecture ▶
Concept
Pick Two — the Fundamental Trade-off
The CAP theorem says a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of three properties: Consistency (every read sees the latest write), Availability (every request gets a response), and Partition tolerance (it keeps working when the network splits). Since networks will partition, partition tolerance isn't optional in practice — so the real choice, during a partition, is consistency vs availability.
Reference
The Three Letters
LetterGuarantee
ConsistencyAll nodes return the same, most-recent data. A read never sees stale values.
AvailabilityEvery request gets a (non-error) response, even if some nodes are down.
Partition toleranceThe system keeps operating even when nodes can't talk to each other.
Note: CAP's "Consistency" is stricter than ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability)'s — it means linearizability (one up-to-date copy), not "constraints hold." Different word, different guarantee.
In Practice
CP vs AP — What You Choose During a Split
CP (consistency)AP (availability)
During a partitionRefuse/blocks writes to stay correctKeep serving, reconcile later
Read might beAlways currentStale for a moment
Good forBanking, inventory, bookingsFeeds, carts, social, DNS (Domain Name System)
Examplesetcd, ZooKeeper, HBaseCassandra, DynamoDB, Riak
Most real systems aren't purely one or the other — they tune per-operation (a shopping cart is AP; the final checkout is CP).
Beyond CAP
Consistency Is a Spectrum
ModelPromise
Strong / linearizableReads always see the latest write — as if one copy existed.
EventualGiven no new writes, all replicas eventually converge. Cheap & available.
Read-your-writesYou always see your own updates (even if others lag).
CausalRelated events are seen in order; unrelated ones may not be.
A related lens, PACELC, extends CAP: even when there's no partition (Else), you still trade Latency vs Consistency — stronger guarantees cost round-trips. There's no free lunch in distributed data.
🕸️ Service Mesh — Istio, Linkerd & the Sidecar Pattern Cloud Native ▶
Concept
Move Networking Concerns Out of Your Code
When one app becomes 50 microservices, every service needs retries, timeouts, TLS (Transport Layer Security), load balancing, and metrics for its calls to the others. Building that into each service — in every language — is repetitive and inconsistent. A service mesh extracts all of it into the infrastructure: a proxy runs alongside each service and handles service-to-service traffic, so your application code just makes a plain request and the mesh does the hard parts.
Architecture
Sidecars & the Two Planes
PieceRole
Sidecar proxyA proxy (often Envoy) deployed next to every service instance. All traffic in/out flows through it — the app is unaware.
Data planeThe collection of all sidecars actually moving the traffic.
Control planeThe brain (e.g. Istio's istiod) that configures every sidecar with routing rules, certs, and policy.
You change behavior by updating the control plane; it pushes config to the sidecars. Newer meshes offer a "sidecar-less" (per-node) mode to cut the per-pod overhead.
Reference
What a Mesh Gives You
CapabilityDetail
mTLS (Mutual Transport Layer Security) everywhereAutomatic mutual-TLS encryption + identity between services — zero app changes.
Traffic controlCanary/blue-green by shifting % of traffic; retries, timeouts, circuit breaking.
ObservabilityUniform metrics, logs, and traces for every call, for free.
PolicyWho may call whom (authorization), rate limits, fault injection for testing.
Trade-offs
Do You Actually Need One?
Detail
Worth it whenMany services, multiple languages, strict security/compliance, and you need uniform mTLS + observability.
Overkill whenA handful of services — the operational complexity and latency/resource overhead outweigh the benefit.
OptionsIstio (powerful, complex), Linkerd (lightweight, simpler), Cilium (eBPF-based), Consul.
A mesh solves the same problems an API (Application Programming Interface) gateway does between internal services — the gateway is the front door for outside traffic; the mesh is the internal road network.
🔃 GitOps — Git as the Source of Truth for Operations DevOps ▶
Concept
If It's Not in Git, It Doesn't Exist
GitOps applies the software workflow you already know — pull requests, review, merge, history — to infrastructure and deployments. The desired state of your whole system lives in a Git repo as declarative config; an automated agent continuously makes the real cluster match it. You never kubectl apply by hand — you change a file, open a PR, and merging is the deploy.
How It Works
Push vs Pull Deployment
Traditional CI pushes changes into the cluster (the pipeline has cluster credentials and runs apply). GitOps flips it: an agent inside the cluster pulls the desired state from Git and reconciles continuously.
StepWhat Happens
1. DeclareDesired state (Kubernetes manifests, Helm, Terraform) is committed to Git.
2. ObserveAn in-cluster agent (Argo CD, Flux) watches the repo.
3. DiffIt compares Git (desired) against the live cluster (actual).
4. ReconcileIt applies changes to close the gap — automatically and continuously.
Reference
Why Teams Adopt It
BenefitDetail
Git is the audit logEvery change is a reviewed, attributed, revertible commit. Rollback = git revert.
No config driftThe agent fixes manual/out-of-band changes automatically — the cluster can't silently diverge.
Better securityCI no longer needs cluster credentials; the pull agent lives inside and reaches out.
ReproducibleRebuild an entire environment from the repo — great for DR and new clusters.
Practical
Tools & Gotchas
PointDetail
ToolsArgo CD and Flux are the two dominant Kubernetes GitOps agents.
SecretsYou can't commit plaintext secrets — use Sealed Secrets, SOPS, or an external secrets operator.
Repo layoutCommon pattern: separate app-code repos from a config repo; a merge to config triggers the deploy.
Fits declarative bestGitOps assumes a system that reconciles to a declared state (Kubernetes shines); imperative steps fit less cleanly.
💰 FinOps — Cloud Cost Management Cloud ▶
Concept
The Cloud Bill Is a Team Sport
In the data-center era, capacity was a big upfront purchase the finance team controlled. In the cloud, any engineer can spin up expensive resources in seconds — and the bill is pay-as-you-go and variable. FinOps is the practice of bringing financial accountability to that model: giving engineers cost visibility, so the people who create spend can make informed trade-offs between speed, quality, and cost. It's a culture, not just a dashboard.
Framework
Inform → Optimize → Operate
PhaseWhat You Do
InformMake cost visible & attributable — tag resources, allocate spend to teams/products, show dashboards.
OptimizeCut waste — rightsize, delete idle resources, buy commitments, pick cheaper options.
OperateMake it continuous — budgets, alerts, and cost as a normal engineering metric.
Reference
Where the Savings Are
LeverWhat It Means
RightsizingMatch instance size to real usage — most VMs (Virtual Machine) are wildly overprovisioned.
Kill idle / zombiesUnattached disks, idle load balancers, forgotten dev environments burn money 24/7.
CommitmentsReserved Instances / Savings Plans trade a 1–3 yr commitment for ~30–70% off steady workloads.
Spot instancesSpare capacity at up to ~90% off — for fault-tolerant, interruptible jobs.
AutoscalingScale to demand (and to zero) instead of provisioning for peak always-on.
Storage tieringMove cold data to cheaper classes; set lifecycle rules.
Egress awarenessData transfer out is a sneaky cost — cross-region/cross-cloud traffic adds up.
Practice
Habits That Keep Costs Sane
HabitWhy
Tag everythingWithout tags for team/env/product, you can't attribute spend or find waste.
Budgets & anomaly alertsCatch a runaway job or a misconfigured autoscaler before the invoice does.
Unit economicsTrack cost per customer / per request, not just the total — growth should scale efficiently.
Right time to optimizeDon't micro-optimize a tiny bill; focus effort where spend is largest.
♾️ What DevOps Actually Is — Culture Over Tools DevOps ▶
Concept
Breaking the Wall Between Dev and Ops
DevOps isn't a job title or a toolchain — it's a culture that removes the traditional wall between developers (who want to ship change) and operations (who want stability). The mantra is "you build it, you run it": the team that writes the code also operates it, so quality and reliability become everyone's job, not a handoff. Tools (CI/CD, IaC, containers) enable it, but adopting them without the culture just automates the old dysfunction faster.
▸ CALMS — THE FIVE PILLARS
PillarMeans
CultureShared ownership, blameless learning, collaboration over silos
AutomationAutomate the repetitive path (build, test, deploy, infra)
LeanSmall batches, remove waste, optimize flow end-to-end
MeasurementInstrument everything; decide with data (see DORA)
SharingOpen knowledge, feedback, and tooling across teams
🔁 The Three Ways — Flow, Feedback, Learning DevOps ▶
Concept
The Principles Behind DevOps (The DevOps Handbook)
The Three Ways are the underlying principles all DevOps practices derive from — a useful lens for judging why a practice helps.
WayPrinciplePractices
1. FlowSpeed work left→right (dev→prod)Small batches, CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery), limit WIP, remove bottlenecks
2. FeedbackFast signal right→leftMonitoring, automated tests, alerting, stop-the-line on failure
3. LearningContinual experimentationBlameless postmortems, chaos drills, psychological safety
Flow gets change out fast; feedback catches problems fast; learning makes the system better over time. Skip feedback and you ship bugs faster; skip learning and you repeat incidents.
📊 DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) Metrics — Measuring Delivery Performance DevOps ▶
Reference
The Four Numbers That Predict Elite Teams
The DORA (DevOps Research & Assessment) research found four metrics that correlate with high-performing organizations. Crucially, speed and stability rise together — elite teams deploy more often and break less. If you measure one thing about delivery, measure these.
MetricQuestionElite
Deploy frequencyHow often do you ship?On-demand / many per day
Lead time for changeCommit → production?< 1 day
Change failure rate% of deploys causing a problem0–15%
MTTR (Mean Time To Repair)Time to restore after an incident< 1 hour
First two = throughput; last two = stability. (A fifth, reliability, was later added.) Use them as a trend, not a stick — gaming "deploy frequency" by shipping trivial changes helps no one.
🗺️ Value Stream Mapping — Find the Bottleneck DevOps ▶
Concept
Where Does the Time Actually Go?
A value stream map traces every step from idea to production, recording for each: process time (actual work) vs wait time (queued, waiting for approval/review/ environment). The revelation is almost always that waiting dwarfs working — a code change might take 2 hours to write and 2 weeks to ship, stuck in queues. You improve flow by attacking the biggest wait, not by making developers type faster.
%C/A (percent complete & accurate) at each step reveals rework loops — if QA (Quality Assurance) sends 40% back, that handoff is your real problem. Map it, find the fattest wait/rework, fix that, remap. It's the Lean tool DevOps borrowed to make "optimize flow" concrete.
🛝 Platform Engineering & the Internal Developer Platform DevOps ▶
Concept
Paving a Golden Path So Every Team Doesn't Reinvent It
"You build it, you run it" can overload product teams with infra complexity — Kubernetes, pipelines, secrets, observability, all per team. Platform engineering answers this by building an Internal Developer Platform (IDP): a self-service layer that packages the infra into golden paths, so a developer can provision a service, database, and pipeline with a form or a CLI (Command Line Interface) command — without becoming a cloud expert.
PrincipleDetail
Self-serviceDevelopers get what they need without filing tickets
Golden pathsPaved, opinionated defaults that are easy to follow and secure by default
Product mindsetThe platform team treats developers as customers (adoption, not mandate)
Not a rename of opsIt's a product, not a gatekeeper — paved roads, not roadblocks
Tools in the space: Backstage (developer portal), Crossplane/Terraform (provisioning), Port/Humanitec (IDP orchestration).
🏭 CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) Pipeline Design — Stages, Gates & Artifacts DevOps ▶
Concept
The Assembly Line From Commit to Production
A pipeline runs a series of stages on every change, each a quality gate that must pass before the next. Build once, produce an immutable artifact, and promote that same artifact through environments — never rebuild per stage, or you're testing something different than you ship.
StageGate
BuildCompiles; produces the artifact (jar, image)
TestUnit + integration pass; coverage threshold
ScanSAST/SCA/secrets clean (fail on high sev)
Deploy → stagingSmoke/e2e tests green
Deploy → prodManual approval or automated canary
CI = integrate + test every change automatically. CD = that artifact is always deployable (Continuous Delivery) or actually auto-deployed (Continuous Deployment). Keep pipelines fast — a 40-minute pipeline kills the feedback loop.
🎬 GitHub Actions — Workflows, Jobs & Secrets DevOps ▶
How-To
CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) Built Into Your Repo
GitHub Actions runs YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) workflows in .github/workflows/ triggered by events (push, PR, schedule). A workflow has jobs (run in parallel by default) made of steps (shell commands or reusable actions). 
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix: { node: [18, 20] }   # test on multiple versions
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '${{ matrix.node }}' }
      - run: npm ci && npm test
      - run: deploy.sh
        env: { TOKEN: '${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}' }
ConceptDetail
MatrixRun the job across a combination of versions/OSes
Secrets${{ secrets.X }} — never hard-code creds
Reusable/compositeFactor shared steps into called workflows/actions
OIDC (OpenID Connect)Assume a cloud role with no stored keys (ties to IAM)
🔧 Jenkins · GitLab CI · CircleCI — The Landscape DevOps ▶
Reference
Which CI Tool, and Why
ToolCharacter
GitHub ActionsNative to GitHub, huge marketplace — the default for GitHub repos
GitLab CIDeeply integrated with GitLab; one .gitlab-ci.yml; strong self-hosted story
JenkinsThe veteran — infinitely pluggable, self-hosted, but you maintain it (Jenkinsfile/Groovy)
CircleCI / Travis / DroneHosted CI, config-as-YAML, fast setup
Argo / TektonKubernetes-native pipelines (GitOps-friendly)
They all share the model — YAML/DSL pipeline, runners/agents, stages, artifacts, secrets. Learn the concepts once; the syntax is a lookup. Pick by where your code lives and whether you want hosted vs self-managed.
🌿 Branching Strategies — Trunk vs GitHub Flow vs GitFlow DevOps ▶
Concept
How Your Team Moves Code to Main
StrategyHowFits
Trunk-basedEveryone commits to main behind feature flags; tiny short-lived branchesHigh-velocity CD; elite DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) teams
GitHub FlowBranch → PR → review → merge → deploy mainMost web teams; simple & effective
GitFlowLong-lived develop/release/hotfix branchesVersioned/released software; heavier
The trend is toward trunk-based: long-lived branches cause painful merges and delay integration (the opposite of "continuous integration"). Short-lived branches + feature flags let you merge constantly and release independently of deploy.
🚦 Progressive Delivery — Flags + Canary in the Pipeline DevOps ▶
Concept
Release ≠ Deploy
Progressive delivery separates deploy (code is on the servers) from release (users see it), and ramps exposure gradually so a bad change hits few people. It stitches together patterns you already know into the pipeline.
TechniqueRole
Feature flagsShip code dark; toggle on for cohorts at runtime
CanaryRoute 1% → 10% → 100% while watching metrics
Blue-greenInstant switch + instant rollback
Automated rollbackBad canary metrics → pipeline reverts automatically
Tools: LaunchDarkly/Unleash/Flagsmith (flags), Argo Rollouts/Flagger (automated canary on Kubernetes). This is how elite teams deploy dozens of times a day with a low change-failure rate — the two DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) goals reconciled.
🐳 Docker Deep — Multi-Stage Builds & Image Slimming DevOps ▶
How-To
Small, Fast, Secure Images
A naive Dockerfile produces bloated, slow, insecure images. Two techniques fix most of it: multi-stage builds (build in a fat image, copy only the artifact into a tiny final image) and layer caching (order instructions so dependencies cache across builds). 
# Stage 1: build
FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.* ./
RUN go mod download        # cached unless go.* changes
COPY . .
RUN go build -o /app

# Stage 2: tiny runtime — just the binary
FROM gcr.io/distroless/base
COPY --from=build /app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
TechniqueWin
Multi-stageMB-sized final image, no build tools shipped
Distroless / AlpineMinimal base = smaller attack surface
Layer orderCopy deps before source → fast rebuilds
Non-root USERDon't run containers as root
.dockerignoreKeep secrets/junk out of the build context
☸️ Kubernetes Objects — The Ones You Actually Use DevOps ▶
Reference
The Building Blocks of a Deployment
Kubernetes has dozens of object types, but day-to-day you use a handful. They compose: a Deployment manages Pods; a Service gives them a stable address; an Ingress routes external traffic in.
ObjectRole
PodThe smallest unit — one or more containers sharing network/storage
DeploymentManages a replicated, self-healing set of Pods + rolling updates
ServiceStable virtual IP/DNS load-balancing to a set of Pods
IngressHTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)(S) routing from outside into Services
ConfigMap / SecretConfig & credentials injected into Pods
StatefulSetPods with stable identity/storage (databases)
NamespaceVirtual cluster for isolation/multi-tenancy
Everything is declarative YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) reconciled to desired state — you describe what you want; the controllers make it so (kubectl apply -f).
⎈ Helm & Kustomize — Packaging Manifests DevOps ▶
Reference
Stop Copy-Pasting YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) Per Environment
Raw manifests don't scale across dev/staging/prod. Two tools solve it differently: Helm templates manifests with variables into reusable "charts" (the K8s package manager); Kustomize layers overlays that patch a common base — no templating language.
HelmKustomize
ApproachTemplating + values.yamlBase + overlay patches
PackagingCharts, repos, releases, rollbackNo packaging
ComplexityPowerful but templating can get gnarlySimple, YAML-native (built into kubectl)
Best forDistributing apps (Postgres, nginx)Your own app across environments
🔒 Kubernetes Security — RBAC (Role-Based Access Control), Network Policies & Pod Security DevOps ▶
Reference
A Cluster Is Insecure by Default
Out of the box, K8s (Kubernetes) is permissive — pods can talk to everything, run as root, and service accounts may be over-privileged. Hardening is a checklist every production cluster needs.
ControlDoes
RBACLeast-privilege for users & service accounts (who can do what)
Network PoliciesDefault-deny pod-to-pod traffic; allow only what's needed
Pod Security StandardsBlock root, privileged, host mounts (restricted profile)
Admission controlOPA/Gatekeeper, Kyverno enforce policy at deploy time
Image scanningTrivy/Grype in CI; only signed images (see supply chain)
SecretsEncrypt at rest (etcd); external secrets operators
This is where the Red Team's "Kubernetes attacks" meet defense — RBAC abuse and container escape are exactly what these controls stop.
⚙️ Configuration Management — Ansible & the Alternatives Config Mgmt ▶
Reference
Make Servers Match a Desired State
Config management enforces how a server is set up — packages, files, services, users — declaratively and repeatably. Ansible dominates because it's agentless (just SSH + Python) and its YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) playbooks are readable. 
# A tiny playbook: install & start nginx, idempotently
- hosts: web
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      ansible.builtin.apt: { name: nginx, state: present }
    - name: Ensure it is running
      ansible.builtin.service: { name: nginx, state: started, enabled: true }
ToolModel
AnsibleAgentless, push, YAML — easiest to adopt
Puppet / ChefAgent-based, pull, mature at large scale
SaltAgent or agentless; very fast event bus
Idempotency is the whole point: run it 100 times, the box ends in the same state. Config management handles mutable servers; it complements Terraform (which provisions the infra) — ties to the IaC (Infrastructure as Code) card.
🔐 Secrets Management — Vault & Kubernetes Secrets Secrets ▶
Concept
Stop Putting Passwords in Git
Hardcoded credentials are one of the most common breach causes. A secrets manager stores them centrally, encrypted, with access control and audit — and the best systems issue short-lived, dynamic creds so a leak expires on its own.
ApproachDetail
HashiCorp VaultCentral secrets + dynamic DB/cloud creds + encryption-as-a-service
Cloud-nativeAWS (Amazon Web Services) Secrets Manager, GCP (Google Cloud Platform) Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault
External Secrets OperatorSync a manager's secrets into K8s (Kubernetes) Secrets
Sealed Secrets / SOPSEncrypt secrets so they're safe to commit to Git (GitOps)
Note: plain Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted at rest by default — enable encryption providers and prefer a real manager. Dynamic short-TTL creds beat static ones every time.
🔗 Software Supply Chain Security — SBOM (Software Bill of Materials), SLSA & Sigstore Supply Chain ▶
Concept
Know & Trust What You Ship
After SolarWinds and Log4Shell, securing the build pipeline itself is a first-class concern. The goal: know every component in your artifact, and prove the artifact came from your pipeline unmodified.
Standard / ToolAnswers
SBOM"What's inside?" — a bill of materials (SPDX/CycloneDX)
SLSA"How was it built?" — build-integrity levels & provenance
Sigstore / cosign"Is it really ours?" — keyless signing of artifacts
Dependency scanningTrivy, Grype, Dependabot — find vulnerable deps (SCA)
# Generate an SBOM and sign an image (keyless, via OIDC)
syft myimage:1.0 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
cosign sign myimage:1.0
cosign verify myimage:1.0 --certificate-identity ...
Then enforce it: an admission controller can reject unsigned images at deploy time — provenance you actually check, not just generate.
📜 Policy as Code — OPA/Rego & Kyverno Governance ▶
Concept
Guardrails That Enforce Themselves
Instead of a wiki page saying "don't deploy public S3 (Simple Storage Service) buckets," policy-as-code makes the rule executable — checked automatically in CI or blocked at admission. Governance becomes a test that fails, not a review someone forgets.
ToolDetail
OPA / RegoGeneral policy engine; Gatekeeper enforces it on K8s (Kubernetes)
KyvernoK8s-native policy in YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) (no new language to learn)
ConftestRun OPA policies against Terraform/JSON/YAML in CI
Cloud-nativeAWS (Amazon Web Services) SCPs (Service Control Policy), GCP (Google Cloud Platform) Org Policy, Azure Policy
Where to enforce: shift left (CI catches it before merge) and defense in depth (admission control catches it at runtime). Ties directly to the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Benchmarks and cloud-security cards.
🗄️ Artifact & Registry Management Delivery ▶
Reference
Where Build Outputs Live
A pipeline builds artifacts — container images, jars, npm packages — that need a trusted, versioned home between build and deploy. Registries provide storage, access control, scanning, and immutability.
RegistryStores
HarborSelf-hosted container registry + scanning + signing
Artifactory / NexusUniversal (Docker, Maven, npm, PyPI…)
GHCR / ECR (Elastic Container Registry) / Artifact RegistryCloud/platform-native registries
Practices: immutable tags (never re-push :v1.2.3), retention policies to prune old images, scan on push, and promote the same digest through dev→staging→prod rather than rebuilding — build once, promote everywhere.
🕸️ Kubernetes Networking & Storage — CNI & CSI Kubernetes ▶
Reference
How Pods Talk and Where Data Lives
Kubernetes defers networking and storage to pluggable interfaces, so the cluster works the same whether you run on AWS (Amazon Web Services), bare metal, or a laptop. CNI wires up pod networking; CSI attaches persistent storage.
LayerDetail
CNI pluginCalico, Cilium, Flannel — gives every pod an IP (Internet Protocol); enforces NetworkPolicy
Service & kube-proxyStable virtual IP + load-balancing across pod replicas
Ingress controllerNGINX, Traefik — HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) routing & TLS (Transport Layer Security) into the cluster
CSI driverProvisions PersistentVolumes from EBS/PD/etc. via a PVC
StorageClassDefines a tier (ssd, standard) for dynamic provisioning
Cilium (eBPF-based) is increasingly the default — it does networking, NetworkPolicy, and observability in one. Storage: a PVC requests, the StorageClass + CSI driver fulfill it.
🎯 Penetration Testing
PT+
5-Phase Methodology · OWASP Top 10 · Engagement Types 29 topics · ~50 min ▾
🎯 Penetration Testing Phases 5-PHASE METHODOLOGY ▶
Methodology
Planning → Recon → Scan → Exploit → Report
Engagement types: Black Box (no info) · White Box (full info) · Grey Box (partial info). Always requires written authorization (Rules of Engagement / Statement of Work).
Planning & Scoping
Define objectives · Rules of Engagement (RoE) · Target IP (Internet Protocol) ranges & apps · Legal authorization · NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement) · SoW · Emergency contacts · Timeline
Reconnaissance & OSINT (Open Source Intelligence)
Passive: WHOIS, DNS (Domain Name System), Shodan, LinkedIn, cert transparency logs · Active: Nmap, banner grabbing, subdomain enumeration, network mapping
Scanning & Enumeration
Vulnerability scanning · Service versioning · SMB/SNMP/LDAP enumeration · Web app scanning (Burp Suite, Nikto) · Credential spraying · Fuzzing
Exploitation & Post-Exploitation
Exploit vulns (Metasploit, custom PoC) · Priv esc · Lateral movement · Persistence (backdoors, scheduled tasks) · Data exfiltration proof · Pivoting
Reporting & Remediation
Executive summary · Technical findings (CVSS scored) · PoC (Proof of Concept) evidence & screenshots · Remediation guidance · Attestation · Clean-up IOCs (Indicator of Compromise) · Retesting
🌐 OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10 (2021) WEB VULNERABILITIES ▶
Reference
Top 10 Web Application Security Risks
A01
Broken Access Control
Restrictions not enforced; IDOR, privilege escalation, force browsing
A02
Cryptographic Failures
Weak/missing encryption, cleartext sensitive data, deprecated algorithms
A03
Injection
SQL (Structured Query Language), OS (Operating System) command, LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), NoSQL injection — untrusted data to interpreter
A04
Insecure Design
Missing controls at design phase; threat modeling failures, insecure patterns
A05
Security Misconfiguration
Default creds, open storage, verbose errors, unnecessary features enabled
A06
Vulnerable & Outdated Components
Unpatched libraries, frameworks, OS components with known CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures)
A07
ID & Auth Failures
Weak passwords, no MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), session fixation, credential stuffing
A08
Software & Data Integrity Failures
Insecure deserialization, CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) pipeline attacks, unsigned updates
A09
Logging & Monitoring Failures
No alerting on failed logins, logs not protected or centralized, no SIEM (Security Information and Event Management)
A10
Server-Side Request Forgery
Server fetches attacker-controlled URL (Uniform Resource Locator); used to reach internal/cloud metadata
💉 SQLmap — SQL (Structured Query Language) Injection Tool Reference PENTEST TOOL ▶
Reference — Source: SQLmap Cheat Sheet
SQLi Attack Types · Target Options · Detection · Enumeration
SQLmap automates SQL injection detection and exploitation. Runs on Python 2.6, 2.7, and 3. Kali Linux: sqlmap. Other: python3 sqlmap.py. Always use with written authorization.
▸ SQL INJECTION ATTACK CATEGORIES
Category Technique Description
In-Band Error-based DB error messages leak config/structure. Flag: -technique=E
Union-based UNION keyword appends attacker query to legitimate result. Flag: -technique=U
Stacked queries Multiple statements joined by ; — modifies/reads DB in one call. Flag: -technique=S
Inline queries Embedded partial SQL in server-side code. Flag: -technique=Q
Out-of-Band DNS (Domain Name System) exfiltration Results sent via DNS/HTTP to separate channel. Use --dns-domain
Inferential (Blind) Boolean-based Tautologies (1=1) change app behavior to infer data. Flag: -technique=B
Time-based Inject sleep/wait — if delay occurs, DB is vulnerable. Flag: -technique=T
BASIC USAGE PATTERN
# Syntax sqlmap [target] [options] # Step 1: Fingerprint the database sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page.php?id=1" -f --batch # Step 2: List all databases sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page.php?id=1" --dbs --batch # Step 3: List tables in specific database sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page.php?id=1" -D mydb --tables --batch # Step 4: Dump specific table columns sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page.php?id=1" -D mydb -T users --columns --batch # Step 5: Dump all data from table sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page.php?id=1" -D mydb -T users --dump --batch # With session cookie (authenticated scan) sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page?id=1" \ --cookie="PHPSESSID=abc123; security=low" \ --tables --batch
▸ KEY OPTIONS REFERENCE
Flag Purpose
-u URL (Uniform Resource Locator) Target URL containing vulnerable parameter (e.g., ?id=1)
-g DORK Google dork — sqlmap will scan matching results
-r FILE Load HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) request from Burp Suite save file
--batch Never prompt — use default answers (scripting)
--dbs Enumerate all accessible databases
--tables Enumerate tables in target database
--columns Enumerate columns in target table
--dump Dump table data
--passwords Enumerate & attempt to crack user password hashes
-p PARAM Specify parameter to test (e.g., -p "id,user-agent")
--dbms=mysql Force back-end DBMS (Database Management System) (mysql/postgresql/mssql/oracle)
--proxy=URL Route through proxy (Burp: http://127.0.0.1:8080)
--tor Route through Tor anonymity network
--random-agent Use random User-Agent header to evade WAF (Web Application Firewall)
--tamper=SCRIPT Apply tamper script to bypass WAF/IPS
--technique=BEUSTQ SQLi techniques: B=Boolean E=Error U=Union S=Stacked T=Time Q=Inline
▸ --LEVEL AND --RISK SETTINGS
Setting Value Behaviour
--level 1 (default) GET/POST params only — minimal requests
--level 2 Also tests Cookie headers
--level 3 Also tests User-Agent and Referer headers
--level 4–5 Null values, edge case payloads
--risk 1 (default) Safe — data unchanged, DB stays operational
--risk 2 Adds heavy time-based tests — may slow DB
--risk 3 OR-based tests — may UPDATE all table rows
🐞Vulnerability ScanningPenTest+ • Vuln▶
SCANNER
OpenVAS / Greenbone
Greenbone's free, full-featured vulnerability scanner. Runs thousands of Network Vulnerability Tests (NVTs) from a maintained feed and reports findings with CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) scores and remediation. The leading open-source alternative to Nessus.
# Greenbone / OpenVAS (Kali)
gvm-setup            # first-time setup
gvm-start            # web UI on https://127.0.0.1:9392
gvm-check-setup      # verify feeds & services
SCANNER
Nessus & InsightVM
Commercial scanners with deep plugin libraries and compliance audits. Nessus (Tenable) is the industry standard; Nexpose / InsightVM (Rapid7) integrates tightly with Metasploit.
WEB
Web Vulnerability Scanners
Nikto checks web servers for known issues, WPScan targets WordPress, and Nuclei runs fast template-based checks at scale.
# Fast templated web scan
nuclei -u https://target -severity high,critical
nikto -h https://target
wpscan --url https://target --enumerate u,vp
WORKFLOW
Scan → Validate → Prioritize
Scanners surface potential issues but generate false positives. Always validate manually before reporting, and rank by CVSS plus real-world exploitability (EPSS / known-exploited).
ScannerTypeNotes
OpenVAS / GreenboneNetworkOpen-source, NVT feed
NessusNetworkCommercial standard (Tenable)
Nexpose / InsightVMNetworkRapid7, Metasploit link
NiktoWeb serverKnown-issue checks
WPScanWordPressPlugin / theme / user enum
NucleiWeb (templated)YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) templates, very fast

🦈Hak5 GearPenTest+ • Hardware▶

Physical & HID Attacks
Hak5 builds small hardware implants for authorized red-team and physical-security testing. Many impersonate trusted devices (keyboards, USB ethernet) to slip past software controls — so they double as awareness-training props.

USB (Universal Serial Bus) Rubber Ducky & DuckyScript
Looks like a USB drive but registers as a keyboard, typing pre-programmed keystrokes in milliseconds (HID injection). Programmed in the simple DuckyScript language.

Pocket multi-tool for sub-GHz radio, 125 kHz RFID (Radio Frequency Identification), NFC (Near Field Communication), infrared, GPIO, and BadUSB (HID). Popular for physical-access and IoT (Internet of Things) testing in authorized engagements.

🛰️C2 & PivotingPenTest+ • C2▶
C2
Command & Control Frameworks
After a foothold, C2 frameworks manage agents/beacons across compromised hosts — tasking, collection, and lateral movement. Cobalt Strike is the commercial standard; Sliver, Mythic, Havoc, and Empire are common open-source options.
PIVOT
Tunneling & Pivoting
Reach segmented internal networks through a compromised host. Chisel and ligolo-ng build fast tunnels; proxychains plus an SSH (Secure Shell) dynamic forward routes tools through the pivot.
# SSH dynamic SOCKS proxy, then route a scan through it
ssh -D 1080 user@pivot-host
proxychains nmap -sT -Pn 10.10.10.0/24

Reverse Engineering
Pull apart binaries to find flaws. Ghidra (NSA, free) and IDA Pro disassemble and decompile; Radare2 / Cutter and GDB+pwndbg aid dynamic analysis; pwntools scripts exploit development.

Cloud Pentest
Assess misconfigured cloud. Pacu attacks AWS (Amazon Web Services); ScoutSuite and Prowler audit AWS/Azure/GCP posture; CloudFox maps attack surface.

Fuzzing
Throw malformed input to crash or break targets. AFL++ fuzzes binaries, while ffuf and wfuzz fuzz web endpoints and parameters.

🎯Methodology & PhasesPenTest+ • PT0-002▶
ENGAGEMENT
Scoping & Authorization
Define targets, exclusions, timing, and a signed authorization (get-out-of-jail letter) before touching anything. Capture constraints, points of contact, and a deconfliction process for accidental impact.
GOVERNANCE
Rules of Engagement (RoE)
The contract for behavior: allowed techniques, working hours, data-handling rules, and escalation paths. No RoE = no test.
TYPES
Test & Team Styles
Black-box (no knowledge), gray-box (partial), white-box (full). External vs. internal vantage. Red (attack), blue (defend), purple (collaborate).

PASSIVE
No-Touch Intel
Collect data without contacting the target: WHOIS, DNS (Domain Name System) records, breach dumps, social media, job posts, and Google dorking. Zero footprint on the target.
ACTIVE
Direct Probing

whois example.com

theHarvester -d example.com -b all

📡Scanning & EnumerationPenTest+ • Discovery▶
HOST/PORT
Nmap Essentials
The workhorse: discover hosts, open ports, service versions, and OS (Operating System), then run NSE scripts for deeper enumeration.
# SYN scan + version + default scripts + OS, all ports
nmap -sS -sV -sC -O -p- -T4 10.0.0.5
# Targeted UDP + NSE vuln scripts
nmap -sU -p 53,161 --script vuln 10.0.0.5
ENUM
Service Enumeration
Pull users, shares, and config from exposed services: SMB (Server Message Block) (enum4linux, smbclient), SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) (snmpwalk), LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), and NFS (Network File System) showmount.
Nmap FlagMeaning

🧒Ethical Hacking 101PenTest+ • Start Here▶
BIG IDEA
What Is a Penetration Test?
A pentest is hiring someone to break into your systems on purpose — with permission — to find the holes before a real attacker does. Think of a hotel paying a locksmith to test every lock and report which ones are weak.
THE LINE
Permission Is Everything
The only difference between a penetration tester and a criminal is written authorization and scope. Same tools, same techniques — but one has a signed 'get-out-of-jail' agreement saying exactly what they're allowed to touch.
STYLES
Black / Gray / White Box
Black-box = the tester knows nothing (like a real outsider). White-box = they get full details and source (a thorough inside review). Gray-box is in between. More knowledge = deeper testing in less time.
MINDSET
Think Like an Attacker
Hacking is mostly curiosity plus stubbornness: 'What happens if I do the unexpected?' Testers chain small, boring weaknesses into one big problem — which is exactly why defenders should fix the 'small' stuff.
PhaseIn Plain English
ReconQuietly learn everything public about the target
ScanningKnock on doors to see what's open
ExploitationUse a weakness to get in
Post-exploitSee how far you can reach once inside
ReportingWrite up findings + how to fix them — the real product
🧾Scoping & Rules of EngagementPenTest+ • Start Here▶
WHY PAPERWORK
The Boring Part Keeps You Out of Jail
Before any hacking, both sides sign what’s allowed. This isn’t bureaucracy for its own sake — it’s the difference between a paid professional and a felony. Scope and authorization are the seatbelt of the job.
SCOPE
What’s In, What’s Off-Limits
Scope lists exactly which systems, addresses, and techniques are fair game — and which are absolutely not (production payroll, third-party clouds, physical break-ins). When in doubt, it’s out of scope.
SAFETY
Deconfliction & the ‘Get-Out-of-Jail’ Letter
Testers carry written authorization in case security catches them (good — that means detection works!). A deconfliction contact lets everyone quickly tell ‘is this the tester, or a real attacker?’ during the engagement.
RoE ItemWhy It’s There
AuthorizationWritten proof you’re allowed
Scope / exclusionsExactly what you may and may not touch
Time windowsWhen testing is permitted
Data handlingHow findings & sensitive data are protected
Emergency contactWho to call if something goes wrong
🔓 Getting Started in Ethical Hacking — The Right Way PENTEST • Start Here ▶
LEGAL FOUNDATION
Authorization Is Everything
Hacking without permission is a federal crime in the US (CFAA) and illegal worldwide. Authorization must be explicit, in writing, before you touch anything. "It was just a test" is not a defense. Ethical hacking means having a signed contract, defined scope, and legal protection before you start.
THE LEARNER'S PATH
Legal Practice Environments
Your own lab: VMs on your laptop (VirtualBox + Kali Linux + vulnerable VMs like Metasploitable, DVWA). 100% legal, full control.
Hack The Box (HTB): paid platform with realistic machines to compromise. Legal by design.
TryHackMe: beginner-friendly guided rooms with hand-holding. Best starting point.
PicoCTF, CTFtime: Capture The Flag competitions. Legal challenges with prizes.
OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) WebGoat: intentionally vulnerable web app for learning web attacks.
FOUNDATION KNOWLEDGE
What to Learn Before "Hacking"
The best hackers are really strong defenders first. Build this foundation:
1. Networking fundamentals (TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, firewalls)
2. Linux command line (file system, permissions, processes, scripting)
3. Programming basics (Python especially — automate, parse, build tools)
4. Web technology (HTML, HTTP methods, cookies, sessions, same-origin policy)
5. OS (Operating System) security concepts (users, privilege, authentication)
6. Cryptography basics (hashing, symmetric, asymmetric)
Then take CompTIA (Computing Technology Industry Association) Security+ → CEH/OSCP path.
CERTIFICATIONS
Industry-Recognized Pentest Certs
CertLevelStyleFocus
CompTIA Security+BeginnerMultiple choiceBroad security concepts
CompTIA PenTest+IntermediateMC + performancePentest methodology
CEH (Certified Ethical Hacker) (EC-Council)IntermediateMultiple choiceTools and techniques (theory-heavy)
OSCP (Offensive Security Certified Professional) (OffSec)Advanced24-hr practical examHands-on exploitation; gold standard
GPEN (GIAC)AdvancedMC + practicalNetwork pentesting
KALI LINUX
The Pentest Distro
Kali Linux (by Offensive Security) is a Debian-based distro pre-loaded with hundreds of security tools: Nmap, Metasploit, Burp Suite, Wireshark, Aircrack-ng, John the Ripper, Hashcat, and more. Don't use Kali as your daily driver — it runs as root by default and is designed for testing, not everyday use. Run it in a VM or bootable USB (Universal Serial Bus) for lab work.
🔍 Basic Recon & Enumeration — Know Your Target PENTEST • Foundation ▶
PASSIVE vs ACTIVE RECON
Invisible vs Detectable
Passive recon — gather information WITHOUT touching the target. No packets sent to their systems. Examples: WHOIS, DNS (Domain Name System) lookups, Google dorking, LinkedIn, Shodan, certificate transparency logs. Hard to detect.
Active recon — directly query the target's systems. Port scans, banner grabbing, web crawling. Generates logs on their end. Only legal with authorization.
NMAP BASICS
The Port Scanner Every Tester Uses
# Quick scan — top 1000 ports nmap 192.168.1.1 # SYN scan (stealthier, requires root) sudo nmap -sS 192.168.1.1 # Service/version detection nmap -sV 192.168.1.1 # OS fingerprinting sudo nmap -O 192.168.1.1 # Full scan: all ports + service + OS + scripts sudo nmap -A -p- 192.168.1.1 # Scan a range nmap 192.168.1.0/24 # Output to file nmap -oA scan_results 192.168.1.1
OSINT TOOLS
Open-Source Intelligence
Shodan — search engine for internet-connected devices. Find exposed cameras, industrial control systems, unpatched servers.
theHarvester — collect emails, subdomains, hosts from public sources.
Maltego — visual relationship mapping (person → email → domain → IP → org).
Google Dorks — advanced Google search operators to find sensitive files: site:example.com filetype:pdf "confidential"
crt.sh — certificate transparency logs; find all subdomains of a domain.
🕸️ Web Application Pentesting — Hacking the Web Safely PENTEST • Methodology ▶
WEB APP ATTACK SURFACE
Where Web Vulnerabilities Live
Web applications are the most attacked surface in modern environments. Unlike network pentesting (ports and protocols), web app testing focuses on application logic, input handling, and authentication. The good news: most web vulnerabilities are predictable and well-documented (OWASP). The bad news: developers keep repeating the same mistakes.
LayerWhat to TestCommon Findings
AuthenticationLogin, password reset, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) bypassWeak passwords, enumeration, broken token reset
AuthorizationHorizontal/vertical privilege escalationIDOR — access other users' data by changing IDs
Input HandlingForms, query params, headers, file uploadsSQLi, XSS (Cross-Site Scripting), XXE (XML External Entity), command injection
Session ManagementCookies, tokens, session fixationPredictable tokens, missing Secure/HttpOnly flags
Business LogicPurchase flows, transfers, state machinesNegative quantities, price manipulation, race conditions
API (Application Programming Interface) EndpointsREST/GraphQL endpointsMissing auth, verbose errors, mass assignment
BURP SUITE BASICS
The Swiss Army Knife for Web Testing
Burp Suite is the industry-standard web proxy for intercepting, modifying, and replaying HTTP/HTTPS traffic. The Community edition is free and powerful enough for most learning. Professional adds the scanner.
ToolPurposeBeginner Use
Proxy → InterceptPause and inspect every requestSee what the browser actually sends
Proxy → HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) HistoryLog of all requests madeFind interesting endpoints and parameters
RepeaterResend and modify individual requestsTest input handling by changing values manually
IntruderAutomated fuzzing with payload listsPassword spraying, parameter enumeration
DecoderEncode/decode base64, URL (Uniform Resource Locator), HTML (HyperText Markup Language), hexDecode tokens and encoded parameters
Scanner (Pro)Automated vulnerability scanningPassive and active scanning
IDOR DEEP DIVE
Insecure Direct Object Reference — The #1 Finding
IDOR (now categorized under Broken Access Control, OWASP A01) occurs when an application uses user-controllable references to access objects without verifying the user is authorized. It's the most common web vulnerability by volume.
# Vulnerable pattern — user ID directly in URL GET /api/users/1234/profile # your profile GET /api/users/1235/profile # someone else's — do you get it? # Vulnerable pattern — order ID in parameter GET /orders?id=8821 # your order GET /orders?id=8820 # try decrementing — another user's order? # Where to look - Numeric IDs in URLs, query params, request bodies - GUIDs (sometimes predictable if v1 — time-based) - Encoded values — decode them first (base64, hex) - Hidden form fields with IDs # How to test 1. Create two test accounts (Alice and Bob) 2. As Alice, perform action that creates a resource → note the ID 3. Log in as Bob, try to access the same resource ID 4. If Bob can access Alice's resource = IDOR
COMMAND INJECTION
When the App Runs Your Input as Shell Commands
Command injection occurs when user input is passed to a system shell without sanitization. If you can get your input executed as OS (Operating System) commands, you typically own the server. Critical severity — always.
# Common in features that: ping IPs, resolve DNS, process files, # run nmap, send email via sendmail, resize images via ImageMagick # Basic test payloads — try in any input field ; id # semicolon chains commands && id # run if first cmd succeeds || id # run if first cmd fails `id` # backtick subshell $(id) # $() subshell (URL: %24%28id%29) | id # pipe output # If you see "uid=33(www-data)" in the response — confirmed! # Blind injection — no output visible, infer via timing ; sleep 5 # if response delays 5s — blind injection exists

WHOISDomain ownership, registrar, dateswhois target.com
