0 0 1 * *   /opt/scripts/monthly_report.sh

# View your current scheduled jobs
crontab -l

# Edit them (opens your default editor)
crontab -e

Many modern Linux systems also offer systemd timers as an alternative — they integrate with journalctl for logging, can express dependencies on other services, and handle "what if the system was off when this should have run?" more gracefully. Cron remains common and perfectly fine for simple jobs; timers shine once your scheduling needs get more sophisticated.

Concept

Idempotency: the property that turns "uh oh" into "no big deal"

A script is idempotent if running it multiple times produces the same end result as running it once. This single property is what determines whether "the job accidentally ran twice" is a non-event or an incident.

# NOT idempotent — running this twice creates two records,
# sends two emails, charges a customer twice...
def process_daily_signups():
    new_users = get_signups_since_last_run()
    for user in new_users:
        send_welcome_email(user)
        create_billing_record(user)

# IDEMPOTENT — checks what's already been done before doing it again
def process_daily_signups():
    new_users = get_signups_since_last_run()
    for user in new_users:
        if not already_sent_welcome_email(user):
            send_welcome_email(user)
            mark_welcome_email_sent(user)
        if not has_billing_record(user):
            create_billing_record(user)

Notice the pattern: instead of just "do the thing," idempotent code asks "has this already been done?" first. That one habit — checking before acting, every time — is what separates scheduled automation you can trust from scheduled automation that occasionally needs a 3 AM apology email to customers.

Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me — assume it WILL run twice someday

"It only runs once a day, what are the odds it overlaps with itself?" is exactly the kind of assumption that holds up fine for months — until a slow database connection causes one run to take 25 hours, and suddenly two copies are running at once, both modifying the same data. Writing scheduled scripts as though they will eventually run concurrently or get interrupted mid-task — using locks, idempotency checks, and transactional updates — costs a little extra effort upfront and saves an enormous amount of cleanup later.

🐍 Python — The Everything Language Language ▶
Reference
Why Python Runs the World
Python is the default language of automation, data science, AI/ML, scripting, and glue code. It is dynamically typed, interpreted, and reads almost like English — indentation is the syntax, so there are no braces. If you learn one language for IT and security work, make it this one: nearly every tool (Ansible, scapy, requests, pandas, PyTorch) has a Python interface.
Syntax
Core Syntax & Data Types
THE ESSENTIALS
# Variables — no type declarations, just assign
name = "Alice"        # str
age = 30             # int
pi = 3.14159        # float
active = True         # bool
items = None          # the "no value" sentinel

# f-strings — the modern way to build text
print(f"{name} is {age}")   # Alice is 30

# The four core containers
nums  = [1, 2, 3]              # list  — ordered, mutable
point = (4, 5)                 # tuple — ordered, immutable
seen  = {1, 2, 3}              # set   — unique, unordered
user  = {"id": 1, "role": "admin"}  # dict  — key/value
Syntax
Control Flow, Functions & Comprehensions
LOGIC & REUSE
# Indentation defines blocks — 4 spaces, no braces
for n in nums:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        print(f"{n} is even")
    else:
        print(f"{n} is odd")

# Functions — default args, type hints (optional but recommended)
def greet(name: str, excited: bool = False) -> str:
    msg = f"Hello, {name}"
    return msg + ("!" if excited else ".")

# Comprehensions — Python's signature one-liners
squares = [n*n for n in range(10)]           # [0,1,4,9,...]
evens   = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
lookup  = {u["id"]: u for u in users}          # dict comprehension
Practical
Files, Errors & a Real Script
A SCRIPT YOU'D ACTUALLY WRITE
import json
from pathlib import Path

# Context manager — file is closed automatically, even on error
with open("servers.json") as f:
    servers = json.load(f)

for host in servers:
    try:
        status = check(host["ip"])
    except ConnectionError as e:
        print(f"{host['name']} unreachable: {e}")
        continue
    print(f"{host['name']}: {status}")

# Guard so the file can be imported without running main()
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Toolchain
Environments, pip & the Standard Library
Command / ModuleWhat It Does
python3 -m venv .venvCreate an isolated virtual environment
source .venv/bin/activateActivate it (deactivate with deactivate)
pip install requestsInstall a package from PyPI into the venv
pip freeze > requirements.txtPin exact versions for reproducible installs
python3 -m pytestRun tests (the standard testing tool)
requestsHTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) for humans — API (Application Programming Interface) calls in 2 lines
json / csvParse and write structured data
pathlibModern, OS-agnostic file paths
subprocessRun shell commands and capture output
argparseBuild proper command-line interfaces
Gotchas
Traps That Bite Beginners
TrapWhy & The Fix
Mutable default argsdef f(x=[]) reuses the same list across calls. Use x=None then x = x or [].
Copying referencesb = a on a list points at the same object. Use a.copy() or list(a).
Integer vs float division/ always gives a float; use // for integer (floor) division.
Indentation mixingNever mix tabs and spaces — Python rejects it. Configure your editor to 4 spaces.
Bare except:Swallows every error including Ctrl-C. Catch specific exceptions instead.
🟦 TypeScript — JavaScript That Scales Language ▶
Concept
Why Add Types to JavaScript
TypeScript is JavaScript with a static type system bolted on. You write types; a compiler (tsc) checks them and then erases them, emitting plain JavaScript that runs anywhere JS runs. The payoff: bugs caught in your editor instead of in production, autocomplete that actually knows your data, and code that documents itself. It has become the default for any JS codebase past "small script" size — React, Node, Deno, and Angular all lean on it.
Syntax
Types, Interfaces & Functions
THE ESSENTIALS
// Primitive annotations — usually inferred, write them at boundaries
let name: string = "Alice";
let age: number = 30;
let tags: string[] = ["admin", "beta"];

// Object shapes — interface (extendable) or type alias
interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email?: string;        // ? = optional
  readonly createdAt: Date;  // can't reassign
}

// Union types — "one of these"
type Status = "active" | "suspended" | "deleted";

// Typed function — params and return
function greet(user: User): string {
  return `Hello, ${user.name}`;
}
Power Tools
Generics, Narrowing & Utility Types
WHERE TYPESCRIPT EARNS ITS KEEP
// Generics — reusable code that keeps its types
function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined {
  return arr[0];
}
const n = first([1, 2, 3]);   // n is number | undefined

// Narrowing — the compiler tracks what a value must be
function len(x: string | string[]): number {
  if (typeof x === "string") return x.length;  // x: string here
  return x.length;                              // x: string[] here
}

// Utility types — transform existing types instead of retyping
type PartialUser = Partial<User>;   // all fields optional
type UserId     = Pick<User, "id">;   // just { id }
type Public     = Omit<User, "email">; // everything but email
Reference
Key Types & Toolchain
▸ TYPES YOU'LL REACH FOR
TypeMeaning
unknownType-safe any — must narrow before use. Prefer over any.
anyOpt out of checking. A code smell — every any is a hole in your safety net.
neverA value that can't exist (exhaustive switches, functions that always throw).
voidFunction returns nothing meaningful.
T | nullExplicit nullability — strictNullChecks forces you to handle it.
as constFreeze a literal to its narrowest type (great for config objects).
▸ TOOLCHAIN
Command / FileWhat It Does
tscThe TypeScript compiler — type-checks and emits JS
tsc --noEmitType-check only (let a bundler handle JS output)
tsconfig.jsonProject config — set "strict": true and never look back
tsx / ts-nodeRun a .ts file directly without a separate build
@types/*Community type definitions for untyped npm packages
Best Practices
Getting the Most From the Type System
DoWhy
Turn on strictEnables null checks, implicit-any errors, and the checks that catch real bugs.
Let inference workDon't annotate what the compiler already knows; type the boundaries (params, exports, API shapes).
Model states as unions"loading" | "error" | "ready" makes impossible states unrepresentable.
Avoid anyIt silently disables checking for everything it touches. Reach for unknown + narrowing.
Types ≠ runtime validationTypes vanish at runtime — validate external data (API/JSON) with a library like Zod.
◈ GraphQL — Ask For Exactly What You Need API ▶
Concept
One Endpoint, Precise Queries
GraphQL is a query language for APIs (Application Programming Interface). Instead of many REST (Representational State Transfer) endpoints each returning a fixed shape, a GraphQL API exposes one endpoint and a typed schema; the client sends a query describing exactly the fields it wants, and gets back JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) in that exact shape — no more, no less. It solves REST's two classic pains: over-fetching (getting fields you don't need) and under-fetching (making 3 calls to assemble one screen).
Example
A Query and Its Response
CLIENT ASKS FOR SPECIFIC FIELDS
# Query — one round trip pulls a user AND their recent posts
query GetUser($id: ID!) {
  user(id: $id) {
    name
    email
    posts(last: 3) {
      title
      publishedAt
    }
  }
}
SERVER RETURNS THAT EXACT SHAPE
{
  "data": {
    "user": {
      "name": "Alice",
      "email": "alice@example.com",
      "posts": [
        { "title": "Intro to GraphQL", "publishedAt": "2026-01-04" }
      ]
    }
  }
}
Reference
The Three Operation Types & the Schema
▸ OPERATIONS
OperationPurposeREST Analogy
queryRead data (no side effects)GET
mutationCreate / update / deletePOST / PUT / DELETE
subscriptionReal-time stream of updates (usually over WebSocket)Webhook / SSE (Server-Sent Events)
▸ SCHEMA DEFINITION (SDL)
type User {
  id: ID!          # ! = non-nullable
  name: String!
  posts: [Post!]!  # non-null list of non-null Posts
}
type Query {
  user(id: ID!): User
}
Trade-offs
GraphQL vs REST — When to Use Which
DimensionRESTGraphQL
FetchingFixed shapes; may over/under-fetchClient picks exact fields
EndpointsMany (one per resource)One
CachingEasy — HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) caches by URL (Uniform Resource Locator)Harder — one URL, needs client-side cache
VersioningOften /v2/ URLsEvolve the schema; deprecate fields
Learning curveLowHigher (schema, resolvers, tooling)
RiskN+1 across endpointsN+1 in resolvers; deep/expensive queries need limits
Rule of thumb: REST shines for simple, cacheable, resource-shaped APIs. GraphQL shines when many clients need many different slices of a richly-connected data graph (think a mobile app and a web app hitting the same backend).
🗄️ Databases — Relational vs NoSQL, ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) & Indexing Data ▶
Concept
Two Families of Database
A relational (SQL) database stores data in tables with a fixed schema and enforces relationships between them — PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL (Structured Query Language) Server. A NoSQL database trades some of that rigor for flexibility and horizontal scale, and comes in several shapes. The real question isn't "which is better" — it's what shape is your data, and what guarantees do you need?
Reference
NoSQL Families
TypeStoresExamplesGood For
DocumentJSON-like documentsMongoDB, CouchbaseFlexible, nested records
Key-ValueSimple key → valueRedis, DynamoDBCaching, sessions, speed
Wide-ColumnRows with dynamic columnsCassandra, HBaseHuge write volume, time-series
GraphNodes & edgesNeo4j, NeptuneRelationships (social, fraud)
Guarantees
ACID — The Transaction Contract
A transaction groups multiple operations so they succeed or fail together. ACID is the promise relational databases make about them:
LetterGuarantee
AtomicityAll operations commit, or none do. No half-finished transfers.
ConsistencyEvery transaction moves the DB from one valid state to another (constraints hold).
IsolationConcurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work.
DurabilityOnce committed, data survives a crash or power loss.
Many NoSQL systems relax these for scale, offering BASE instead (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) — writes propagate over time rather than instantly.
Performance
Indexing — Why the Right Index Is 1000× Faster
Without an index, finding a row means a full table scan — reading every row. An index is a sorted lookup structure (usually a B-tree) that turns that into a fast search, the way a book's index beats flipping every page. The trade: indexes speed up reads but slow down writes (every insert updates the index) and use disk.
CREATE AN INDEX & CHECK IT'S USED
-- Slow: full scan of a big table
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- Add an index on the filtered column
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);

-- EXPLAIN shows the planner's strategy — look for "Index Scan"
-- instead of "Seq Scan" (Postgres) after adding the index
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
▸ INDEXING RULES OF THUMB
DoWhy
Index columns you filter/join/sort onThat's where scans hurt
Use a composite index for multi-column filtersOne index can serve WHERE a=? AND b=?
Don't index everythingEach index taxes every write and eats storage
Read the query planEXPLAIN tells you what the DB actually does — measure, don't guess
Design
Normalization vs Denormalization
ApproachWhatTrade-off
NormalizeSplit data so each fact lives in exactly one place (no duplication)Clean writes, no update anomalies — but more joins on read
DenormalizeDuplicate data to avoid joinsFaster reads — but you must keep copies in sync
Relational databases start normalized; you denormalize deliberately for read performance. Document databases often start denormalized (embed related data) and trade write-side duplication for single-read fetches.
🔴 WebSockets & SSE (Server-Sent Events) — Real-Time on the Web Web ▶
Concept
Push, Don't Poll
Plain HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is request/response: the client asks, the server answers, the connection closes. That's terrible for live data — chat, notifications, dashboards, multiplayer — where the server needs to speak first. The old workaround was polling (ask "any news?" every few seconds — wasteful and laggy). WebSockets and Server-Sent Events keep a connection open so the server can push the instant something happens.
Reference
Three Ways to Get Live Data
TechniqueDirectionBest For
PollingClient pulls repeatedlySimple, infrequent updates; last resort
SSE (EventSource)Server → client, one-wayFeeds, notifications, live logs, progress
WebSocketFull-duplex, both waysChat, games, collaborative editing, trading
Reach for SSE when only the server needs to push (it's just HTTP, auto-reconnects, and is dead simple). Reach for WebSockets when the client must send too, in real time.
Example
WebSocket & SSE Clients
WEBSOCKET — TWO-WAY
const ws = new WebSocket("wss://example.com/chat");

ws.onopen  = () => ws.send(JSON.stringify({ join: "room-7" }));
ws.onmessage = (e) => render(JSON.parse(e.data));
ws.onclose = () => scheduleReconnect();   // you handle reconnect
SSE — SERVER-TO-CLIENT (AUTO-RECONNECTS)
const es = new EventSource("/api/updates");
es.onmessage = (e) => append(e.data);
es.addEventListener("price", (e) => updateTicker(e.data));
Practical
Gotchas in Production
IssueWhat To Know
Use wss://The encrypted (TLS) scheme — like HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) for sockets. Never ship plain ws://.
ReconnectionWebSockets don't auto-reconnect — implement backoff. SSE reconnects for you and can resume via Last-Event-ID.
HeartbeatsSend periodic pings so proxies/load balancers don't kill an idle connection.
ScalingOpen connections are stateful — many servers need a shared pub/sub layer (e.g. Redis) to broadcast across nodes.
AuthBrowsers can't set custom headers on a WebSocket handshake — pass a token via a cookie or a short-lived ticket in the URL (Uniform Resource Locator).
🧩 API (Application Programming Interface) Design — Versioning, Pagination, Rate Limits & Idempotency Web ▶
Concept
The Contract Others Build On
Once people depend on your API, its shape is a promise. Good API design is mostly about the boring-but-critical concerns that keep that promise as the API grows: not breaking existing clients, returning large result sets safely, protecting the service from abuse, and behaving predictably when the network retries. Get these four right and the rest is detail.
Reference
Versioning — Don't Break Existing Clients
StrategyExampleNotes
URL (Uniform Resource Locator) path/v2/usersMost common, visible, easy to route
HeaderAccept: application/vnd.api+json;v=2Cleaner URLs; harder to test by hand
Query param?version=2Simple but easy to forget
Rule: an additive change (new optional field) is backward-compatible and needs no new version. Removing/renaming a field or changing its type is breaking — that's when you bump the version and keep the old one running during a deprecation window.
Reference
Pagination & Rate Limiting
▸ PAGINATION — NEVER RETURN "ALL"
StyleHowTrade-off
Offset/limit?offset=40&limit=20Simple; slow & wobbly on big/changing data
Cursor/keyset?after=<id>&limit=20Fast & stable at scale; can't jump to page N
▸ RATE LIMITING — RESPONSE HEADERS
# Server tells the client its budget
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
Retry-After: 30          # wait 30s before retrying
Return 429 when a client exceeds its budget; a well-behaved client backs off using Retry-After. Common algorithms: token bucket (allows bursts) and sliding window (smooth).
Reliability
Idempotency — Safe Retries
Networks drop responses. If a client retries a payment because it never got the reply, you must not charge twice. An idempotency key — a unique ID the client sends with the request — lets the server recognize a duplicate and return the original result instead of doing the work again. 
POST /charges
Idempotency-Key: a1b2c3-unique-per-attempt

# First call: process, store result under the key.
# Retry with the SAME key: return the stored result, don't re-charge.
▸ WHICH HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) METHODS ARE ALREADY IDEMPOTENT?
MethodIdempotent?
GET, PUT, DELETEYes — same call, same end state
POSTNo — needs an idempotency key to be safe to retry
⚙️ gRPC & Protocol Buffers — High-Performance RPC (Remote Procedure Call) API ▶
Concept
Calling a Remote Function Like a Local One
gRPC is a framework for Remote Procedure Calls — you call a method on another service as if it were a local function, and gRPC handles the networking. It runs over HTTP/2 (HyperText Transfer Protocol version 2) and serializes data with Protocol Buffers (protobuf): a compact binary format defined by a schema. The result is dramatically smaller and faster than JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) over REST (Representational State Transfer) — which is why it's the default for internal microservice-to-microservice communication.
Example
Define Once in a .proto File
user.proto — THE CONTRACT
syntax = "proto3";

// A message = a typed record; numbers are field tags (wire IDs)
message UserRequest {
  int32 id = 1;
}
message User {
  int32  id    = 1;
  string name  = 2;
  string email = 3;
}

// A service = the callable methods
service UserService {
  rpc GetUser(UserRequest) returns (User);
}
A compiler (protoc) turns this into typed client + server code in your language — both sides share one source of truth, so a mismatched field is a compile error, not a 3 a.m. surprise.
Reference
Four Call Styles
TypeShapeUse
Unary1 request → 1 responseOrdinary calls
Server streaming1 request → stream of responsesLive feeds, large results
Client streamingStream of requests → 1 responseUploads, telemetry
BidirectionalBoth stream at onceChat, real-time sync
Streaming comes free from HTTP/2's multiplexing — a big reason gRPC picked it as the transport.
Trade-offs
gRPC vs REST — Pick the Right Tool
gRPCREST/JSON
PayloadCompact binaryHuman-readable text
SpeedFaster (binary + HTTP/2)Slower
ContractStrong (.proto schema)Looser (OpenAPI optional)
Browser supportNeeds a proxy (gRPC-Web)Native everywhere
Debug by handHard (binary)Easy (curl)
Best forInternal microservicesPublic/browser APIs (Application Programming Interface)
📊 OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) vs OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) — Transactional vs Analytical Data Data ▶
Concept
Two Jobs, Two Very Different Databases
Databases do two fundamentally different kinds of work. OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) runs the live application — many small, fast reads and writes: place an order, update a profile. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) answers big questions over history: "revenue by region by quarter for three years." Trying to run heavy analytics on your production OLTP database is a classic mistake — the giant scan slows down every customer's checkout.
Comparison
OLTP vs OLAP Side by Side
OLTPOLAP
PurposeRun the applicationAnalyze & report
QueriesMany small reads/writesFew huge aggregations
TouchesA few rows by keyMillions of rows, few columns
Optimized forFast writes, low latencyFast scans & aggregates
DataCurrent, detailedHistorical, often aggregated
ExamplesPostgres, MySQLBigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift
Why
Row Stores vs Column Stores
The performance gap comes down to physical layout. OLTP databases are row-oriented — a whole record sits together, so reading or writing one order is one fast seek. OLAP databases are column-oriented — each column is stored together, so summing one column over millions of rows reads only that column (and compresses beautifully, since a column holds similar values).
Row storeColumn store
Great atFetch/modify whole recordsAggregate a few columns over many rows
CompressionModestExcellent (like values together)
In Practice
You Use Both — Connected by a Pipeline
A typical stack keeps them separate: the app writes to an OLTP database, and a data pipeline (ETL/ELT) periodically copies and reshapes that data into an OLAP warehouse for analysts and dashboards. This isolates the two workloads so analytics never slows the live app, and lets each database be tuned for its job. (A newer category, HTAP, tries to serve both from one system — handy, but the separated pattern still dominates.)
🧱 WebAssembly (WASM) — Near-Native Speed in the Browser Web ▶
Concept
A Fast, Portable Compile Target for the Web
JavaScript is the only language browsers natively run — but it's not ideal for CPU-heavy work like video editing, games, or CAD. WebAssembly is a compact binary instruction format that runs at near-native speed in the browser. You write in C, C++, Rust, or Go, compile to a .wasm module, and it executes in the same secure sandbox as JS — often 10–100× faster for number-crunching. It doesn't replace JavaScript; it runs alongside it for the heavy lifting.
Reference
Why It's Fast & Safe
PropertyDetail
Binary formatCompact to download and quick to parse/compile vs parsing text JS.
Predictable performanceStatically typed, ahead-of-time-friendly — no JIT (Just-In-Time) warm-up guessing.
SandboxedRuns in the same memory-safe browser sandbox as JS — can't touch the system directly.
Language-agnosticAny language with a WASM backend compiles to it (Rust, C/C++, Go, C#…).
How It Works
JS Loads and Calls It
// JS instantiates the module and calls exported functions
const { instance } = await WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming(
  fetch("image-filter.wasm")
);
const result = instance.exports.applyBlur(ptr, len);
JS and WASM share memory via a typed ArrayBuffer. Modern toolchains (Emscripten for C/C++, wasm-pack for Rust) generate the glue so you mostly call WASM like a normal library.
Reference
Where It Shines — and WASI Beyond the Browser
Use caseExample
Compute-heavy appsFigma, Photoshop web, video/audio editing, 3D/CAD, games
Port existing codeBring a mature C/C++ library to the web unchanged (ffmpeg, SQLite)
Server / edgeVia WASI, WASM runs outside the browser — fast-starting, sandboxed serverless & plugins
Not for everything: WASM can't directly touch the DOM (Document Object Model) (it calls back into JS for that), and simple UI (User Interface) logic is still easier in plain JavaScript. Reach for it when performance is the bottleneck.
📱 Progressive Web Apps (PWA) — Web Apps That Feel Native Web ▶
Concept
One Codebase, App-Like Experience
A Progressive Web App is a website that uses modern browser capabilities to behave like an installed app — it can be added to the home screen, work offline, load instantly, and send push notifications — all from a single web codebase, no app store required. "Progressive" means it works as a normal site everywhere and enhances where the browser supports more. It's the middle ground between a website and a native app.
Reference
The Three Core Ingredients
PieceWhat It Provides
Service WorkerA script that runs in the background between the page and network — enables offline, caching, and push. The heart of a PWA.
Web App ManifestA JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) file describing the app (name, icons, colors, display mode) so it can be installed to the home screen.
HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure)Required — service workers only run over secure connections (they're powerful, so they must be trusted).
Key Idea
The Service Worker — Offline & Caching
A service worker sits between your app and the network as a programmable proxy. It can intercept every request and decide: serve from cache, fetch from network, or both. That's what makes a PWA load instantly and keep working with no connection. 
// Cache-first: serve from cache, fall back to network
self.addEventListener("fetch", (e) => {
  e.respondWith(
    caches.match(e.request)
      .then((hit) => hit ?? fetch(e.request))
  );
});
Common strategies: cache-first (assets), network-first (fresh data), and stale-while-revalidate (fast + eventually fresh).
Trade-offs
PWA vs Native
PWANative app
CodebaseOne (web)Per platform
InstallFrom a URL (Uniform Resource Locator), no storeApp store
Device APIs (Application Programming Interface)Growing, but limitedFull access
UpdatesInstant (it's a website)Store review + user update
iOS supportPartial (some APIs gated)Full
Great for content, commerce, and productivity apps where reach and instant updates matter; native still wins for deep hardware access and demanding games.
♿ Web Accessibility (a11y) — Building for Everyone Web ▶
Concept
The Web Should Work for Every User
Accessibility (abbreviated a11y — "a", 11 letters, "y") means building sites people can use regardless of ability: someone navigating by keyboard, hearing a screen reader, zooming to 400%, or avoiding motion. It's not a niche — it overlaps with good UX (User Experience) for everyone (captions help in loud rooms; keyboard support helps power users), it's often a legal requirement (ADA, EU EN 301 549), and the standard to aim for is WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) at level AA.
Framework
POUR — The Four Principles
PrincipleMeans
PerceivableUsers can sense the content — alt text on images, captions on video, sufficient color contrast.
OperableEverything works by keyboard, not just mouse; enough time; no seizure-inducing flashing.
UnderstandableClear language, predictable navigation, helpful error messages.
RobustWorks across browsers and assistive tech — valid, semantic HTML (HyperText Markup Language).
Practical
The Highest-Impact Habits
DoWhy
Use semantic HTMLA real <button> is focusable, clickable, and announced correctly for free. A <div onclick> is none of those.
Alt text on imagesDescribe meaningful images; use empty alt="" for decorative ones so screen readers skip them.
Label every inputA <label> tied to its field tells users what to type.
Keyboard + visible focusTab through the whole page; never remove the focus outline without replacing it.
Color contrast ≥ 4.5:1Body text must stand out from its background (WCAG AA).
Respect reduced motionHonor prefers-reduced-motion for users who get motion sickness.
Reference
ARIA — Use Sparingly
ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) adds roles and states (role, aria-label, aria-expanded) so screen readers understand custom widgets. But the first rule of ARIA is: don't use ARIA if native HTML can do it — a real <nav>/<button>/<input> beats a div patched with attributes. Bad ARIA is worse than none.
TestingHow
Automatedaxe, Lighthouse, WAVE — catch ~30–40% of issues fast.
ManualUnplug the mouse and navigate; turn on a screen reader (VoiceOver, NVDA). No tool replaces this.
🦀 Rust — Safe Systems Programming Language ▶
Reference
Memory Safety Without a Garbage Collector
Rust's ownership and borrow checker guarantee memory safety at compile time — no GC, no use-after-free, no data races. That's why it's winning in systems, WASM (WebAssembly), CLI (Command Line Interface) tools, and increasingly the Linux kernel. 
fn main() {
    let mut nums = vec![1, 2, 3];
    nums.push(4);
    let sum: i32 = nums.iter().sum();   // 10
    println!("sum = {sum}");
}
ConceptDetail
Ownership / borrowEach value has one owner; borrows are checked at compile time
Option / ResultNo null; errors are values you must handle
CargoBuild tool + package manager (crates.io)
TraitsShared behavior (like interfaces) with zero-cost generics
Trade-off: a steep learning curve ("fighting the borrow checker") buys you C-like speed with safety guarantees. If it compiles, a whole class of bugs is simply gone.
☕ Java — The Enterprise Workhorse Language ▶
Reference
Write Once, Run Anywhere on the JVM
Java compiles to bytecode that runs on the JVM, making it portable and battle-tested for large backends. Statically typed, object-oriented, with a massive ecosystem (Spring) and a mature GC. 
public class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var nums = List.of(1, 2, 3);
        int sum = nums.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
        System.out.println("sum = " + sum);
    }
}
ConceptDetail
JVM / bytecodePortable runtime; also hosts Kotlin, Scala, Clojure
Spring BootThe dominant framework for services
Maven / GradleBuild & dependency management
Modern JavaRecords, sealed types, virtual threads (Project Loom)
Kotlin is the modern, less-verbose JVM language (and Android's default) — worth reaching for on new JVM projects.
🎯 C# & .NET — Microsoft's Cross-Platform Stack Language ▶
Reference
Java's Sibling, Now Open & Everywhere
C# runs on .NET, which is now open-source and cross-platform. Strong tooling (Visual Studio), first-class async, and used for web (ASP.NET), desktop, games (Unity), and cloud. 
var nums = new[] { 1, 2, 3 };
var sum = nums.Sum();            // LINQ
Console.WriteLine($"sum = {sum}");
ConceptDetail
.NET (Core)Cross-platform runtime & SDK (Software Development Kit) (dotnet CLI (Command Line Interface))
LINQQuery collections/DBs with a fluent, SQL-like syntax
async/awaitC# pioneered the pattern most languages now copy
ASP.NET Core / BlazorWeb APIs (Application Programming Interface) & SPA-in-C# via WASM (WebAssembly)
Familiar if you know Java; NuGet is the package manager. Unity makes C# a major game-development language too.
💎 Ruby — Optimized for Developer Happiness Language ▶
Reference
Elegant, Dynamic, and All About Rails
Ruby is a dynamic, purely object-oriented language prized for readable, expressive code. Its killer app is Ruby on Rails, the convention-over-configuration framework that shaped modern web development. 
nums = [1, 2, 3]
sum = nums.reduce(0, :+)   # or nums.sum
puts "sum = #{sum}"
ConceptDetail
Everything is an objectEven numbers; blocks & iterators everywhere
RailsMVC (Model-View-Controller), "convention over configuration", rapid CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) apps
Gems / BundlerPackages & dependency locking
MetaprogrammingPowerful DSLs (Domain-Specific Language) (Rails leans on this heavily)
Great for startups and prototyping — you go from idea to CRUD app fast. Trade-off: dynamic typing and slower raw speed than compiled languages.
🐘 PHP — The Language That Runs the Web Language ▶
Reference
Still Powering the Majority of Websites
PHP is a server-side language built for the web — it powers WordPress, and thus a huge share of all sites. Modern PHP (8.x) is genuinely good: typed, fast, with a strong framework in Laravel. 
<?php
$nums = [1, 2, 3];
$sum = array_sum($nums);
echo "sum = $sum";
ConceptDetail
Request-per-scriptClassic model: each request runs a script fresh
ComposerThe modern package manager (Packagist)
Laravel / SymfonyFull-featured modern frameworks
PHP 8+JIT (Just-In-Time), typed properties, enums, attributes, fibers
Don't judge it by 2005 — modern PHP is a competent, fast web language. Its ubiquity in shared hosting and WordPress keeps demand high.
🔩 C — Close to the Metal Language ▶
Reference
The Language Everything Else Is Built On
C is small, fast, and gives you direct control over memory via pointers. Operating systems, embedded firmware, databases, and language runtimes are written in it. Learning C teaches how computers actually work. 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {1, 2, 3}, sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) sum += nums[i];
    printf("sum = %d\n", sum);
    return 0;
}
ConceptDetail
PointersVariables that hold memory addresses — power & footguns
Manual memorymalloc/free — you own leaks & use-after-free
CompilationPreprocess → compile → link (gcc/clang, make)
Undefined behaviorOff-the-rails when you break the rules (buffer overflows)
C's manual memory is exactly what Rust set out to make safe. Its lack of guardrails is why memory-safety bugs dominate CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) — the security case for newer languages.
⚙️ Assembly & How Programs Actually Run Fundamentals ▶
Concept
Registers, the Stack & the CPU (Central Processing Unit)'s Real Job
Under every language is machine code the CPU executes. Assembly is the human-readable form. You rarely write it, but understanding it demystifies performance, debugging, and — crucially — how exploits like buffer overflows work (ties to the reverse-engineering material).
ConceptDetail
RegistersTiny ultra-fast CPU storage (rax, rsp, rip…)
The stackGrows down; holds locals, args & return addresses
Calling conventionRules for passing args & returns (System V, stdcall)
Instructionsmov, push, call, ret, jmp
Why it matters: overwriting a saved return address on the stack is the classic buffer-overflow exploit — and why we have stack canaries, ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization), and NX. Reading disassembly is core to malware analysis and CTF (Capture The Flag) pwn/rev challenges.
🏷️ Semantic Versioning & Dependency Management Fundamentals ▶
Reference
What ^1.2.3 Actually Means
SemVer gives version numbers meaning so tools can update safely. MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new backward-compatible features, PATCH for fixes.
RangeAllows
^1.2.3≥1.2.3, <2.0.0 (compatible: minor+patch)
~1.2.3≥1.2.3, <1.3.0 (patch only)
1.2.3Exactly that version (pinned)
Lockfiles (package-lock.json, poetry.lock, Cargo.lock) pin the exact resolved tree so builds are reproducible — commit them. Ranges say "what's allowed"; the lockfile says "what you actually got." A 0.x version signals anything may break at any time.
🌊 Apache Kafka — The Distributed Event Log Data Eng ▶
Reference
The Backbone of Streaming Data
Kafka is a durable, distributed append-only log. Producers write events to topics; consumers read at their own pace. Because the log is retained and replayable, it decouples systems and underpins event-driven architectures.
ConceptDetail
Topic / partitionA stream, split into ordered partitions for parallelism
OffsetA consumer's position in a partition — replay by rewinding
Consumer groupConsumers share partitions to scale out
RetentionKeep events for days/forever — the log is the source of truth
vs a queue: a classic queue deletes on read; Kafka keeps the log so many consumers replay independently. It's the practical engine behind Event Sourcing, CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation), and the Outbox pattern (ties to the engineering cards).
✨ Apache Spark — Big-Data Processing Data Eng ▶
Reference
Compute Across a Cluster, in Memory
Spark processes datasets too big for one machine by distributing the work across a cluster and keeping data in memory. You write DataFrame/SQL code; Spark plans and parallelizes it. 
# PySpark: read, aggregate, write — runs distributed
df = spark.read.parquet("s3://data/events/")
(df.groupBy("country")
   .count()
   .write.parquet("s3://out/by_country/"))
ConceptDetail
DataFrame / Spark SQL (Structured Query Language)The high-level API (Application Programming Interface) most people use
Lazy + DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)Transformations build a plan; actions trigger execution
Structured StreamingSame API for batch & streaming
DatabricksThe managed commercial platform
When: data outgrows pandas/one box. For smaller data, single-node tools (DuckDB, Polars) are simpler and often faster — don't reach for a cluster you don't need.
🗓️ Orchestration — Airflow & Dagster Data Eng ▶
Reference
Scheduling & Wiring Data Pipelines
Data pipelines are graphs of dependent tasks ("load, then transform, then report"). Orchestrators schedule them, handle retries and backfills, and show you what failed and why.
ToolModel
AirflowThe incumbent — Python DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graph) of tasks; huge operator ecosystem
DagsterAsset-oriented — declare the data assets, it derives the graph
PrefectPythonic, dynamic flows; lighter than Airflow
Key features: a DAG (no cycles), scheduling, retries, and backfills (re-run history after a fix). Asset-based tools (Dagster) shift thinking from "run these tasks" to "produce these datasets," which maps better to lineage and data quality.
🔧 dbt & the Modern Data Stack Data Eng ▶
Reference
Software Engineering for SQL (Structured Query Language)
dbt brought engineering discipline to analytics: you write transformations as version-controlled SQL SELECTs (models), and dbt handles dependencies, testing, and documentation — all running inside your warehouse.
ConceptDetail
ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) (not ETL)Load raw first, transform in the warehouse (Snowflake/BigQuery)
ModelsA SQL SELECT = a table/view; ref() builds the DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)
Tests & docsAssert not-null/unique; auto-generate a data catalog
The stackFivetran/Airbyte (ingest) → warehouse → dbt → BI (Business Intelligence) (Looker)
Why it stuck: analytics code gets Git, code review, CI, and tests — treating pipelines like software. ELT works because cloud warehouses are cheap and powerful enough to transform in place.
⭐ Dimensional Modeling — Star & Snowflake Schemas Data Eng ▶
Concept
Designing a Warehouse for Analytics
Transactional (OLTP) schemas are normalized for writes; analytics (OLAP) wants fast aggregation over huge tables. Dimensional modeling (Kimball) organizes data into facts and dimensions for exactly that.
ConceptDetail
Fact tableThe measurements/events (sales, clicks) — long & numeric
Dimension tableThe context (date, product, customer) — descriptive
Star schemaFacts in the center, dimensions around — few joins, fast
SnowflakeDimensions further normalized — less duplication, more joins
SCD (Type 2)Track history when a dimension changes (keep old rows)
Slowly Changing Dimensions answer "what was the customer's tier when they bought?" — Type 2 keeps versioned rows so history stays accurate. Star schemas are the default; snowflake only when storage or governance demands it.
📱 Kotlin, Swift & Scala — Modern Typed Application Languages Languages ▶
Why Together
Three Answers to "Fix the Language, Keep the Platform"
Each of these arrived to replace an entrenched language without leaving its ecosystem. Kotlin fixes Java while running on the JVM. Swift replaces Objective-C while keeping the Apple frameworks. Scala brought functional programming to the JVM. So all three share a family resemblance — strong static types, null safety, type inference, immutability by default, expressions instead of statements — because they are all reactions to the same 1990s pain points.
LanguageRuns onReplaces / joinsHome turf
KotlinJVM (also native, JS)JavaAndroid, increasingly server-side
SwiftNative (LLVM)Objective-CiOS/macOS; some server & systems use
ScalaJVM (also JS, native)Joins JavaBig data (Spark), typed FP shops
Shared Ideas
Null Safety and the Expression Habit
The one feature to carry away is null in the type system. A plain String cannot be null; a String? might be, and the compiler forces you to handle the difference before you can call a method on it. That single move eliminates the most common crash in the languages they replaced. The second shared habit is that almost everything is an expression that returns a value — an if, a when/match — so you assign its result rather than mutating a variable inside branches. 
// Kotlin — null safety and when-as-expression
val name: String? = user.nickname          // may be null
val shown = name?.uppercase() ?: "GUEST"    // safe call + default

val tier = when (score) {                    // returns a value
    in 90..100 -> "A"
    in 80..89  -> "B"
    else       -> "C"
}
// Swift — optionals are the same idea, different syntax
let name: String? = user.nickname
let shown = name?.uppercased() ?? "GUEST"
if let real = name { greet(real) }          // unwrap safely
Where They Diverge
Pragmatic vs Pure
Kotlin is deliberately pragmatic — coroutines make async code read like sequential code, and Java interop is seamless, which is why Google made it the Android default. Swift leans on value types (structs copied, not shared) and, rather than a garbage collector, uses ARC — automatic reference counting decided at compile time, whose one sharp edge is the retain cycle you break with a weak reference. Scala is the most powerful and the steepest: a full functional type system, immutable-first, beloved where correctness is worth a hard learning curve and easy to overcomplicate where it is not.
λ Elixir, Haskell & the Functional / Niche Languages Languages ▶
Why Learn One
A Different Language Rewires How You Think
You will likely never ship Haskell to production, and that is not the point. Languages built on ideas your daily one lacks — enforced purity, the actor model, a type system that proves things — leave habits behind that make your everyday code better: smaller functions, less shared mutable state, thinking about failure as data. Each language below is worth a weekend for the idea it forces on you.
LanguageThe idea it teaches
Elixir / ErlangFault tolerance through isolated processes and "let it crash"
HaskellPurity, laziness, and a type system that carries real proof
LuaHow small an embeddable language can be
RStatistics and data as a first-class, vectorized concern
MATLABMatrix maths as the native datatype (engineering, DSP)
Elixir & the BEAM
"Let It Crash" Is a Design, Not a Shrug
Elixir runs on the BEAM, Erlang's virtual machine, built for telephone switches that must not go down. The model: millions of tiny isolated processes, sharing nothing, communicating only by messages. When one hits an error it dies cleanly and a supervisor restarts it in a known-good state — so instead of defensively guarding every edge case, you let a failed process crash and be reborn. That is how the BEAM reaches nine-nines uptime, and it is a genuinely different answer to reliability than try/catch everywhere. 
# Elixir — spawn a process, send it a message
pid = spawn(fn -> receive do
  {:hello, name} -> IO.puts("hi #{name}")
end end)
send(pid, {:hello, "world"})
# Pattern matching everywhere; immutability is the default.
Haskell
The Compiler as a Proof Checker
Haskell is purely functional: a function given the same input always returns the same output and changes nothing else, so anything with a side effect — I/O, state, randomness — is marked in its type. That sounds academic until you feel the payoff: "if it compiles, it usually works" is close to true, because the type system has ruled out whole categories of bug before the program ever runs. It is also lazy — nothing is computed until its value is needed, which makes infinite data structures ordinary and evaluation order occasionally surprising. The vocabulary it makes concrete — pure functions, immutability, effects as values — is exactly what shows up, gently, in modern JavaScript, Rust and Kotlin.
The others, briefly: Lua is the go-to embedded scripting language — game engines, nginx, Redis — because the whole interpreter is tiny and trivially bound to C. R and MATLAB are domain tools rather than general-purpose languages: R for statistics and its plotting, MATLAB for matrix-heavy engineering and signal processing. Reach for them when the domain is the point, not the software.

💙 PowerShell — Windows (and Cross-Platform) Scripting SHORTCUTS • Scripting ▶
POWERSHELL VS CMD
Why PowerShell Replaced Command Prompt
CMD (Command Prompt) is ancient — 1980s DOS heritage. PowerShell is a modern scripting environment built on .NET. Everything is an object (not just text), making it far more powerful. PowerShell Core (PS 7+) runs on Linux and Mac too — making it cross-platform. Windows admins and security teams must know it.
FeatureCMDPowerShell
Output typePlain text.NET objects (piped, filtered, sorted)
ScriptingBatch files (.bat) — limitedFull scripting language (.ps1) with loops, functions, classes
PipingText pipesObject pipes — access properties directly
Windows integrationLimitedFull access to WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation), .NET, COM, Registry
Cross-platformWindows onlyPowerShell 7+ runs on Linux/Mac
Security loggingMinimalTranscription, ScriptBlock logging
CORE CONCEPTS
Cmdlets, Objects, and the Pipeline
PowerShell commands are called cmdlets (pronounced "command-lets"). They follow a Verb-Noun naming pattern (Get-Process, Set-Item, New-Item). Output is objects with properties — you can access, filter, and pipe them.
# Get-Help is your best friend Get-Help Get-Process Get-Help Get-Process -Examples Get-Help *service* # find cmdlets about services # Basic navigation (aliases match Linux commands) ls # alias for Get-ChildItem cd C:\Users\Alice # alias for Set-Location pwd # Print Working Directory cat file.txt # alias for Get-Content cp source dest # alias for Copy-Item rm file.txt # alias for Remove-Item mkdir NewFolder # alias for New-Item -ItemType Directory # Object pipeline — output is objects, not text Get-Process # list all processes Get-Process | Where-Object {$_.CPU -gt 50} # filter by CPU Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 Get-Process | Select-Object Name, CPU, WorkingSet
COMMON TASKS
PowerShell Cheat Sheet
# Services Get-Service # list all services Get-Service -Name "wuauserv" # Windows Update service Start-Service -Name "wuauserv" Stop-Service -Name "wuauserv" Restart-Service -Name "wuauserv" Set-Service -Name "wuauserv" -StartupType Disabled # Files and text Get-Content C:\log.txt # read file Get-Content C:\log.txt | Select-String "error" # grep equivalent "Hello World" | Out-File C:\output.txt Add-Content C:\log.txt "new line" # append # Network Test-NetConnection google.com # ping + port check Test-NetConnection google.com -Port 443 # test specific port Get-NetIPAddress # your IP addresses Resolve-DnsName google.com # DNS lookup Get-NetTCPConnection # netstat equivalent # System info Get-ComputerInfo # detailed system info Get-EventLog -LogName Security -Newest 20 # security log Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_LogicalDisk # disk info # Users Get-LocalUser # list local accounts New-LocalUser -Name "alice" -Password (ConvertTo-SecureString "P@ss!" -AsPlainText -Force) Add-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" -Member "alice"
SCRIPTING
Writing PowerShell Scripts
# Variables start with $ $name = "Alice" $count = 42 $pi = 3.14159 # String interpolation Write-Host "Hello, $name!" # Hello, Alice! Write-Host "Pi is approximately $pi" # Arrays $fruits = @("apple", "banana", "cherry") $fruits[0] # apple $fruits.Count # 3 $fruits += "date" # add element # Hash tables (dicts) $user = @{ Name = "Alice"; Age = 30; Role = "Admin" } $user["Name"] # Alice $user.Role # Admin # If / ForEach / While if ($count -gt 10) { Write-Host "Big" } elseif ($count -gt 5) { Write-Host "Medium" } else { Write-Host "Small" } foreach ($fruit in $fruits) { Write-Host "I like $fruit" } 1..10 | ForEach-Object { Write-Host "Item $_" } # 1 to 10 # Functions function Get-Greeting { param([string]$Name = "World") return "Hello, $Name!" } Get-Greeting -Name "Alice"
EXECUTION POLICY
Why Your Script Won't Run
PowerShell's execution policy restricts which scripts can run. This is a security feature — not a permission system. On a new Windows machine, scripts are often blocked by default.
# Check current policy Get-ExecutionPolicy # Policy levels (most to least restrictive) Restricted # No scripts (default on Win clients) AllSigned # Only code-signed scripts RemoteSigned # Local scripts OK; downloaded must be signed Unrestricted # All scripts run (prompt for remote) Bypass # Nothing blocked (used in automation) # Set for current user (doesn't require admin) Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser # Run a script bypassing policy (one-time) powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File myscript.ps1
🌳 Git Power User — Beyond add, commit, push SHORTCUTS • Version Control ▶
STASHING
Set Work Aside Temporarily
You're mid-change and suddenly need to switch branches for an urgent fix — but your work isn't ready to commit. git stash shelves your changes so you have a clean working directory, then restores them later.
git stash # shelve current changes git stash -u # include untracked files git stash list # see all stashes git stash pop # restore most recent & remove from list git stash apply # restore but KEEP in stash list git stash drop # delete a stash git stash save "wip: login" # named stash
REBASE
Rewrite History for a Clean Timeline
Rebasing moves your commits to start from a different base — useful for keeping a linear, clean history instead of merge bubbles. Golden rule: never rebase commits you've already pushed to a shared branch (it rewrites history others depend on).
# Update your feature branch with latest main (linear) git checkout feature git rebase main # replay your commits on top of main # Interactive rebase — clean up your last N commits git rebase -i HEAD~3 # edit/squash/reorder last 3 commits # In the editor: pick / squash / reword / drop / edit # If conflicts arise during rebase # fix files, then: git add <files> git rebase --continue git rebase --abort # bail out, restore original state
UNDOING THINGS
The Commands That Save You
GoalCommand
Unstage a file (keep changes)git restore --staged file
Discard local changes to a filegit restore file
Amend the last commitgit commit --amend
Undo last commit, keep changes stagedgit reset --soft HEAD~1
Undo last commit, keep changes unstagedgit reset HEAD~1
Nuke last commit and changes (danger)git reset --hard HEAD~1
Safely undo a pushed commitgit revert <hash> (makes a new inverse commit)
Recover "lost" commitsgit reflog (your safety net — shows ALL HEAD moves)
GIT BISECT
Binary Search to Find the Bug-Introducing Commit
A bug appeared somewhere in the last 200 commits but you don't know where. git bisect does a binary search — you test the midpoint, tell git "good" or "bad", and it homes in on the exact commit that broke things in ~log₂(n) steps.
git bisect start git bisect bad # current commit is broken git bisect good v1.0 # this old tag worked # Git checks out a commit halfway between. Test it, then: git bisect good # this one works # — or — git bisect bad # this one is broken # Repeat. Git narrows down to the exact culprit commit. git bisect reset # done — return to where you started # Automate it with a test script! git bisect run ./test.sh # git runs the script at each step
INSPECTING
Useful Investigation Commands
git log --oneline --graph --all # visual branch history git blame file.py # who changed each line and when git show <hash> # view a specific commit's changes git diff main..feature # compare two branches git log --grep="bug" # search commit messages git log -p file.py # full history of one file git log --author="alice" # commits by author
🪟 tmux — Never Lose a Session Again SHORTCUTS • Productivity ▶
WHY TMUX
The Persistent, Splittable Terminal
tmux (terminal multiplexer) solves two huge problems: (1) Persistence — your session keeps running on the server even if your SSH (Secure Shell) connection drops or you close your laptop. Reconnect and everything's exactly where you left it. (2) Layout — split one terminal into multiple panes and windows. For anyone who works on remote servers, tmux is life-changing. A long-running job no longer dies when your Wi-Fi hiccups.
THE PREFIX KEY
Everything Starts with Ctrl+b
tmux commands begin with a prefix — by default Ctrl+b — then a key. Notation: C-b means Ctrl+b, release, then press the next key. (Many people remap the prefix to Ctrl+a for ergonomics.)
# Session management (from the shell) tmux # start a new session tmux new -s work # named session "work" tmux ls # list sessions tmux attach -t work # reattach to "work" tmux kill-session -t work # THE killer feature: detach and reattach # C-b d → detach (session keeps running on the server) # Later: tmux attach → everything's still there
PANES & WINDOWS
Splitting and Navigating
Keys (after C-b)Action
%Split pane vertically (left/right)
"Split pane horizontally (top/bottom)
arrow keysMove between panes
oCycle to next pane
zZoom pane to fullscreen (toggle)
xClose current pane
cCreate a new window (like a tab)
n / pNext / previous window
0-9Jump to window by number
,Rename current window
[Enter scroll/copy mode (q to exit)
CONFIG
A Sensible ~/.tmux.conf Starter
# ~/.tmux.conf # Remap prefix to Ctrl+a (easier reach) unbind C-b set -g prefix C-a # Start windows/panes at 1, not 0 set -g base-index 1 # Enable mouse (scroll, click panes, resize) set -g mouse on # More scrollback history set -g history-limit 10000 # Easier splits that remember current path bind | split-window -h -c "#{pane_current_path}" bind - split-window -v -c "#{pane_current_path}" # Reload config without restarting: C-a r bind r source-file ~/.tmux.conf \; display "Reloaded!"
⚡ Text Processing Mastery — Combining the Classic Tools SHORTCUTS • Power User ▶
THE UNIX PHILOSOPHY
Small Tools That Do One Thing, Piped Together
The power of the command line comes from composing small, focused tools with pipes (|). Each tool does one thing well; the pipe feeds one's output into the next. Mastering a handful of these — and how to chain them — lets you answer questions about logs and data in seconds that would take ages in a GUI (Graphical User Interface).
GREP — FIND LINES
Search Text Like a Pro
grep "ERROR" app.log # lines containing ERROR grep -i "error" app.log # case-insensitive grep -r "TODO" ./src # recursive through dir grep -v "DEBUG" app.log # INVERT — lines WITHOUT DEBUG grep -c "404" access.log # count matching lines grep -n "fail" app.log # show line numbers grep -A3 -B3 "panic" app.log # 3 lines After + Before context grep -E "warn|error|fatal" app.log # regex (extended) OR grep -oE "[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+" log # extract just IPs
FIND — LOCATE FILES
Search the Filesystem by Any Attribute
find . -name "*.log" # by name pattern find / -type f -size +100M # files over 100MB find . -mtime -1 # modified in last 24h find /var/log -mtime +30 -delete # delete logs older than 30 days find . -type f -name "*.sh" -perm -u+x # executable scripts # find + exec / xargs — act on results find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; # delete each match find . -name "*.py" | xargs grep "import os" # grep in matches
THE CLASSIC PIPELINE
cut · sort · uniq · awk — Together
# "Top 10 IPs hitting my web server" — a legendary one-liner cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10 # cut field 1 (IP) → sort → count dups → sort by count desc → top 10 # Count HTTP status codes awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn # Sum a column (e.g., total bytes transferred) awk '{sum += $10} END {print sum}' access.log # Unique users who logged in today grep "$(date +%Y-%m-%d)" auth.log | grep "session opened" \ | awk '{print $NF}' | sort -u # Find the 5 largest files under /var, human-readable find /var -type f -printf '%s %p\n' | sort -rn | head -5 \ | awk '{printf "%.1f MB %s\n", $1/1048576, $2}'
MODERN ALTERNATIVES
Faster, Friendlier Replacements
ClassicModernWhy
grepripgrep (rg)Much faster, respects .gitignore, nicer output
findfdSimpler syntax, fast, sane defaults
catbatSyntax highlighting, line numbers
lseza / lsdColors, icons, git status
tophtop / btopInteractive, visual
Learn the classics first — they're on every server, everywhere, forever. The modern tools are great for your own machine but won't be on that random production box at 3am.
⌨️ Intermediate Vim — Editing as a Language SHORTCUTS • Power User ▶
THE BIG IDEA
Vim Is a Language: Verb + Motion
Vim's power isn't memorizing hundreds of commands — it's that commands compose like a language. You combine a verb (operator: what to do) with a motion (where). Learn a handful of each and you can express thousands of edits. d (delete) + w (word) = dw "delete word." Once it clicks, editing becomes thought-speed.
# GRAMMAR: [count] operator motion dw # delete word d3w # delete 3 words c$ # change to end of line y} # yank (copy) to next blank line >i{ # indent inside { } block =G # auto-indent to end of file
OPERATORS (VERBS)
What to Do
OperatorAction
dDelete (cut)
cChange (delete + enter insert mode)
yYank (copy)
> / <Indent / dedent
=Auto-format/indent
gu / gULowercase / uppercase
MOTIONS & TEXT OBJECTS
Where to Act
MotionMoves / Selects
w / b / eWord forward / back / end
0 / $Start / end of line
gg / GTop / bottom of file
f{char} / t{char}Jump to / before next char
%Matching bracket
iw / awText object: inner / a word
i" / i( / i{Inside quotes / parens / braces
it / ipInside tag / paragraph
Text objects are the superpower: ci" = "change inside quotes" (deletes text between quotes, drops you in insert mode) — works no matter where your cursor is in the string. di( = delete inside parens. dit = delete inside HTML (HyperText Markup Language) tag. These feel magical once learned.
HIGH-VALUE COMMANDS
Things That Save Real Time
. # REPEAT last change (incredibly powerful) ciw # change inner word, then . to repeat on others * # search for word under cursor ggVG # select entire file (gg, Visual, G) :%s/old/new/g # replace all "old" with "new" in file :%s/old/new/gc # ...with confirmation each time u / Ctrl-r # undo / redo A # jump to end of line + insert o / O # open new line below / above >G # indent from cursor to end of file Ctrl-v # VISUAL BLOCK — edit columns (great for tables)
The . command repeats your last change — pair it with a motion-based edit and you can fix dozens of spots with single keystrokes. Mastering "edit once, repeat with ." is the hallmark of a fluent Vim user.
Beginner Browser Power Moves – Tabs, History, and DevTools Shortcuts
Concept

Most people use 10% of their browser

If you spend your day in a browser — and almost everyone in IT does — a handful of muscle-memory shortcuts can save you dozens of clicks an hour. These work across Chrome, Edge, and Firefox unless noted otherwise (swap Ctrl for Cmd on macOS).

Reference

Tab and window management

ShortcutWhat it does
Ctrl+TOpen a new tab
Ctrl+Shift+TReopen the last closed tab (works multiple times — it's a stack!)
Ctrl+Tab / Ctrl+Shift+TabJump to the next / previous tab
Ctrl+1 through Ctrl+8Jump directly to tab 1–8 by position
Ctrl+9Jump to the last tab, no matter how many are open
Ctrl+L or Alt+DJump straight to the address bar (faster than clicking)
Ctrl+Shift+NOpen a new incognito/private window — handy for testing as a "logged out" user
Reference

Navigation, search, and page tools

ShortcutWhat it does
Ctrl+FFind text on the current page — your fastest way to locate something in a long doc or log dump
Ctrl+HOpen browsing history — useful for re-finding "that ticket from yesterday"
Alt+Left / Alt+RightBack / forward (faster than reaching for the mouse)
Ctrl+R / F5Reload the page
Ctrl+Shift+RHard reload — bypasses the cache (your go-to when "the page looks wrong" after a deploy)
Ctrl+DBookmark the current page
Hands-on

DevTools shortcuts every helpdesk and dev should know

ShortcutWhat it does
F12 or Ctrl+Shift+IOpen Developer Tools — your window into what the page is actually doing
Ctrl+Shift+JJump straight to the Console tab (where JavaScript errors show up)
Ctrl+Shift+C"Inspect element" mode — click anything on the page to see its underlying HTML/CSS
Network tab + Ctrl+RWatch every request the page makes as it loads — essential for "why is this slow / broken?"

When a user reports "the website is broken," opening the Console tab before doing anything else often shows you the actual JavaScript error in seconds — turning a vague complaint into an actionable bug report you can hand to a developer.

Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me

"It works fine for me" is rarely the end of the story — it might be a cached version of the page, a browser extension interfering, or a cookie holding onto stale session data. Before assuming the user is "doing something wrong," try Ctrl+Shift+N for a clean incognito window: if the problem disappears there, you've just proven it's local to their browser profile, not the website — and saved everyone a lot of back-and-forth.

Beginner Tmux Survival Kit – Never Lose a Terminal Session Again
Concept

The problem tmux solves: "the SSH (Secure Shell) connection dropped, and I lost everything"

Tmux (terminal multiplexer) lets you create terminal sessions that keep running even after you disconnect — whether your laptop sleeps, your VPN (Virtual Private Network) drops, or you just want to walk away and resume later from a different machine. Without it, a long-running command in an SSH session dies the instant the connection does. With it, you simply reconnect and find everything exactly where you left it, still running.

Concept

The mental model: sessions, windows, and panes

ConceptThink of it as...Why it matters
SessionAn entire workspace — everything you're doing on this server right nowYou can detach from it and it keeps running; reattach later from anywhere
WindowA tab within that sessionSwitch between separate tasks (editing, monitoring logs, running tests) without separate connections
PaneA split within a window — multiple terminals visible side by sideWatch logs in one pane while running commands in another, all on one screen
Reference

The shortcuts that get you 90% of the way there

Every tmux command starts with a "prefix" key — by default Ctrl+b — released, then followed by another key. Below, "prefix" means "press Ctrl+b, let go, then press the next key."

ShortcutWhat it does
tmux new -s workStart a new named session called "work" (naming sessions makes them MUCH easier to find later)
prefix dDetach from the current session — it keeps running in the background
tmux attach -t workReattach to that session from anywhere — even a different computer
tmux lsList all running sessions — "what do I have going on right now?"
prefix cCreate a new window (tab) in the current session
prefix n / prefix pMove to the next / previous window
prefix %Split the current pane vertically (side by side)
prefix "Split the current pane horizontally (stacked)
prefix arrow-keyMove between panes in that direction
Hands-on

A realistic first session, start to finish

# 1. SSH into a remote server, then start a named session
ssh admin@server.example.com
tmux new -s deploy

# 2. Kick off something long-running — a deployment, a big sync, a build
./run_deployment.sh

# 3. Your laptop goes to sleep / VPN hiccups / you close the lid.
#    The deployment KEEPS RUNNING on the server — tmux doesn't care
#    that your connection dropped.

# 4. Reconnect later (even from a different machine entirely)
ssh admin@server.example.com
tmux attach -t deploy
# ...and there it is, exactly where you left it, still running

# 5. When you're completely done with it
exit   # closes the window/session from inside
# or from outside: tmux kill-session -t deploy
Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me — name your sessions

"I'll remember which session is which" is a confident assumption at 2 PM and a source of genuine confusion at 2 AM when tmux ls shows four unnamed sessions and you can't recall which one has the thing you actually need. The thirty seconds it costs to type tmux new -s deploy-prod-db-migration instead of tmux new pays for itself the very first time you have more than one session running — which, if you use tmux at all regularly, will be sooner than you think.

🧰 VS Code — Setup, Settings & Profiles VS Code ▶
How-To
Make It Yours — and Keep It Everywhere
VS Code is configured through settings.json (per-user and per-workspace). Settings Sync pushes your settings, keybindings, and extensions to every machine via your GitHub/Microsoft account. Profiles let you keep clean, separate setups per stack (a lean Python profile vs a heavy web profile) so extensions don't pile up.
▸ SETTINGS WORTH SETTING (settings.json)
{
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,       // auto-format every save
  "editor.rulers": [80, 120],       // visual line-length guides
  "files.autoSave": "onFocusChange",
  "editor.minimap.enabled": false,
  "workbench.editor.enablePreview": false,  // stop tabs replacing each other
  "editor.bracketPairColorization.enabled": true
}
Tip: commit a .vscode/settings.json to a repo to share team defaults, and a .editorconfig for cross-editor consistency.

How-To
Edit Locally, Run Anywhere
VS Code's Remote Development splits the editor (your machine) from the workspace (elsewhere): a server component runs on the target and the UI (User Interface) stays local, so it feels native even though the code, terminal, and extensions execute remotely.
ModeRuns your code…
Remote-SSHOn a remote server over SSH (Secure Shell)
WSLInside the Linux subsystem on Windows

Your Setup, Version-Controlled & Portable
Your shell config, editor settings, git config, and aliases (the "dotfiles" — .bashrc, .gitconfig, …) are your personal productivity layer. Put them in a Git repo so a new machine is one command away from feeling like home, and you never lose that alias you set up two years ago.

How-To
The Right Language Version, Per Project
Project A needs Node 18, Project B needs Node 22; one needs Python 3.11, another 3.13. Version managers let you install many versions and switch automatically per directory — no more "works on my machine" from a version mismatch.
ToolManages

🤖 AI (Artificial Intelligence) Pair Programming — Using It Well Dev Env ▶
Reference
A Force Multiplier — If You Stay in Charge
AI assistants (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, and others) generate code, explain unfamiliar code, write tests, and draft boilerplate fast. Used well they're a big accelerant; used blindly they introduce subtle bugs and security holes. You stay the engineer — the AI drafts, you own.
DoWatch out for
Great for boilerplate, tests, glue codePlausible-but-wrong code (hallucinated APIs)
Explaining a codebase / errorInsecure defaults (no input validation)
Refactoring with a clear specOutdated patterns from training data
Review every line before you commitLeaking secrets/proprietary code to a service
Treat AI output like a junior's PR: read it, test it, understand it before it ships. The engineers who benefit most are the ones who could have written it themselves and can spot when it's wrong.
💻 Terminal Productivity — Work Faster at the Command Line SHORTCUT • Practical ▶
BASH READLINE SHORTCUTS
Move Without the Arrow Keys
ShortcutAction
Ctrl+AMove cursor to beginning of line
Ctrl+EMove cursor to end of line
Ctrl+F / Ctrl+BMove forward/back one character
Alt+F / Alt+BMove forward/back one WORD
Ctrl+WDelete word before cursor
Alt+DDelete word after cursor
Ctrl+KDelete from cursor to end of line
Ctrl+UDelete from cursor to beginning of line

Ctrl+GCancel current history search

HISTORY TRICKS
Never Retype Long Commands
# See your command history history | tail -20 # Run command #42 from history !42 # Run last command starting with "nmap" !nmap # Substitute in last command (fix typos fast) # If you typed: cat /etc/paaswd ^paaswd^passwd # re-runs with correction # Search history with fzf (install separately) Ctrl+R # built-in incremental search
TMUX BASICS
Multiple Terminals in One Window
tmux is a terminal multiplexer — splits your terminal into multiple panes, creates persistent sessions that survive network disconnects, and lets you detach/reattach from long-running tasks.
# Start new session tmux new -s mysession # Detach (leaves session running) Ctrl+B then D # Reattach later tmux attach -t mysession # Key bindings (all start with Ctrl+B, the prefix) # Split horizontally Ctrl+B then % # Split vertically Ctrl+B then " # Move between panes Ctrl+B then arrow key # New window (tab) Ctrl+B then C # Switch windows Ctrl+B then N / P # Kill current pane Ctrl+B then X
ALIASES
Shortcut Your Most-Used Commands
# Add to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc # Shorter ls with detail alias ll='ls -lah --color=auto' # Never accidentally remove files alias rm='rm -i' # Quick git shortcuts alias gs='git status' alias gd='git diff' alias gl='git log --oneline --graph -20' # SSH with key timeout alias ssha='eval $(ssh-agent) && ssh-add' # Python shortcut alias py='python3' # Apply changes source ~/.bashrc
PIPES & REDIRECTION
Compose Powerful One-Liners
# | pipes output of one command into next ps aux | grep python | grep -v grep # > overwrites file, >> appends echo "hello" > output.txt echo "world" >> output.txt # 2> redirects stderr, 2>&1 merges with stdout command > out.log 2>&1 # /dev/null discards output command > /dev/null 2>&1 # tee: write to file AND stdout simultaneously ls -la | tee listing.txt # xargs: turn output into arguments find . -name "*.tmp" | xargs rm -f

Voice / chatVia the companion extension
Great for: remote pairing, mob programming, interviews, and mentoring. The guest doesn't need the repo cloned or the toolchain installed — they're borrowing yours. Pairs naturally with Codespaces above.
🦀 Modern CLI (Command Line Interface) Tools — ripgrep, fzf, bat, jq & eza Terminal ▶
Reference
Faster, Friendlier Replacements for the Classics
A wave of (mostly Rust) tools reimagine the Unix classics — faster, with sensible defaults, color, and git-awareness. Learning a handful genuinely speeds up daily terminal work.
ToolReplacesWhy
ripgrep (rg)grepBlazing fast; respects .gitignore by default
fdfindSimpler syntax, fast, sane defaults
fzf—Fuzzy finder — pipe anything into an interactive picker
batcatSyntax highlighting + line numbers + git marks
ezalsColors, icons, a --tree view, git status
jq / yq—Slice, filter & transform JSON/YAML on the CLI
zoxidecdJumps to frequent dirs (z proj)
deltadiff/pagerGorgeous side-by-side git diffs
# fzf + ripgrep + bat: interactively search & preview matches
rg --line-number . | fzf --preview 'bat --color=always {1} --highlight-line {2}'

# jq: pull a field from an API response
curl -s api.example.com/users | jq '.[] | {name, email}'
Start with three: rg, fzf, and jq pay for themselves immediately. Wire fzf into your shell (Ctrl-R history, Ctrl-T files) and it becomes muscle memory. jq is essential glue for any API/DevOps work.

🐙 GitHub & Git — Command Reference DEV · VERSION CONTROL ▶
Concept
Git vs GitHub
Git is a distributed version-control system that runs locally — it tracks changes, branches, and history entirely on your machine. GitHub is a cloud hosting service for Git repositories that adds pull requests, Actions CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery), Issues, and collaboration features. You push local Git commits to a remote GitHub repository.
Reference
Core Workflow — Init · Clone · Stage · Commit · Push
▸ SETUP & REPO CREATION
CommandWhat It Does
git initCreate a new Git repo in the current directory
git clone <url>Download a remote repo and all its history
git remote add origin <url>Link local repo to a remote (usually GitHub)
git remote -vList all configured remotes and their URLs (Uniform Resource Locator)
git config --global user.name "Name"Set your display name for commits globally
git config --global user.email "e@x.com"Set your email for commits globally
▸ STAGE & COMMIT
CommandWhat It Does
git statusShow staged, unstaged, and untracked files
git add <file>Stage a specific file for the next commit
git add .Stage all changed files in current directory
git commit -m "message"Save staged snapshot with a descriptive message
git commit --amendEdit the last commit message or add staged changes to it
git diffShow unstaged changes line by line
git diff --stagedShow staged changes that will go into the next commit
▸ PUSH & PULL
CommandWhat It Does
git push -u origin mainPush main branch & set upstream tracking for future pushes
git pushPush current branch to its tracked remote branch
git pullFetch remote changes and merge into current branch
git fetch originDownload remote changes without merging them
git push origin --delete <branch>Delete a branch on the remote
▸ BRANCHING & MERGING
CommandWhat It Does
git branchList all local branches (* = current)
git branch <name>Create a new branch at current commit
git switch <name>Switch to an existing branch (modern syntax)
git switch -c <name>Create and switch to a new branch in one step
git merge <branch>Merge named branch into current branch
git rebase mainReplay current branch commits on top of main (cleaner history)
git branch -d <name>Delete a local branch (safe — fails if unmerged)
▸ INSPECTION & HISTORY
CommandWhat It Does
git log --onelineCompact one-line-per-commit history
git log --oneline --graphASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) branch graph alongside commit log
git show <commit>Display diff and metadata for a specific commit
git blame <file>Show who last changed each line of a file
git tag v1.0.0Create a lightweight tag at current commit
▸ UNDO & RECOVERY
CommandWhat It Does
git restore <file>Discard unstaged changes to a file (permanent)
git restore --staged <file>Unstage a file (keeps changes on disk)
git revert <commit>Create a new commit that undoes a past commit (safe for shared repos)
git reset --soft HEAD~1Undo last commit but keep changes staged
git reset --hard HEAD~1Undo last commit AND discard changes entirely (destructive)
git stashShelve current changes to a temporary stack
git stash popApply most-recent stash and remove it from the stack
▸ GITHUB CLI (Command Line Interface) (gh)
CommandWhat It Does
