gh repo createCreate a new GitHub repo interactively
gh repo clone <owner/repo>Clone a GitHub repo by owner/name shorthand
gh pr createOpen a pull request for the current branch
gh pr listList open pull requests in the current repo
gh pr mergeMerge the current pull request
gh issue createCreate a new issue in the current repo
gh issue listList open issues in the current repo
gh run listList recent GitHub Actions workflow runs
gh run viewView details and logs for a workflow run
🔑 API (Application Programming Interface) Keys & Gateways — Netlify · GitHub · REST (Representational State Transfer) DEV · WEB · DEPLOY ▶
Concept
What Is an API Key?
An API key is a unique string a server issues to identify and authorize a client. When you make a request to an external service (weather data, payment processor, AI model), you include the key so the server knows who you are and what you're allowed to do. Keys are like passwords for machines — they should never be hard-coded in source code or committed to Git.
Reference
API Key Types & Token Formats
▸ KEY & TOKEN TYPES
TypeHow It WorksExample Use
API Key (static)A long random string sent with every requestOpenWeather, Stripe publishable key
Secret KeyServer-side only — never exposed to browsersStripe secret key, Twilio auth token
Bearer Token (OAuth 2.0)Short-lived token exchanged after auth flowGoogle APIs, GitHub OAuth (Open Authorization) Apps
Personal Access Token (PAT)Long-lived user token with scoped permissionsGitHub PAT (Port Address Translation), GitLab personal token
JWT (JSON Web Token)Self-contained signed payload: header.payload.sigAuth0, Firebase, custom auth backends
Service Account KeyJSON (JavaScript Object Notation) credential file for machine-to-machine authGoogle Cloud service accounts
Webhook SecretHMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) signature to verify incoming webhook payloadsGitHub webhooks, Stripe webhooks
▸ HOW API KEYS ARE SENT
MethodExampleNotes
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) Header (preferred)Authorization: Bearer <token>Most secure — not in logs or browser history
Custom HeaderX-API-Key: <key>Common with REST APIs (e.g. AWS, Twilio)
Query Parameter?api_key=<key>Convenient but appears in server logs — avoid for secrets
Request Body{ "api_key": "..." }Used by some legacy APIs; only safe over HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure)
Basic AuthAuthorization: Basic base64(user:pass)Username = key, password = secret (e.g. Twilio)
▸ API GATEWAY PATTERNS
Gateway TypeProtocolKey Trait
REST APIHTTP/HTTPSStateless; uses GET/POST/PUT/DELETE + JSON responses
GraphQLHTTP/HTTPSSingle endpoint; client specifies exactly what data it needs
WebSocketws:// / wss://Persistent two-way connection; used for real-time data
WebhookHTTP/HTTPSServer pushes data to YOUR URL (Uniform Resource Locator) when an event occurs
gRPCHTTP/2 (HyperText Transfer Protocol version 2)Binary protocol; used for high-performance microservices
Netlify FunctionsHTTPSServerless endpoints at /.netlify/functions/<name>
Platform
Netlify — Environment Variables & Deploy Keys
Netlify injects environment variables at build time and into serverless functions. Never hard-code secrets in netlify.toml — store them in the Netlify dashboard under Site settings → Environment variables.
▸ KEY NETLIFY VARIABLES
VariableWhat It Holds
NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKENPersonal access token for the Netlify CLI (Command Line Interface) and API
NETLIFY_SITE_IDUnique ID of the target site (used by netlify deploy)
NODE_VERSIONNode.js version to use during build (e.g. 18)
CONTEXTBuild context: production, deploy-preview, branch-deploy
DEPLOY_URLURL of this specific deploy (injected automatically by Netlify)
URLPrimary site URL (e.g. https://mysite.netlify.app)
BRANCHGit branch that triggered this build
COMMIT_REFFull SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) of the Git commit that triggered the build
▸ NETLIFY CLI COMMANDS
CommandWhat It Does
netlify loginAuthenticate CLI with your Netlify account via browser
netlify initLink current directory to a Netlify site (or create one)
netlify devRun local dev server that emulates Netlify Functions & redirects
netlify buildRun the build command locally (same as the Netlify CI build)
netlify deployDeploy site to a draft URL for preview
netlify deploy --prodDeploy site to the production URL
netlify env:listList all environment variables for the linked site
netlify env:set KEY valAdd or update an environment variable in the Netlify dashboard
netlify env:get KEYPrint the value of a single environment variable
netlify functions:listList all serverless functions deployed on the site
▸ netlify.toml — KEY CONFIG FIELDS
FieldPurposeExample
[build] commandBuild command Netlify runs"npm run build"
[build] publishFolder containing built output to deploy"dist"
[build] functionsFolder containing serverless function files"netlify/functions"
[build.environment]Non-secret env vars baked into the buildNODE_VERSION = "18"
[[redirects]]URL redirect / rewrite rulesfrom = "/*" to = "/index.html"
[[headers]]HTTP response headers to add to matched pathsCSP (Content Security Policy), CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing), caching headers
Platform
GitHub — Personal Access Tokens & Actions Secrets
GitHub uses Personal Access Tokens (PATs) to let scripts, CI pipelines, and tools authenticate as you without needing your password. GitHub Actions has a built-in GITHUB_TOKEN automatically available in every workflow — no setup needed.
▸ TOKEN TYPES
TokenScopeUse Case
Classic PATCoarse — whole account, broad permission bucketsQuick scripts, legacy integrations
Fine-grained PATSpecific repos + specific permissions (read/write)Preferred for new integrations — least privilege
GITHUB_TOKENAuto-scoped to current repo during the workflow runGitHub Actions — push, comment on PRs, publish packages
Deploy KeySSH (Secure Shell) key tied to a single repo (read or read/write)Server-side deploys, CI systems without a user account
OAuth App TokenUser grants specific scopes via OAuth flowThird-party apps that need to act on behalf of users
GitHub App TokenInstallation token issued per-repo, short-livedAutomated bots, CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) integrations (preferred for orgs)
▸ GITHUB ACTIONS SECRETS
How ToSteps
Add a secretRepo → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret
Use in workflow${{ secrets.MY_SECRET }} in any step's env: or command
Org-level secretOrg → Settings → Secrets → can be shared across multiple repos
Built-in token${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} — always available, no setup needed
▸ COMMON PAT PERMISSION SCOPES
ScopeGrants Access To
repoFull read/write access to private and public repos
public_repoRead/write access to public repos only
workflowCreate and update GitHub Actions workflow files
read:userRead your public profile data
user:emailRead your verified email addresses
packagesUpload/download GitHub Packages
delete_repoDelete repositories (avoid granting unless needed)
Best Practices
Keeping API Keys Secure
RuleWhy It Matters
Never commit keys to GitOnce pushed (even deleted later), keys are in git history forever and can be scraped
Use .env files locally.env holds secrets for local dev — always add it to .gitignore
Use platform secret storesNetlify env vars, GitHub Actions secrets, AWS (Amazon Web Services) Secrets Manager — not plain config files
Least privilegeGrant only the minimum permissions the key actually needs — limits blast radius if leaked
Rotate regularlyExpire and replace tokens on a schedule; immediately rotate any key that may have been exposed
Separate keys per environmentDev, staging, and production should each have their own keys so a test leak doesn't hit prod
Use secret scanningGitHub scans pushes for known token formats and alerts you (or blocks the push) automatically
Use HTTPS onlySending a key over plain HTTP exposes it to anyone watching the network
🏛️ Philosophy & Thought
Ideas
Stoicism · Machiavelli · Buddhism · Taoism · Existentialism · Wicca · Paganism · Druidism · Minimalism · Mental Models · Decision-Making 14 topics · ~30 min ▾
🏛️ Stoicism — The Art of Rational Endurance PHILOSOPHY ▶
CORE
The Dichotomy of Control
Focus only on what is up to you — your judgments and actions — and accept the rest. Live by the four virtues: wisdom, justice, courage, temperance.
FIGURES
The Big Three
Marcus Aurelius (Meditations), Epictetus (Enchiridion), and Seneca (Letters). Roots in Zeno of Citium, c. 300 BCE.
PRACTICE
Daily Exercises
Negative visualization (premeditatio malorum), memento mori (remember mortality), and amor fati (love your fate) build resilience and gratitude.
Ancient Greek · Roman
Core Doctrines & Daily Practice
Founded ~300 BC by Zeno of Citium. Stoics held that virtue alone is sufficient for happiness and that emotions rooted in false judgements must be overcome through reason.
▸ THE FOUR CARDINAL VIRTUES
Wisdom (Sophia)
Knowing what is good, bad, and indifferent. The foundation of all other virtues.
Justice (Dikaiosyne)
Acting rightly toward others. Social duty; fairness in all dealings.
Courage (Andreia)
Facing hardship, pain, and death without flinching. Moral as well as physical.
Temperance (Sophrosyne)
Self-discipline and moderation. Mastery over appetites and impulses.
▸ CORE PRINCIPLES
Principle Meaning Practice
Dichotomy of Control Some things are "up to us" (prohairesis) — judgements, impulses, desires. Everything else is external and indifferent. Ask "Is this in my control?" before reacting to any event.
Memento Mori "Remember you will die." Mortality awareness as a tool for gratitude and urgency. Morning reflection: treat each day as a gift, not a given.
Amor Fati "Love of fate." Accept and embrace everything that happens — not mere tolerance, but affirmation. Reframe obstacles as opportunities; say "it was meant to be" and mean it.
Negative Visualization (Premeditatio Malorum) Deliberately imagine loss — of health, relationships, possessions — to appreciate what you have. Evening: briefly imagine losing what you value most, then feel gratitude for its presence.
Sympatheia All things are interconnected in one rational whole (the Logos). We are citizens of the universe. When frustrated by others: "They act from ignorance, not malice. I would do the same without better judgement."
▸ KEY FIGURES & TEXTS
Figure Era Key Work Contribution
Marcus Aurelius 121–180 AD Meditations Roman Emperor. Private journal of self-discipline; applied Stoicism in governance.
Epictetus 50–135 AD Enchiridion, Discourses Former slave. Focused on inner freedom regardless of external circumstance.
Seneca 4 BC–65 AD Letters to Lucilius, On the Shortness of Life Statesman and playwright. Practical moral essays on time, wealth, and death.
Zeno of Citium 334–262 BC — Founder of the Stoic school in Athens' painted porch (Stoa Poikile).
▸ DAILY STOIC PRACTICE
AM
Morning Journal
What obstacles might I face today? How will I respond virtuously? Rehearse the day — adversities and all.
MID
Pause & Label
When emotion arises, name it: "I notice anger." The gap between stimulus and response is where virtue lives.
PM
Evening Review
What did I do well? What could I have done better? No self-flagellation — just honest assessment. (Seneca's method)
♟️ Machiavellianism — Power, Realism & Strategy POLITICAL PHILOSOPHY ▶
SOURCE
The Prince (1532)
Niccolò Machiavelli analyzed power as it is, not as it should be. A ruler must master virtù (skill/decisiveness) to manage fortuna (chance).
IDEAS
Realpolitik
Outcomes can justify hard means; it is safer to be feared than loved if you cannot be both. Pragmatic statecraft over idealism.
NOTE
Two Meanings
Distinguish the political philosophy from the psychology term 'Machiavellianism' — a dark-triad trait describing manipulative, self-serving behavior.
Niccolò Machiavelli · 1469–1527
The Prince & the Discourses — Realpolitik Framework
Machiavelli separated political science from ethics. His work describes how power actually operates, not how it ideally should. Often misread as endorsing cruelty; actually a clinical observer of political reality.
▸ CORE CONCEPTS
Concept Meaning
Virtù Not "virtue" but prowess — strength, skill, cunning, willpower. The ruler's capacity to shape events through force of character and action.
Fortuna Fortune/chance — the unpredictable half of all outcomes. Virtù can master ~50% of fate; the rest is Fortuna. She favors the bold.
The Lion & the Fox A ruler must be both: the lion to frighten wolves (force), the fox to recognize traps (cunning). Neither alone is sufficient.
Economy of Violence Cruelties must be committed all at once; benefits distributed gradually. Sudden harshness is quickly forgotten; lingering harm festers.
Appearance vs. Reality It is unnecessary to actually possess virtues — it is sufficient to appear to have them. People judge by what they see, not what is.
Love vs. Fear It is safer to be feared than loved if you cannot be both. But avoid being hated — hatred is fatal; fear can be managed.
▸ THE 48 LAWS — ROBERT GREENE'S SYNTHESIS
Never Outshine the Master
Always make those above you feel superior. Conceal your talent when needed.
Conceal Your Intentions
Keep people off-balance. Reveal purpose only when it cannot be stopped.
Guard Your Reputation
Reputation is the cornerstone of power. A single crack and you are vulnerable.
Play on People's Need to Believe
People crave meaning. Offer a cause, a vision — they will follow willingly.
▸ DARK TRIAD CONTEXT (Psychology)
Trait Core Distinction
Machiavellianism Cynical worldview, strategic manipulation, delayed gratification Calculating and patient; manipulates for long-term gain
Narcissism Grandiosity, entitlement, need for admiration Emotional; manipulates for ego supply and status
Psychopathy Low empathy, impulsivity, callousness Reactive; least strategic of the three
🧠 Psychology — Mind, Behavior & Biases COGNITIVE SCIENCE ▶
SCHOOLS
Major Approaches
Psychodynamic (unconscious drives), behavioral (conditioning), cognitive (thinking patterns), and humanistic (growth & self-actualization).
APPLIED
Useful Frameworks
CBT links thoughts→feelings→behavior. Classical vs. operant conditioning explains learned responses. Maslow's hierarchy ranks human needs. The DSM-5 is the diagnostic standard (for clinicians, not self-diagnosis).
Cognitive BiasWhat It Is
Confirmation biasFavoring info that fits beliefs
AnchoringOver-weighting the first number seen
Dunning-KrugerLow skill, high confidence
Sunk costContinuing because of past investment
AvailabilityJudging by what comes to mind easily
Applied Psychology
Cognitive Biases · Defense Mechanisms · Frameworks
Psychology studies the mind and behavior. Understanding your cognitive architecture is the first step to overcoming it. "Knowing yourself is the beginning of all wisdom." — Aristotle
▸ KEY COGNITIVE BIASES
Bias Description Example
Confirmation Bias Seek info that confirms existing beliefs; ignore contradicting evidence Only reading news aligned with your politics
Dunning-Kruger Effect Incompetent people overestimate ability; experts underestimate theirs Beginner investor convinced they've outsmarted the market
Sunk Cost Fallacy Continue bad decisions because of past investment (time/money/effort) Finishing a terrible book because you've read half of it
Availability Heuristic Judge probability by how easily examples come to mind Fear flying after seeing news of a crash; ignoring car risk
Fundamental Attribution Error Over-attribute others' behavior to character; under-attribute to situation "They cut me off — they're a bad person" (vs. they're late for hospital)
Anchoring Over-rely on first piece of information encountered $100 item marked down to $70 feels like a deal regardless of value
Negativity Bias Negative events register more strongly than equally positive ones One criticism outweighs ten compliments
Halo Effect One positive trait causes assumption of other positive traits Attractive people assumed to be more competent
▸ EGO DEFENSE MECHANISMS (Freud / Anna Freud)
Mechanism Description
Repression Unconsciously pushing threatening thoughts out of awareness
Rationalization Creating logical explanations to justify unacceptable behavior
Projection Attributing your own unacceptable feelings to others
Denial Refusing to acknowledge a painful reality
Displacement Redirecting emotion from original source to safer target
Sublimation Channeling unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activity (e.g., aggression → sport)
▸ KEY FRAMEWORKS
Maslow's Hierarchy
Physiological → Safety → Love/Belonging → Esteem → Self-Actualization. Lower needs must be satisfied before higher ones motivate.
Locus of Control
Internal: outcomes result from your actions. External: outcomes are luck/fate. Internal LoC correlates strongly with resilience and achievement.
Growth vs Fixed Mindset
Carol Dweck. Fixed: ability is innate and static. Growth: ability is developed through effort. Growth mindset predicts higher achievement and resilience.
Flow State (Csikszentmihalyi)
Optimal experience at the intersection of high challenge + high skill. Time distorts. Deep absorption. Intrinsic reward. Cultivated through deliberate practice.
📜 Philosophy — Schools of Thought WESTERN TRADITION ▶
Epistemology · Metaphysics · Ethics · Logic
Major Schools & Key Thinkers
▸ MAJOR SCHOOLS
School Era Core Claim Key Figures
Rationalism 17th–18th c. Knowledge derived primarily from reason, not senses. Innate ideas exist. Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz
Empiricism 17th–18th c. All knowledge derives from sensory experience. The mind starts as a blank slate (tabula rasa). Locke, Hume, Berkeley
Pragmatism 19th–20th c. Truth is what works in practice. Ideas are tools; their value is in their consequences. Peirce, James, Dewey
Existentialism 20th c. Existence precedes essence. Individuals create their own meaning in an indifferent universe. Sartre, Camus, Heidegger, de Beauvoir
Utilitarianism 18th–19th c. The morally right action maximizes overall happiness (utility) for the greatest number. Bentham, Mill
Kantian Ethics (Deontology) 18th c. Act only according to maxims you could will to be universal laws. Duty above consequences. Immanuel Kant
Virtue Ethics Ancient Greek Focus on developing good character (virtues) rather than rules or outcomes. Aristotle, MacIntyre
Nihilism 19th–20th c. Life has no intrinsic meaning, purpose, or value. Traditional morality is groundless. Nietzsche (critic), Cioran
▸ ESSENTIAL CONCEPTS
Concept Definition
Cogito ergo sum "I think, therefore I am." Descartes' foundational certainty — even a deceiver cannot doubt the existence of the doubter.
Categorical Imperative Kant: act only on maxims that could become universal laws. Treat humanity never merely as means but always as ends.
Absurdism Camus: life is inherently meaningless yet humans persistently seek meaning — this conflict is the Absurd. Response: revolt (not suicide, not faith).
Veil of Ignorance Rawls: design a just society without knowing your position in it. Ensures impartiality — you'd design fairness since you might be disadvantaged.
Übermensch Nietzsche's "Overman" — one who creates their own values after the "death of God." Not a racial concept; a call to self-overcoming.
Solipsism Only one's own mind is certain to exist. All else may be illusion. A logical extreme rarely endorsed but philosophically significant.
☸️ Buddhism — The Path to Liberation SPIRITUAL PHILOSOPHY ▶
CORE
Four Noble Truths
Life contains suffering (dukkha); craving causes it; it can cease; and the Eightfold Path is the way out. Reality is marked by impermanence and non-self (anatta).
SCHOOLS
Traditions
Theravada (elder teaching), Mahayana (great vehicle), Zen (direct insight), and Vajrayana (Tibetan). Meditation (samatha & vipassana) is central.
Eightfold PathGroup
Right View / IntentionWisdom
Right Speech / Action / LivelihoodEthics
Right Effort / Mindfulness / ConcentrationMental discipline
Siddhartha Gautama · ~563–483 BC
Four Noble Truths · Eightfold Path · Core Concepts
Buddhism is both a religion and a philosophy. Its goal is the cessation of dukkha (suffering) through understanding the nature of mind and reality. Not theistic in the Western sense — the Buddha is a teacher, not a god.
▸ THE FOUR NOBLE TRUTHS (Catvāri Āryasatyāni)
1
Dukkha (Suffering)
Life inherently contains suffering, dissatisfaction, and imperfection. Birth, aging, sickness, death, getting what we don't want, not getting what we want — all are dukkha.
2
Samudāya (Origin)
The origin of suffering is craving (tanha) — for pleasure, for existence, for non-existence. Attachment and aversion are the roots.
3
Nirodha (Cessation)
Suffering can cease. Nirvana is the complete extinguishing of craving — a state of peace, freedom, and liberation.
4
Magga (The Path)
The Noble Eightfold Path is the way to end suffering. Practical and systematic — not metaphysical belief but lived practice.
▸ THE NOBLE EIGHTFOLD PATH
Path Category Meaning
Right View Wisdom Understanding the Four Noble Truths; seeing reality as it is, not as we wish it to be.
Right Intention Wisdom Commitment to non-attachment, non-ill-will, and non-harmfulness.
Right Speech Ethics Abstaining from lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter.
Right Action Ethics Abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Right Livelihood Ethics Earning a living that does not cause harm to others or oneself.
Right Effort Meditation Cultivating wholesome states and abandoning unwholesome ones continuously.
Right Mindfulness Meditation Present-moment awareness of body, feelings, mind-states, and phenomena.
Right Concentration Meditation Developing deep meditative absorption (jhanas) as foundation for insight.
▸ CORE CONCEPTS (THE THREE MARKS OF EXISTENCE)
Anicca — Impermanence
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent. Clinging to what is transient is the source of suffering. Release attachment.
Dukkha — Unsatisfactoriness
Even pleasant experiences carry an undercurrent of dissatisfaction because they end. Nothing conditioned can permanently satisfy.
Anatta — Non-Self
The "self" is not a fixed, permanent entity but a changing process of aggregates (skandhas). Liberating when truly understood.
☯️ Taoism — The Way of Nature CHINESE PHILOSOPHY ▶
CORE
The Tao & Wu Wei
The Tao is the natural way underlying everything. Wu wei — effortless action — means moving with nature's flow rather than forcing it.
FIGURES
Texts & Symbols
Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching and Zhuangzi's writings are foundational. Yin-yang expresses complementary opposites in dynamic balance.
Lao Tzu · ~6th–4th c. BC
Tao Te Ching — The Classic of the Way and Its Power
The Tao (道) — the Way — is the fundamental, unnamed principle underlying all of reality. It cannot be named or fully grasped, only lived. "The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao."
▸ CORE PRINCIPLES
Principle Meaning Application
Wu Wei (無為) "Non-action" or effortless action. Acting in harmony with the natural flow rather than forcing outcomes. Avoid unnecessary struggle. Like water: yield, go around, persist gently.
Pu (樸) — Simplicity The uncarved block. Original nature before social conditioning. Simplicity as strength. Strip away pretense. Return to what is essential and natural.
Te (德) — Virtue/Power Inner virtue or power that arises naturally when aligned with the Tao. Not morality imposed from outside but integrity from within. Be genuinely good, not performatively good.
Yin-Yang (陰陽) All opposites are interdependent and contain each other's seed. Darkness within light, light within darkness. Change is constant. Stop seeing circumstances as purely good or bad. Both are transforming.
Ziran (自然) Self-so, naturalness. Things should be allowed to follow their own nature. Stop trying to control what is inherently wild and self-organizing.
▸ WATER AS TAOIST METAPHOR
Water is the supreme Taoist metaphor. It is:
· Soft yet wears down the hardest rock (persistence)
· Low — it always seeks the lowest point (humility)
· Yielding — flows around obstacles rather than fighting them
· Essential — all life depends on it, yet it does not demand recognition
"Nothing in the world is as soft and yielding as water, yet nothing is better at dissolving the hard and inflexible."
🌑 Existentialism & Absurdism 20TH C. PHILOSOPHY ▶
CORE
Existence Precedes Essence
We are not born with a fixed purpose; we create meaning through free choices and bear full responsibility for them.
THEMES
Freedom, Absurd, Authenticity
Camus framed the absurd (seeking meaning in a silent universe); the answer is to live authentically rather than in 'bad faith'.
FIGURES
Key Thinkers
Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Sartre, Camus, and Simone de Beauvoir — spanning religious and atheist existentialism.
Sartre · Camus · Kierkegaard · Heidegger
"Existence precedes essence" — Building meaning in a meaningless universe
Existentialism holds that there is no pre-given human nature or purpose. We exist first, then create ourselves through choices. This is both terrifying (radical freedom) and liberating.
▸ KEY CONCEPTS
Concept Thinker Meaning
Radical Freedom Sartre We are "condemned to be free" — there is no escape from choice. Even refusing to choose is a choice. Total responsibility for self.
Bad Faith (Mauvaise Foi) Sartre Pretending you have no choice; adopting a fixed identity to escape freedom. E.g., "I can't help it, that's just who I am."
The Absurd Camus The conflict between humans' need for meaning and the universe's silent indifference. Three responses: physical suicide (wrong), philosophical suicide (religion — bad faith), or revolt (the only authentic response).
Authenticity Heidegger Owning your existence — facing death (Being-toward-death) rather than fleeing into das Man (the "they-self" of conformity).
Leap of Faith Kierkegaard Rational thought cannot resolve the deepest questions. Authentic existence requires a passionate, subjective commitment despite uncertainty.
Thrownness (Geworfenheit) Heidegger We are "thrown" into existence — we did not choose our time, place, language, culture. But we are responsible for what we do with this situation.
▸ THE MYTH OF SISYPHUS — CAMUS
Sisyphus is condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity — it always rolls back down. Camus argues this is the human condition.

The resolution: "One must imagine Sisyphus happy."
Not because the task is meaningful in any cosmic sense, but because the struggle itself fills his heart. Revolt against absurdity — continuing to live, create, love — is the only authentic response.
🧭Mental Models & Folk WisdomLifestyle • Practical Wisdom▶
BOUNDARIES
“Not my circus, not my monkeys.”
A Polish proverb (nie mój cyrk, nie moje małpy) meaning: this drama isn’t mine to manage. When a mess belongs to someone else — their emotions, their choices, their chaos — you can still care without taking ownership of it. Before leaping in to fix things, ask whose circus this actually is. It pairs perfectly with the Stoic dichotomy of control: spend your energy on your own monkeys.
VERIFY
“Assume makes an ass out of u and me.”
Break the word apart — ASS·U·ME — and it’s a built-in memory hook: unchecked assumptions end up embarrassing everyone involved. Don’t fill gaps in what you know with guesses; ask, confirm, and write it down. In IT especially, assuming ‘someone else handled it’ or ‘that config is fine’ is how outages are born. Trade “I assumed…” for “Let me verify…”
ACCEPTANCE
“You can’t make someone make the right choice — but you can pick up the pieces afterward.”
You don’t control other people’s decisions, only your response to them. Advise, warn, and offer help — then release the outcome, because it was never yours to steer. And when their choice goes wrong, you can still show up with grace and help them rebuild. It’s the dichotomy of control plus compassion: let go of a steering wheel you were never holding, and keep your hands free to help pick up the pieces.
SayingCore LessonUse It When…
Not my circus, not my monkeysHealthy boundariesYou’re tempted to own someone else’s drama
Assume = ass / u / meVerify, don’t guessYou catch yourself filling in unknowns
Can’t make the right choice…Release + compassionYou’re trying to control another’s decision
🧠More Models for a Clear HeadLifestyle • Decision-Making▶
CHARITY
Hanlon’s Razor
“Never attribute to malice what is adequately explained by carelessness or a bad day.” Most slights aren’t attacks — they’re someone rushed, tired, or unaware. Assuming clumsiness over evil lowers your stress and usually turns out to be correct.
SIMPLICITY
Occam’s Razor
When you have competing explanations, start with the simplest one that fits the facts. The server is probably unplugged before it’s a sophisticated hacker. Simple guesses are faster to test — rule them out first.
CONTROL
The Serenity Principle
Sort every worry into two buckets: things I can change and things I can’t. Act on the first bucket; make peace with the second. Almost all anxiety comes from pouring effort into the wrong bucket.
FOCUS
Circle of Control
Picture three rings: what you control (your actions), what you influence (others, by asking), and what you only care about (the weather, the economy). Push your attention inward toward the center — that’s where your power actually is.
PROGRESS
Done Beats Perfect
Perfectionism is procrastination in a nice outfit. A finished, slightly rough thing helps people today; a perfect thing that never ships helps no one. Ship it, then improve it.
🧭Decision-MakingLifestyle • Judgment▶
DOORS
One-Way vs. Two-Way Doors
Some decisions are reversible (a two-way door — try it, walk back if wrong) and some aren’t (a one-way door). Spend real deliberation on the one-way doors; move fast and experiment on the rest. Most choices are two-way.
TRADE-OFFS
Opportunity Cost
Saying yes to one thing is saying no to everything else you could do with that time or money. The real cost of a choice isn’t just its price — it’s the best thing you gave up to make it.
ENOUGH
Good Enough Beats Endless Search
Chasing the absolute best (maximizing) often costs more than it returns. Decide what ‘good enough’ looks like up front, pick the first option that clears the bar, and move on. Done decisions free your mind.
PAUSE
Sleep On the Big Ones
Strong emotion is a bad time to decide. For anything major, give it a night; tomorrow’s calmer brain sees options today’s couldn’t. Urgency is often manufactured — real deadlines survive a good night’s sleep.

⬜ Minimalism & Intentional Living LIFESTYLE ▶
CORE
Less, But Better
Own and do fewer things, chosen deliberately, so attention and resources go to what matters most. Subtraction as a path to clarity.
PRACTICE
Applying It
Declutter to essentials, resist mindless consumption, and extend the idea to time and screens (digital minimalism: tools serve values, not the reverse).
Modern Practice
Intentionality · Essentialism · Deep Work
▸ CORE PRINCIPLES
Essentialism (Greg McKeown)
The disciplined pursuit of less. Not about doing more things — about doing the right things. "If it's not a clear yes, it's a no."
Deep Work (Cal Newport)
Cognitively demanding tasks performed in a state of distraction-free concentration. The skill of the 21st century. Rare + valuable = leverage.
KonMari Method
Keep only what "sparks joy." Tidy by category, not location. The goal: create an environment that supports who you want to become.
Parkinson's Law
Work expands to fill the time allotted. Impose artificial constraints. Deadlines create focus. Less time + clear priority = better output.
▸ HIGH-PERFORMANCE LIFESTYLE FRAMEWORKS
Framework Key Idea Source
80/20 Principle (Pareto) 80% of results come from 20% of efforts. Identify and double down on the vital few. Ruthlessly eliminate the trivial many. Vilfredo Pareto / Tim Ferriss
Atomic Habits Systems over goals. 1% better every day = 37x better in a year. Identity-based habits: "I am a writer" vs "I want to write." James Clear
Ikigai Japanese: reason for being. The intersection of what you love, what you're good at, what the world needs, and what you can be paid for. Japanese philosophy
Memento Vivere "Remember to live." The counterpoint to Memento Mori — not just contemplating death, but using that awareness to fully inhabit life. Stoic tradition
Wabi-Sabi Japanese aesthetic: find beauty in imperfection, transience, and incompleteness. A cracked bowl repaired with gold (Kintsugi) is more beautiful for its history. Japanese philosophy

⏳Habits & TimeLifestyle • Getting Things Done▶
COMPOUNDING
1% Better
Tiny improvements compound. Getting 1% better each day isn’t flashy, but over a year it stacks into a transformation. Big results are usually small habits repeated longer than other people are willing to.
START SMALL
The Two-Minute Rule
To beat procrastination, shrink the task until starting takes under two minutes: “write one sentence,” “open the file,” “put on the shoes.” Starting is the hard part; momentum does the rest.
PRIORITIES
Eat the Frog
Do your most important (often most dreaded) task first, while your energy and willpower are fresh. Everything after it feels downhill, and you’re not dragging the dread around all day.
IdeaIn One Line
Pareto (80/20)A few efforts produce most of the results
Parkinson’s LawWork expands to fill the time you give it
Time-boxingGive a task a fixed slot, then stop
Don’t-break-the-chainMark each day you do the habit; keep the streak
🧠 Learning How to Learn — Build the Skill Behind All Skills LIFESTYLE • Foundation ▶
THE FORGETTING CURVE
You Forget 90% If You Don't Review
Ebbinghaus (1885) showed that without review, humans forget ~40% of new material within 20 minutes, ~70% within a day, ~90% within a week. The cure isn't reading more — it's spaced repetition: review material at increasing intervals (1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks, 1 month).
ACTIVE vs PASSIVE LEARNING
Watching ≠ Knowing
Passive: watching a video tutorial, reading, highlighting. Feels like learning, but retention is low (~5-10%).
Active: writing code from scratch, teaching, explaining concepts aloud, doing practice questions, building projects. Retention climbs to 70-90%.
For every hour of video, spend two hours doing something with the material. The discomfort of struggle IS the learning.
FEYNMAN TECHNIQUE
If You Can't Explain It Simply, You Don't Know It Yet
1. Pick a concept you're studying.
2. Explain it as if teaching a 12-year-old — no jargon allowed.
3. Where you stumble or grab for words → that's your gap.
4. Go back and study only that gap.
5. Repeat until the explanation is smooth.
This technique cuts through the illusion of familiarity ("I've seen this 10 times" ≠ "I understand it").
DELIBERATE PRACTICE
Push the Edge, Get Feedback, Adjust
Random repetition doesn't produce mastery. Deliberate practice does:
• Work at the edge of your ability — if it's easy, it's review, not growth
• Get immediate, accurate feedback (run the code; take the quiz)
• Focus on weaknesses, not strengths
• Rest and consolidate — sleep is when the brain cements learning
COMPOUNDING KNOWLEDGE
Small Daily Gains Add Up Exponentially
1% better every day for a year = 37× improvement (1.01^365 ≈ 37.8). The hard part is that the gains are invisible at first. The graph looks flat for months, then curves sharply upward. Most people quit in the flat zone. Don't compare your chapter 3 to someone else's chapter 20. Stack small wins daily, stay consistent, trust the process.
⏱️ Time Management — Making Your Hours Count LIFESTYLE • Productivity ▶
THE CORE PROBLEM
Tech Work Is Constantly Interrupted
Deep work — the focused, uninterrupted concentration that produces real output — takes approximately 23 minutes to recover from each interruption. A day of constant Slack pings and meetings produces the feeling of work with very little actual output. Protecting your focus is a technical skill, not a personality preference.
THE POMODORO TECHNIQUE
Work in Focused Sprints
Francesco Cirillo's technique: work in 25-minute focused blocks (a "pomodoro"), then take a 5-minute break. Every 4 pomodoros, take a 15-30 minute break. Simple and effective for fighting procrastination and tracking what you actually accomplished.
# Pomodoro pattern [25 min work] → [5 min break] # 1 pomodoro [25 min work] → [5 min break] # 2nd [25 min work] → [5 min break] # 3rd [25 min work] → [25 min break] # 4th — long break # Linux terminal timer (simple) sleep 1500 && echo "Pomodoro done!" | wall # 25 min # Or use the timer command if installed timer 25m "Focus session done"
THE EISENHOWER MATRIX
Prioritize by Urgency and Importance
UrgentNot Urgent
ImportantQ1: DO FIRST
Production is down. Security incident. Deadline today.		Q2: SCHEDULE
Learning new skills. Planning. Preventing future problems.
Not ImportantQ3: DELEGATE
Most interruptions. Many meetings. Someone else's urgent.		Q4: ELIMINATE
Social media scrolling. Busywork. Unnecessary reports.
The trap: most people spend too much time in Q1 (reactive firefighting) and Q3 (other people's urgency). High performers protect Q2 — this is where growth and prevention happen. If you never invest in Q2, Q1 grows forever.
ASYNC FIRST
Protect Deep Work Time
TacticHow To Implement
Batch notificationsCheck Slack/email at 9am, noon, 4pm — not constantly
Time blockingBlock 2-4 hour "deep work" blocks in your calendar — treat them like meetings
Do Not DisturbOS-level DND during focus blocks. People survive without instant responses.
Default to asyncIf it doesn't need an immediate decision, use email/ticket — not a meeting
Weekly reviewEvery Friday: what did I accomplish? What are next week's top 3 priorities?
🏯 The Japanese Mastery Loop — Kata, Poka-Yoke, Hansei, Kaizen, Shokunin LIFE • Learning Systems ▶
Core Concept

Fast mastery is a correction system, not an absence of failure

Five practices from Japanese manufacturing and craft traditions compose into a learning loop that has nothing to do with talent and everything to do with how quickly a mistake becomes information. Soichiro Honda is the standing example: he left school young, learned mechanical work through apprenticeship, and went back to study metallurgy part-time only after his piston rings failed Toyota's quality tests. Honda has been the world's largest motorcycle manufacturer since 1959. The failure was not the detour — the targeted study that followed it was the method.

Say the obvious thing plainly: this is a transferable framework that happens to have Japanese names, not a claim that Japanese people learn faster for some innate reason. Every one of these practices was invented by someone solving a specific problem, which is exactly why they transfer.

Reference

The five practices and what each one does

PracticeIts job in the loopWhat it looks like when you study
Kata 型
the form		Gives you a model to copy before you improviseWork through solved examples before attempting blank problems. Type the tutorial's commands exactly once before changing anything
Poka-yoke ポカヨケ
mistake-proofing		Makes the error harder to commit, or impossible to missRedesign the setup so a mistake announces itself — a linter, a checklist, a lab you can reset
Hansei 反省
reflection		Converts what went wrong into information you can act onFifteen minutes at the end of a session, written down, on what broke and why
Kaizen 改善
continuous improvement		Changes one variable at a time so you can tell what workedAlter one thing about how you study per week — not five
Shokunin 職人
the craftsman's standard		Gates advancement on demonstrated mastery, over a horizon of yearsDon't move on because you finished the chapter. Move on because you can rebuild it from memory

Read as a cycle: copy a form → make errors visible → reflect on them → change one thing → refuse to advance until it holds. Most self-teaching skips steps two and three entirely, which is why it feels like effort without traction.

Concept

Poka-yoke came from a missing spring, and the rename matters

In 1961 at Yamada Electric, workers assembling a push-button switch sometimes forgot to place a small spring underneath. Shigeo Shingo did not issue a warning or retrain anyone. He changed the process so that a missing spring became immediately visible — the error could still happen, but it could no longer travel.

The technique was first called baka-yoke, "fool-proofing", and was renamed poka-yoke, "mistake-proofing", because the first name insulted the people doing the work. That rename is the whole philosophy in one word: the error is a property of the process, not a defect in the person. Applied to studying, it stops the useless move of resolving to "be more careful" and starts the useful one of asking what would have caught this.

Concept

Andon — stopping the line is the expensive part, and that's the point

Toyota's andon system gives a production worker the authority to signal a problem and halt the line so the underlying defect gets fixed rather than passed downstream. Notice what that costs: stopping a line is expensive and visible, and the system accepts that cost because a defect that keeps moving is more expensive still.

The study equivalent is the uncomfortable one. When you hit something you do not actually understand, the cheap move is to keep reading and hope it resolves. Andon says stop, find the real gap, fix it, then resume. Every hour spent on chapter nine while chapter four is still broken is a defect travelling downstream.

Concept

Kumon — what a mastery gate actually is

In 1954 a high-school maths teacher, Toru Kumon, started writing daily incremental worksheets for his son Takeshi after a poor test result. The design rule is the interesting part: the sheets advance in small steps, and only after correction and demonstrated mastery. Not after time spent, not after completion — after mastery. Kumon's own history reports that Takeshi reached calculus by sixth grade; the method later scaled to millions of students.

Two honest notes. That calculus claim comes from Kumon, an interested party, so treat it as the company's account rather than an independent finding. And the mechanism is not mysterious — a gate that only opens on mastery makes it impossible to accumulate the quiet debt that makes later material feel impossible.

The trap

Adopting the vocabulary instead of the loop

It is easy to put "kaizen" in a journal and change nothing. Three specific failure modes:

TrapWhy it fails
Kaizen as "improve everything constantly"Kaizen is one variable at a time. Change five things and you have learned nothing about any of them — you have run an experiment with no control
Kata as "never deviate"The form is a stage, not a destination. Traditional arts name three: shu (keep the form), ha (break it), ri (leave it). Copying is where you start, and staying there is its own failure
Hansei as self-criticismReflection that produces feeling bad is not reflection. The output of hansei is a specific change to make next session — if there is no change, it did not happen
In practice

Running the loop on this site

The tools here already implement three of the five, which makes the loop cheap to run rather than something extra to maintain:

PracticeWhat to use
Shokunin — mastery gatesGrade flashcards honestly. Pressing Again is a mastery gate refusing to open; pressing Good on a card you half-knew defeats the whole scheduler
Hansei — reflectionThe notepad. One entry per session: what broke, and the one change for next time
Poka-yoke — visible errorsThe quizzes, and the ✓ reviewed markers. A wrong quiz answer is an error made visible on the spot rather than discovered in an exam
Kata — copy the form firstRun the commands in a card exactly as written once, in a lab you can reset, before adapting them
Kaizen — one variableChange one thing a week: session length, time of day, deck size, or where you study. Note it in the notepad so next week's comparison means something

Framework and historical claims summarised from BetterU's "Why the Japanese Master Anything Faster Than Anyone" sources page, which cites Britannica on Honda and kaizen, documented accounts of the poka-yoke spring incident, Toyota andon practice, and Kumon's own company history.

🪞 Hansei — The 15 Minutes That Beat 15 More LIFE • Learning Systems ▶
Core Concept

The finding

In a field experiment at an Indian business-process-outsourcing company, employees in technical training were split: one group spent the final 15 minutes of each training day writing reflections on what they had learned, the other group spent those 15 minutes working. The reflection group scored roughly 23% better on the final assessment.

Same clock. Same material. The difference is entirely in what the last quarter-hour was spent on. The primary paper is "Learning by Thinking: How Reflection Can Spur Progress Along the Learning Curve", summarised in Harvard Business Review as "The Power of Reflection at Work".

Why it matters

It inverts the instinct

When time is short, nearly everyone spends the last fifteen minutes doing one more module, one more video, one more page. This result says that is the worse trade — and it is a *trade*, not an addition, which is why it is actionable for anyone who genuinely has no spare time. You are not being asked to find fifteen minutes. You are being asked to spend fifteen you already have differently.

The mechanism is well-supported by learning research more broadly: retrieving and articulating what you just learned consolidates it, while passive additional exposure mostly produces the feeling of learning. This site has a card on that too — see Learning How to Learn.

Hands-on

Four prompts, fifteen minutes, written down

# Written, not thought. Thinking about it feels identical to
# doing it and produces much less. The notepad on this site works.

# 1. What did I actually learn today? (not "what did I cover")
   Subnetting: the /26 case finally clicked - 4 subnets, 62 hosts.

# 2. Where did I get stuck, and what was the real cause?
   Kept miscounting host bits. Real cause: doing it in my head
   instead of writing the octet out.

# 3. What would have caught that error sooner?  (poka-yoke)
   Write the binary octet every time, even when it feels obvious.

# 4. What ONE thing changes next session?  (kaizen)
   Binary octet on paper for every question, no exceptions.

Prompt 1 is the retrieval. Prompts 2 and 3 are where the reflection earns its keep — a cause and a countermeasure, not a mood. Prompt 4 is the only line that has to survive until tomorrow.

The trap

Reflection that produces no change is a diary

Hansei in its original setting is not about feeling bad — it is structurally the opposite. It identifies a cause and a countermeasure, and in Toyota's practice the countermeasure belongs to the process rather than the person. Applied to study, the test is simple: if a session's reflection produced no specific change to how you work tomorrow, it did not happen. "Should focus more" is not a countermeasure. "Phone in another room, timer for 25 minutes" is.

The second trap is scale. One change per session, reviewed weekly. A reflection that generates six countermeasures produces none of them.

Honest limits

What the 23% figure does and does not support

It is one field experiment, in technical training, at one company, with a short assessment horizon. That is a genuinely good study design — a randomised field trial with a demanding control group who spent the time working rather than idling — but a single effect size does not transfer as a guarantee, and 23% is not a number to expect on your own study log.

What it supports well is the direction: at the margin, time spent consolidating beats time spent covering. That direction is corroborated by a large body of independent work on retrieval practice and the testing effect, which is the reason to act on it. Treat the specific figure as a headline and the direction as the finding.

🏛️ The Memory Palace — Method of Loci for Ordered Lists LIFE • Learning Systems ▶
Core Concept

Trade a weak memory for a strong one

Human memory for arbitrary ordered lists is poor. Human memory for places you have walked through is extraordinary — you can mentally tour your childhood home right now, room by room, in order, without effort. The method of loci exploits the gap: you attach each item you need to remember to a specific location along a route you already know, and then recall becomes a walk rather than a retrieval.

It is old. The technique is set out in the Rhetorica ad Herennium (roughly the first century BCE) and discussed by Cicero and Quintilian as standard equipment for orators speaking for an hour without notes. The origin story — the poet Simonides identifying crushed banquet guests by where they had been seated — is a traditional legend rather than documented history, but the technique it describes was taught as a professional skill for centuries.

Why it matters

Memory athletes are not built differently — they use a strategy

This is the finding worth knowing, because it changes what you conclude about your own memory. A study of World Memory Championship competitors published in Nature Neuroscience (Maguire and colleagues, 2003) found no structural brain differences between superior memorizers and controls, and no difference on general intelligence measures. What differed was which brain regions they engaged — spatial and navigational areas — consistent with nearly all of them reporting use of loci-based methods.

A later training study (Dresler and colleagues, Neuron, 2017) took people with ordinary memory, trained them in loci-based mnemonics for six weeks, and found large and durable improvements in list recall, alongside connectivity patterns shifting toward those of memory athletes. The capability is trainable, and the ceiling is much higher than most people assume theirs is.

Hands-on

Building one, using the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) layers

# 1. Pick a route you know cold. Your home, your commute, your
#    old school. Fixed order, no ambiguity about what comes next.
#    Seven stops for seven layers.

# 2. Walk it once in your head and name the stops out loud.
#    Front door -> hallway -> kitchen -> stairs -> landing ->
#    bathroom -> bedroom.  Lock the ORDER before adding anything.

# 3. Place one item per stop, as a concrete absurd image.
#    Absurd is not decoration - distinctive images survive,
#    sensible ones blur together.

Front door   L1 Physical    - a fat CAT-6 cable used as a door chain
Hallway      L2 Data Link   - MAC addresses stencilled on every coat hook
Kitchen      L3 Network     - a satnav on the counter routing the kettle
Stairs       L4 Transport   - a courier hauling parcels up, demanding
                              a signature for each  (TCP)
Landing      L5 Session     - a bouncer with a clipboard, logging who's
                              still connected
Bathroom     L6 Presentation- a mirror translating your reflection into
                              another language  (encoding, encryption)
Bedroom      L7 Application - your laptop open on the bed, browser running

# 4. Walk it forwards. Then BACKWARDS - that is the test that
#    proves the locations are doing the work, not a sing-song
#    mnemonic sentence you memorised instead.

Backwards recall is the honest check. A first-letter mnemonic ("Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away") only runs one direction and collapses if you forget one word. A palace is random-access: ask "what's layer 4?" and you go straight to the stairs.

Reference

What on this site is worth a palace

Good fit — ordered and arbitraryBad fit — use something else
The OSI 7 layers, and the TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol) 4 in parallelSubnetting maths — that needs practice, not storage
Incident response phases (PICERL), the forensics process, the vulnerability management lifecycleWhy TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) needs a handshake — that is understanding, and a palace will paper over its absence
The SF form series: 700, 701, 702, 703, 704, 705, 706–712 with their coloursReading a packet capture — a skill, built by doing
Port numbers and the protocols on themAnything you will touch daily; repetition will handle it for free
The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) functions, the five Kaizen practices, any "N steps of X" frameworkConcepts you need to apply under variation
The trap

A palace stores; it does not explain

This is the failure mode that matters, and most enthusiastic accounts of the technique skip it. You can build a flawless palace for the seven OSI layers and still not be able to say which layer a problem lives at — because naming a list and understanding a model are different skills, and the technique only delivers the first. Worse, fluent recall feels exactly like understanding, so a palace can hide a gap rather than reveal one.

Use it for the index, not the content. Loci gets the seven layers into permanent, random-access storage in twenty minutes so that your actual study time goes on what happens at each one. Two further honest limits:

LimitWhat to do about it
Encoding costs real effort up frontOnly build one for material that is arbitrary, ordered, and that you have already failed to remember the normal way
Reusing a route overwrites the old contentsKeep a dedicated route per subject, or accept the palace is disposable — fine for an exam, not for a career
In practice

Where it sits alongside the tools here

Loci and spaced repetition solve different halves of the same problem and work well together. The palace gets a list in fast; the scheduler keeps it there. Build the palace once, then let the flashcards on this site surface the same list on the usual intervals — the review takes seconds because you are walking a route, not straining for an answer, and each successful walk strengthens both.

If the list is one you keep failing on, that is the signal to build a palace for it rather than grade it Again for the fifth time. Repeated failure on the same card is information about the method, not about you.

🌙 Sleep — Where the Studying Actually Sticks LIFE • Learning Systems ▶
Core Concept

Studying encodes. Sleep is what files it

Everything else on this site — flashcards, quizzes, spaced repetition, reflection — is encoding. It gets material in. The process that converts a fragile new trace into something durable happens largely while you are asleep, and it is not passive: during deep non-REM sleep the hippocampus replays the day's material and hands it off to the cortex for long-term storage. This is the consolidation the scheduler on this site is implicitly betting on.

Which produces an uncomfortable arithmetic. An extra hour of study taken out of sleep is not a straight trade of rest for revision. You are paying for the encoding with the consolidation, and the consolidation is the part that decides what you still know next month.

Reference

Sleep matters on both sides of a study session

WhenWhat it does
Sleep before learningPrepares the hippocampus to encode at all. Sleep-deprived subjects show measurably reduced hippocampal activity while trying to learn new material — the deficit is in taking it in, not just in keeping it
Sleep after learningConsolidation. Deep non-REM is associated with declarative material — facts, definitions, the things flashcards hold. REM is more associated with procedural skill and emotional processing
NapsA nap long enough to reach deep sleep can measurably help recall of material learned beforehand. Real but modest; a nap is a supplement to a night, not a substitute for one
ConsistencyA stable wake time matters alongside total duration — an erratic schedule produces the effects of short sleep even when the hours roughly add up

The practical shape: study, then sleep. Reviewing material in the evening and sleeping on it puts consolidation immediately after encoding, which is the ordering the mechanism wants. Cramming until 3am inverts it.

The trap

You lose the ability to notice you are impaired

This is the finding that matters most, and the reason "I do fine on five hours" is not evidence. In controlled chronic sleep-restriction studies, objective performance keeps degrading day after day while subjective sleepiness levels off. People adapt to how being impaired feels long before they stop being impaired. You are not calibrated to judge this about yourself, and neither is anyone else.

So treat the self-report as unreliable and look at outcomes instead: how many cards you are failing on the second pass, whether you reread paragraphs, whether you are irritable at things that would not normally irritate you.

The genuine short-sleeper phenotype — people who function normally on very little sleep, associated with rare gene variants — exists and is very rare. The base rate makes it a bad bet about yourself, and the people who claim it are overwhelmingly in the first category rather than the second.

Honest limits

What this card will not tell you

Sleep is where the self-improvement genre is at its worst, so it is worth being explicit about the edges of the claim:

ClaimStatus
"Sleep 4 hours and feel like 8"Not supported. You can reduce how bad it feels — caffeine does that — without recovering the function you lost
"7–9 hours for adults"A consensus recommendation across a population, not a personal prescription. Individual need genuinely varies; the variation is smaller than people want it to be
Specific sleep-stage percentages you should hitConsumer trackers estimate stages from movement and heart rate and are not reliable at that resolution. Useful for spotting duration and consistency trends; not for optimising a hypnogram
Catching up at the weekendPartially works for sleepiness. Does not retroactively consolidate what you failed to encode on Wednesday

And the obvious one: persistent trouble sleeping despite decent habits is a medical question, not a discipline problem. Insomnia and sleep apnoea are treatable and are not fixed by a better bedtime routine.

Hands-on

The short list, in order of how much it buys you

# 1. Fix the WAKE time first, not the bedtime. It is the anchor
#    the rest of the rhythm hangs off, and it is the one you can
#    actually control with an alarm.

# 2. Caffeine has a half-life of roughly 5-6 hours. A 4pm coffee
#    still has meaningful caffeine on board at 10pm. It blocks the
#    signal that you are tired - it does not clear the tiredness.

# 3. Alcohol is a sedative, not a sleep aid. It gets you under
#    faster and then fragments the second half of the night and
#    suppresses REM - the half where consolidation is finishing.

# 4. Put the last review session BEFORE sleep, not instead of it.
#    Twenty minutes of flashcards at 22:30 beats two hours at 02:00,
#    and it is not close.

# 5. If you are going to lose sleep anyway - an incident, a
#    newborn, a deadline - spend the compromised day on ROUTINE
#    work and move the learning. Encoding is what degrades first.
In practice

On-call makes this a professional problem, not a personal one

A rotation that wakes you at 03:00 is not just unpleasant — it removes the deep sleep in which the week's learning was going to consolidate, and it does so on a schedule you did not choose. That is worth naming out loud when a rota is being designed: follow-the-sun coverage, a compensating day, and a hard limit on consecutive nights are sleep-protection measures, not perks. See Surviving On-Call and Burnout on this site for the rest of that argument.

And if you are studying for a certification while on a rotation, expect the schedule to be the constraint rather than your discipline. Plan for fewer, better-timed sessions instead of assuming you will make up the difference by trying harder.

🎯 Attention — Task Switching, Residue & the Cost of Interruption LIFE • Learning Systems ▶
Core Concept

You do not multitask. You switch, and switching is not free

For anything requiring thought, the brain does not run two tasks at once — it alternates, and each alternation costs time and accuracy while it reconfigures. This is one of the more robust findings in cognitive psychology, and the practical consequence is blunt: two things done alternately take longer and come out worse than the same two done in sequence.

Which makes IT work structurally hostile to learning. The job is built out of interruptions — pages, tickets, chat, "quick question" — and a study session squeezed into that texture is mostly switch cost.

Concept

Attention residue — the part that explains the frustration

The switch cost is not just the moment of switching. Research by Sophie Leroy describes attention residue: after moving to a new task, part of your attention stays on the previous one, degrading performance on the new task for some time. You are physically at the new task while a fraction of you is still on the last one.

The useful nuance is when residue is worst: leaving a task unfinished and unplanned. Leroy's work indicates that having a concrete plan for how you will resume substantially reduces the residue — the mind appears to let go of an interrupted task more readily once there is a recorded intention to return to it. That turns an unpleasant finding into a two-line habit.

Observational studies of office work also report interruption recovery taking on the order of twenty minutes. That figure gets quoted with a precision the underlying research does not really support, so treat it as an order of magnitude — the direction is solid, the exact number is not a constant.

Hands-on

The parking note — the highest-value two lines you will write

# Before you answer the page, take the interrupt, or close the
# laptop mid-thought, write these two lines. Ten seconds.

WAS: tracing why the VLAN 40 hosts can't reach the gateway.
     Confirmed the trunk carries 40. Next: check the SVI is up.

# That is it. "WAS" kills the residue - the task is recorded,
# so you can stop holding it. "Next" removes the worst part of
# resuming, which is not the work but re-deciding where you were.

# The notepad on this site is a fine place for these. So is a
# sticky note. The medium does not matter; writing it does.
Reference

Protecting attention, cheapest first

MoveWhy it works
Notifications off by default, not per-app whack-a-moleEvery notification is a switch you did not choose. Allowlist the handful that genuinely cannot wait — a real page — and silence the rest
Phone in another room while studyingNot in a pocket, not face-down on the desk. This is cheap and reversible, which is the main argument for it: you lose nothing by testing it for a week
Batch the interruptible workTwo or three deliberate passes through chat and tickets, rather than a continuous trickle. The trickle costs more in switches than the batch costs in latency
One deck at a time on this sitePick a single domain in the flashcard or quiz picker rather than All domains. A deck that jumps between subnetting and Stoicism adds switching for no benefit
Protect a block, and tell peopleAn unannounced focus block gets interrupted. A stated one usually does not, and stating it is most of the work
The trap

Believing you are the exception

People who multitask the most tend to rate themselves as best at it and to perform worst on objective switching measures. Some of the specific studies in this area have had a mixed replication record, so hold the effect size loosely — but the self-assessment problem is the same one as with sleep, and it is the actionable part: your confidence about your own attention is not measurement.

The second trap is treating focus as a character trait. It is mostly environment and structure. Someone who cannot concentrate with a phone buzzing and six tabs of chat open is not undisciplined; they are in a room designed to prevent concentration. Change the room before concluding anything about yourself.

Third: a long unbroken block is not automatically better. Sustained hard focus degrades, and deliberately spacing study — which the scheduler on this site does for you — beats one heroic session. The goal is uninterrupted blocks, not maximum duration.

In practice

Two hours, honestly measured

A useful and slightly deflating exercise: for one study session, tally a mark in the notepad every time your attention leaves the material — a check of a phone, a tab switch, a thought about work. Do not try to change anything, just count. Most people are surprised, and the count is a far better baseline than a memory of how the session felt.

Then change one thing next session and count again — which is the Kaizen rule from The Japanese Mastery Loop, applied to your own attention instead of to the material.

📝 Note-Taking for Learning — Notes You Never Reopen Are Theatre LIFE • Learning Systems ▶
Core Concept

A note does two jobs, and most people only ever get one

Writing a note has an encoding function — the act of deciding what matters and putting it in your own words is itself the learning — and a storage function, where the note is a record you come back to. Both are real. The failure is that almost everyone optimises for storage, produces beautiful complete notes, and never reopens them. That gets you neither: the transcription was too shallow to teach you anything, and the archive is never read.

The single test worth applying to any note-taking system: does it force me to process the material, and does it produce something I will actually use later? If the answer to either is no, it is a hobby.

The trap

The collector's fallacy

Highlighting, saving, bookmarking and copying all feel like progress and produce almost none. The feeling comes from the effort and the visible output — 200 Kindle highlights, a tidy folder, a page of clean notes — and it is uncoupled from whether you know anything. Rereading has the same problem: it is the most popular study method and among the least effective, precisely because familiarity feels like knowledge.

The uncomfortable diagnostic: if you cannot remember roughly what is in a set of notes without opening them, they have not taught you anything yet. That is not an argument against notes — it is an argument that the note is the raw material and not the result.

Reference

Two kinds of note, and conflating them ruins both

This is the most useful distinction in the whole topic, and it matters especially in IT because so much of the material is commands.

Reference notesLearning notes
PurposeFind it again at 03:00 under pressureBuild understanding you carry without the note
Should beVerbatim, complete, exact — flags, paths, versionsParaphrased, sparse, in your own words
Success looks likeYou grep it and it works first timeYou never need to open it again
ExampleThe exact tcpdump incantation that captured the thingWhy a SYN (Synchronize) flood exhausts the backlog queue
Failure modeParaphrasing it, so the command is subtly wrong when you need itTranscribing it, so you wrote it down instead of understanding it

Keep them in different places, or at minimum different sections. A runbook that has been "summarised in your own words" is dangerous. A conceptual note that is a verbatim copy of a paragraph is useless. Most people's notes are an unhelpful average of the two.

Reference

The three systems worth knowing

SystemHow it worksBest for
Cornell
Walter Pauk, Cornell University, 1950s		Split the page: a narrow cue column on the left, notes on the right, a summary across the bottom. Fill the notes while learning; write the cue column afterwards as questions; cover the notes and answer from the cuesLearning. It is the only one of the three with retrieval practice designed into the page — the cue column turns notes into a self-test by default rather than by discipline
Zettelkasten
Niklas Luhmann's slip-box		One idea per note, each in your own words, each explicitly linked to related notes. Value accumulates in the links, not the countLong-horizon work where you are building a body of understanding and want to find non-obvious connections. Overkill for passing an exam in six weeks
Progressive summarisation
layered highlighting		Keep the source, then highlight within it, then bold within the highlights, then summarise — each pass only on what survivedLong documents you will genuinely revisit. Note this is a popular practice rather than a research finding — treat it as a sensible workflow, not an evidenced method

If you adopt one thing from this card, adopt the Cornell cue column. Not the paper layout — the habit of converting every note into a question the same day you take it.

Hands-on

The cue column, applied to something on this site

# NOTES column - written while reading the OSPF card
Areas limit LSA flooding. Area 0 is the backbone; every
other area must touch it. ABR sits between areas and
summarises. Non-backbone areas reach each other THROUGH 0.
Virtual link = a bodge to reattach an orphaned area.

# CUE column - written AFTERWARDS, as questions.
# This is the part that does the work. Ten questions beats
# ten more paragraphs of notes.
Q: What problem do OSPF areas solve?
Q: What must every non-backbone area connect to, and why?
Q: What does an ABR do?
Q: If two areas can't reach area 0, what's the fix - and
   why is it a smell rather than a design?

# SUMMARY - one or two lines, from memory, notes covered.
# If you can't write this, you did not learn it yet, and
# that is worth knowing NOW rather than in an exam.
OSPF scales by splitting the flooding domain into areas
that all hang off a mandatory backbone.

# Then: cover the notes. Answer the cues out loud.
# Anything you fail becomes a flashcard, not a re-read.

Notice the asymmetry in effort. The notes column took two minutes and taught you a little. The cue column took two minutes and is where nearly all the value is, because writing a good question about material requires knowing what the material is for.

Honest limits

On handwriting versus typing

You will have heard that handwriting notes beats typing them. That comes from a well-known 2014 study (Mueller and Oppenheimer, "The Pen Is Mightier Than the Keyboard"), which found longhand note-takers did better on conceptual questions. It has since had a mixed replication record — later attempts, including a larger 2019 study, did not reproduce the key effects. So do not treat "always use paper" as settled.

What survives is the proposed mechanism, and it is the part worth acting on: typing makes verbatim transcription easy, and transcription is shallow processing. Handwriting helps only because it is too slow to transcribe, forcing you to select and paraphrase. If you type but deliberately refuse to transcribe — paraphrase, compress, write questions — you get the benefit without the wrist ache. If you handwrite but copy the slide word for word, the paper does not save you.

The medium is not the variable. Paraphrasing is the variable.

In practice

Using this with the site's own tools

StepWhere
Learning notes, in your own words, one topic at a timeThe notepad. Not a copy of the card — the card is already saved and does not need duplicating
Turn each note into a question the same dayThe notepad, as a cue list. This is the Cornell column and the single highest-value habit here
Anything you fail on the cues★ the topic so it lands in your study list, then grade it in flashcards — that is what the scheduler is for
Reference notes — exact commands and flagsKeep separately from the above, verbatim. A personal runbook is a different artifact with different rules
End-of-session reviewFold the cue answers into the Hansei prompts — see Hansei — The 15 Minutes That Beat 15 More

The through-line across every card in this group: the output of studying should be a question you can answer, not a document you can show. Notes are how you get there, and they are not the destination.

🧩 Study Systems That Survive a Brain That Won't Cooperate PRODUCTIVITY • Executive Function ▶
Scope

What this card is, and what it deliberately is not

This is about structure: how to build a study system that keeps working when initiation is hard, attention is inconsistent, and time does not feel like it passes at a steady rate. Those difficulties are common in ADHD (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder) and are also common without it — under stress, on shift work, during burnout, in a job made of interruptions.

It is not a diagnostic tool and contains no symptom checklist on purpose. Whether you have ADHD is a clinical question for a clinician, and a study system is not a substitute for assessment or treatment where those are indicated. What follows is useful regardless of the answer, which is why it is written this way.

Core Concept

Design for the bad day, not the good one

Most study plans are built by a motivated person on a good evening, for a person who will also be motivated on every future evening. That person does not reliably show up. A plan that requires consistency to work will fail the first week it does not get consistency — and then the failure gets read as a character flaw rather than as a design fault.

The inversion: assume you will miss days, assume some sessions will be four minutes, and build something where that is fine and the system still functions. A system that survives a bad week beats a better system that does not.

Reference

Five structural moves, and what each is actually solving

MoveThe problem it addressesWhat it looks like
Externalise everythingHolding intentions in your head is the expensive part, and the load is invisible until it drops somethingWritten parking notes, a visible next-action, alarms that carry meaning. Out of your head, into the environment
Cut initiation cost to near zeroStarting is very often the bottleneck — not effort, not capability, not wanting toLeave the laptop open on the card. Queue the deck the night before. Make the first action so small it is embarrassing to refuse
Make time visibleTime passing is not reliably felt, so "I'll just check one thing" becomes forty minutes with no internal alarmA visible countdown, not a clock. An alarm for the end of a session, not just the start
Shorter blocks, more of themA two-hour block is a commitment you will avoid making; fifteen minutes is notFifteen honest minutes daily beats a heroic Sunday that happens twice
Use interest deliberatelyEngagement is not evenly available across topics; forcing the dullest material first often produces nothing at allStart on the interesting thing to get moving, then ride the momentum into the dull one. Rotate topics rather than grinding one
The trap

Streaks, and other systems that punish a missed day

A streak counter converts one missed day into a reason to stop entirely. It is a motivational device that works well for people who rarely miss and works actively against people who sometimes do — which is precisely backwards, because the second group is the one that needs to find restarting cheap.

The single most important property of a study system here is that restarting costs nothing. No streak to lose, no "start the plan over", no backlog that greets you with a number designed to make you feel behind. Anything done today counts, including four minutes.

Worth being straight about a limitation of the tools on this site: the spaced-repetition scheduler does accumulate due cards while you are away, so a week off produces a large number on the study button. That number is not a debt and it is not a verdict. Cap the session — twenty cards, then stop — and let the rest come back tomorrow. Clearing a backlog in one sitting is the least useful thing you can do with it.

Hands-on

Body doubling, and why it is worth trying despite thin evidence

Working alongside someone else — same room, or a video call with both of you silently working — is widely reported to make starting and sustaining much easier. The evidence base is mostly practice and self-report rather than trials, so it is offered here as worth testing, not as established. The reason to test it anyway: it is free, it takes one session to evaluate, and the downside is a wasted hour.

# A session designed to be easy to start, not impressive.

Night before : queue ONE deck. Laptop open on it. That is
               the whole preparation.
Start        : timer visible, 15 minutes, one deck only.
First action : answer one card. Not "study" - one card.
If it flows  : keep going, no upper limit, stop when it stops.
If it does not: you did 15 minutes. That is a completed
               session, not a failed one. Close it.
End          : one line in the notepad - what to start on
               next time. Kills the residue and removes
               tomorrow's hardest decision.

Notice that the plan has no failure state. There is no outcome where you "didn't really study", which is the point — a system with a failure state will eventually be avoided to prevent triggering it.

In practice

What on this site already does this

Structural moveWhere
ExternaliseThe notepad — parking notes, next-action lines, the end-of-session line above
Low initiation cost⌘K quick jump; the ⏰ Review due deck, which decides what to study so you only have to decide whether
Small blocksPick one domain deck, not All domains. A 9-card deck is a session you will actually start
Interest firstThe 🎲 random-topic button, genuinely — landing somewhere unexpected is often enough to get moving
No streaksDeliberate: nothing on this site counts consecutive days, and nothing is lost by missing one

And the framing that runs through the rest of this domain, stated once more because it matters most here: this is environment and structure, not character. Difficulty starting is not laziness, and a system that keeps failing is information about the system. See Attention for the same argument applied to interruption, and Sleep for the physical floor underneath all of it.

🧠 Mind & Wellbeing
Inner Game
Imposter Syndrome · Burnout · Resilience · Failure · On-Call · Communication 12 topics · ~30 min ▾
🗣️Communication & RelationshipsLifestyle • People▶
LISTEN
Seek First to Understand
Most arguments are two people waiting to talk. Try to truly understand the other side first — repeat it back until they say “yes, exactly.” You can’t be persuasive to someone who doesn’t feel heard.
OWN IT
Use “I” Statements
“I felt ignored when the change shipped without a heads-up” lands far better than “you always ignore me.” Describe your experience instead of accusing, and the other person can hear you instead of defending.
CHARITY
Assume Good Intent
Walk in assuming people are doing their best with what they know (see Hanlon’s Razor). It’s usually true, it lowers your blood pressure, and it leaves room to be pleasantly surprised.
MANNERS
Praise in Public, Correct in Private
Recognition feels best with an audience; criticism stings worst with one. Flip the venues and people trust you with hard feedback because you never made it humiliating.
💪Resilience & PerspectiveLifestyle • Inner Game▶
REFRAME
It’s Not What Happens, It’s How You Read It
Two people hit the same traffic jam: one fumes, one catches up on a podcast. The event is identical; the story you tell about it is the part you control — and the story decides how it feels.
GRATITUDE
Name Three Good Things
A nightly habit of naming three things that went right rewires attention toward what’s working. It’s nearly free and quietly powerful against a brain wired to dwell on threats.
PERSPECTIVE
This Too Shall Pass
Good times and hard times are both weather, not climate. Remembering that keeps you humble in the highs and hopeful in the lows. A smooth sea never made a skilled sailor.
GROWTH
Add the Word “Yet”
“I can’t do this” becomes “I can’t do this yet.” Skills are built, not bestowed — the expert was once a beginner who didn’t quit. Struggle is the feeling of learning happening.
ProverbThe Lesson
Measure twice, cut onceA little planning prevents big waste
