• Async communication — send a message that doesn't require instant response; not everything needs a meeting
• Documented decisions — remote work requires more writing; decisions made verbally get forgotten or disputed
• Time zone awareness — know your teammates' working hours; don't expect a response at 7pm their time
• Intentional social interaction — remote work is isolating; deliberately build in non-work contact
VISIBLE WORK
Make Your Contributions Visible
In an office, people see you working. Remote, you must communicate your work explicitly. Share what you've accomplished, what you're blocked on, and what you're planning. This isn't bragging — it's helping your manager advocate for you and keeping the team aligned. Daily standups, weekly summaries, and clear status updates protect your reputation and ensure your work is recognized.
THE WISDOM LOOP
Experience → Reflection → Wisdom
Experience alone doesn't create wisdom — anyone can do the same job for 20 years and learn very little. Wisdom comes from experience + deliberate reflection. Keep a journal. Review your week. Ask "What worked? What didn't? What would I do differently?" The people who grow fastest aren't those who do the most — they're those who learn the most from what they do.

Decoding Any Staff Designator
Military staff designators follow a consistent three-part formula. Letter = which organization/level this staff belongs to. First number = the functional area (what they do). Second number (optional) = the branch or sub-section within that function.

🔤 Prefix Letters — J · G · S · N · A · C · M · F ALL PREFIXES ▶
Reference — All Major Prefixes
Organization Level & Service Branch Designators
The prefix letter indicates which command level and which military service the staff section belongs to. The same number (e.g., 3 = Operations) means the same function regardless of letter prefix.
Prefix Stands For Used By / Level Example Commands Numbers Used
J Joint Unified & combatant commands with two or more service branches CENTCOM, INDOPACOM, SOCOM, DIA, CJCS, USFK, NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) HQ J1–J9
G General Staff Army divisions, corps, and above (General Officer-led commands) 82nd Airborne HQ, 1st Cav HQ, Army corps HQs G1–G9
S Staff Army & Marine Corps at battalion and brigade level (below division) 1-8 Infantry Bn, 2d Marines Regt, Brigade Combat Teams S1–S6 (S7–S9 uncommon)
N Navy Navy headquarters, fleet commands, and naval installations CNO staff, NAVAIR, NAVSEA, Fleet Forces Command N1–N9
A Air Force HAF (Headquarters Air Force) and major command (MAJCOM) staff HAF, ACC, AMC, AFSOC, PACAF, USAFE A1–A10
AF Air Force (alt form) Used in some Air Force numbered air force HQs and wing-level staff for formal documents 1st Air Force, 12th Air Force Same as A-series
M Marine Corps Marine Expeditionary Force (MEF) and Marine division level I MEF, II MEF, III MEF, MARFORPAC M1–M9 (MEF uses G at div, S at bn)
C Combined Multinational/coalition commands where two or more nations operate together Combined Forces Command Korea, NATO Allied Command Ops C1–C9
F Fleet / Force Navy fleet-level commands; also used for some Air Force force-level designations 3rd Fleet, 7th Fleet, U.S. Fleet Forces Command F1–F9
CG Coast Guard U.S. Coast Guard headquarters and district commands COMDT staff, Coast Guard districts CG-1 through CG-9
ⓘ Combined vs Joint: Joint (J) = multiple US military services working together. Combined (C) = multiple nations working together. A command can be both — e.g., Combined Joint Task Force = multinational + multi-service.
🔢 Functional Numbers 1 through 9 — What Each Number Means ALL NUMBERS ▶
Reference — Universal Functional Areas
Numbers are consistent across ALL prefix letters
Regardless of whether the prefix is J, G, S, N, or A — the number always means the same functional area. A J3 and an S3 both handle Operations — just at different command levels.
1
Manpower & Personnel
Human resources, strength reporting, assignments, promotions, awards, disciplinary actions, casualty reporting, morale and welfare. The "HR department" of a military headquarters. J1 · G1 · S1 · N1 · A1
2
Intelligence
All-source intelligence: HUMINT, SIGINT, GEOINT, OSINT (Open Source Intelligence), MASINT. Threat assessments, enemy order of battle, ISR (Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance), targeting. J2 · G2 · S2 · N2 · A2
3
Operations
Current and ongoing operations — the main effort of any HQ. Battle rhythm, OPORD execution, fires coordination, battle tracking, exercises, and training management. The largest and busiest staff section. J3 · G3 · S3 · N3 · A3
4
Logistics & Supply
Sustainment: supply (Class I–IX), maintenance, transportation, field services, mortuary affairs, contracting. Ensures the force has what it needs to fight and survive. J4 · G4 · S4 · N4 · A4
5
Plans & Strategy
Future operations planning — from 96 hours out through long-range strategy. Operational plans (OPLANs), concept development, war gaming, campaign design, interagency coordination. Distinct from J3 (current ops). J5 · G5 · S5 · N5 · A5
6
Communications, Signal & IT
All networks, radios, satellite comms, data links, IT infrastructure, cybersecurity, COMSEC (communications security), and information management. The military's IT department. J6 · G6 · S6 · N6 · A6
7
Training & Force Development
Exercise planning, readiness reporting, individual and collective training programs, force generation, leader development. Air Force A7 = installations & mission support. Usage varies by branch. J7 · G7 · A7
8
Financial Management & Resources
Budgeting, resource allocation, comptroller functions, program objective memoranda (POM), contracts oversight, cost analysis, financial reporting to higher commands. J8 · G8 · N8 · A8
9
Civil Affairs & Interagency
Civil-military operations, host-nation relations, NGO/IGO coordination, reconstruction, PSYOP (Psychological Operations) coordination, USAID partnerships, governance support in conflict zones. J9 · G9 · S9 · A9
🔭 Sub-Designators — The Third Digit (e.g., J63) BRANCH LEVEL ▶
Reference — Sub-Sections Within Directorates
Third Digit = Branch Within the Functional Directorate
Large headquarters (combatant commands, service HQs) further divide each directorate into branches. The third digit follows the same 1–9 logic: 1=Manpower, 2=Intel, 3=Ops, 4=Logistics within that function. Smaller units (battalions, brigades) rarely use sub-designators.
▸ UNIVERSAL SUB-DESIGNATOR LOGIC
Sub # Function Within the Directorate Example in J6
X1 Manpower & Personnel within that function — staffing, billets, HR for the directorate J61 — J6 manpower & workforce management
X2 Requirements, Architecture & Assessment — needs analysis, doctrine, policy J62 — Network architecture & requirements
X3 Operations — day-to-day execution, current operational support J63 — Network operations & comms ops center
X4 Logistics, Resources & Programs — budget, contracts, sustainment of the function J64 — IT programs, resource management
X5 Plans & Strategy — future development, long-range planning within the function J65 — Comms policy & interoperability plans
X6 Communications within the function — less common at sub-level J66 — COMSEC & crypto management
X7 Training & Exercises within the function J67 — Comms training & exercise support
X8 Financial management specific to the function J68 — IT budget & acquisition oversight
X9 Interagency / special programs within the function J69 — Coalition network integration

⚖️ Branch Comparison — Same Number, Different Context SIDE-BY-SIDE ▶
Cross-Branch Reference
How Each Branch Uses the Same Numbers Differently
The number means the same function, but the scope, size, and tools differ dramatically between a battalion S-section and a combatant command J-directorate.
▸ FUNCTION 1 — PERSONNEL
Code Level Focus & Scope
S1 Battalion (400–1000 personnel) Leave requests, promotions, awards, strength reports, casualty notification for the battalion. Usually 2–4 people.
G1 Division (10,000–20,000 personnel) Same functions but manages policy across multiple brigades. Interfaces with Army HRC (Human Resources Command).
J1 Combatant Command (multi-service, global) Manages manpower for all services assigned to the command; joint manning documents; handles inter-service personnel policy conflicts.
N1 Navy HQ Total force management for all Navy personnel: recruiting, retention, career development, diversity programs.
A1 Headquarters Air Force Manpower & personnel for the entire Air Force: force structure decisions, officer/enlisted development, Air Force Personnel Center (AFPC) oversight.
▸ FUNCTION 3 — OPERATIONS (THE MAIN EFFORT)
Code Level Focus & Scope
S3 Battalion Plans and supervises all battalion training and combat operations. Runs the battalion Tactical Operations Center (TOC). Usually a Major.
G3 Division Synchronizes maneuver, fires, aviation, and combat support across the division. Manages the Division Main CP battle rhythm.
J3 Combatant Command Executes the commander's operational concept across all services globally. Runs the 24/7 Joint Operations Center (JOC). Often a 2-star billet.
N3 Navy Fleet Fleet operational employment; ship deployment scheduling; current fleet operations and readiness.
A3 Air Force Largest Air Force staff directorate. Oversees air operations, flying hour programs, readiness, and airpower employment globally.
▸ FUNCTION 6 — COMMUNICATIONS & IT
Code Level Focus & Scope
S6 Battalion Maintains radios (SINCGARS, SOCOM radios), tactical comms, NIPR/SIPR terminal at battalion level. Often a Warrant Officer or Captain.
G6 Division Division network (Tactical LAN), frequency management, satellite terminals, Signal Battalion oversight.
J6 Combatant Command Enterprise-level network operations. Manages the Joint Information Environment (JIE); classified and unclassified networks; cyber integration with USCYBERCOM.
N6 Navy Navy enterprise networks (NMCI/ONE-Net), shipboard comms systems, spectrum management, Navy COMSEC program.
A6 Air Force AFNET, Air Force IT infrastructure, C2 (Command and Control) systems, spectrum, cyberspace capabilities integration into air operations.

🧒Reading Military Codes (Beginner)MIL • Start Here▶
BIG IDEA
Why the Letters and Numbers?
Militaries need to communicate fast and without confusion. So they standardize: a letter says which level/branch a staff section is, a number says its job, and a phonetic alphabet keeps spoken letters from being misheard over a noisy radio.
DECODE IT
Letter + Number
Read the letter, then the number. The letter is the echelon/service (S, G, J…), the number is the function (1 = people, 2 = intel, 3 = operations…). So J2 is Joint Intelligence and S4 is unit-level Logistics.
SPELL IT OUT
NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) Phonetic Alphabet
To avoid 'B' vs 'D' mix-ups, each letter gets a word: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta… 'CAT' becomes 'Charlie-Alpha-Tango.' Pilots, police, and IT support all borrow this trick for spelling things aloud.
CLOCK
24-Hour (Military) Time
No AM/PM confusion: the day runs 0000 to 2359. 1:00 PM is 1300 ('thirteen hundred'). Subtract 12 from afternoon hours to get back to a 12-hour clock.
NumberStaff Function
1Personnel (people / admin)
2Intelligence (information)
3Operations (the mission)
4Logistics (supply)
6Communications / Cyber
🎖️Ranks & Echelons (Very Basic)MIL • Start Here▶
THREE GROUPS
Enlisted, NCO, Officer
Most militaries have three broad tiers. Enlisted are the trained doers; NCOs (non-commissioned officers, like sergeants) are experienced leaders risen from the ranks; officers are commissioned leaders who plan and command. NCOs are often called ‘the backbone.’
SIZE LADDER
From Squad to Division
Units nest like Russian dolls, each led by a more senior person: a handful of troops form a squad, squads form a platoon, platoons a company, and so on up. Bigger unit = higher-ranking commander.
Unit (Army, roughly)SizeLed By (roughly)
Squad~8–12Sergeant
Platoon~30–40Lieutenant
Company~100–150Captain
Battalion~500–800Lt. Colonel
Brigade~3,000+Colonel
Division~10,000+Major General
📻 Military Communication Standards — Clear, Concise, Correct MIL • Foundation ▶
WHY MILITARY COMMS
When Miscommunication Costs Lives
Military communication standards were designed for high-stress, noisy, partial-information environments where a misunderstood message can have catastrophic consequences. These principles apply directly to IT operations, incident response, and emergency management — anywhere clarity under pressure matters.
SALUTE REPORT
Size · Activity · Location · Unit · Time · Equipment
A SALUTE report is a standardized format for reporting enemy contact or suspicious activity. Gives responders exactly what they need, in the right order, nothing extra.
LetterFieldExample
SSize3 individuals
AActivityMoving northbound along the road
LLocationGrid 123456, 500m east of checkpoint
UUnit/UniformCivilian clothing, no visible insignia
TTime0830 local
EEquipmentArmed, backpacks, one vehicle
IT application: Use SALUTE-style structured reporting for security incidents — "3 systems affected, lateral movement detected, VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 10, identified at 14:32 UTC, using PSExec and Mimikatz."
SITREP
Situation Report — Periodic Status Update
A SITREP (Situation Report) is a standardized periodic update on current status. Key elements:
Current situation — what is happening right now
What has been accomplished — progress since last report
Next actions — what you're about to do
Issues/requests — what you need from higher command
Format matters: be concise, use the same structure every time, report at agreed intervals (even "no change" is information).
RADIO PROCEDURE
Pro-Words (Procedural Words)
Pro-WordMeaning
OVERMy transmission is complete; I expect a reply
OUTConversation is finished; no reply expected
ROGERI received and understood your last message
WILCOI understand and WILL comply (includes Roger)
SAY AGAINRepeat your last transmission (not "repeat" — that has an artillery meaning)
BREAKShort pause in a long transmission
STANDBYWait, I'll get back to you
NEGATIVENo / incorrect
AFFIRMYes / correct
BREVITY IN ALL COMMS
Say It Once, Say It Right
Military communication demands brevity because radio time is shared, batteries die, and enemies can intercept. The principle: say everything necessary, nothing more. In IT: this same discipline makes incident bridge calls, escalation emails, and Slack channels dramatically more effective. State the problem, the impact, what you've tried, what you need — then stop talking.
🎯 OODA (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) Loop — Decision-Making Under Pressure MILITARY • Decision Frameworks ▶
WHAT IS THE OODA LOOP
The Framework Behind Fast, Good Decisions
Developed by Air Force Colonel John Boyd after studying why American pilots won more dogfights despite flying inferior aircraft in Korea. The answer: they could cycle through decisions faster. Boyd codified this as the OODA Loop — Observe, Orient, Decide, Act. The fighter who gets inside the opponent's OODA loop wins. Directly applicable to incident response, red teaming, and any competitive situation.
THE FOUR PHASES
OODA — Breaking Down Each Stage
PhaseWhat HappensCybersecurity Application
ObserveGather information from the environment. Sensory data, signals, telemetry — raw uninterpreted facts.SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) alerts, network telemetry, threat intel feeds, user reports
OrientMake sense of what you observed. Filter through mental models, prior experience, cultural tradition, analysis. This is the most important phase — your worldview shapes everything.Apply threat knowledge (ATT&CK TTPs), understand adversary motivation, contextualize the alert
DecideChoose a course of action from available options based on your orientation.Contain vs. monitor, escalate vs. handle, which remediation path
ActExecute the decision. Then immediately begin observing again — it's a loop.Block IP (Internet Protocol), isolate host, patch, notify stakeholders
IT APPLICATION
Incident Response Through the OODA Lens
The fastest incident responders have fast OODA loops — not because they skip steps, but because their Orient phase is automatic from experience and training. This is why tabletop exercises, purple team exercises, and studying past incidents matter: they pre-load the Orient phase.
GoalHow to Achieve It
Speed up ObserveBetter tooling: more log sources, better SIEM, endpoint visibility (EDR)
Speed up OrientTraining, experience, runbooks, tabletop exercises, threat intel
Speed up DecidePre-approved playbooks, clear authority (who can approve isolation?), escalation paths
Speed up ActAutomation (SOAR), prepared scripts, pre-staged remediation tools
Disrupt attacker's loopDeception (honeypots), rapid changes (rotate credentials), unpredictable responses
📋 Commander's Intent — Empowering Action Without Micromanaging MILITARY • Leadership ▶
THE CONCEPT
Two Levels Up, Two Levels Down
In military doctrine, every order includes Commander's Intent — a clear statement of the end state (what does success look like?) and purpose (why are we doing this?). When the plan breaks down (and it always does — "no plan survives first contact with the enemy"), subordinates can make independent decisions that align with the intent rather than freezing to wait for orders.
The rule: know your commander's intent two levels up (why your boss's boss wants this), and ensure your subordinates know yours two levels down. This creates adaptive, decentralized execution.
IT APPLICATION
How Commander's Intent Applies to Tech Teams
Military ConceptIT/Tech Equivalent
Commander's IntentBusiness goal behind a project — "why are we building this?" Engineers who know the why make better tradeoff decisions when specs change
Plan breaks downRequirements change mid-sprint, production incident during deploy, API (Application Programming Interface) partner goes down
Decentralized executionOn-call engineers making incident decisions without waiting for management approval
Two levels upDevelopers understanding the business context; analysts understanding org risk tolerance
Two levels downTeam leads ensuring ICs (Individual Contributor) understand the outcome, not just the task
MISSION-TYPE ORDERS
Tell Them What and Why — Not Always How
The German military concept of Auftragstaktik (mission tactics): give subordinates the objective and constraints, then trust them to figure out the method. This produces faster, more adaptive results than prescriptive orders — because the person closest to the problem has the most relevant information.
Applied to IT: instead of "run these exact five commands in this order," a good manager says "we need the backup restored and the service healthy before 8am Monday — you have authority to make it happen." The engineer has context the manager doesn't.
📝 After-Action Review — Learning From Every Event MILITARY • Continuous Improvement ▶
WHAT IS AN AAR
The Army's Structured Debrief
The After-Action Review (AAR) is a U.S. Army practice for learning from any event — a mission, an exercise, a failure. It's a structured, honest discussion conducted immediately afterward while memories are fresh. The civilian tech world adopted it as the "post-mortem" or "retrospective." It's one of the highest-leverage habits a team can build: every incident becomes a lesson instead of just a scar.
THE FOUR QUESTIONS
The Core of Every AAR
QuestionPurpose
1. What was supposed to happen?Establish the plan/expectation
2. What actually happened?Establish the facts, honestly
3. Why was there a difference?Root cause analysis — the real learning
4. What do we do differently next time?Actionable improvements, assigned owners
THE BLAMELESS PRINCIPLE
Hunt for Causes, Not Culprits
The single most important rule: AARs (and post-mortems) must be blameless. The moment people fear punishment, they hide information — and you lose the lessons. The premise is that everyone acted reasonably given what they knew at the time. The goal is to fix the system (better tooling, clearer process, more training) that allowed the mistake, not to punish the person. This maps directly to IT incident post-mortems: when engineers can speak freely about what went wrong, the organization actually improves.
Blameless (Good)Blameful (Toxic)
"The deploy process let an untested change reach prod""Bob broke production"
"Our runbook was unclear about the rollback step""You should have known better"
People share mistakes openly → org learnsPeople hide mistakes → org repeats them
🧭 Troop Leading Procedures — A Framework for Planning Anything MILITARY • Planning ▶
THE 8 STEPS (BMNT)
How Small-Unit Leaders Plan and Prepare
Troop Leading Procedures (TLP) are the 8-step process small-unit leaders use to plan and execute a mission. The genius is in step 3 — issue a warning order early so the team can start preparing in parallel while you finish planning. This concept maps perfectly to running an IT project or incident response.
StepMilitaryIT/Project Equivalent
1. Receive the missionGet the order/taskReceive the ticket/project/incident
2. Issue a warning orderAlert the team early"Heads up team, big task coming — start prepping"
3. Make a tentative planInitial course of actionDraft approach, identify resources
4. Initiate movementStart positioningProvision environments, gather access
5. Conduct reconnaissanceRecon the terrainInvestigate the system/codebase/logs
6. Complete the planFinalize detailsFinalize the runbook/design
7. Issue the orderBrief the teamKickoff: assign roles, confirm understanding
8. Supervise & refineExecute, adjust, rehearseExecute, monitor, adapt as you learn
PARALLEL PLANNING
Don't Make Your Team Wait on You
The biggest lesson from TLP for civilian work: warning orders enable parallel work. A weak leader plans everything in silence, then dumps a finished plan on the team at the last minute. A strong leader gives early, partial information ("we'll be migrating the database this weekend — start reviewing the schema") so the team prepares simultaneously. This compresses timelines dramatically and respects your team's ability to contribute.
📡 PACE Planning — Redundancy by Design MILITARY • Resilience ▶
WHAT IS PACE
Primary, Alternate, Contingency, Emergency
PACE is a military communications planning method: for any critical capability, you pre-plan four methods ranked by preference. If the Primary fails, you fall back to Alternate, then Contingency, then Emergency — no panic, no improvising, because the fallbacks were decided in advance. It's a discipline of building redundancy before you need it, and it maps perfectly to IT resilience planning.
LevelMeaningComms ExampleIT Example
PrimaryBest, normal methodEncrypted radioSlack / primary monitoring
AlternateNearly as goodSatellite phoneEmail / secondary tool
ContingencyWorkable but degradedRunner with written messagePhone bridge / SMS
EmergencyLast resortSignal flaresPersonal phones / physical meet
PACE FOR IT
Apply It to Anything Critical
The brilliance of PACE is that it forces you to ask "what if this fails?" three times — before the crisis. During a major incident, your primary tools may be down (what if the outage takes out Slack and the monitoring dashboard?). A PACE plan means the team already knows where to go.
CapabilityA PACE Plan Might Be
Incident communicationP: Slack → A: Email → C: Conference bridge → E: Personal cell phones
AuthenticationP: SSO (Single Sign-On) → A: Local admin → C: Break-glass account → E: Console/physical access
Internet connectivityP: Primary ISP (Internet Service Provider) → A: Secondary ISP → C: Cellular failover → E: Manual hotspot
Backups/restoreP: Hot replica → A: Cloud backup → C: Offsite tape → E: Rebuild from IaC (Infrastructure as Code)
RISK MANAGEMENT WORKSHEET
The Military's 5-Step Risk Process
The Army's Composite Risk Management (now Risk Management, ATP 5-19) is a simple, repeatable process used before any operation. It mirrors how IT teams assess change risk — and it's worth internalizing as a mental checklist before any risky action.
StepActionIT Parallel
1. Identify hazardsWhat could go wrong?Threat model the change
2. Assess hazardsHow likely × how bad?Risk = likelihood × impact
3. Develop controlsHow do we reduce risk?Mitigations, rollback plan, testing
4. Implement controlsPut them in placeApply guardrails, schedule maintenance window
5. Supervise & evaluateMonitor, adjust, learnWatch metrics, AAR afterward
🎖️ Leadership — Styles, Mission Command & Cohesion MILITARY • Leadership ▶
LEADERSHIP STYLES
Match the Style to the Situation
There's no single "best" leadership style — effective leaders adapt to the situation, the people, and the stakes. The military teaches this explicitly, and it maps directly to leading technical teams and incidents.
StyleWhen It WorksIT Example
Directive (autocratic)Crisis, no time to debate, clear dangerActive incident — "isolate that host NOW"
ParticipativeSkilled team, time to deliberateArchitecture decisions, planning
DelegativeHighly capable, trusted people"You own this project — keep me posted"
TransformationalNeed to inspire change/growthDriving a culture or major modernization
ServantDay-to-day team enablementRemoving blockers so the team can deliver
The skill is the switch: a leader who is directive during an outage but participative in planning earns far more than one stuck in a single mode. Reading which the moment needs is the art.
MISSION COMMAND
Decentralized Execution Through Trust
Mission Command is the modern military's core leadership philosophy: leaders provide clear intent and the "why," then empower subordinates to use disciplined initiative to achieve it — without waiting for detailed orders. It rests on mutual trust, shared understanding, and accepting prudent risk. In fast-moving situations (combat or a production incident), the people closest to the problem must be able to act. Micromanagement is too slow and doesn't scale.
PrincipleMeaning
Build cohesive teams through trustTrust is earned over time; it's the foundation
Create shared understandingEveryone knows the goal and the why
Provide clear commander's intentThe end state, so people can adapt the how
Exercise disciplined initiativeAct toward the intent without being told
Use mission ordersSay what + why, not every how
Accept prudent riskPerfect certainty never comes; act anyway
UNIT COHESION
What Makes Teams Perform Under Stress
The military invests heavily in cohesion because cohesive units perform dramatically better under pressure — and the research (e.g., Google's Project Aristotle) found the same for tech teams: the #1 predictor of high-performing teams is psychological safety — members feel safe to take risks, admit mistakes, and speak up. This connects directly to blameless post-mortems: people who fear punishment hide problems, and hidden problems compound. Leaders build cohesion by sharing hardship, being competent and fair, communicating honestly, and putting the team's welfare above their own ego. Take care of your people, and they'll take care of the mission.
Beginner OPSEC – Operational Security in Cyber & Real Life
Core Concept
What Is OPSEC?
OPSEC (Operational Security) originated in the military but now applies universally to anyone who needs to protect sensitive information or activities from adversaries.

The core question: "What information, if known by the wrong person, would allow them to harm me, my organisation, or my mission?"

The five-step OPSEC process:
1. Identify critical information — what do I need to protect? (credentials, plans, personnel, locations).
2. Analyse threats — who wants this information and why? (criminals, competitors, nation-states, insiders).
3. Analyse vulnerabilities — where could I accidentally expose this? (social media, email, public logs).
4. Assess risk — likelihood × impact for each vulnerability.
5. Apply countermeasures — reduce the vulnerability (encryption, access control, need-to-know, training).

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — if sensitive information belongs to your organisation, don't share it even with colleagues who don't need it. Need-to-know is a core OPSEC principle.
Digital OPSEC
Personal Digital Security Hygiene
Every IT professional is a target. Apply OPSEC to yourself:
PERSONAL OPSEC CHECKLIST ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── CREDENTIALS [ ] Use a password manager (Bitwarden, 1Password) — unique passwords everywhere [ ] Enable MFA on every account that supports it (TOTP app, not SMS) [ ] Never reuse passwords — one breach = one compromised account, not many COMMUNICATIONS [ ] Sensitive work: use encrypted email (ProtonMail) or end-to-end encrypted chat [ ] Assume corporate email is monitored and archived [ ] Don't discuss sensitive projects on public Slack workspaces / Discord SOCIAL MEDIA [ ] Don't post photos that reveal physical security details (badge readers, screens) [ ] Job posting recon: attackers read your LinkedIn to map tech stack [ ] Don't announce travel dates publicly — burglars and social engineers note it DEVICE SECURITY [ ] Full-disk encryption on laptops (BitLocker/FileVault/LUKS) [ ] Screen lock within 2 minutes of inactivity [ ] VPN on untrusted Wi-Fi (coffee shops, hotels, airports) [ ] Webcam cover when not in use WORK HABITS [ ] Clear desk policy — sensitive docs face down or locked away [ ] Shred documents before disposal; don't put them in recycling [ ] Be aware of shoulder surfing in public spaces [ ] Verify caller identity before providing information (voice phishing = vishing)
Org OPSEC
Protecting Sensitive Information at Scale
Organisational OPSEC controls applied in enterprise security:

• Information classification: Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted — policies dictate how each is handled.
• Data Loss Prevention (DLP): software that blocks classified files from being emailed externally or uploaded to personal cloud storage.
• Privileged Access Workstations (PAW): a dedicated, hardened device used only for admin tasks — never for browsing or email.
• Air-gapped networks: classified systems with no internet connection; data moves via signed, approved media only.
• Red team deception: honeytokens — fake credentials or files planted in your system; if accessed, you know an attacker has them.
# Create a honeytoken file (plant it; alert if accessed) # On Linux: use inotifywait to alert when the file is read touch /home/admin/.aws/credentials_BACKUP_2023 inotifywait -m /home/admin/.aws/credentials_BACKUP_2023 -e access | while read path action file; do echo "HONEYTOKEN ACCESSED: $path$file at $(date)" | mail -s "ALERT: Honeytoken read" security-team@corp.example.com done # AWS honeytoken: create an IAM key that only fires CloudTrail events # Canarytokens.org generates free honeytokens for: # AWS keys, Word docs, PDFs, URLs, DNS names
Mindset
"Assume Breach" – The Modern Security Posture
"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — but in security, the one assumption you should make is that you have already been breached.

The Assume Breach philosophy:
• Design systems as if an attacker already has a foothold — use micro-segmentation, least privilege, and mutual TLS (Transport Layer Security) between services.
• Invest in detection and response as much as prevention — because prevention eventually fails.
• Run red-team exercises to find gaps before real attackers do.
• Know your mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to respond (MTTR) — measure and improve them continuously.

You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — an attacker who got in through a phishing email is not your fault; the speed and quality of your response is entirely within your control.
Beginner Leadership – Military Principles Applied to IT Teams
Core Concept
Why Military Leadership Models Translate
Military leadership doctrine has been refined over centuries under the highest-stakes conditions imaginable — and a surprising amount of it maps directly onto leading an IT team through an outage, a project crunch, or simply day-to-day operations.

Both environments share key features: high-pressure decisions with incomplete information, the need to coordinate people who can't all see the whole picture, and consequences that compound when communication breaks down.

You don't need a title to lead — the engineer who keeps a calm head during an outage and gets the team organised is leading, regardless of what the org chart says.
Commander's Intent
"Commander's Intent" – Goals Over Scripts
In the military, a leader gives Commander's Intent: a clear statement of the end goal and the "why" — not a rigid step-by-step script. This way, when the situation changes (and it always does), subordinates can adapt without waiting for new orders.

In IT, this looks like:
Bad delegation: "Run these five exact commands in this order."
Good delegation: "We need this service back online with zero data loss — here's what I know about the failure. Use your judgment; call me if you hit something I haven't covered."

Good intent-based delegation does two things: it grows your team's capability, and it means the mission survives even if the leader is unreachable — exactly when it matters most (3 AM incidents).
After-Action Review
The After-Action Review (AAR) Process
The military's After-Action Review is the direct ancestor of the modern "blameless postmortem." Four simple questions, asked after every significant event:
THE AFTER-ACTION REVIEW — FOUR QUESTIONS ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 1. WHAT WAS SUPPOSED TO HAPPEN? "The deploy was supposed to complete in 10 minutes with zero downtime." 2. WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED? "The deploy took 47 minutes and caused a 12-minute outage." 3. WHY WAS THERE A DIFFERENCE? "The database migration locked a table longer than expected because the table had grown 3x since the migration was last tested." 4. WHAT WILL WE DO DIFFERENTLY NEXT TIME? "Test migrations against a copy of production-sized data. Add a pre-flight check that estimates migration duration. Add an automatic abort if a migration runs longer than 5 minutes." RULES THAT MAKE IT WORK: - No rank in the room — the newest hire's observation counts as much as the senior engineer's - Focus on the SYSTEM, not the PERSON ("the process allowed this" not "Dave messed up") - Write it down — verbal lessons evaporate; written ones compound
Mission Mindset
Putting It All Together — Leading Through Chaos
These three phrases — central to this entire guide — are themselves leadership principles refined into short, memorable forms (the way good military doctrine often is):

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — a leader protects their team's focus. Shield people from drama and scope creep that doesn't serve the mission; redirect it to whoever owns it.

"Assume makes an ass out of you and me" — a leader verifies before committing resources. "I think the backup ran" is not the same as "I confirmed the backup completed and is restorable."

"You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards" — a leader's real value often shows after something goes wrong: staying calm, organising the recovery, protecting the team from blame spirals, and turning the failure into the team's next strength.

Master these three, lead with clear intent, and run honest AARs — and you'll out-perform leaders with twice your technical knowledge but none of this foundation.
Beginner Translating Military Experience into IT Resume Language
Why this matters

The translation gap is real — and fixable

A hiring manager reading "Maintained communications equipment for a forward-deployed unit under field conditions" may not immediately connect that to "can troubleshoot hardware, manage inventory, and keep systems running with no backup support nearby." The skills transfer; the vocabulary doesn't, automatically. Translating your experience into civilian IT language isn't dishonesty or exaggeration — it's making sure the reader understands what you actually did.

Concept

Side-by-side: military experience to IT resume language

What you didHow it translates
Stood watch / monitored systems on shift rotations"Performed continuous system monitoring and incident triage across rotating shift schedules — directly applicable to SOC/NOC environments"
Maintained or repaired communications/radio/radar equipment"Diagnosed and resolved hardware faults under time pressure with limited resources — comparable to field/desktop support and infrastructure troubleshooting"
Managed property, parts inventory, or supply accountability"Tracked and reconciled asset inventories using accountability systems — transferable to IT asset management (ITAM)"
Trained junior personnel on procedures or equipment"Developed and delivered technical training to incoming team members — translates to documentation and knowledge-transfer responsibilities"
Operated under a clearance, handled sensitive information"Held [clearance level]; managed sensitive information per strict handling protocols — directly relevant to compliance-driven environments (GRC, government contracting)"
Followed and enforced strict procedures / checklists"Executed and audited compliance with documented standard operating procedures — maps to change management, runbooks, and audit readiness"
Concept

Lead with impact, not just duties

Civilian resumes reward quantified outcomes over lists of responsibilities. Compare:

# Weak — describes a duty, says nothing about the outcome
"Responsible for maintaining unit IT equipment."

# Strong — same underlying experience, framed around impact
"Maintained 40+ workstations and network devices supporting a 120-person
unit with zero unplanned downtime over a 12-month deployment, reducing
average ticket resolution time by replacing ad-hoc fixes with a
documented troubleshooting checklist."

If you don't have exact numbers, reasonable estimates are fine — "approximately," "more than," and "supported a team of roughly X" all read as honest and specific. What recruiters are scanning for is scale and outcome, not decimal-point precision.

Mindset

Not my circus, not my monkey — but also, it's now your circus

Military culture often instills "stay in your lane, don't volunteer for extra work" as survival wisdom — and that instinct can undersell you in interviews. The civilian IT world rewards people who *did* step outside their narrow job description: the radio tech who also fixed everyone's laptop issues, the supply clerk who built a spreadsheet that automated half the unit's paperwork. Those moments where you picked up something that "wasn't your job" are often the most resume-worthy stories you have. Don't bury them out of habit.

Beginner Using the GI Bill and Tuition Assistance for IT Certifications
Why this matters

Education benefits are some of the best-kept "secrets" in the military community

Many service members and veterans leave significant education benefits unused — not from lack of eligibility, but from not knowing the programs exist, assuming the paperwork is too complicated, or believing (often incorrectly) that the benefit only covers traditional four-year degrees. IT certifications are frequently fundable through these same programs, and stacking several certs can be a faster, cheaper path into the field than a full degree program — especially if your goal is to start working sooner rather than later.

Concept

The major programs, at a glance

ProgramWho it's generally forWhat it can cover
Post-9/11 GI BillVeterans and some active-duty members meeting service requirementsTuition, housing allowance (BAH), and — important for this audience — licensing & certification exam reimbursement
Tuition Assistance (TA)Active-duty service members, by branch programCourses and, in some programs, certification training while still serving
VR&E (Chapter 31)Veterans with a service-connected disability affecting employabilityTraining, certification costs, and career counseling support — often more comprehensive than people expect
State veteran education benefitsVaries — many states offer additional programs on top of federal benefitsVaries by state; worth checking your state's department of veterans affairs directly

Note specifically: the Post-9/11 GI Bill's licensing and certification reimbursement is separate from its tuition coverage and is often overlooked — it can directly fund the exam fee for things like CompTIA (Computing Technology Industry Association) Security+, AWS (Amazon Web Services) certifications, or Cisco credentials, without needing to be enrolled in a degree program at all.

Hands-on

A practical first-steps checklist

# 1. Confirm your eligibility and remaining benefit balance
#    — VA.gov and your installation's education center are the
#    authoritative sources; don't rely on secondhand information

# 2. Ask SPECIFICALLY about certification/licensing reimbursement
#    — this is frequently a different process than degree-program
#    tuition, with its own forms and approval steps

# 3. Confirm the certification you want is on an approved list
#    — most IT vendor certs (CompTIA, AWS, Microsoft, Cisco) are
#    commonly approved, but verify with your education office BEFORE
#    you pay out of pocket and try to get reimbursed after the fact

# 4. Keep every receipt, confirmation email, and exam voucher
#    — reimbursement claims move much faster with complete
#    documentation than with "I'm pretty sure I paid for that"

# 5. Talk to your installation's education office or a
#    Veteran Service Organization (VSO) — they exist specifically
#    to help you navigate this, and the help is free
Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me — verify your specific situation

Benefit rules change, vary by branch, by discharge status, by years of service, and by which specific program you're using — what worked for a friend who left the service three years ago may not apply to you today. Don't assume you're ineligible because of something you heard secondhand, and don't assume a benefit covers something without confirming it in writing first. A 20-minute conversation with an education counselor or VSO representative can save you from either missing out on something you qualified for, or getting an unpleasant reimbursement surprise after the fact.

Beginner Networking Events Without the Awkwardness – A Veteran's Field Guide
Why this matters

"Networking" sounds fake until it gets you a job

Plenty of capable people — veterans especially, coming from a culture that often values humility and "letting your work speak for itself" — find the idea of "networking" deeply uncomfortable, even slightly dishonest-feeling. Reframe it: networking is just having genuine conversations with people who do interesting work, and staying in touch. The job-finding part is a side effect of doing that consistently — not the awkward main event it's often made out to be.

Concept

Where IT networking actually happens (most of it isn't fancy galas)

VenueWhat it actually looks likeWhy it works
Local user groups / meetupsA monthly gathering of people who use the same tools (Linux, AWS, cybersecurity) — usually free, usually casualLow-pressure, recurring — you become a familiar face over a few months without ever "selling" yourself
Veteran-focused tech programsOrganizations specifically built to connect transitioning service members with IT employers and mentorsEveryone there already understands your background — no translation needed, no awkward "so, tell me about your service" small talk
Online communitiesSubreddits, Discord servers, LinkedIn groups focused on specific certifications or technologiesLower social pressure than in-person events — you can build relationships entirely on the strength of your questions and contributions
Certification study groupsPeople preparing for the same exam, often meeting weekly to quiz each otherBuilt-in shared goal — conversation starts itself, friendships form naturally around mutual struggle and progress
Hands-on

A simple script for your first conversation (genuinely, not cynically)

# The goal of a first conversation is NOT "get a job out of this person."
# It's "have one genuine, useful exchange." That's it. Everything
# else follows from doing that consistently, many times, over months.

# An opener that works because it's true and specific:
"Hey, I'm transitioning out of [your role] and getting into IT —
 working through my Security+ right now. What got you started
 in this field?"

# A good follow-up that shows you're actually listening:
"That's interesting — how is that different day-to-day from
 what I'd expect coming from [your background]?"

# The single most useful thing you can do afterward — not
# during the conversation, but within 48 hours of it:
"Hey [name], really enjoyed talking about [specific thing they
 said] — wanted to say thanks for the perspective. I'll let you
 know how the Security+ exam goes!"

# That last message is the entire "secret" — most people never
# follow up at all, which means simply doing it puts you ahead
# of nearly everyone else they met that night.
Mindset

Not my circus, not my monkey — but this circus is worth joining

It's tempting to think "I'll network once I actually have something impressive to show" — but that backwards thinking keeps a lot of talented people invisible right when visibility would help them most. The people who'll eventually want to help you get hired are the same people you'd be meeting now, while you're still learning. Showing up consistently while you're a beginner — asking good questions, being genuinely curious, following up — builds the exact relationships that turn into opportunities later. You don't need to be impressive yet. You need to be present, and real.

🏷️ Classification Levels & Markings — Damage, Not Importance MILITARY • Classified Handling ▶
Core Concept

The level is a damage estimate, not a measure of how interesting it is

Every classification level in the US system is defined by one question: what would reasonably be expected to happen to national security if this were disclosed to someone unauthorized? Not "how secret does this feel", not "how senior is the person who wrote it" — the expected damage. Executive Order 13526 sets three levels and nothing else. There is no "Super Secret", no "Eyes Only" level, and no fourth tier above Top Secret. What people mean when they say something is "higher than Top Secret" is usually a compartment (SCI or a SAP) layered on top of Top Secret, which restricts who may see it — not a new level.

Reference

The three levels and the standard behind each

LevelDamage standard if disclosedColour convention
Top SecretExceptionally grave damage to national securityOrange
SecretSerious damage to national securityRed
ConfidentialDamage to national securityBlue
CUI (Controlled Unclassified Information)Not classified at all — unclassified information that still has handling rules under law or policyPurple banner in DoD (Department of Defense) usage
UnclassifiedNo damage standard; may still be marked to prove it was reviewedGreen

Learn the three adjectives in order — damage, serious damage, exceptionally grave damage. They come up in briefings, on exams and in adjudication language, and they are the actual legal test.

Concept

What a properly marked document carries

MarkingWhereWhat it does
Banner lineTop and bottom of every pageStates the overall classification of the whole document — always the highest level anything in it reaches
Portion markingStart of every paragraph, title, bullet, table and caption(U), (C), (S), (TS) — so a reader can extract the unclassified parts without guessing
Classification authority blockBottom of the first pageClassified By, Derived From, Reason, Declassify On — who decided, on what basis, and when it stops
Declassification instructionIn the authority blockA date, an event, or 50X1-HUM-style exemption codes. "Indefinitely" is not an option
The trap

Aggregation — three unclassified facts can add up to a classified one

The single most common way careful people get this wrong is assuming that a document made entirely of unclassified paragraphs is unclassified. It often is not. Compiling individually harmless facts — a schedule, a location, a capability, a name — can reveal something none of them revealed alone, and the compilation is classified at the level of what it reveals. This is why the banner line is not computed by scanning the portion marks for the highest one; it is a judgement made by someone with derivative classification authority. If you are compiling, ask. The same logic is why an unclassified network can still be the wrong place for a spreadsheet of unclassified rows.

In practice

Why this sits on an IT site

On a cleared contract you will meet these markings before you touch a system, and they drive technical decisions you will be asked to implement: which network a workload runs on, which drives may be moved between rooms, what a data-loss-prevention rule looks for, and what your backup retention may legally do. DISA (Defense Information Systems Agency) STIGs (Security Technical Implementation Guide), CMMC (Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification) and media sanitisation standards are the machine half of this; the markings are the human half, and the human half is the part that gets people walked out of the building.

📄 Cover Sheets — SF (Standard Form) 703, SF 704 & SF 705 MILITARY • Classified Handling ▶
Core Concept

The colour is the control

A cover sheet is a single sheet of coloured card stapled or clipped to the front of a classified document while it is out of the safe. Its whole job is to be visible from across a room and from a doorway: it stops a passer-by reading the first page, and it tells anyone who walks in what protection the stack in front of you requires. The colours are standardised precisely so recognition needs no reading — you are meant to identify the level at a glance, at an angle, upside down, from the far side of the office.

Reference

The three cover sheets

FormLevelColour
SF 703Top SecretOrange
SF 704SecretRed
SF 705ConfidentialBlue

Numbers ascend as classification descends — 703 is the highest level, 705 the lowest. That is the opposite of most people's first guess, and it is the detail that shows up on tests. The mnemonic that sticks: 703 is the hottest number and orange is the hottest colour.

Reference

On and off — when a cover sheet applies

SituationCover sheetWhy
Document out on a desk, in useOnThis is the case it exists for
Being hand-carried within a facilityOnPlus whatever the local policy requires for transit
Left unattended for any periodShould not happenA cover sheet is not a substitute for the safe — it buys seconds, not permission
Stored in an approved containerOff (per local policy)The container is the control now; sheets in the safe just waste them
Being mailed or shippedOff — inner wrapper markings apply insteadTransmission has its own double-wrapping rules; a cover sheet on the outside would advertise the contents
DestroyedOff — sheets are reusableThe cover sheet itself is unclassified
The trap

The top sheet must match the highest thing in the stack

Put a Secret document on top of a Top Secret one, and a red SF 704 now sits over a stack that is really Top Secret. Everyone who glances at it — including you, in a hurry, at the end of a long day — will treat it as Secret. This is the mechanism behind a large share of real handling violations, and it is not an exotic failure: it is what happens when someone tidies a desk. The cover sheet describes the stack, not the page it is stapled to. If the stack changes, the sheet changes.

The same reasoning explains a rule that surprises newcomers: a cover sheet is never the marking of record. Removing it does not declassify anything. The banner lines on the pages are the marking; the sheet is a warning label.

💾 Media & Equipment Labels — SF (Standard Form) 706 Through SF 712 MILITARY • Classified Handling ▶
Core Concept

Media inherits the classification of the highest data ever written to it

A drive is not classified by what is on it now — it is classified by the highest level it has ever processed, until it is sanitised or destroyed by an approved method. Deleting the file does not lower the label. Reformatting does not lower the label. This is why a labelled drive that "only has unclassified stuff on it now" is still handled at its label, and why the labels are adhesive and meant to stay put.

Reference

The label series

FormMarksColourNote
SF 706Top SecretOrangeMatches the SF 703 cover sheet colour
SF 707SecretRedMatches SF 704
SF 708ConfidentialBlueMatches SF 705
SF 709ClassifiedPurpleLevel not yet determined — a holding label, not a permanent state
SF 710UnclassifiedGreenOnly required in mixed environments, so that "no label" never means "probably fine"
SF 711Data Descriptor—Not a level: records dates, content description, compartments and handling caveats
SF 712Classified SCIYellowSensitive Compartmented Information — a compartment on top of a level
The trap

SF 710 green exists because "unlabelled" is ambiguous

In a room where classified and unclassified media sit side by side, an unlabelled drive is not evidence of anything — it might be unclassified, or it might be classified media someone forgot to label. Marking the unclassified media too removes the ambiguity entirely: in a properly run mixed environment, every piece of media carries a label, so an unlabelled one is immediately an anomaly worth stopping for. The green label is not bureaucratic excess; it is what makes the absence of a label meaningful.

In practice

What this means for the IT side of the job

Purple SF 709 is the label you reach for when a system has processed data of unknown provenance — a machine that touched something it should not have, pending determination. It is deliberately a temporary state; a room full of purple labels means a backlog, not a filing system. And SF 711's data descriptor is where the useful operational detail lives: dates, compartments, and the caveats that decide whether a drive may cross a room, a building or a boundary. Sanitisation and destruction standards — degaussing, approved shredders, and why a "secure erase" is not automatically sufficient for classified media — are the technical follow-on, and they live in the operations material on this site.

🔐 Container & End-of-Day Forms — SF (Standard Form) 700, SF 701 & SF 702 MILITARY • Classified Handling ▶
Core Concept

Three forms, three different questions

These get confused constantly because they all live on or near the same safe. They answer different questions: who owns this container and what is its combination (SF 700), did we secure the whole room tonight (SF 701), and did anyone open, close or check this specific container (SF 702).

Reference

The three container forms

FormNameAnswersLives
SF 700Security Container InformationWho is responsible, how to reach them after hours, and — in a sealed envelope — the combinationInside the container's locking drawer; the sealed part is stored at the classification of the container's contents
SF 701Activity Security ChecklistWas the area secured — safes locked, desks clear, screens off, windows and doors checkedBy the exit, signed at end of day
SF 702Security Container Check SheetEvery open, every close, and the independent end-of-day check, each with initials and timeOn the container itself
The trap

The second signature is the whole point of SF 702

An SF 702 has a column for the person who closed the container and a separate column for the person who checked that it was closed. Signing both yourself defeats the control entirely — the design assumes the closer is the one most likely to believe a drawer is latched when it is not, because they are the one who just latched it. Two people, two initials. The same logic explains why the sheet stays with the container rather than in a binder: the record has to be where the check happens.

A missed check is not a paperwork slip. It triggers a security inspection of the container, and — because nobody can prove the contents were protected overnight — the possibility of a reportable incident. That is the honest reason the form is taken seriously by people who otherwise dislike forms.

In practice

A change of combination is a change of SF 700

Combinations change when someone with access departs, when the container is compromised, at the interval local policy sets, and whenever the container is taken out of service. Each of those means a new SF 700 with a newly sealed envelope — and the old one destroyed, not filed. The parallel to IT is exact: the SF 700 is a credential record, the sealed envelope is an escrow, and the offboarding rule is the same one that should already be rotating shared credentials when a person leaves a team.

📋 Clearance Paperwork — SF (Standard Form) 86, SF 312 & SF 714 MILITARY • Classified Handling ▶
Reference

The three forms you will actually be handed

FormWhat it isWhen
SF 86Questionnaire for National Security Positions — the long one: residences, employment, foreign contacts, finances, substance use, police recordBefore investigation; updated at reinvestigation
SF 312Classified Information Nondisclosure Agreement — the binding contract you sign before accessAt indoctrination, before you see anything
SF 714Financial Disclosure — required for some programs and compartmentsProgram-specific, alongside or after SF 86
Core Concept

A clearance is eligibility. It is not permission

Three conditions must all hold before anyone may see a classified thing: an appropriate clearance level, a signed SF 312, and a demonstrated need to know. The third is the one people forget, and it is not a formality. A Top Secret clearance does not entitle its holder to read a Top Secret document about a program they have no role in — and asking a colleague to "just tell me the gist" is a request to commit a violation, however casually it is meant. Need-to-know is judged per item, by the holder of the information, every time.

Reference

The adjudicative guidelines — what is actually assessed

GuidelineConcern
Allegiance · Foreign influence · Foreign preferenceDivided loyalty, or family and financial ties that create leverage
Personal conductIncluding lying on the SF 86 itself
Financial considerationsUnmanageable debt as a motive; the concern is pressure, not poverty
Alcohol · Drug involvement · Psychological conditionsJudgement and reliability — treatment sought voluntarily is generally mitigating, not disqualifying
Criminal conduct · Handling protected information · Outside activities · IT systems misuseDemonstrated rule-following, especially with information already entrusted to you

The whole-person concept applies: a single adverse fact is weighed with its recency, frequency, the circumstances, and whether it has been mitigated.

The trap

The cover-up is the disqualifier far more often than the thing

Personal conduct — which explicitly covers deliberate omission or falsification on the SF 86 — takes down more applications than the underlying issues it was meant to hide. Old debt, a decade-old arrest, past drug use and treatment for a mental health condition are all routinely adjudicated favourably in context. Concealing any of them is evidence about how you behave when a rule is inconvenient, which is the exact question the process is asking. Disclose it, and let the whole-person concept do its job.

In practice

Continuous evaluation changed the rhythm

The old model was a periodic reinvestigation every five or ten years depending on level. Continuous vetting replaces much of that with automated, ongoing checks against financial, criminal and other records — so a significant change surfaces in weeks rather than at the next cycle. Practically, this means self-reporting matters more than it used to: reporting your own event first is a routine conversation, while being asked about something the system found is a different one. The reportable list typically includes foreign travel and contacts, financial changes, arrests, and changes in marital or cohabitation status.

🚨 Spills, Sanitisation & Reporting — The First Ten Minutes MILITARY • Classified Handling ▶
Core Concept

A spill is classified data on a system not approved for it

Most spills are accidents of routing, not of malice: a Secret paragraph pasted into an unclassified email, a document attached from the wrong drive, a file saved to the wrong share. The term of art is a classified message incident or contamination. The system that received it is now classified at that level, along with its backups, its mail queues, the search index that crawled it, and every workstation that opened it. That blast radius is why the response is heavier than the mistake feels.

Staged flow

What to do, in order

#DoWhy
1Stop. Do not delete it.Deleting destroys evidence, spreads the data into deleted-item stores and backups, and does not sanitise anything. It also makes an accident look like a cover-up
2Keep the system where it is — do not power it off unless told toPreserves state for the people who have to scope the incident
3Report to your security officer immediately, in person or by an approved channelMinutes matter for containment, and reporting is your obligation regardless of who caused it
4Do not discuss it over the contaminated channelAn email about the spill, sent on the spilled-to system, extends the spill
5Do not forward, print, screenshot or "quarantine" it yourselfEvery copy is another system in scope
6Write down what you did and when, while you rememberScoping depends on an accurate timeline more than on anything technical
The trap

"I'll just delete it and nobody needs to know" is the career-ending version

Spilling classified data by accident is a common, survivable, usually non-disciplinary event — it is treated as an incident to be scoped and cleaned. Concealing one is a different act with a different name. The reporting obligation is on you, it is not discharged by hoping someone else noticed, and it does not lapse because a week has passed. Report late rather than not at all.

Reference

Clear, purge, destroy — the three sanitisation outcomes

OutcomeResistsTypical use
ClearRecovery with ordinary tools and system functionsMedia staying at the same classification, inside the same environment
PurgeRecovery with laboratory techniquesMedia leaving control, or being moved down in classification where policy allows it at all
DestroyEverything — the media no longer exists as mediaThe default for classified media at end of life

Two practical notes that catch IT people out. A drive's own "secure erase" is a clear at best and is not automatically accepted for classified media — the approved method is set by policy, not by the vendor's datasheet. And degaussing is for magnetic media only: it does nothing to a solid-state drive, which is why the approved answer for classified flash storage is so often physical destruction.

🗺️ MDMP & the OPORD — The Planning Cycle and the Five-Paragraph Order Leadership • Planning ▶
Core Concept
A Repeatable Way to Turn a Problem Into a Plan
The Military Decision-Making Process is a seven-step staff process for producing a plan under uncertainty and time pressure. Strip the uniform off it and it is a project-planning method any incident commander or engineering lead already half-uses: understand the problem, generate options, wargame them against what can go wrong, pick one, and write it down so others can act without you in the room. Its discipline is that every step has an output the next step consumes — you cannot skip ahead and still have a plan.
StepProducesCivilian parallel
1 Receipt of missionInitial timeline and warning"We have an incident" — start the clock
2 Mission analysisThe restated problem + constraintsWhat are we actually solving, and what's fixed?
3 Course-of-action developmentSeveral distinct optionsBrainstorm real alternatives, not one plan and two strawmen
4 COA analysis (wargaming)Each option stress-testedPremortem: play it forward against failures
5 COA comparisonA decision matrixScore options on agreed criteria
6 COA approvalThe chosen planDecision-maker commits
7 Orders productionThe OPORDWrite it so people can execute it
Reference
The OPORD — Five Paragraphs, Always the Same Order
The operations order is the output, and its power is that it is always the same five paragraphs in the same sequence, so anyone can find what they need under fire. The single most valuable line for civilian use is buried in paragraph 2: commander's intent — the purpose and end state — which is what lets people improvise correctly when the plan meets reality. See Commander's Intent — Empowering Action Without Micromanaging.
#ParagraphAnswers
1SituationWhat's going on — friendly, hostile, and the environment
2MissionWho, what, when, where and why — one clear sentence
3ExecutionIntent, the concept, and each element's specific tasks
4SustainmentLogistics, medical, supply — how it's kept running
5Command & signalWho's in charge, and how everyone communicates
An incident-response runbook or a launch plan written in these five paragraphs is instantly readable by anyone who knows the format — which is the whole point of a standard.
Pitfall
Analysis That Outlives the Decision Window
MDMP scales down on purpose — under time pressure you run an abbreviated version, and the rule of thumb is to give subordinates two-thirds of the available time and keep one-third for your own planning. A plan delivered after the moment for it has passed is worse than a rougher plan delivered in time. The OODA Loop — Decision-Making Under Pressure is the fast end of the same spectrum: MDMP for deliberate planning, OODA (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) for the seconds you actually have.
🛰️ The Intelligence Cycle — Direction, Collection, Processing, Dissemination Planning • SecOps ▶
Core Concept
Data Is Not Intelligence Until It Answers a Question Someone Asked
The intelligence cycle is the loop that turns raw collection into a decision-maker's answer, and its first step is the one everyone skips: direction. Intelligence starts with a specific question from whoever must act — not with collecting everything and hoping insight falls out. This is the exact same cycle a cyber threat-intel team runs, which is why it appears in Threat Intelligence Lifecycle almost verbatim.
PhaseWhat happensFailure if skipped
DirectionThe decision-maker states what they need to knowYou collect noise nobody asked for
CollectionGather from every relevant sourceGaps, or over-reliance on one source
ProcessingTranslate, decrypt, collate into usable formRaw feeds no analyst can actually read
AnalysisTurn information into assessed meaningA data dump mistaken for a judgment
DisseminationDeliver it to who needs it, in time to actThe right answer, filed where no one reads it
FeedbackDid it help? Refine the next roundThe cycle never improves
Reference
The Collection Disciplines
Sources are grouped by how they collect — the "-INT" families — because each has different reliability and different ways to be fooled. A sound assessment triangulates across several rather than trusting one, since any single discipline can be spoofed by an adversary who knows you rely on it.
DisciplineSource
OSINT (Open Source Intelligence)Open sources — public, and the civilian's main one; see the OSINT cards in `threat`
HUMINTHuman sources
SIGINTIntercepted signals and communications
GEOINT / IMINTImagery and geospatial data
MASINTMeasurement and signature — the technical residue of an activity
Why It Transfers
Every "Monitoring" Effort Is This Cycle
A SOC (Security Operations Center), a business-analytics team and a competitive-intelligence function all run this loop, and all fail in the same place: they collect prodigiously and never nailed down the direction, so they produce dashboards nobody uses to decide anything. If you take one habit from the model, take the first step — make someone name the decision the intelligence is for before you collect a byte.
🎯 Red Teaming as a Discipline — Premortems & Structured Contrarian Thinking Decision-Making ▶
Core Concept
Assigning Someone to Attack the Plan, on Purpose
Red teaming here is not the offensive-security kind (that lives in the `redteam` domain) — it is the decision discipline of deliberately assigning people to challenge a plan, assumption or organization before reality does. The premise is that groups converge on a preferred answer and then defend it, so agreement has to be manufactured back into disagreement by design. A good red team is chartered, protected, and pointed at the assumptions everyone treats as settled.
TechniqueWhat it does
Premortem"It's a year later and this failed — why?" Surfaces risks that optimism hides
Devil's advocateA chartered role to argue against, so dissent isn't a career risk
Red team / blue teamOne group plans, another attacks the plan on its own terms
Key-assumptions checkList what must be true; ask how you'd know if it weren't
Analysis of competing hypothesesScore evidence against every explanation, not just the favourite
The Premortem
The Cheapest, Highest-Value Version
The premortem is the one to actually run, because it costs fifteen minutes and defuses the social pressure that silences doubts. Instead of asking "any concerns?" — which invites nobody to speak — you state the failure as fact: "assume this launch failed badly; write down why." Prospective hindsight makes people far more willing and far more specific, because they are explaining a failure rather than criticizing a colleague's plan. It maps directly onto MDMP's wargaming step and onto any engineering design review.
The condition that makes it work: it must be safe to be the bearer of bad news. A red team whose findings get the messenger punished produces reassuring findings — which is worse than none, because now the blind spot has a rubber stamp. Charter it, protect it, and reward the uncomfortable finding.
Why It Transfers
The Same Failure, in Every Field
Groupthink, confirmation bias and overconfidence are not military problems; they are human ones, and they sink product launches, security architectures and incident calls exactly as they sink operations. Structured contrarian thinking is the countermeasure that scales, because it does not depend on having one brave skeptic in the room — it builds the skeptic into the process. Pair it with the honest self-examination in After-Action Review — Learning From Every Event: red teaming before, AAR after.
🔴 Red Team & Offensive Tooling
PT+ OSCP
Recon · Exploitation · AD Attacks · C2 · Password & Wireless 43 topics · ~30 min ▾
⚠️ Rules of Engagement — Read This First Ethics ▶
Authorized Use Only
These Tools Are for Permission-Based Testing
Every tool in this domain is a reference for authorized penetration testing, CTF (Capture The Flag) competitions, home-lab practice, and cert prep (PenTest+, OSCP, CEH). Running them against systems you don't own or lack written permission to test is illegal in most jurisdictions (CFAA, Computer Misuse Act, etc.). Always work inside a signed scope / rules of engagement, stay within the authorized targets and time window, and handle any data you touch responsibly. Each card pairs offense with a blue-team detection note — because knowing how an attack looks on the wire is what makes you good at both sides.
🗺️ Nmap — The Network Mapper (Deep Dive) Recon ▶
Reference
The Swiss-Army Knife of Discovery
Nmap is the default tool for host discovery, port scanning, service/version detection, and OS (Operating System) fingerprinting. Its scripting engine (NSE) extends it into vuln checks and light exploitation. Authorized targets only.
▸ SCAN TYPES & ESSENTIALS
nmap -sS 10.0.0.0/24        # SYN "half-open" scan (default, fast, needs root)
nmap -sT target             # full TCP connect (no root)
nmap -sU target             # UDP scan (slow; DNS/SNMP/DHCP live here)
nmap -sV -O target          # service versions + OS detection
nmap -p- target             # all 65535 ports (default scans top 1000)
nmap -sC -sV -oA scan target # default scripts + versions, save all formats
nmap -T4 -Pn target          # faster timing; skip host-discovery ping
▸ NSE (SCRIPTING ENGINE)
FlagDoes
-sCRun the default safe script set
--script vulnKnown-vuln checks
--script smb-enum-sharesCategory/named scripts (~600 available)
-AAggressive: -sV -O -sC + traceroute
Blue-team note: a SYN (Synchronize) scan shows up as many connections with no completed handshake from one source — IDS (Intrusion Detection System) (Suricata/Zeek) and firewall logs flag the fan-out. -T4/-T5 timing is loud; real adversaries scan slow.
⚡ Masscan & RustScan — Internet-Scale Port Discovery Recon ▶
Reference
When Nmap Is Too Slow
Masscan is an asynchronous scanner that can probe the entire IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) space in minutes by sending packets without waiting for replies. RustScan finds open ports fast, then hands them to Nmap for deep inspection — best of both. Authorized scope and rate limits only; unbounded scanning is disruptive. 
# Masscan — set a sane rate (packets/sec); high rates can DoS the target
masscan 10.0.0.0/16 -p1-65535 --rate 1000 -oL out.txt

# RustScan → auto-pipe discovered ports into nmap -sV -sC
rustscan -a target --range 1-65535 -- -sV -sC
Blue-team note: extremely high packet rates from a single IP (Internet Protocol) to sequential ports are the signature — netflow/IDS thresholds catch it instantly. Attackers throttle to blend in.
🌾 theHarvester & Recon-ng — OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) Frameworks OSINT ▶
Reference
Passive Intelligence Before You Touch the Target
theHarvester gathers emails, subdomains, hosts, and names from public sources (search engines, certificate transparency, PGP keyservers). Recon-ng is a full framework with a Metasploit-style module system for structured OSINT into a local database. These are passive — they query third parties, not the target directly. 
theHarvester -d example.com -b all      # emails/subdomains from all sources

# Recon-ng — modular, DB-backed
recon-ng
[recon-ng] > marketplace install all
[recon-ng] > modules load recon/domains-hosts/hackertarget
[recon-ng] > options set SOURCE example.com
[recon-ng] > run
Blue-team note: passive OSINT is nearly invisible to the target — the defense is reducing your footprint: scrub metadata, limit what's public, monitor certificate-transparency logs for look-alike domains.
🔭 Amass & Subfinder — Subdomain Enumeration OSINT ▶
Reference
Mapping the Full Attack Surface
Organizations expose far more subdomains than they realize — dev, staging, forgotten apps. Amass (OWASP) and Subfinder aggregate dozens of sources (cert transparency, DNS, APIs) to enumerate them. Finding the forgotten old-admin.example.com is often the way in. 
subfinder -d example.com -all -o subs.txt   # fast, passive
amass enum -passive -d example.com            # passive aggregation
amass enum -active -d example.com -brute       # active: resolves + brute-forces
Blue-team note: maintain your own asset inventory the same way — you can't defend subdomains you forgot you own. Watch for dangling DNS (Domain Name System) records (subdomain takeover risk).
🛰️ Shodan & Censys — Search Engines for Exposed Devices OSINT ▶
Reference
The Internet, Already Scanned for You
Shodan and Censys continuously scan the internet and index every exposed service — banners, ports, TLS (Transport Layer Security) certs, default logins, ICS/SCADA, webcams. Searching them is passive (you query their database, not the target), making them a favorite first step.
▸ SHODAN SEARCH FILTERS
QueryFinds
org:"Example Corp"All indexed hosts for an org
ssl:example.comHosts by TLS certificate
port:3389 country:USExposed RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) in a region
product:MongoDBA specific service/version
"default password"Banners advertising defaults
Blue-team note: search Shodan/Censys for your own org regularly — it's the fastest external-exposure audit there is. Anything you find, an attacker already has.
🔎 Google Dorking, Maltego & SpiderFoot OSINT ▶
Reference
Advanced Search & Automated Link Analysis
Google Dorking uses advanced operators to surface exposed data indexed by search engines (the Google Hacking Database catalogs thousands of proven queries). Maltego and SpiderFoot automate OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) into visual link graphs — connecting domains, emails, people, and infrastructure.
▸ USEFUL DORKS
OperatorFinds
site:example.com filetype:pdfDocuments on a domain
intitle:"index of" site:example.comOpen directory listings
inurl:admin site:example.comAdmin panels
"password" filetype:logLeaked logs/creds
Blue-team note: dork your own domain to find accidental exposure; use robots.txt, auth, and Google Search Console removal for anything sensitive that's indexed.
🧪 Burp Suite — The Web Pentest Workbench Web ▶
Reference
Intercept, Modify, Replay
Burp Suite is the industry-standard web app testing platform. It sits as a proxy between your browser and the target, letting you inspect and tamper with every request. Authorized targets only.
ToolDoes
ProxyIntercept + edit requests/responses on the fly
RepeaterManually tweak & resend a single request (the core manual-testing loop)
IntruderAutomate payloads over positions — fuzzing, brute force, enumeration
ScannerAutomated vuln crawl (Pro)
Decoder / ComparerEncode/decode & diff responses
Typical flow: browse the app through the proxy to map it → send an interesting request to Repeater → probe for injection/auth flaws by hand → automate with Intruder. Blue-team note: app-layer WAF (Web Application Firewall) + anomaly detection on parameter tampering and high request volume from one session.
⚡ OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) ZAP — The Open-Source Web Scanner Web ▶
Reference
Burp's Free Cousin — Great for CI
OWASP ZAP is a free, open-source web proxy/scanner with much of Burp's core: intercepting proxy, spider, active/passive scanning, and fuzzing. Its automation-friendliness makes it the go-to for DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) in CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) — run a baseline scan on every build against a staging deploy. 
# Baseline (passive) scan — safe for CI, no attacks
zap-baseline.py -t https://staging.example.com

# Full active scan (authorized targets only)
zap-full-scan.py -t https://staging.example.com
Blue-team crossover: because ZAP is a defensive tool too, wire it into your own pipeline to catch OWASP Top 10 regressions before release.
💉 sqlmap — Automated SQL (Structured Query Language) Injection Web ▶
Reference
Detect & Exploit SQLi, End to End
sqlmap automates finding and exploiting SQL injection — from detection through data extraction, and even OS (Operating System) shell where the DB permits. Powerful and noisy; authorized scope only. 
sqlmap -u "https://site/item?id=1" --batch    # test a parameter
sqlmap -r request.txt --level 3 --risk 2   # from a saved Burp request
sqlmap -u "..." --dbs                     # list databases
sqlmap -u "..." -D shop -T users --dump    # dump a table
FlagMeaning
--level / --riskHow hard/aggressive to test (1–5 / 1–3)
--tamperEvasion scripts (encode payloads past filters/WAF)
--batchNon-interactive (accept defaults)
Blue-team note: the fix is parameterized queries, not a WAF (Web Application Firewall) — but a WAF + DB query logging will scream at sqlmap's payload patterns and error-based probing.
📁 ffuf & Gobuster — Content & Parameter Fuzzing Web ▶
Reference
Finding the Hidden Endpoints
