🔑 AWS (Amazon Web Services) IAM (Identity and Access Management) — Users, Roles & Policies AWS ▶
How-To
Who Can Do What, to Which Resources
IAM is the heart of AWS security — and the #1 source of breaches when done sloppily. It answers: which principal (user/role) can perform which actions on which resources, under what conditions. Everything is deny-by-default; access must be explicitly granted by a policy.
ConceptWhat
UserA long-lived human/app identity (avoid keys where possible)
RoleAn identity you assume temporarily — the preferred pattern (no stored keys)
GroupA bucket of users sharing policies
PolicyJSON (JavaScript Object Notation) document granting/denying permissions
▸ A POLICY (JSON)
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*",
  "Condition": { "IpAddress": { "aws:SourceIp": "10.0.0.0/8" } }
}
Golden rule: grant least privilege — start with nothing, add the specific actions needed. Never attach *:* ("AdministratorAccess") to app roles.
🎫 AWS (Amazon Web Services) IAM (Identity and Access Management) Deep — AssumeRole, STS (Security Token Service) & Boundaries AWS ▶
How-To
Temporary Credentials Done Right
Long-lived access keys are the thing that leaks. The modern pattern is roles + STS: you assume a role and get temporary credentials that auto-expire (minutes to hours). Cross-account access, CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery), and EC2/Lambda all use this.
MechanismUse
sts:AssumeRoleSwap into a role (incl. cross-account) for short-lived creds
Trust policyOn the role — says who is allowed to assume it
Instance/Task roleEC2/ECS/Lambda auto-receive creds — no keys on disk
Permission boundaryA ceiling on the max perms an identity can ever have
IAM Identity CenterSSO (Single Sign-On) for humans → short-lived console/CLI sessions
OIDC (OpenID Connect) federationLet GitHub Actions assume a role with no stored secret
Policy evaluation: an explicit Deny always wins; otherwise you need an explicit Allow. Effective permission = intersection of identity policy, resource policy, permission boundary, and any SCP (Service Control Policy) (org guardrail).
🔑 GCP (Google Cloud Platform) IAM (Identity and Access Management) — Members, Roles & Hierarchy GCP ▶
How-To
Who (member) Can Do What (role) on Which Resource
GCP IAM binds a member (user, group, or service account) to a role (a bundle of permissions) on a resource. Because of the resource hierarchy, a binding at the project or folder level is inherited by everything beneath it — powerful and easy to over-grant.
Role typeDetail
BasicOwner/Editor/Viewer — broad, legacy, avoid in prod
PredefinedFine-grained, service-specific (e.g. roles/storage.objectViewer)
CustomYour own hand-picked permission set for true least-privilege
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-proj \
  --member="user:alice@example.com" \
  --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"
Prefer predefined/custom roles over basic ones, and bind as low in the hierarchy as possible (project > folder > org).
🤖 GCP (Google Cloud Platform) Service Accounts & Workload Identity GCP ▶
How-To
Machine Identity Without Leaking Keys
A service account (SA) is an identity for an app or VM (Virtual Machine) rather than a person. The trap is downloaded SA key files — long-lived JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) secrets that leak and rarely rotate. Workload Identity is the modern answer: it lets workloads (GKE pods, or external systems like GitHub Actions and even AWS) obtain short-lived SA credentials automatically, with no key file at all.
ApproachVerdict
Downloaded SA key (.json)Long-lived secret — avoid; the #1 GCP credential leak
Attached SA (on a VM/pod)Metadata server issues short-lived tokens automatically
Workload Identity FederationExternal identities (GitHub/AWS) assume an SA keylessly
Rule: if you're storing a .json key, ask whether Workload Identity can replace it. Usually it can.
⚠️ Cloud IAM (Identity and Access Management) Pitfalls & Privilege Escalation Security ▶
Security
How Over-Permissive IAM Becomes a Breach
Most cloud compromises aren't zero-days — they're IAM misconfigurations an attacker chains into full control. Knowing the traps is how you avoid (and, on a red team, find) them.
PitfallWhy It's Dangerous
Wildcards (*:*)"Just make it work" grants admin — the classic root cause
iam:PassRole / actAsLets a low-priv identity hand a powerful role to a service it controls → escalation
Overbroad AssumeRole trustA role anyone can assume is a role attackers assume
Long-lived access keysLeak in code/logs/laptops; rarely rotated
SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) → metadata serviceApp-layer SSRF steals the instance's role creds (IMDSv2 mitigates on AWS)
Public resource policiesA bucket/queue open to "Principal": "*"
Defenses: least privilege, no wildcards, IMDSv2, short-lived creds, and continuous scanning with CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management) tools (Prowler, ScoutSuite, Steampipe) that flag these exact patterns.
🌐 AWS (Amazon Web Services) VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) — Subnets, Security Groups & NACLs (Network Access Control List) AWS ▶
How-To
Your Private Slice of the AWS Network
A VPC is an isolated virtual network you define with a CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) block (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16). Inside it you carve subnets, control routing, and layer two firewalls. Getting the public/private split right is the foundation of a secure architecture.
PieceRole
Public subnetRoute to an Internet Gateway (IGW) — for load balancers, bastions
Private subnetNo direct inbound; outbound via a NAT (Network Address Translation) Gateway — for app servers, DBs
Route tableDecides where a subnet's traffic goes (IGW, NAT, peering)
Security GroupStateful firewall on the instance — allow rules only; return traffic auto-allowed
NACLStateless firewall on the subnet — allow + deny; must allow both directions
Remember: Security Groups are stateful (the common case, instance-level); NACLs are stateless (subnet-level, coarse). Put databases in private subnets and never give them a public IP (Internet Protocol).
🔀 AWS (Amazon Web Services) Load Balancing & DNS (Domain Name System) — ELB (Elastic Load Balancing), Route 53, CloudFront AWS ▶
How-To
Getting Traffic to the Right Place, Fast
ServiceDoes
ALB (Application Load Balancer) (Application LB)Layer 7 — routes HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)(S) by path/host, WebSockets, target groups
NLB (Network Load Balancer) (Network LB)Layer 4 — ultra-fast TCP/UDP, static IPs (Internet Protocol), extreme throughput
Route 53DNS + health checks + routing policies (latency, weighted, failover, geo)
CloudFrontCDN (Content Delivery Network) — caches content at edge locations near users; also DDoS/TLS termination
A typical web path: Route 53 → CloudFront → ALB → targets across multiple AZs (Availability Zone). Route 53's failover routing + health checks is how you build multi-region resilience.
🌐 GCP (Google Cloud Platform) VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) — Global Networks & Firewall Rules GCP ▶
How-To
One Network That Spans the Planet
GCP's big networking difference: a VPC is global, not regional. One VPC can hold subnets in every region, and instances in different regions talk over Google's private backbone without extra peering. Subnets are regional; the VPC that contains them is global.
PieceRole
VPC (global)The whole network; subnets are regional within it
Firewall rulesStateful; applied by network tags or service accounts, not per-instance objects
Cloud NAT (Network Address Translation)Managed egress for private instances (no per-VM NAT gateway)
Cloud RouterDynamic (BGP) routing for hybrid/VPN links
Firewall rules being tag-based is the mental shift from AWS (Amazon Web Services): tag an instance web, write a rule "allow 443 to tag:web" — no security-group object to attach.
🔀 GCP (Google Cloud Platform) Load Balancing & DNS (Domain Name System) GCP ▶
How-To
A Single Global Anycast IP (Internet Protocol)
GCP's global load balancer is a standout: one anycast IP serves users worldwide, automatically routing each to the nearest healthy backend — no per-region IPs or DNS tricks needed. It scales instantly without pre-warming.
ServiceDoes
Global External LBOne IP, worldwide HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)(S) routing to nearest backend
Regional LBL4/L7 within a region
Cloud DNSManaged, scalable DNS with 100% SLA (Service Level Agreement)
Cloud CDN (Content Delivery Network)Edge caching, enabled on the LB backend
🔗 Hybrid Connectivity — VPN (Virtual Private Network), Interconnect & Peering Cloud ▶
Reference
Wiring the Cloud to Your Datacenter (and Itself)
Real deployments connect cloud networks to on-prem and to each other. The options trade cost against bandwidth and reliability.
NeedAWS (Amazon Web Services)GCP (Google Cloud Platform)
Encrypted over internetSite-to-Site VPNCloud VPN
Private dedicated lineDirect ConnectCloud Interconnect
Connect two VPCs (Virtual Private Cloud)VPC Peering / Transit GatewayVPC Peering / Network Connectivity Center
Reach a managed service privatelyPrivateLink / VPC EndpointsPrivate Service Connect
VPN is cheap and quick but rides the public internet; Direct Connect / Interconnect is a private circuit — pricier, but consistent low latency and high bandwidth for production hybrid workloads. PrivateLink-style endpoints keep traffic to cloud services off the public internet entirely.
🖥️ AWS (Amazon Web Services) Compute — EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud), AMIs (Amazon Machine Image) & Auto Scaling AWS ▶
How-To
Renting Virtual Machines That Scale Themselves
EC2 is AWS's virtual-machine service. You launch instances from an AMI (a machine image), pick an instance type (family + size), and — critically — put them behind an Auto Scaling Group so capacity follows demand instead of running fixed (and overpaying).
ConceptDetail
AMISnapshot template an instance boots from (OS + config)
Instance familyt/m = general, c = compute, r = memory, g/p = GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)
Auto Scaling GroupMin/desired/max; adds/removes instances on metrics
Launch templateThe blueprint an ASG uses to create instances
User dataBoot script to configure an instance on launch
▸ PRICING MODELS
ModelUse
On-DemandPay per second; spiky/unpredictable
Savings Plans / Reserved1–3 yr commit → ~30–70% off steady load
SpotSpare capacity ~90% off; can be reclaimed → fault-tolerant jobs
📦 AWS (Amazon Web Services) Serverless & Containers — Lambda, ECS (Elastic Container Service), EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service), Fargate AWS ▶
How-To
Run Code Without (Managing) Servers
ServiceWhat
LambdaFunctions triggered by events; scale-to-zero, pay per ms
ECSAWS's own container orchestrator (simpler than K8s)
EKSManaged Kubernetes (when you need K8s portability)
FargateServerless container compute — runs ECS/EKS tasks with no EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) to manage
App RunnerPush a container/repo → get a URL (Uniform Resource Locator); simplest path
Decision: event-driven glue → Lambda; long-running services in containers → ECS/EKS on Fargate (no servers) or EC2 (cheaper at scale, more ops). Fargate is the "I don't want to manage nodes" answer for containers.
🖥️ GCP (Google Cloud Platform) Compute — Compute Engine & MIGs GCP ▶
How-To
VMs (Virtual Machine) on Google's Infrastructure
Compute Engine is GCP's VM service. Two nice differentiators: per-second billing with sustained-use discounts applied automatically (no upfront commit needed for savings), and custom machine types — pick exact vCPU/RAM instead of fixed sizes.
ConceptAWS (Amazon Web Services) Analog
Machine image / familyAMI (Amazon Machine Image) / instance family (e2, n2, c3…)
Managed Instance Group (MIG)Auto Scaling Group — autoscaling + auto-healing
Instance templateLaunch template
Preemptible / Spot VMsSpot — deep discount, reclaimable
Sustained-use discountAutomatic; no reservation needed
🏃 GCP (Google Cloud Platform) Serverless & Containers — Cloud Run, Functions, GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine) GCP ▶
How-To
Cloud Run Is the Star
Cloud Run is GCP's standout: give it a container, get a scalable HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) endpoint that scales to zero and bills per request — serverless containers with almost no config. It's often the simplest way to deploy a web service on any cloud.
ServiceWhat
Cloud RunServerless containers (scale-to-zero, per-request)
Cloud FunctionsEvent-driven functions (like Lambda)
GKEManaged Kubernetes — the reference K8s experience (Google created K8s)
GKE AutopilotK8s where Google manages the nodes for you
Rule of thumb: a stateless web service or API (Application Programming Interface) → Cloud Run. Event glue → Cloud Functions. You genuinely need Kubernetes (complex microservices, existing K8s manifests) → GKE.
🧭 Choosing Compute — VM (Virtual Machine) vs Container vs Serverless Reference ▶
Reference
A Decision Guide
Pick…When
Serverless functionsEvent-driven, spiky, short tasks; you want zero ops & scale-to-zero
Serverless containers (Cloud Run / Fargate)Web services/APIs you want managed, but with a real container & no cold-start-only limits
Managed KubernetesMany services, complex networking, portability, an existing K8s investment
Plain VMsLegacy apps, special OS/kernel needs, GPUs (Graphics Processing Unit), or maximum control
The trend runs left-to-right toward more managed — start as serverless as the workload allows and drop down to VMs only when you need the control. Less to operate = less to break.
💾 AWS (Amazon Web Services) Storage — S3 (Simple Storage Service) Classes, EBS (Elastic Block Store) & EFS (Elastic File System) AWS ▶
How-To
Three Storage Types for Three Jobs
AWS storage splits into object (S3), block (EBS — a virtual disk for one EC2), and file (EFS — a shared NFS mount for many). Pick by access pattern; mixing them up is a classic mistake. (See the Object Storage topic for S3 fundamentals — here we focus on the AWS-specific pieces.)
ServiceTypeUse
S3ObjectFiles, backups, static sites, data lakes
EBSBlockBoot/data volume for one EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) (like a disk)
EFSFileShared filesystem mounted by many instances
FSxFileManaged Windows/Lustre file systems
▸ S3 STORAGE CLASSES (cost vs access)
ClassFor
StandardHot, frequent access
Standard-IA / One Zone-IAInfrequent access, cheaper storage
Intelligent-TieringAuto-moves objects by usage
Glacier / Deep ArchiveCold archive — pennies to store, slow/paid retrieval
Use lifecycle rules to age objects into colder classes automatically. EBS volumes are AZ-locked — snapshot to S3 for backup/restore across AZs (Availability Zone).
🗃️ AWS (Amazon Web Services) Databases — RDS (Relational Database Service), Aurora & DynamoDB AWS ▶
How-To
Managed SQL (Structured Query Language) & NoSQL
ServiceWhat
RDSManaged relational (Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, MariaDB) — patching, backups, replicas handled
AuroraAWS's cloud-native MySQL/Postgres-compatible engine — faster, auto-scaling storage, Serverless v2
DynamoDBManaged key-value/document NoSQL — single-digit-ms at any scale, serverless
ElastiCacheManaged Redis/Memcached (caching, sessions)
Choosing: relational data with joins/transactions → RDS/Aurora. Massive scale with simple key-based access → DynamoDB (design around your access patterns — no ad-hoc joins). Always enable Multi-AZ for production databases (automatic failover).
💾 GCP (Google Cloud Platform) Storage — Cloud Storage, Persistent Disk & Filestore GCP ▶
How-To
The Same Three Types, Google's Names
ServiceTypeAWS (Amazon Web Services) Analog
Cloud StorageObjectS3 (Simple Storage Service)
Persistent DiskBlockEBS (Elastic Block Store)
FilestoreFile (NFS)EFS (Elastic File System)
Cloud Storage classes mirror S3: Standard → Nearline → Coldline → Archive, from hot to cheap-cold. A nice touch: one API/bucket namespace with a per-object storage class, and lifecycle rules to auto-tier. Persistent Disks can be resized live and snapshotted globally.
🗃️ GCP (Google Cloud Platform) Databases — Cloud SQL (Structured Query Language), Spanner & Firestore GCP ▶
How-To
Including the One Only Google Has
ServiceWhat
Cloud SQLManaged Postgres/MySQL/SQL Server (≈ RDS)
SpannerGlobally-distributed, strongly-consistent relational DB that scales horizontally — unique to Google
FirestoreServerless document NoSQL (≈ DynamoDB), great for app backends
BigtableWide-column NoSQL for huge analytical/time-series workloads (≈ Cassandra/HBase)
Spanner is the standout — it breaks the usual "you can't have global scale AND strong consistency" rule (via TrueTime atomic clocks). Reach for it when you genuinely need both; otherwise Cloud SQL is the everyday relational choice.
📊 BigQuery — Serverless Data Warehouse GCP ▶
How-To
Query Terabytes With SQL (Structured Query Language), No Cluster
BigQuery is GCP (Google Cloud Platform)'s flagship analytics warehouse: fully serverless (no infrastructure to size), it runs SQL over terabytes-to- petabytes in seconds by massively parallelizing the scan. It's the OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) counterpart to the transactional databases above (see the OLTP vs OLAP topic).
TraitDetail
ServerlessNo clusters; it scales compute (slots) automatically
ColumnarReads only the columns your query touches → fast + cheap
Cost modelPriced by bytes scanned (or flat-rate slots) — SELECT * on a huge table is expensive
BQ ML (Machine Learning)Train ML models in SQL, in place
Cost tip: select only needed columns and use partitioned/clustered tables — you pay for data scanned, so pruning saves real money. AWS (Amazon Web Services)'s equivalent is Redshift (and Athena for S3).
🛡️ AWS (Amazon Web Services) Security Stack — CloudTrail, GuardDuty & Security Hub AWS ▶
How-To
See, Detect, and Govern Your Account
AWS security starts with visibility. These services layer together: log everything, detect threats, check config, and aggregate it all. CloudTrail is non-negotiable — turn it on day one.
ServiceDoes
CloudTrailRecords every API (Application Programming Interface) call — the audit log of who did what
ConfigTracks resource configuration over time + rules for compliance
GuardDutyML/threat-intel detection on logs (crypto-mining, recon, exfil)
Security HubAggregates findings from all of them + CIS/AWS benchmarks
InspectorAutomated vuln scanning of EC2/ECR/Lambda
MacieFinds sensitive data (PII) in S3 (Simple Storage Service)
Pattern: CloudTrail + Config feed GuardDuty + Security Hub, which stream findings to your SIEM/SOAR. This is the AWS-native version of the Blue Team stack.
🔐 AWS (Amazon Web Services) Data Protection — KMS (Key Management Service) & Secrets Manager AWS ▶
How-To
Encryption & Secrets, Managed
KMS (Key Management Service) creates and controls encryption keys; most AWS services integrate with it for encryption-at-rest with a checkbox. Secrets Manager stores credentials/API keys with automatic rotation, so secrets never live in code or env files.
ServiceDetail
KMSManaged keys; envelope encryption; per-key IAM (Identity and Access Management) policies + audit via CloudTrail
Secrets ManagerStore + auto-rotate DB creds/API keys; fetch at runtime
Parameter StoreCheaper config + secret storage (SSM)
Enable default encryption on S3/EBS/RDS with KMS, and pull secrets from Secrets Manager at runtime — the two habits that close the most common data-exposure gaps.
🛡️ GCP (Google Cloud Platform) Security — Cloud Audit Logs & Security Command Center GCP ▶
How-To
The Google-Side Equivalents
ServiceDoesAWS (Amazon Web Services) Analog
Cloud Audit LogsAdmin/data-access API (Application Programming Interface) audit trailCloudTrail
Security Command CenterCentral posture + threat findings dashboardSecurity Hub + GuardDuty
Cloud Logging / MonitoringLogs, metrics, alertingCloudWatch
ChronicleGoogle's SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) at scale—
SCC is the single pane for GCP security posture — it surfaces misconfigurations, vulnerabilities, and active threats across your projects, mapped to standards.
🔐 GCP (Google Cloud Platform) Data Protection — Cloud KMS (Key Management Service), Secret Manager & VPC-SC GCP ▶
How-To
Keys, Secrets & a Data-Exfil Perimeter
ServiceDetail
Cloud KMSManaged encryption keys (like AWS KMS); CMEK on most services
Secret ManagerVersioned secret storage with IAM (Identity and Access Management) + audit
VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) Service ControlsA security perimeter around services to stop data exfiltration — GCP-distinctive
DLP (Data Loss Prevention) API (Application Programming Interface)Discover & redact sensitive data (PII)
VPC-SC is the standout: it draws a boundary so that even a stolen credential can't pull data out to the internet — mitigating the exact SSRF/exfil chains from the IAM Pitfalls card.
🔎 CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management) — Prowler, ScoutSuite & Steampipe Security ▶
Reference
Continuously Audit Your Cloud Posture
Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) tools scan your accounts for misconfigurations — public buckets, over-broad IAM (Identity and Access Management), unencrypted volumes, disabled logging — against benchmarks (CIS). This is the bridge between the Cloud and Blue Team domains: run them regularly to find gaps before attackers (using the same tools) do.
ToolDetail
ProwlerOpen-source AWS/GCP/Azure security assessments (CIS, NIST, etc.)
ScoutSuiteMulti-cloud config auditing → HTML (HyperText Markup Language) report
SteampipeQuery your cloud with SQL (Structured Query Language) (find issues with a SELECT)
Cloud-nativeSecurity Hub / SCC do continuous CSPM too
🏗️ Terraform on AWS (Amazon Web Services) & GCP (Google Cloud Platform) IaC ▶
How-To
One Tool for Every Cloud
Terraform's superpower in the cloud is being provider- agnostic — the same HCL workflow (init/plan/apply) provisions AWS, GCP, Azure, and 100+ others. You declare a provider, then resources. (See the Terraform topic for the core workflow — here's the cloud-specific shape.) 
provider "aws"    { region  = "us-east-1" }
provider "google" { project = "my-proj", region = "us-central1" }

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "data"   { bucket = "my-data" }
resource "google_storage_bucket" "data" { name = "my-data", location = "US" }
Cloud essentials: store state remotely (S3 + DynamoDB lock, or GCS) so a team shares it; use modules for reusable stacks (a "VPC module"); and never edit cloud resources by hand once Terraform manages them (drift).
📜 AWS-Native IaC (Infrastructure as Code) — CloudFormation & CDK (Cloud Development Kit) AWS ▶
Reference
Terraform's In-House Rivals
CloudFormation is AWS (Amazon Web Services)'s native IaC — YAML/JSON templates, deeply integrated, no state file to manage (AWS tracks it as a "stack"). CDK (Cloud Development Kit) lets you write infra in a real programming language (TypeScript, Python) that synthesizes to CloudFormation — loops, conditions, and abstractions instead of sprawling YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language).
CloudFormationCDKTerraform
LanguageYAML/JSONReal code → CFNHCL
ScopeAWS onlyAWS onlyMulti-cloud

🏛️ Azure Hierarchy, RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) Scopes & Policy Azure ▶
Foundation
Four Levels, and Everything Inherits Downward
Almost every "why can't I do this?" in Azure is answered by knowing which scope a setting was applied at. Permissions, policy and cost all flow down the same four-level tree, and nothing flows back up.
ScopeWhat it isWhat you attach here
Management groupA container for subscriptions; nests up to six levels under the tenant rootOrg-wide policy, broad role assignments
SubscriptionThe billing and quota boundary — roughly an AWS (Amazon Web Services) accountBudgets, quotas, environment separation (prod / non-prod)
Resource groupA lifecycle container; resources in it are deployed and deleted togetherTeam-level RBAC, locks, tags
ResourceThe individual VM (Virtual Machine), storage account, key vault…Narrow, exception-level access
The gotcha: a resource group is not a security boundary by itself and it is not a network boundary at all — two VMs in different resource groups can sit in the same subnet and talk freely.
Access vs Shape
RBAC Answers "Who", Policy Answers "What"
These two get confused constantly. A role assignment decides whether you may act. A policy decides whether the resource is allowed to exist in that shape. A deployment can fail on either, and the error text tells you which.
Azure RBACAzure Policy
ControlsActions a principal may performProperties a resource may have
Made ofPrincipal + role definition + scopeCondition + effect, grouped into initiatives
EffectsAllow (deny assignments are rare and system-made)Audit, Deny, Modify, DeployIfNotExists, AuditIfNotExists
Failure looks likeAuthorizationFailed — 403RequestDisallowedByPolicy — names the policy
FixAssign the role at the right scope, then wait for propagationChange the request, or exempt the scope deliberately
 
# Who has access here, and inherited from where?
az role assignment list --scope "/subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-prod" --include-inherited -o table

# Why did that deployment get blocked? Ask the policy engine directly
az policy state list --resource "<resource-id>" --filter "complianceState eq 'NonCompliant'" -o table

# Built-in roles are usually enough — check before writing a custom one
az role definition list --custom-role-only false --query "[?contains(roleName,'Contributor')].roleName"
Least privilege in practice: Reader for everyone by default, Contributor scoped to a resource group, and Owner or User Access Administrator handed out only through PIM (Privileged Identity Management) with approval and a time limit. Resource locks (CanNotDelete / ReadOnly) are a separate, dumber safety net — they stop even an Owner, which is exactly why prod deployments sometimes fail mysteriously.
🕸️ Azure Networking — VNet (Virtual Network), NSG (Network Security Group) & the Load-Balancer Family Azure ▶
Reference
Filtering, Routing and Reaching Out
A virtual network is the private address space; everything else is a decision about what may cross it. Network security groups filter, route tables steer, and peering or a gateway connects it to somewhere else.
Building blockWhat it doesWorth remembering
Virtual network / subnetPrivate address space, carved into subnetsAzure reserves five addresses per subnet — .0, .1, .2, .3 and the broadcast
Network security groupStateful allow/deny rules on a subnet and/or a NIC (Network Interface Card)Priority 100–4096, lowest number wins; default rules allow intra-VNet and deny inbound internet
Application security groupA named group of NICs you can use as a rule source or destinationLets rules say "web tier → app tier" instead of listing addresses
Route table / UDRUser-defined routes that override Azure's system routesThe usual way traffic is forced through a firewall appliance
VNet peeringPrivate, low-latency link between two virtual networksNot transitive — A↔B and B↔C does not give you A↔C
VPN gateway / ExpressRouteEncrypted tunnel over the internet / a private circuitExpressRoute skips the public internet entirely; VPN is cheaper and slower
Azure FirewallManaged stateful firewall with FQDN (Fully Qualified Domain Name) and threat-intel filteringSits in its own subnet named AzureFirewallSubnet
Private endpointA private IP (Internet Protocol) inside your VNet for a PaaS (Platform as a Service) serviceNeeds a matching private DNS (Domain Name System) zone or names still resolve public
Service endpointKeeps traffic to a PaaS service on the Azure backboneCheaper than a private endpoint, but the service keeps its public IP
Choosing
Four Load Balancers, One Right Answer
ServiceLayerReachReach for it when
Load Balancer4 — TCP/UDPRegionalYou need raw throughput and any protocol
Application Gateway7 — HTTP/SRegionalPath/host routing, TLS (Transport Layer Security) termination, WAF (Web Application Firewall) on a regional app
Front Door7 — HTTP/SGlobalWorldwide entry point with caching, WAF and failover between regions
Traffic ManagerDNSGlobalYou need to steer by DNS answer — including to non-Azure endpoints
Traffic Manager hands out an answer, not a connection. Clients cache DNS, so failover is only as fast as the record's TTL (Time To Live) — if you need instant failover at the HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) layer, that is Front Door's job.
💽 Azure Compute & Storage — Picking the Right SKU (Stock Keeping Unit) Azure ▶
Compute
From Virtual Machines to "No Machine at All"
OptionYou manageGood for
Virtual MachinesThe OS (Operating System) and everything on itLift-and-shift, anything needing full control
Virtual Machine Scale SetsAn image and a scaling ruleIdentical VMs that grow and shrink on demand
App ServiceYour code and the plan sizeWeb apps and APIs (Application Programming Interface) where a VM is overkill
Azure FunctionsA function and its triggerEvent-driven glue; Consumption plan bills per execution
Container AppsA container and scale rulesMicroservices without operating Kubernetes
AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service)The cluster's workloads and node poolsTeams already invested in Kubernetes
Sizing shorthand: B = burstable and cheap, D = general purpose, E = memory-heavy, F = compute-heavy, L = storage-heavy, N = GPU (Graphics Processing Unit). Availability: an availability set spreads VMs across fault and update domains inside one datacenter; availability zones spread them across physically separate datacenters in the region. Zones are the stronger guarantee, and not every region or SKU offers them.
Storage
Redundancy, Tiers and Who Holds the Key
RedundancyCopiesSurvives
LRS (Locally Redundant Storage)3, one datacenterA disk or rack failure
ZRS (Zone-Redundant Storage)3, across zones in one regionLosing a whole datacenter
GRS (Geo-Redundant Storage)LRS locally + 3 in a paired regionLosing a region (read access only after failover)
GZRS (Geo-Zone-Redundant Storage)ZRS locally + LRS in the paired regionBoth a zone and a region loss
RA-GRS (Read-Access Geo-Redundant Storage) / RA-GZRSAs above, plus a readable secondary endpointSame, but you can read the copy any time
Access tiers trade storage cost against retrieval cost: Hot for active data, Cool (30-day minimum), Cold (90-day) and Archive (180-day, and it must be rehydrated before you can read it). Lifecycle management rules move blobs between them automatically. 
# Prefer Entra ID over account keys — keys are shared secrets nobody rotates
az storage blob list --account-name stprod01 --container-name backups --auth-mode login -o table

# If you must hand out temporary access, a user-delegation SAS is the safest kind:
# it is signed with an Entra credential, so revoking the identity revokes the link
az storage blob generate-sas --account-name stprod01 --container-name backups \
  --name report.csv --permissions r --expiry 2026-01-01T00:00Z --auth-mode login --as-user
📈 Azure Monitor, Log Analytics & KQL (Kusto Query Language) Azure ▶
Observability
Metrics Are Free, Logs Are Opt-In
Platform metrics are collected automatically and kept for 93 days. Resource logs are not collected at all until you add a diagnostic setting pointing the resource at a Log Analytics workspace. The single most common monitoring complaint — "there's nothing in the logs" — is usually that nobody ever turned them on.
TableWhat lands in it
AzureActivityControl-plane operations — who created, changed or deleted a resource
AzureDiagnosticsResource logs from services that use the shared schema
HeartbeatAgent check-ins; the fastest way to spot a machine that stopped reporting
Perf / InsightsMetricsCPU (Central Processing Unit), memory, disk and network counters from monitored machines
SigninLogs / AuditLogsEntra ID sign-ins and directory changes
SecurityEvent / SyslogWindows security events and Linux syslog
AppRequests / AppExceptionsApplication Insights telemetry for your own code
 
// Who deleted things in the last day, and did it succeed?
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where OperationNameValue endswith "/DELETE"
| project TimeGenerated, Caller, OperationNameValue, ActivityStatusValue, ResourceGroup
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Machines that have stopped sending a heartbeat in the last 15 minutes
Heartbeat
| summarize LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
| where LastSeen < ago(15m)

// Failed sign-ins by error code — the shape of an attack, or of a broken app
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) and ResultType != 0
| summarize attempts = count() by ResultType, ResultDescription, AppDisplayName
| order by attempts desc

// Top CPU offenders, bucketed for a chart
Perf
| where ObjectName == "Processor" and CounterName == "% Processor Time"
| summarize avg(CounterValue) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| render timechart
The KQL that covers most days: where to filter, project to pick columns, extend to compute one, summarize … by to aggregate, bin() to bucket time, join to correlate two tables, and render to chart it. Filter on TimeGenerated first — it is the difference between a fast query and an expensive one. The same language drives Sentinel, Defender and Resource Graph.
🩺 Azure Troubleshooting Playbook Azure • Ops ▶
Method
Five Questions, In This Order
Azure failures nearly always fall into one of five buckets. Asking them in order saves you from packet-capturing a problem that was a missing role assignment.
#QuestionWhere to look
1Is Azure itself broken?Service Health for regional incidents, Resource Health for this specific resource
2Did the action even reach Azure — and who made it?Activity Log: the operation, the caller, the status and the correlation ID
3Am I allowed to do it?RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) at every scope, plus any policy assignment or resource lock
4Can the packets get there?Network Watcher — effective rules, effective routes, connection troubleshoot
5Is the thing inside the box healthy?Boot diagnostics, serial console, Run Command, app logs
Always capture the correlation ID. Every Azure Resource Manager operation carries one, it ties the portal error to the Activity Log entry to the deployment operation — and it is the first thing support asks for.
Toolkit
The Commands That Answer Each Question
# 2 — what actually happened, and under whose identity
az monitor activity-log list --resource-group rg-prod --offset 2h \
  --query "[?status.value=='Failed'].{op:operationName.value,by:caller,msg:properties.statusMessage}" -o table

# 2 — a failed template/Bicep deployment: the top-level error hides the real one
az deployment group show -g rg-prod -n my-deploy --query properties.error
az deployment operation group list -g rg-prod -n my-deploy \
  --query "[?properties.provisioningState=='Failed'].properties.statusMessage"

# 3 — effective permissions for a principal at a scope
az role assignment list --assignee user@contoso.com --all --include-inherited -o table

# 4 — will this packet be allowed? (evaluates every NSG in the path)
az network watcher test-ip-flow --vm web01 -g rg-prod --direction Inbound \
  --protocol TCP --local 10.0.1.4:443 --remote 203.0.113.10:51234

# 4 — what the NIC actually sees after all inheritance
az network nic list-effective-nsg --name web01-nic -g rg-prod -o table
az network nic show-effective-route-table --name web01-nic -g rg-prod -o table

# 4 — end-to-end reachability including DNS and the next hop
az network watcher test-connectivity --source-resource web01 -g rg-prod \
  --dest-address api.internal.contoso.com --dest-port 443

# 5 — the VM is unreachable: look at the screen and the boot log
az vm boot-diagnostics get-boot-log --name web01 -g rg-prod
az vm run-command invoke --name web01 -g rg-prod --command-id RunPowerShellScript \
  --scripts "Get-Service W3SVC | Select Status"
Error Reference
What the Message Actually Means
ErrorReal causeFirst move
AuthorizationFailedNo role assignment grants that action at that scopeCheck the scope, not just the role — and allow for propagation delay
RequestDisallowedByPolicyAn Azure Policy deny effect blocked the shape of the requestThe message names the policy; fix the request or file an exemption
ScopeLockedA CanNotDelete or ReadOnly lock is in the wayRemove the lock deliberately, then put it back
QuotaExceeded / SkuNotAvailableSubscription vCPU quota, or that size isn't offered in the region/zoneRequest a quota increase, or pick another size or region
ZonalAllocationFailedCapacity in that specific zone, right nowRetry, try another zone, or use a different VM (Virtual Machine) family
429 / TooManyRequestsResource Manager or a data plane is throttling youHonour Retry-After, back off exponentially, batch the calls
InvalidTemplateDeploymentA nested or dependent resource failed, not the template syntaxRead the inner error from the deployment operations
Name resolves to a public IP (Internet Protocol)Private endpoint exists, private DNS (Domain Name System) zone isn't linked to the VNet (Virtual Network)Link the zone, confirm with nslookup from inside the VNet
Public network access is disabledThe PaaS (Platform as a Service) firewall is on and your client isn't on the allow listAdd the IP or subnet, or go through the private endpoint
A pattern worth internalising: if something worked yesterday and fails today with no deployment in between, check the Activity Log for a policy or lock added at a parent scope. Inheritance means someone can break your resource group without ever touching it.
🪪 Entra ID — Sign-In & Conditional Access Troubleshooting Azure • Identity ▶
Method
The Sign-In Log Already Knows Why
Nearly every "I can't get in" ends at one row in the Entra sign-in logs. Find the attempt by user and time, then read three fields: the failure code, the Conditional Access tab showing which policies evaluated and what each one decided, and the device details. Guessing before reading that row wastes the afternoon.
CodeMeansFix
AADSTS50126Wrong username or passwordGenuinely a credential problem — check for lockout and password spray
AADSTS50076MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) required for this resourceExpected; the client must be able to prompt interactively
AADSTS50079User must enrol in MFA firstSend them through registration, or use temporary access pass
AADSTS53003Blocked by a Conditional Access policyThe log names the policy — check device compliance and location
AADSTS50105User isn't assigned to the applicationAssign the user or group to the enterprise app
AADSTS700016App not found in this tenantWrong tenant, or the service principal was never consented
AADSTS90094Admin consent requiredGrant consent for the delegated permission
AADSTS50058Silent sign-in failed — no sessionUsually benign; the client then prompts interactively
 
# On the device: is it joined, and does it hold a usable PRT?
dsregcmd /status
# AzureAdJoined : YES  |  AzureAdPrt : YES  — if PRT is NO, SSO and device-based CA will fail

# Least-risk way to test a policy change before anyone feels it
# Entra admin center ▸ Conditional Access ▸ What If  — simulate user + app + device + location
# then ship the policy in Report-only mode and read the results for a week
The three rules that prevent most Conditional Access outages: keep a break-glass account excluded from every policy and monitored for use; roll every new policy out in report-only first; and remember that a policy requiring a compliant device silently depends on Intune — if compliance evaluation breaks, sign-ins break with it. That seam is why endpoint and identity engineers end up in the same incident bridge.
🧮 Computer Science Fundamentals
Theory
Complexity · Data structures · Algorithms · Graphs · Probabilistic structures 33 topics · ~1h 05m ▾
📉 Big-O in Practice — What the Notation Hides CS • Complexity ▶
Orientation
You Already Know What Big-O Measures; This Is Where It Misleads
Big O Notation — Measuring Algorithm Efficiency in the Scripting domain covers the notation itself. This card is the follow-up nobody gets taught: Big-O deliberately discards information, and the discarded information is what decides which code is faster on the machine you actually own.
The definition throws away constant factors and lower-order terms because it describes behaviour as n grows without bound. Real inputs are finite, often small, and run on hardware with a memory hierarchy that the model does not represent at all.
Where it breaks
Four Ways the Better Complexity Loses
SituationWhat actually happens
Small n Insertion sort beats quicksort below roughly 10–20 elements, which is why real sort implementations switch to it for small partitions rather than recursing further
Constant factors A linear scan of a contiguous array frequently beats a hash lookup for a few dozen items — no hashing, no pointer chasing, and the whole array is in cache
Memory layout A linked list and an array are both O(n) to traverse. The array can be an order of magnitude faster, because Big-O counts operations and cannot see cache misses
Worst vs typical Quicksort is O(n²) worst case and the usual default anyway, because that case is rare and its typical constant is excellent
The verdict: use Big-O to reject algorithms that will not survive growth, which is what it is genuinely good at. Do not use it to choose between two survivors — measure those, on representative data.
Failure mode
Optimising the Term That Was Never the Problem
The most common waste in performance work is improving an O(n²) loop over 200 items — microseconds — inside a request that spends 40 milliseconds waiting on a database. The complexity analysis was correct and the work was pointless.
Before optimising an algorithm, establish that computation is the cost. In most application code it is not: input/output dominates, and the useful numbers are the ones in Memory Layout & Cache Locality — Why Arrays Beat Linked Lists — roughly nanoseconds for memory, microseconds for local storage, milliseconds for a network round trip. Those three orders of magnitude decide more than an exponent usually does.
📊 Amortized Analysis — Why a Dynamic Array Is O(1) "On Average" CS • Complexity ▶
The idea
Averaging an Expensive Operation Across the Cheap Ones That Earned It
Appending to a dynamic array — a Python list, a Go slice, a C++ vector — is usually writing one value: O(1). Occasionally the backing store is full, and the whole thing is copied to a larger one: O(n). Calling append O(n) because of that would be true and useless.
Amortized analysis asks what a sequence of operations costs. Because the array grows by a constant factor — typically doubling — each resize is twice as expensive as the last but happens half as often. The copying work across n appends sums to less than 2n, so the average cost per append is constant.
The load-bearing detail is "by a factor". Growing by a fixed amount instead — 10 more slots each time — makes appending O(n) amortized, because resizes stop becoming rarer. This is a real bug people write when implementing their own buffer.
Distinction
Amortized Is Not Average-Case
MeansGuarantee
Average-caseExpected cost over a distribution of inputsProbabilistic — a bad input can defeat it
AmortizedWorst-case cost of a sequence, divided by its lengthGuaranteed — no input sequence beats it
Amortized is the stronger claim. Hash table lookup is average-case O(1), and an adversary who can choose keys can force collisions — see Hash Tables. Dynamic array append is amortized O(1), and no sequence of appends can make it worse.
Failure mode
Where the Average Is the Wrong Thing to Care About
Amortized guarantees say nothing about when the expensive operation lands. In a real-time or latency-sensitive path, the occasional O(n) resize is a latency spike, and "it averages out" is no comfort to the request that hit it. The same argument applies to garbage collection pauses.
The mitigations are the same in both cases: pre-size the structure if you know roughly how large it will get, or choose an implementation with worse average throughput and better worst-case bounds. Latency and throughput are different goals, and amortized analysis only speaks to the second. 
# Pre-sizing removes the resizes entirely when the size is known
buf = [None] * n_expected          # Python
buf := make([]int, 0, nExpected)     # Go: length 0, capacity reserved
⚖️ Time vs Space Trade-offs — What Caching Actually Costs CS • Complexity ▶
The pattern
Nearly Every Speed-Up Is Memory You Agreed to Spend
Precomputation, indexes, memoisation, lookup tables and caches are one idea in different clothes: store an answer so you do not compute it twice. The cost is memory, and — far more often the real problem — the obligation to keep the stored answer correct.
TechniqueBuysCosts
MemoisationRepeated calls become freeUnbounded growth unless evicted; wrong if the function is not pure
Database indexLookups go from scan to seekSlower writes, more disk, and a planner that may ignore it
Lookup tableArithmetic becomes an array readOnly wins if the table stays in cache
Denormalised copyNo join at read timeTwo sources of truth to reconcile
The verdict: the memory is the advertised cost and rarely the one that hurts. Invalidation is the real price — every cache is a claim that stored data still matches its source, and nothing enforces that claim for you.
Failure mode
A Lookup Table Bigger Than the Cache Is Slower Than the Maths
Replacing computation with a table assumes the read is cheap. Once the table exceeds the processor's cache, each read is a main-memory access of roughly a hundred nanoseconds — enough time to have executed hundreds of arithmetic instructions.
Modern processors are fast enough that recomputing a small value frequently beats looking it up. This is a genuine reversal from older guidance, and it is why measure is the whole answer here rather than a hedge.
🔁 Recursion & Induction — Trusting a Function That Calls Itself CS • Correctness ▶
The method
Do Not Trace It — Prove It
The reason recursion feels hard is that people try to simulate it mentally, unwinding each call. That does not scale past two levels. The working technique is induction, and it needs exactly three checks:
CheckAsk
Base caseIs there an input that returns without recursing, and is its answer right?
Inductive stepAssuming the call on a smaller input is correct, is my answer correct?
ProgressDoes every call move strictly toward the base case?
Assume the recursive call works. That is not a cheat — it is the inductive hypothesis, and it is the entire reason the technique exists. If all three checks hold, the function is correct, and you never traced a single call.
Failure mode
Progress Is the Check People Skip
Base case and inductive step are usually obvious. Progress is where real bugs live: recursing on n instead of n - 1 on one branch, or on a sub-list that is only sometimes smaller. The result is a stack overflow on a specific input rather than a wrong answer on all of them, which makes it a production bug rather than a test failure. 
# Progress fails when the pivot is the smallest element: the right
# partition never shrinks and the recursion never terminates.
def quicksort(a, lo, hi):
    if lo >= hi: return              # base case
    p = partition(a, lo, hi)
    quicksort(a, lo, p)              # BUG: should be p - 1
    quicksort(a, p + 1, hi)
Python defaults to a recursion limit near 1000 frames, which turns unbounded recursion into a clean exception. C and C++ have no such courtesy: the stack simply runs out, and a deep recursion on attacker-controlled input is a denial-of-service bug.
Practicalities
Tail Calls, and Why Python Will Not Help You
A tail call is a recursive call that is the last thing a function does. Some languages — Scheme, and most functional languages — are required to reuse the stack frame, making such recursion equivalent to a loop. Others, notably Python and CPython-adjacent runtimes, deliberately do not, because keeping the frames makes tracebacks readable.
The practical rule: recursion is the clearer expression for genuinely tree-shaped problems — parsing, directory walks, divide and conquer. For linear problems, write the loop. Where depth is bounded by data you do not control, convert to an explicit stack so the limit is memory you can measure rather than a frame count you cannot.
🧩 P, NP & Knowing When to Stop Looking for an Exact Answer CS • Tractability ▶
The distinction
Easy to Check Is Not the Same as Easy to Find
P is the set of problems solvable in polynomial time. NP is the set whose proposed answers can be verified in polynomial time. Every problem in P is in NP — checking is never harder than solving — and whether the reverse holds is the open question.
A useful example: given a schedule for 300 staff, confirming it satisfies every constraint takes seconds. Finding an optimal one may take longer than the age of the universe. Nothing about the checking speed implies anything about the finding speed, and that gap is the entire subject.
Why you care
Recognising One Saves You From Promising a Delivery Date
NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP: solve one efficiently and you have solved all of them. Nobody has, in over fifty years of trying. The practical consequence is that recognising your problem as one of them is a result, not a defeat — it tells you to stop searching for an exact efficient algorithm and change what you are promising.
Shows up asClassic name
Fitting jobs onto machines or VMs (Virtual Machine) onto hostsBin packing
Rostering staff or timetabling roomsGraph colouring
Routing a vehicle through many stopsTravelling salesman
Choosing what fits in a fixed budgetKnapsack
Dependency resolution with version constraintsBoolean satisfiability
The verdict: that last row is why package managers occasionally hang for a very long time. Dependency resolution is genuinely NP-complete, and the resolver is not badly written — it is running a solver on a hard instance.
What to do instead
Four Honest Exits
ExitGive upGood when
ApproximationOptimality — take within 5% of bestNearly always. Most businesses cannot tell optimal from good
HeuristicAny guarantee at allInstances look alike and you can measure results
Constrain the inputGeneralityThe hard cases do not occur in your data
Off-the-shelf solverWriting it yourselfAlways try this first — solvers beat hand-rolled search badly
The failure mode is not choosing an exit: an exact algorithm ships, works on the test data, and hangs eighteen months later when a customer's input crosses a threshold nobody documented. Decide which guarantee you are dropping, and write it down where the next person will find it.
🧱 Memory Layout & Cache Locality — Why Arrays Beat Linked Lists CS • Data Structures ▶
Orientation
Which Structure to Pick Is Covered; This Is Why the Table Lies
Choosing the Right Data Structure in the Scripting domain has the operation-cost table. This card explains why that table mispredicts real performance so often: it counts operations, and the machine charges for memory access patterns.
Memory does not arrive one byte at a time. It arrives in cache lines, typically 64 bytes. Reading one integer from main memory fetches its fifteen neighbours whether you want them or not — so a structure whose elements sit next to each other gets the next fifteen reads nearly free.
The consequence
Same Big-O, Order-of-Magnitude Difference
ArrayLinked list
Traversal complexityO(n)O(n)
Elements per memory fetch~16 (64-byte line, 4-byte ints)1, plus a pointer to chase
Prefetcher can helpYes — the stride is predictableNo — the next address is unknown until arrival
Memory overheadNoneA pointer per element, often doubling the size
Genuinely better atEverything you iterateSplicing when you already hold the node
The verdict: linked lists are taught early and used rarely. Unless you need stable references to elements or O(1) splice with a node already in hand, an array or dynamic array wins — including for insert-in-the-middle at small sizes, because memmove of a contiguous block is extremely fast.
Applying it
Struct of Arrays, and Why Databases Went Columnar
If you process one field across many records, storing an array per field beats an array of records: the fetched cache lines contain only data you asked for. This is the same insight behind columnar storage — see Columnar Engines — Parquet, DuckDB & ClickHouse in the Data domain — and behind why a scan over a column store outruns a row store on analytics by so much. 
# Array of structs: summing one field drags every other field into cache
struct P { float x, y, z; char name[64]; };
P people[N];              # 76 bytes/record; ~0.8 useful bytes per line

# Struct of arrays: the summed field is contiguous
float xs[N], ys[N], zs[N];
char names[N][64];        # every fetched line is all x values
Do not reach for this by default — it makes code harder to read and only pays where a hot loop touches a subset of fields over many records. It is a profiling result, not a style.
#️⃣ Hash Tables — Collisions, Load Factor & the DoS (Denial of Service) That Exploits Them CS • Data Structures ▶
Mechanism
O(1) Is a Statement About Luck, Not a Guarantee
A hash function maps a key to a bucket index. Two keys landing in the same bucket is a collision, and it is not an edge case — by the birthday argument, collisions begin appearing once the table holds roughly the square root of its capacity in items. Every real implementation is mostly collision-handling machinery.
StrategyHowWeakness
ChainingEach bucket holds a listPointer chasing; degrades to a list under attack
Linear probingTry the next slot alongClustering, but excellent cache behaviour
Robin HoodProbe, stealing slots from luckier keysComplex deletion; very even probe lengths
Load factor — items divided by buckets — is the number that governs all of them. Beyond roughly 0.7 for open addressing, probe sequences lengthen sharply, so tables resize and rehash to stay under it. That resize is the same amortized cost described in Amortized Analysis, and the same latency spike.
Failure mode
Hash Flooding — Turning O(1) Into O(n) On Purpose
If the hash function is deterministic and public, an attacker can compute thousands of distinct keys that collide into one bucket. Every lookup then walks a long chain, and a single HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) request with a crafted form body or JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) object consumes seconds of CPU (Central Processing Unit). One request, one core, no authentication needed.
This broke essentially every web framework simultaneously in 2011, because they all parsed request parameters straight into a hash table. The fix is hash randomisation: seed the hash function per process, so an attacker cannot precompute colliding keys. 
# Python randomises string hashing per process by default since 3.3.
# Same string, two processes, two hashes — that is the mitigation working.
$ python3 -c "print(hash('collide'))"
$ python3 -c "print(hash('collide'))"

# PYTHONHASHSEED=0 disables it. Only ever for reproducing a bug.
Never hard-code a hash seed in production, and never rely on iteration order. If you need a stable order, sort explicitly. Code that depends on dictionary ordering works until the day someone enables randomisation, and then fails somewhere unrelated.
Practicalities
Mutable Keys, and Equality That Disagrees With Hashing
A hash table's contract is that equal objects hash equally, and that a key's hash never changes while it is stored. Break either and entries become unreachable — present in memory, invisible to lookup, and undetectable by reading the calling code.
This is why Python refuses to hash a list, and why overriding equality without overriding hashing is a bug in Java, C# and Python alike. If you write one, write both, from the same fields, and make those fields immutable.
🌳 Trees — BST (Binary Search Tree), Balanced, Heap & Trie, and What Each Is Actually For CS • Data Structures ▶
Choosing
Four Trees, Four Different Jobs
"Tree" is not one structure. These four solve genuinely different problems, and confusing them is the usual reason someone reaches for the wrong one.
StructureAnswersReach for it when
BST / balanced treeOrdered lookup, range queries, predecessorYou need sorted order as well as lookup
HeapOnly "what is the minimum?"Priority queues, scheduling, top-k
TriePrefix matching, autocompleteKeys are strings sharing prefixes
B-treeOrdered lookup with few disk readsThe data is on disk — this is your database index
The verdict: if you only need "is this present?", a hash table beats all of them. Trees earn their place when order matters — range scans, nearest neighbours, or reading everything sorted without a sort.
Why balance
An Unbalanced BST Is a Linked List With Extra Steps
A plain BST built from already-sorted input degenerates completely: every insert goes right, and lookup becomes O(n). Since sorted input is extremely common — importing records by ID, replaying a log — this is the normal case rather than the pathological one.
Self-balancing variants (red-black, AVL) rotate on insert to keep depth logarithmic. You will rarely implement one; you should know that your language's ordered map is one, and that a hand-rolled BST in production code is a latent O(n).
Disk
B-trees Exist Because a Disk Read Is Enormous
A balanced binary tree over a million keys is about 20 levels deep. On disk that is 20 seeks, and a seek costs roughly a hundred thousand times a memory access. B-trees fix this by making each node hold hundreds of keys — one page — so the same million keys sit three levels deep and cost three reads.
This is the single most important structure in databases, and Indexes Explained — B-tree, Hash & Covering in the Data domain covers the query-planning side. The theory answer to "why not a binary tree on disk?" is: the memory hierarchy has a cliff in it, and B-trees are shaped around the cliff.
🕸️ Graphs — Representation, Traversal & the Four Algorithms Worth Knowing CS • Data Structures ▶
Recognising one
Most Hard Problems Are Graph Problems Wearing a Costume
Package dependencies, network topology, permission inheritance, build pipelines, service call chains, Active Directory attack paths — all graphs. Recognising the shape is most of the work, because the algorithms are standard once you have.
QuestionAlgorithmCost
Fewest hops from here to there?Breadth-first searchO(V + E)
Is there a cycle? What order can I build in?Topological sortO(V + E)
Cheapest path with weights?DijkstraO(E log V)
Cheapest path, some weights negative?Bellman-FordO(V·E) — slower, but Dijkstra is simply wrong here
Dijkstra with negative weights does not produce a slightly worse answer — it produces a wrong one, because it finalises a node's distance on first visit and a negative edge can invalidate that later. This is a genuine trap: the code runs, returns a path, and the path is not shortest.
Representation
Adjacency List Unless the Graph Is Dense
Adjacency listAdjacency matrix
SpaceO(V + E)O(V²) regardless of edges
"Is there an edge u→v?"O(degree)O(1)
Iterate a node's neighboursOptimalO(V) even for one neighbour
Real graphs are overwhelmingly sparse — a machine has a handful of neighbours, not thousands — so adjacency lists win almost always. A matrix over 100,000 nodes is 10 billion entries for a graph that probably has a few hundred thousand edges.
Failure mode
Traversal Without a Visited Set
Any graph with a cycle will loop forever if traversal does not record visited nodes. The same bug in a slightly different form — marking visited on dequeue rather than on enqueue — lets a node enter the queue many times, quietly turning a linear traversal into something far worse on dense graphs. 
from collections import deque

def bfs(adj, start):
    seen = {start}                     # mark on ENQUEUE, not on dequeue
    q = deque([start])
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()
        yield node
        for nxt in adj[node]:
            if nxt not in seen:
                seen.add(nxt)
                q.append(nxt)
Cycles also make "dependency resolution" fail in the field: a build system reporting a cycle is doing topological sort correctly, and the cycle is real. Fix the dependencies, not the tool.
🎲 Probabilistic Structures — Bloom Filters, HyperLogLog & Sketches CS • Data Structures ▶
The trade
Give Up Exactness, Get Constant Memory
These structures answer questions about enormous sets in kilobytes, by being wrong in a bounded and known direction. That last part is what makes them engineering tools rather than approximations: the error is one-sided, so you can build correct systems on top.
StructureAnswersWrong how
Bloom filterHave I seen this?False positives only — never a false negative
HyperLogLogHow many distinct?~2% error in ~12 KB, for billions of items
Count-min sketchHow often did this appear?Overestimates only — never under
The one-sidedness is the design. A Bloom filter saying "no" is definitive, so it is used as a cheap gate in front of an expensive check: databases consult one before reading a disk block, and a "no" skips the read entirely.
Bloom filters
A Bit Array, k Hashes, and No Deletion
Insert by hashing an item k ways and setting those k bits. Query by checking the same k bits: any zero means definitely absent; all ones means probably present. Nothing stores the item itself, which is why memory does not grow with item size.
You cannot delete. Clearing a bit would also delete every other item sharing it. The false-positive rate is fixed by bits-per-item and k, so the size must be chosen from the expected item count in advance — roughly 10 bits per item gives about 1%. Over-fill it and the rate climbs until every answer is "probably present".
Use one when a false positive costs only a wasted lookup, never where it costs correctness or safety. "Probably breached password" is a fine use; "probably authorised" is not.
🔤 Sorting & Searching — Why Your Language Picked the One It Did CS • Algorithms ▶
The real question
You Will Never Write a Sort; You Will Choose One By Accident
Implementing a sort is an interview exercise. The decision that matters in real code is which one your runtime already calls, because that choice determines whether your sort is stable, how it behaves on nearly-sorted data, and whether an adversary can push it into its worst case.
Used byAlgorithmStableChosen because
Python, Java objectsTimsortYesReal data arrives partly sorted; Timsort finds and merges existing runs
C++ std::sortIntrosortNoQuicksort speed, switching to heapsort to cap the worst case at O(n log n)
Rust sort_unstablePattern-defeating quicksortNoFastest in place; the stable version is offered separately and costs memory
DatabasesExternal merge sortUsuallyThe data does not fit in memory, which changes the problem entirely
Stability is the property that bites. A stable sort keeps equal elements in their original relative order, which is what makes "sort by date, then sort by name" produce what users expect. Do that with an unstable sort and the second pass silently scrambles the first — a bug that looks like a data problem.
Searching
Binary Search Is Easy to Describe and Famously Easy to Get Wrong
Binary search was published in 1946 and the first correct published implementation appeared in 1962. The standard Java version carried an overflow bug for nine years. The lesson is not that it is hard, but that off-by-one boundaries deserve real care — so call your standard library's version. 
# The classic bug: lo + hi overflows on large arrays in fixed-width ints.
mid = (lo + hi) // 2          # overflows in C/Java
mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2     # does not

# Python: use the library. bisect returns an insertion point,
# which is more useful than a found/not-found boolean.
from bisect import bisect_left
i = bisect_left(sorted_items, target)
found = i < len(sorted_items) and sorted_items[i] == target
Sorting to enable one binary search is a losing trade: O(n log n) to save O(n). It pays only when you will search the same data many times — which is exactly the argument for a database index.
🗝️ Divide & Conquer, Greedy, Dynamic Programming — Recognising Which Applies CS • Algorithms ▶
Recognising
Three Strategies, and the Question That Separates Them
These are not interchangeable techniques to try in turn. Each requires a specific property of the problem, and applying one whose property does not hold produces an answer that is confidently wrong rather than slow.
StrategyRequiresFails how
Divide & conquerIndependent subproblems that recombineRecombination is harder than the split
GreedyA locally best choice is always globally safeSilently returns a suboptimal answer
Dynamic programmingOverlapping subproblems, optimal substructureState explosion — memory, not correctness
Greedy is the dangerous one. It is easy to write, usually plausible, and wrong in a way no test catches unless someone knew the optimum independently. Making change with coins of 1, 3 and 4: greedy takes 4+1+1 for six, while the optimum is 3+3. Before shipping a greedy algorithm, either prove the exchange argument or say plainly that the result is approximate.
DP in practice
Memoise the Recursion; Do Not Start With the Table
Dynamic programming is taught bottom-up, with a table and indices, which is why it has a reputation for being impenetrable. The practical route is the opposite: write the naive recursion, confirm it is correct, then add a cache. The result is the same complexity with none of the index arithmetic. 
from functools import lru_cache

# Naive recursion: correct, exponential, obviously right.
# One decorator makes it linear. That is the whole technique.
@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def ways(n):
    if n < 0: return 0
    if n == 0: return 1
    return ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2)
Convert to a bottom-up table only when you need it — to avoid recursion depth, or to drop memory from O(n) to O(1) by keeping just the rows still in use. Both are optimisations of a working solution, not the starting point.
🔡 String Algorithms — Matching, Edit Distance & Where Regex Fits CS • Algorithms ▶
Matching
Naive Search Is Usually Fine, Until the Data Is Adversarial
Checking a pattern at every position is O(n·m) worst case and close to O(n) on natural text, because mismatches happen early. Real substring search in a standard library is already better than naive, and the classic algorithms matter mainly for knowing why the worst case exists.
AlgorithmIdeaGood for
Knuth-Morris-PrattPrecompute how far to skip after a mismatchGuaranteed O(n + m), streaming input
Boyer-MooreMatch right to left, skip ahead on a bad characterLong patterns — often sublinear in practice
Rabin-KarpRolling hash, compare hashes not charactersSearching many patterns at once; plagiarism detection
Aho-CorasickA trie of all patterns, matched in one passThousands of patterns — intrusion detection, filters
Aho-Corasick is the one worth recognising operationally: it is how a signature engine scans traffic for ten thousand indicators in a single pass rather than ten thousand.
Failure mode
Catastrophic Backtracking — When a Regex Becomes a Denial of Service
A regular expression describing a regular language can be matched in linear time. Most production engines — Python, Java, JavaScript, PCRE — instead use backtracking, because it supports backreferences and lookaround. On a pattern with nested quantifiers, that backtracking can be exponential. 
# Nested quantifier over overlapping alternatives. Add one character
# to the input and the match time roughly doubles.
pattern = r"^(a+)+$"
subject = "a" * 30 + "!"        # no match, and it will take a while

# Mitigations, in order of preference:
#  1. Avoid nested quantifiers and overlapping alternations
#  2. Anchor, and make quantifiers possessive/atomic where supported
#  3. Use a linear-time engine (RE2, Rust regex) for untrusted patterns
#  4. Impose a timeout — the last resort, not the design
Never run a user-supplied regular expression on a backtracking engine. This is a real and regularly exploited class of outage, and it has taken down major services. If users must supply patterns, use an engine with linear-time guarantees.
Edit distance
Levenshtein Is Dynamic Programming You Will Actually Use
Edit distance counts the insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to turn one string into another. It powers spelling suggestions, "did you mean", fuzzy record matching and command-line typo correction, and it is the clearest small example of dynamic programming — a table where each cell depends on three neighbours.
It costs O(n·m) time and memory, so it does not scale to comparing one string against millions. The standard approach is to narrow candidates cheaply first — a prefix index, a trie, or blocking on a key — and compute edit distance only within the shortlist.
🎰 Randomised Algorithms — Sampling, Reservoirs & Monte Carlo CS • Algorithms ▶
Why randomise
Randomness Removes the Adversary's Advantage
A deterministic algorithm has a worst case, and anything that can choose your input can find it. Randomising a choice the algorithm makes means no fixed input is reliably bad — the same reasoning behind hash seed randomisation, and behind picking a random pivot in quicksort.
Two families worth telling apart: Las Vegas algorithms are always correct and take a random amount of time (randomised quicksort). Monte Carlo algorithms take bounded time and are occasionally wrong, with a probability you choose (primality testing).
Reservoir sampling
A Fair Sample From a Stream of Unknown Length
Take k items uniformly at random from a stream you cannot buffer and whose length you do not know in advance — log lines, telemetry, a large file. Keep the first k, then for item i replace a random one with probability k/i. Every item ends equally likely, in O(k) memory and one pass. 
import random

def reservoir(stream, k):
    keep = []
    for i, item in enumerate(stream):
        if i < k:
            keep.append(item)
        else:
            j = random.randint(0, i)     # inclusive
            if j < k:
                keep[j] = item
    return keep
This is how sampled logging and distributed tracing keep a representative slice without knowing the request volume ahead of time. The alternative people reach for — "keep every hundredth" — is not a uniform sample and correlates badly with periodic traffic.
Failure mode
The Wrong Random Number Generator
A default generator is built for speed and statistical quality, not unpredictability. Its output is reproducible from its seed, which is a feature for simulation and a vulnerability for anything security-relevant.
UsePythonNever use for
Simulation, sampling, shuffling display orderrandomTokens, passwords, keys, session IDs
Anything an attacker benefits from predictingsecrets—
Predictable password-reset tokens are a recurring real-world breach, and the code that produced them looked entirely reasonable. If the value protects something, use the cryptographic generator — it costs nothing here.
🎯 Algorithm Interview Patterns — The Eight That Cover Most Questions CS • Interview ▶
The patterns
Recognition Beats Recall
Interview questions are drawn from a small set of shapes. Memorising solutions does not transfer; recognising the shape does, because the shape tells you the data structure and the data structure writes most of the code.
Signal in the questionReach for
Sorted array, find a pair or tripleTwo pointers from both ends
Longest/shortest contiguous run meeting a conditionSliding window
Top k, or a running medianHeap — two heaps for the median
"Have I seen this before", counting, groupingHash map
Shortest path in an unweighted graph or gridBreadth-first search
All combinations, permutations, board placementsBacktracking
Count the ways, or best value under a limitDynamic programming
Ordering with dependenciesTopological sort
Sliding window and two pointers cover a surprising share alone. Both turn an O(n²) nested loop into O(n) by never re-examining what the window already summarised — and both are far easier to derive live than to remember.
Method
State the Brute Force First — It Is Worth Marks, Not Lost Ones
Candidates routinely stay silent hunting for the clever answer. Saying "the brute force is O(n²) — I check every pair; let me see whether I can avoid re-scanning" establishes a correct baseline, shows the analysis, and frequently leads to the optimisation. It also leaves something working if time runs out.
Then: clarify input constraints before coding, say the complexity of what you are about to write, and test on an empty input and a single element. Most failed submissions are edge cases, not algorithms. See Interview Preparation — Getting the Job in the Career domain for the surrounding process.
⏱️ Processes, Threads & Scheduling — What a Context Switch Costs CS • Operating Systems ▶
Orientation
Linux Covers the Commands; This Is Why the Numbers Come Out That Way
Processes & Signals — Running Programs in Linux and Process Management – Finding and Taming Runaway Processes in the Linux domain cover finding and controlling processes. This card is the model underneath: what the kernel is actually choosing between, and why adding threads so often fails to make anything faster.
ProcessThread
Address spaceIts own — isolatedShared with siblings
Crash blast radiusItselfThe whole process
CommunicationPipes, sockets, shared memory — explicitOrdinary variables — and therefore races
Switch costHigher — address space changesLower, but not free
The verdict: the choice is about failure isolation more than performance. Threads share memory, which makes communication trivial and makes every shared variable a correctness problem. Processes make you say what you are sharing — which is why browsers and web servers put untrusted work in separate processes.
The cost
A Context Switch Is Cheap Directly and Expensive Indirectly
The direct cost — saving registers, swapping page tables — is on the order of a microsecond. The real cost is that the new task arrives to a cache full of the previous task's data, so it runs slowly until the cache refills. That indirect cost is invisible to every timer and can dominate.
This is why running far more runnable threads than cores makes throughput worse, and why thread-pool sizing is roughly core-count for CPU-bound work but much higher for I/O-bound work, where threads are blocked rather than competing.
Measure switches directly before theorising: vmstat 1 reports context switches per second in the cs column, and pidstat -w attributes them per process. A high voluntary switch count means blocking on I/O (Input/Output); a high involuntary count means CPU (Central Processing Unit) contention. Those two point at opposite fixes.
🗺️ Virtual Memory — Paging, the TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) & Swap's Bad Reputation CS • Operating Systems ▶
The mechanism
Every Address Your Program Uses Is a Lie the Kernel Maintains
Programs address virtual memory; hardware translates each access to a physical address through page tables. That indirection buys isolation between processes, memory that can be larger than RAM (Random Access Memory), and shared read-only pages — one copy of a library serving every process using it.
Translation itself would be ruinously slow if performed every access, so the processor caches recent translations in the TLB. A TLB miss costs a page-table walk; this is why large pages exist, and why a workload with a scattered access pattern can be slow for reasons no profiler attributes to memory.
Reputation
Swap Is Not the Problem — Thrashing Is
"Disable swap for performance" is common advice and mostly wrong. Swap lets the kernel evict pages that are genuinely never touched — initialisation code, an idle daemon — and use the reclaimed memory as cache. A system with swap and no swapping is healthier than one without swap.
The pathology is thrashing: the working set exceeds RAM, so pages are evicted and immediately faulted back. Throughput collapses because every access waits on storage. Disabling swap does not fix that — it converts a slow system into one where the out-of-memory killer terminates something instead.
Watch the paging rate, not the swap usage. Used swap is a historical fact and often harmless; si/so in vmstat staying non-zero is the live problem. The two get confused constantly, and only the second is an incident.
🔐 Concurrency Primitives — Mutexes, Semaphores, Conditions & Atomics CS • Operating Systems ▶
Choosing
Four Tools, and They Are Not Interchangeable
PrimitiveAnswersTypical misuse
MutexOnly one at a time in hereHeld across an I/O (Input/Output) call, serialising everything
SemaphoreAt most N at a timeUsed as a mutex, losing the "who owns it" check
Condition variableWait until something is trueWaiting without a loop — spurious wakeups are real
AtomicThis one operation is indivisibleAssuming two atomics compose atomically
The last one is the subtle one. Two atomic operations are not an atomic pair: an atomic read followed by an atomic write is a race, because something can intervene between them. That is why compare-and-swap exists — it makes read-check-write a single indivisible step.
Failure mode
The Lock You Held for Too Long
The most common concurrency bug in production is not a race — it is a mutex held across something slow. A lock held during a network call or a disk write turns a concurrent service into a serial one, and the symptom is latency that climbs with load while CPU (Central Processing Unit) stays low. 
# Serialises every caller behind one network round trip
with lock:
    row = db.fetch(key)          # slow, and holding the lock
    cache[key] = transform(row)

# Do the slow work outside; hold the lock only for the shared state
row = db.fetch(key)
value = transform(row)
with lock:
    cache[key] = value           # may overwrite a concurrent write — usually fine
The second version can do duplicate work under contention. That is nearly always the right trade: duplicated computation is cheap, and a serialised service is not. Decide deliberately rather than by where the with happened to go.
🔒 Deadlock & Livelock — The Four Conditions, and Which One to Break CS • Operating Systems ▶
Diagnosis
Deadlock Needs All Four; Removing Any One Prevents It
ConditionBreak it by
Mutual exclusionUsing immutable data or per-thread copies
Hold and waitAcquiring everything at once, or nothing
No pre-emptionTimeouts — take the lock or give up and retry
Circular waitA global lock ordering — the usual answer
Lock ordering is the practical fix. Define an order — by address, by identifier, by name — and require every code path to acquire in that order. The classic deadlock is two account transfers running in opposite directions; ordering by account number removes it entirely, and costs one comparison.
Livelock
Everything Is Running and Nothing Is Progressing
Livelock is deadlock's harder-to-spot relative: threads are not blocked, they are busy responding to each other and never advancing. Two people stepping aside in a corridor, repeatedly. It is worse than deadlock diagnostically, because CPU (Central Processing Unit) is busy and every thread looks alive.
The usual cause is a naive retry: detect a conflict, back off, retry immediately, collide again. Fix it the same way networks did — exponential backoff with jitter. Without jitter, retries stay synchronised and collide in lockstep forever.
Database deadlocks are normal and expected. The engine detects a cycle and aborts one transaction with a retryable error — so application code that talks to a database must handle deadlock as a retry case, not as a fatal exception. Code that does not is the source of the intermittent failures nobody can reproduce.
💾 Filesystems From the Inside — Inodes, Journaling & Crash Consistency CS • Operating Systems ▶
Structure
A Filename Is a Pointer, Not the File
The file is the inode: metadata plus the location of its data. A directory entry is just a name pointing at an inode number. Several names may point at the same inode — hard links — and the data survives until the last one is removed.
Two consequences that explain real behaviour.
