Deleting a file being held open by a process frees no space, because the descriptor is still a reference — which is why a disk can stay full after deleting a log, until the writer is restarted. And "disk full" with free space showing means inode exhaustion: millions of tiny files, checkable with df -i, which almost nobody runs first.
Crash consistency
Journaling Protects the Filesystem, Not Your Data
A write touches several structures — the data, the inode, the free-space map. Interrupted halfway, the filesystem is inconsistent. A journal records the intent first, so recovery replays or discards the whole operation and the structure is always valid.
The default mode journals metadata only, because journaling data as well halves write throughput. So after a crash the filesystem mounts cleanly and a file may still contain garbage or an old version: the guarantee is about the filesystem, not the file contents, and that distinction disappoints people at the worst moment. 
# The durability sequence applications must actually perform
# A write() is in the page cache, not on the device.
fd = os.open(path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT)
os.write(fd, data)
os.fsync(fd)                     # the file's data is now durable
os.close(fd)
dir_fd = os.open(os.path.dirname(path), os.O_RDONLY)
os.fsync(dir_fd)                 # and now its NAME is durable too
The second fsync is the one everybody omits. Renaming a temporary file into place is atomic, but the directory entry itself is buffered — crash before that is flushed and the file is durable under a name that no longer exists. This is the bug behind a well-known class of "my config file was empty after a power cut".
🕰️ Time in Distributed Systems — Why Timestamps Cannot Order Events CS • Distributed ▶
The problem
Two Clocks Never Agree, and One of Them Runs Backwards
Ordering events across machines by wall-clock timestamp is the most common distributed systems mistake, because it looks like it works. Clocks drift, and NTP (Network Time Protocol) corrects them by stepping — which means a timestamp can go backwards, and two events can carry identical times.
The consequences are real: last-write-wins silently discards the wrong update, log correlation across services shows effects before causes, and a certificate can appear expired on one host and valid on another.
Use a monotonic clock for durations and a wall clock only for display. Measuring elapsed time by subtracting two wall-clock readings is a bug that surfaces rarely and confusingly — every mainstream language offers a monotonic source precisely for this.
The alternative
Logical Clocks Count Causality Instead of Seconds
A Lamport clock is a counter each node increments on every event and sends with every message; a receiver takes the maximum of its own and the sender's, plus one. This guarantees that if A caused B then A's number is lower — but not the reverse, so a lower number does not prove causality.
A vector clock carries one counter per node, which does capture the reverse: comparing two vectors tells you that one happened before the other, or that they are genuinely concurrent — neither caused the other.
Detecting concurrency is the point. Concurrent writes are a real conflict, and a system that knows this can surface both versions and ask, rather than silently picking the one with the larger timestamp. The cost is a vector that grows with the number of nodes, which is why production systems bound it or use hybrid logical clocks instead.
🤝 Consensus — Raft and Paxos, Without the Paper CS • Distributed ▶
The problem
Getting a Group of Machines to Agree on One Value
Consensus is how a cluster decides who the leader is, whether a transaction committed, or what the current configuration is — with machines failing and messages being lost or delayed. Every strongly consistent distributed system has one of these at its core: etcd and Kubernetes, Consul, ZooKeeper, most modern databases.
Raft is the one to learn, because it was explicitly designed to be understandable and the mechanism is three ideas: elect a leader, replicate an ordered log from that leader, and commit an entry once a majority has stored it.
Majorities
Quorum Is Why Cluster Sizes Are Odd
NodesMajorityFailures tolerated
321
431 — no better than 3
532
Four nodes tolerate no more failures than three and cost more to coordinate. That is the entire reason clusters are 3, 5 or 7. Requiring a majority also makes split-brain impossible: two halves of a partitioned network cannot both hold a majority, so at most one side stays writable.
Failure mode
Losing Quorum Is Correct Behaviour, and It Looks Like an Outage
When enough nodes fail that no majority remains, the cluster stops accepting writes. It is not broken — it is refusing to risk divergence. Under CAP it has chosen consistency over availability, deliberately.
The operational trap is forcing a new configuration to "get it back up". That can commit a state the old majority never agreed, and when the missing nodes return the histories conflict. Restore the nodes if there is any chance of it; forcing quorum is a data-loss decision and should be recorded as one. See CAP Theorem & Consistency Models in the DevOps domain for the trade-off this sits inside.
📡 Failure Detection & FLP — Why "Is It Down?" Has No Perfect Answer CS • Distributed ▶
The result
A Slow Node and a Dead Node Are Indistinguishable
If a node has not replied, it may be dead, or overloaded, or the network may have dropped the reply. From the outside these are identical, and no amount of waiting resolves the ambiguity — waiting longer only reduces how often you are wrong.
The FLP result proves this is fundamental: in an asynchronous system where even one node may fail, no algorithm can guarantee consensus in bounded time. Real systems get around it not by beating the proof but by adding timeouts — accepting that they will occasionally declare a live node dead.
Every timeout is a guess about the network. Too short and you evict healthy nodes during a traffic spike, causing the outage you were detecting. Too long and real failures go unnoticed. There is no correct value — only one tuned to your network's actual latency distribution.
Consequences
Fencing, Because the Old Leader May Not Know It Was Replaced
A node declared dead and replaced may still be running — paused by garbage collection, or on the far side of a partition. When it resumes it believes it is still the leader and may write. That is split-brain, and it corrupts data rather than causing downtime.
The standard defence is a fencing token: every leadership term carries a monotonically increasing number, and the storage layer rejects any write bearing a number lower than the highest it has seen. The stale leader's writes are refused by the resource itself rather than by agreement it cannot participate in.
This is why distributed locks are harder than they look. A lock with a lease and no fencing is not safe — the lease can expire while the holder is paused, and the holder has no way to notice before it writes. If you are implementing one, the token is not optional.
🏔️ Caches & the Memory Hierarchy — The Numbers Every Engineer Should Know CS • Architecture ▶
The numbers
Six Orders of Magnitude, and Where Your Latency Actually Went
Storage is a hierarchy: small and fast at the top, enormous and slow at the bottom. The gaps are not incremental — they span six orders of magnitude, and knowing roughly where each level sits explains more production latency than any profiler.
LevelRoughlyScaled to 1 second = 1 ns
L1 cache~1 ns1 second
L2 cache~4 ns4 seconds
Main memory~100 ns2 minutes
NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) read~100 µs1 day
Same-datacentre round trip~0.5 ms6 days
Cross-continent round trip~150 ms5 years
These are order-of-magnitude figures, not benchmarks — they shift with hardware, and the ratios matter far more than the values. The practical conclusion is blunt: no amount of algorithmic cleverness recovers a network round trip you did not need. Remove the trip before optimising the loop.
Consequence
Cache Lines Explain False Sharing
Memory moves in 64-byte lines, and cache coherency operates on whole lines. Two threads writing to different variables that happen to share a line will invalidate each other's caches on every write — the code is correct, contends on nothing logically, and runs several times slower than the single-threaded version.
This is false sharing, and it is the standard explanation for parallel code that gets slower as you add threads. The fix is padding hot per-thread counters onto separate lines. Diagnose it by suspicion rather than by profiler: the signature is negative scaling with thread count on a workload that should be embarrassingly parallel. See Memory Layout & Cache Locality — Why Arrays Beat Linked Lists for the single-threaded side of the same mechanism.
🔢 Number Representation — Two's Complement, IEEE-754 & the Bugs Each Causes CS • Architecture ▶
Integers
Overflow Is Silent, and the Minimum Has No Positive Twin
Two's complement represents negatives by inverting and adding one, which is why addition and subtraction need no special cases — and why the range is asymmetric. A 32-bit int spans −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647: one more negative than positive.
So abs(INT_MIN) is negative. Negating the minimum overflows, and in C that is undefined behaviour the optimiser may assume cannot happen. The classic exploitable form is a length check passing because an attacker-supplied size overflowed to negative, and the subsequent allocation being far too small.
Floats
0.1 + 0.2 Is Not 0.3, and Money Is Not a Float
IEEE-754 stores a sign, an exponent and a fraction in base two. Tenths are not representable in base two any more than a third is in base ten, so the stored value is the nearest representable one and the error compounds across operations. 
# Not a language quirk — the hardware representation, everywhere
>>> 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
False
>>> from decimal import Decimal
>>> Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3")
True
Store money as integer minor units, or as a decimal type. Never as a float. And never compare floats with == — compare against a tolerance appropriate to the magnitudes involved, because a fixed epsilon is wrong at both ends of the range.
Failure mode
The Special Values That Propagate Silently
IEEE-754 defines infinities, two zeros, and NaN (Not a Number). NaN is the dangerous one: it is not equal to itself, so a single NaN entering a pipeline propagates through every arithmetic operation and survives most validity checks written as comparisons.
A metric that reads NaN on a dashboard usually entered as a division by zero many steps upstream. Check with the language's dedicated predicate — math.isnan(), not x == float('nan'), which is always false. And note that x != x being true is the portable NaN test, which looks like a bug and is not.
👻 Speculative Execution & Its Security Cost — Spectre and Meltdown CS • Architecture ▶
Why processors guess
Waiting for a Branch Wastes a Hundred Cycles, So the CPU (Central Processing Unit) Does Not Wait
Instructions execute in a pipeline, several in flight at once. A conditional branch stalls it — the processor cannot know which way to go until the condition resolves, and if that depends on memory, resolving may take hundreds of cycles.
So it predicts, and executes ahead speculatively. If the guess was right, the work is already done. If wrong, the architectural results are discarded. Modern prediction accuracy is well above 95%, and this is a large part of why processors are fast.
The flaw
Discarded Work Leaves Traces in the Cache
Speculation discards architectural state — registers, memory. It does not undo microarchitectural state: data loaded during a mis-speculation stays in the cache. An attacker who can time cache access can therefore learn something about speculatively-read memory they were never permitted to read.
MeltdownSpectre
AbusesOut-of-order execution past a permission checkBranch prediction, trained by the attacker
ReadsKernel memory from user spaceMemory within the victim's own address space
Fixable in softwareYes — page table isolationNot generally; it is mitigated, not fixed
Spectre is the one that matters, because it is a property of speculation itself. Meltdown was an implementation bug and was fixed. Spectre is mitigated per-pattern — compiler barriers, index masking, isolating untrusted code in its own process — and new variants keep arriving, because the underlying optimisation is not going away.
What it means for you
Process Isolation Stopped Being Paranoia
Practical consequences most engineers actually meet: browsers reduced timer precision and put each site in its own process; cloud providers stopped co-locating untrusted tenants on one physical core; and mitigations cost real performance — single-digit to low-double-digit percentages on system-call-heavy workloads.
The transferable lesson is broader than these vulnerabilities: an abstraction that is correct architecturally can still leak through its implementation. Timing, cache state and power draw are all side channels, and none of them appear in the model the code was written against.
⚙️ Instruction Execution — Pipelining, Superscalar & Why Branches Are Expensive CS • Architecture ▶
The model
A Processor Is an Assembly Line, Not a Loop
The textbook cycle — fetch, decode, execute, write back — describes one instruction. Real processors overlap them, so while one instruction executes, the next is decoding and a third is being fetched. Throughput approaches one instruction per cycle even though each takes several.
Superscalar designs go further and issue several instructions per cycle across duplicated units, and out-of-order execution reorders them around stalls. The consequence worth internalising: instruction count is a poor predictor of speed. What matters is whether the pipeline stays full.
Stalls
Three Ways to Empty the Pipeline
HazardCauseMitigated by
DataAn instruction needs a result not yet producedForwarding; reordering
ControlA branch — which instruction comes next is unknownPrediction, and speculation
StructuralTwo instructions want the same unitDuplicating units
A mispredicted branch costs 15–20 cycles — the pipeline is flushed and refilled. Prediction is well above 95% accurate on typical code, which is exactly why unpredictable branches are so costly: a condition that is genuinely random defeats the predictor every other time.
Applying it
Sorting the Input Made the Loop Faster — and It Is Not a Trick
The famous demonstration: a loop summing values above a threshold runs several times faster over sorted data than unsorted, with identical instruction counts. Sorted input makes the branch predictable — long runs of taken, then long runs of not-taken — and the predictor gets it right almost every time.
The engineering lesson is not "sort your data". It is that branchless code can beat branching code where the condition is unpredictable: a conditional move, arithmetic on the comparison result, or a lookup table has no branch to mispredict. Worth reaching for only in a measured hot loop — it is harder to read, and the compiler often does it already.
🧬 Instruction Sets — x86-64, ARM64, RISC-V & Why the Shift Is Happening CS • Architecture ▶
The comparison
The RISC-vs-CISC Argument Is Over; the Licensing One Is Not
The old distinction — few simple instructions versus many complex ones — has largely dissolved. Modern x86 decodes its complex instructions into simple internal operations, so internally it looks much like a RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) machine. What still differs is instruction encoding, memory ordering, and who is allowed to build one.
x86-64ARM64RISC-V
Instruction lengthVariable, 1–15 bytesFixed 4 bytesFixed, with extensions
Memory modelStrong — mostly orderedWeak — reordering allowedWeak
LicensingTwo vendorsLicensed from ArmOpen, royalty-free
Where you meet itDesktops, most serversPhones, Apple silicon, cloud instancesEmbedded, and growing
Variable-length encoding is the real cost. Finding where each instruction ends is itself work, which makes wide parallel decode harder — one of the structural reasons ARM (Advanced RISC Machines) designs reach high instruction throughput more easily.
Failure mode
The Memory Model Is the Bug You Only See After Porting
x86 has a strong memory model: writes become visible in roughly program order. ARM does not — it may reorder freely unless told otherwise. Concurrent code that relies on incidental ordering therefore works on x86 for years and fails on ARM, intermittently.
The code was always wrong; x86 was hiding it. This became a widespread discovery when Apple silicon and ARM cloud instances arrived, and it is why the correct primitives — atomics with explicit ordering, or the language's memory model — are not optional pedantry. See Concurrency Primitives — Mutexes, Semaphores, Conditions & Atomics.
Practical consequence for operations: a container image is built for an architecture. exec format error on an ARM node means an amd64 image; multi-architecture images exist precisely for this, and forgetting them is the most common ARM migration incident.
🏗️ How a Compiler Works — Lexing, Parsing, IR (Incident Response) & Codegen CS • Compilers ▶
The pipeline
Four Stages, and Knowing Which One Failed
A compiler is a pipeline of translations, each producing a form easier to work with than the last. The practical value in knowing the stages is diagnostic: the stage that failed tells you what kind of mistake you made.
StageProducesError looks like
LexingTokensUnterminated string; stray character
ParsingA syntax tree"Unexpected token" — grammar broken
Semantic analysisA checked, typed treeUndefined name; type mismatch
Optimise & generateMachine codeRarely an error — usually a slow binary or a miscompile
A parse error's reported line is where the parser gave up, not where you went wrong. A missing closing brace is usually reported many lines later, at the first construct that cannot follow. Look upward from the reported line, not at it.
Why IR
An Intermediate Representation Turns N×M Into N+M
Supporting N languages on M targets needs N×M compilers written directly — or N front-ends and M back-ends sharing one intermediate representation. That is the whole architecture of LLVM, and the reason a new language can target every processor by emitting one IR.
It also explains a practical asymmetry: optimisations written once in the middle benefit every language using it. A new front-end inherits decades of optimisation work for free, which is why modern languages start faster than their authors could have made them alone.
🔥 Interpreters, Bytecode & JIT (Just-In-Time) — The Spectrum From Python to the JVM CS • Runtimes ▶
The spectrum
"Compiled vs Interpreted" Is a Property of Implementations, Not Languages
There is no interpreted language, only interpreted implementations. C has interpreters; Python compiles to bytecode. The real question is when translation to machine code happens, and how much run-time information is available when it does.
ApproachTranslatesTrade
Ahead-of-timeBefore runningFast start, predictable; no run-time knowledge
Bytecode interpreterTo bytecode, then walks itPortable, simple, slower
JITHot paths, while runningPeak speed, slow warm-up, memory cost
A JIT can beat ahead-of-time compilation, which surprises people. It observes what actually happens — which branch is taken, which concrete type flows through — and specialises for it, then de-optimises if the assumption breaks. That information does not exist at build time.
Failure mode
Warm-Up Invalidates Your Benchmark and Your Health Check
A JIT-compiled service is slow for its first seconds or minutes, then several times faster. Two consequences bite in production: a benchmark that measures the first thousand iterations measures the interpreter, and an instance added to a load balancer the moment its health check passes receives full traffic while still cold.
Hence warm-up requests before accepting traffic, and gradual ramping rather than an instant share. This is also why autoscaling a JIT runtime for a traffic spike helps later than expected — the new instances need time to become fast, and the spike may be over before they are.
🏷️ Type Systems — Static, Dynamic, and What Types Actually Buy You CS • Languages ▶
Two axes
Static vs Dynamic Is Not Strong vs Weak
These get conflated constantly and they are independent. Static/dynamic is when types are checked — compile time or run time. Strong/weak is how much the language will silently convert for you.
StrongWeak
StaticRust, Java, GoC — an int is a pointer if you insist
DynamicPython — "1" + 1 raisesJavaScript — "1" + 1 is "11"
Python is dynamically and strongly typed, which surprises people who assume dynamic means permissive. The bug class that hurts is weak typing, not dynamic typing: a silent coercion produces a plausible wrong answer, where a raised error produces a stack trace.
What they buy
Types Are a Machine-Checked Subset of the Documentation
A type signature states what a function accepts and returns, and unlike a comment it cannot drift — the compiler rejects it when it stops being true. That is the durable argument for static types, and it strengthens as a codebase outlives the people who wrote it.
What types do not buy is correctness. A function returning int can return the wrong int. Types eliminate a category of error — roughly, "this value is not the shape you expected" — and leave the logic entirely to you. Teams that expect more from them are the ones disappointed by them.
Practicalities
Gradual Typing, and the Boundary That Lies
TypeScript, Python's annotations and similar systems add optional static checking to dynamic languages. They are genuinely valuable and share one sharp edge: the types are erased before running, so nothing enforces them at the boundary. A value arriving from JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), a database or an untyped library is whatever it actually is, regardless of the annotation.
Validate at the boundary and trust the types inside it. A parse step that checks incoming data against a schema is what makes the annotations true; without one, a wrong assumption propagates deep into typed code that the checker has already certified as safe. See Data Validation — Never Trust Input in the Scripting domain.
♻️ Garbage Collection — Generational Collectors, Pauses & Tuning CS • Runtimes ▶
The core idea
Most Objects Die Young, and Collectors Are Built Around That
The generational hypothesis is an empirical observation: the overwhelming majority of allocations become garbage almost immediately. Collectors exploit it by splitting the heap — new objects in a small young generation collected frequently and cheaply, survivors promoted to an old generation collected rarely.
A young collection is fast because it costs time proportional to the objects that survived, not to the garbage. Allocating a million short-lived objects is nearly free to collect; keeping a million alive is what costs.
Pauses
Reference Counting Has No Pauses and a Different Problem
Tracing (JVM, Go, .NET)Reference counting (CPython, Swift)
Cost timingBursty — pausesSpread continuously
CyclesCollectedLeaked without a cycle detector
ThroughputHigherLower — every assignment updates a count
Neither is free; they place the cost differently. Reference counting is why CPython frees most objects the instant the last name goes away — and why two objects referring to each other need gc to notice.
Failure mode
Tuning the Collector When the Problem Is the Allocation Rate
The instinct on seeing GC pauses is to change collector flags. That is almost always the wrong first move: pause frequency is driven by how fast the application produces garbage, and by how much survives. Reducing allocation in a hot path fixes the cause; flags redistribute the symptom.
The one tuning decision that reliably matters is heap size, and it trades against pause length: a bigger heap collects less often and takes longer each time. Decide from the service's latency target — and note that a memory leak in a managed language is nearly always an unintended reference, most often a cache or a listener list nobody removes from. See Amortized Analysis — Why a Dynamic Array Is O(1) "On Average" for the same latency-versus-throughput trade in another form.
💥 Undefined Behaviour & Memory Safety — The Class Behind Most CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) CS • Languages ▶
The category
Roughly Two Thirds of Serious Vulnerabilities Are One Bug Class
Buffer overflows, use-after-free, double-free and uninitialised reads share a root: languages where the programmer manually guarantees that memory access is valid. Microsoft and Google have each reported that around 70% of their high-severity vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues — a figure worth treating as an order of magnitude rather than a precise number.
BugWhat happens
Buffer overflowWrite past an allocation, corrupting adjacent memory
Use-after-freeAccess memory already returned — an attacker may control what is there now
Double freeCorrupts the allocator's own bookkeeping
Uninitialised readReads whatever the previous occupant left
Undefined behaviour
The Compiler Is Allowed to Assume It Never Happens
In C and C++, undefined behaviour does not mean "unpredictable result" — it means the standard imposes no requirement at all, so the optimiser may assume it cannot occur and reason from there. This is why a null check after a dereference can be deleted: the dereference already implied the pointer was non-null. 
// The dereference tells the optimiser p cannot be null,
// so the check below is dead code and may be removed.
int v = *p;
if (p == NULL) return ERROR;   // deleted at -O2
Undefined behaviour is not a runtime concept. It changes what the compiler emits, which is why a bug can appear only at higher optimisation levels, or only after a compiler upgrade, and why "it works in debug" proves nothing.
What to do
Sanitisers Now, Safer Languages at the Boundary
Rewriting a working C codebase is rarely justified. The standard advice — from the same organisations that published the 70% figure — is to write new code in a memory-safe language and prioritise the parts that parse untrusted input, which is where the exploitable bugs concentrate. 
# Catch it in CI rather than in a CVE. Both are cheap to enable.
clang -fsanitize=address,undefined -g -O1 prog.c
valgrind --leak-check=full ./prog
Sanitisers find these bugs only on code paths your tests actually execute — so their value is bounded by coverage, and pairing them with fuzzing is what makes the combination effective. Rust's guarantee is stronger precisely because it is a property of the type system rather than of the tests.
🏛️ Software Engineering & Architecture
ARCH SWE
System Design · Architecture · Craft · Reliability · Career 36 topics · ~40 min ▾
📈 Scalability 101 — Vertical vs Horizontal System Design ▶
Concept
Two Ways to Handle More Load
Vertical scaling (scale up) means a bigger machine — more CPU/RAM. Simple, but there's a ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means more machines behind a load balancer — effectively unlimited and fault-tolerant, but only if your app is designed for it. The design requirement is statelessness: any server can handle any request, so session/state lives in a shared store (Redis, DB), not in one server's memory.
Vertical (up)Horizontal (out)
HowBigger boxMore boxes
CeilingHardware limit~Unlimited
FailureSingle pointRedundant
ComplexityLowNeeds LB + stateless design
Real systems do both: scale up the database (hard to shard) and scale out the stateless app tier. Shared-nothing architecture — nodes share no memory/disk — is what makes horizontal scaling clean.
⚖️ Load Balancing & Sharding System Design ▶
Concept
Spreading Requests, Then Spreading Data
A load balancer spreads incoming requests across servers; sharding spreads the data across databases when one can't hold or serve it all. Both are "divide the work," at different layers.
▸ LOAD-BALANCING ALGORITHMS
AlgorithmSends request to…
Round robinEach server in turn
Least connectionsThe least-busy server
WeightedBigger servers get more
IP (Internet Protocol) hash / stickySame client → same server
▸ SHARDING STRATEGIES
StrategySplit byWatch out
RangeKey ranges (A–M, N–Z)Hot ranges
Hashhash(key) % NResharding pain
Consistent hashingRing of hashesAdding nodes moves few keys — the standard
The enemy is the hot shard — one key or range getting disproportionate traffic (a celebrity user). Choose a shard key with even distribution and no cross-shard joins on the hot path.
🧮 Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation System Design ▶
Reference
Numbers Every Engineer Should Know
Before designing, sanity-check scale with rough math. Knowing that memory is ~1000× faster than disk, and a cross-region round trip is ~150 ms, tells you where the bottleneck will be without building anything.
▸ LATENCY NUMBERS (orders of magnitude)
Operation~Time
L1 cache reference~1 ns
Main memory reference~100 ns
SSD (Solid State Drive) random read~100 µs
Network round trip (same DC)~0.5 ms
Disk (HDD) seek~10 ms
Round trip across continents~150 ms
▸ CAPACITY MATH (worked)
1M daily active users, 10 requests/user/day = 10M req/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ ~115 req/s average. Peak is typically 2–3× average → design for ~300 req/s. Storage: 10M writes/day × 1 KB × 365 × 5 yr ≈ ~18 TB. These two numbers (QPS + storage growth) drive most of the architecture.
🛟 Designing for Failure System Design ▶
Concept
Everything Fails — Plan for It
At scale, hardware dies, networks partition, and dependencies time out constantly. Robust systems assume failure and stay up anyway. The core moves: eliminate single points of failure, contain damage, and degrade gracefully instead of collapsing.
TechniqueWhat It Buys
Redundancy (N+1)No single point of failure — replicate across AZs (Availability Zone)
Health checks + failoverRoute away from dead instances automatically
BulkheadsIsolate resources so one overloaded feature can't sink the rest
Graceful degradationServe a cached/limited response instead of an error (show stale prices, hide recommendations)
Blast-radius limitsCell-based / sharded design so an outage hits 5% of users, not 100%
Pair with the resilience patterns (circuit breaker, retry-with-backoff, timeout) at the call level. The mindset: "what happens when this dependency is down?" should have an answer for every dependency.
🧩 The System Design Interview — A Framework Career ▶
Reference
A Repeatable Structure for an Open-Ended Question
"Design Twitter" has no single right answer — interviewers assess how you think. A structure keeps you from freezing and shows senior judgment: drive requirements, estimate, sketch, then go deep where it matters.
StepDo
1. ClarifyNail functional + non-functional requirements. Who uses it? Read/write ratio? Consistency vs availability?
2. EstimateQPS (Queries Per Second), storage, bandwidth — back-of-envelope (previous card). Sets the scale.
3. API (Application Programming Interface)Define the core endpoints/contract — forces concreteness.
4. Data modelEntities, access patterns → SQL (Structured Query Language) vs NoSQL choice.
5. High-level designBoxes & arrows: clients → LB → services → DB/cache/queue.
6. Scale & deepenFind bottlenecks; add caching, sharding, replicas, CDN (Content Delivery Network), async queues.
7. Trade-offsName what you gave up. There is no perfect design — only fit-for-purpose.
The senior signal is talking trade-offs out loud and tying decisions back to the requirements — not memorizing one "correct" architecture.
🏗️ Monolith vs Microservices vs Modular Monolith Architecture ▶
Concept
The Most Consequential Architecture Choice
A monolith is one deployable unit — simple to build, test, and deploy, but hard to scale teams and selectively scale parts. Microservices split the system into independently deployable services — great for large orgs and independent scaling, but you trade code complexity for operational complexity (networking, data consistency, observability). The modular monolith is the underrated middle: one deployable, but with strict internal module boundaries — so you get simplicity now and can extract services later if you actually need to.
MonolithMicroservices
DeployOne unitMany, independent
ScaleWhole appPer service
Team fitSmall teamsMany teams
DataOne DB, easy joins/txnsDB-per-service, distributed txns
FailureAll-or-nothingIsolated (if done right)
Ops costLowHigh
Default advice: start with a (modular) monolith. Microservices solve organizational scaling problems you probably don't have yet — adopting them too early buys distributed-systems pain for no benefit.
📡 Event-Driven Architecture Architecture ▶
Concept
React to Facts, Don't Call in Lockstep
Instead of service A calling B calling C, components emit events ("OrderPlaced") to a broker, and interested services react. This decouples producers from consumers: add a new consumer (email, analytics, fraud) without touching the producer. It's the architecture behind responsive, extensible systems — at the cost of harder debugging and eventual consistency.
StyleHowTrade-off
ChoreographyEach service reacts to events independentlyLoose coupling; flow is emergent/hard to trace
OrchestrationA coordinator directs the stepsClear flow; the orchestrator is a coupling point
Watch for: event ordering, duplicate delivery (make consumers idempotent), and schema evolution (version your events). Pairs with the Message Queues topic and CQRS/Event Sourcing below.
⬡ Clean / Hexagonal Architecture Architecture ▶
Concept
Keep Business Logic Independent of Frameworks
Clean Architecture (and its cousin Hexagonal / Ports & Adapters) organizes code so your business logic sits at the center, knowing nothing about the database, web framework, or UI (User Interface). Those outer concerns are adapters that plug into ports (interfaces) the core defines. Swap Postgres for Mongo, REST (Representational State Transfer) for gRPC, without touching the core.
The key rule is the dependency rule: dependencies point inward. The domain never imports the framework; the framework imports the domain. Concretely: the core defines a UserRepository interface; a PostgresUserRepository in the outer layer implements it. This makes the core trivially unit-testable (mock the ports) and resistant to framework churn — the business rules outlive the tech stack.
LayerContains
Entities / DomainCore business rules (no dependencies)
Use casesApplication-specific orchestration
AdaptersDB, web, external APIs (Application Programming Interface) — the replaceable edge
✂️ CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) & Event Sourcing Architecture ▶
Concept
Split Reads from Writes; Store Events, Not State
CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) uses separate models for writing (commands) and reading (queries) — so each can be optimized and scaled independently (e.g. a normalized write DB + denormalized read replicas). Event Sourcing goes further: instead of storing current state, store the full sequence of events that produced it. Current state is a replay of the log.
PatternGainCost
CQRSIndependent read/write scaling & modelsTwo models to keep in sync (eventual consistency)
Event SourcingFull audit trail; time-travel; rebuild any viewComplexity; schema/versioning; snapshots for speed
Powerful together, but not free — they add real complexity. Use them where audit, temporal queries, or extreme read/write asymmetry genuinely demand it (banking, ledgers), not by default.
1️⃣2️⃣ The Twelve-Factor App Architecture ▶
Reference
The Checklist for Cloud-Native Services
The Twelve-Factor methodology is a battle-tested set of rules for building services that deploy cleanly to modern platforms and scale horizontally. You don't need to memorize all twelve — internalize the handful that bite hardest.
FactorRule
ConfigStore config in the environment, never in code
Backing servicesTreat DBs/queues as attachable resources (via URL)
ProcessesStateless & share-nothing — state goes to a backing service
Port bindingExport services via a port; self-contained
DisposabilityFast startup / graceful shutdown (scale & recover fast)
Dev/prod parityKeep environments as similar as possible
LogsTreat logs as event streams to stdout — the platform routes them
Follow these and your app runs the same on a laptop, in a container, or across 100 nodes — the foundation for autoscaling, twelve-factor is why containers and PaaS (Platform as a Service) "just work."
🗂️ Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Design ▶
Concept
Model the Business, Not the Database
DDD is an approach to complex software that puts the business domain at the center. Developers and domain experts build a shared ubiquitous language — the same words in conversation and in code — and split the system into bounded contexts where each term has one precise meaning ("account" means something different to Billing vs Auth).
ConceptMeaning
Bounded contextA boundary where a model & language are consistent (often → a service)
Ubiquitous languageShared vocabulary used identically by experts & code
EntityObject with identity that persists over time (a User)
Value objectDefined only by its attributes, immutable (an Address, Money)
AggregateA cluster of objects with one root that guards invariants
Bounded contexts are why DDD and microservices pair so well — a well-drawn context is a natural service boundary. Start with the language; the model follows.
🧱 SOLID (Single responsibility, Open-closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion) Principles Design ▶
Reference
Five Rules for Maintainable OO Code
SOLID is five principles that keep object-oriented code flexible and testable. You don't apply them dogmatically — you reach for them when code becomes rigid or hard to change.
PrincipleMeans
SSingle ResponsibilityA class has one reason to change
OOpen/ClosedOpen to extension, closed to modification
LLiskov SubstitutionSubtypes must be usable as their base type
IInterface SegregationMany small interfaces > one fat one
DDependency InversionDepend on abstractions, not concretions
The throughline is manage dependencies: isolate what changes, program to interfaces, and keep the direction of dependency pointing at stable abstractions (this is the engine behind Clean Architecture).
🔗 Coupling & Cohesion Design ▶
Concept
The Two Words That Describe Good Structure
Almost every design principle reduces to two ideas. High cohesion: things that change together live together (a module does one job well). Low coupling: modules depend on each other as little as possible, through narrow interfaces. Aim for both — you want tight-inside, loose-between.
PropertyGoodBad
CohesionHigh — focused moduleLow — grab-bag of unrelated code
CouplingLow — few, clean dependenciesHigh — change one, break many
The Law of Demeter ("only talk to your neighbors" — avoid a.getB().getC().doThing()) is a practical way to keep coupling low. When a change ripples across many files, that's high coupling telling you the boundaries are wrong.
📐 API-First & Contract-Driven Design Design ▶
Concept
Design the Interface Before the Implementation
API-first means the API (Application Programming Interface) contract (e.g. an OpenAPI or Protobuf spec) is written and agreed before anyone builds the backend. Frontend, backend, and consumers all code against the same contract in parallel, and you can generate clients, mocks, and docs from it. The interface becomes the source of truth, not an afterthought.
BenefitDetail
Parallel workTeams build against the spec + a mock, not a finished server
CodegenClients, server stubs, docs, validation from one spec
Consumer-driven contractsConsumers publish expectations; a broken change fails CI (Pact)
GovernanceConsistent conventions, versioning, and review across APIs
This is what makes microservices and public platforms manageable — the contract is a stable boundary that lets teams move independently without constant breakage (ties to the API Design topic).
🧮 Idempotency & Exactly-Once — Safe Retries Reliability ▶
Concept
The Property Distributed Systems Live and Die By
In any networked system, messages get lost, duplicated, and retried. An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once — the single most important property for correctness under retries. "Charge $10" is dangerous to retry; "set balance to $90" is safe.
TechniqueHow
Idempotency keyClient sends a unique ID; server dedupes and returns the original result
Natural idempotencyDesign ops as "set to X" (absolute) not "add X" (relative)
Dedup storeTrack processed message IDs; skip repeats
Outbox patternAtomically write state + the event to publish, so neither is lost
True "exactly-once" delivery is famously near-impossible; the practical answer is at-least-once delivery + idempotent consumers = effectively-once processing. Build every consumer and API (Application Programming Interface) assuming it will see duplicates.
✍️ Clean Code & Naming Craft ▶
Concept
Code Is Read Far More Than It's Written
You write a line once; it's read dozens of times over its life. Clean code optimizes for the reader — clarity beats cleverness. The highest-leverage skill is naming: a good name removes the need for a comment.
PrincipleDetail
Intention-revealing nameselapsedDays > d; say what it is
Small functionsDo one thing; a screenful is a smell
Few arguments0–2 ideal; many args hint at a missing object
No surprisesA function does exactly what its name says, nothing hidden
Comments explain whyNot what — the code shows what; comments justify the non-obvious
The Boy Scout Rule: leave the code a little cleaner than you found it. Small, constant improvements beat big rewrites.
👀 Code Review — Doing It Well Craft ▶
Concept
The Highest-ROI Quality Practice
Review catches bugs, spreads knowledge, and keeps a codebase coherent — but only if done with care. Bad reviews (nitpicky, slow, ego-driven) poison a team; good ones make everyone better.
As reviewerAs author
Review promptly (unblock people)Keep PRs small & focused
Comment on the code, not the personExplain the "why" in the description
Distinguish must-fix from nit (label it)Respond to every comment
Ask questions, don't demandDon't take feedback personally
Approve when good enough, not perfectLet the machine catch style (linters)
Automate the boring parts (formatting, lint, tests in CI) so humans review what matters: correctness, design, edge cases, and clarity.
🧪 Testing Strategy — The Test Pyramid Craft ▶
Concept
Many Fast Tests, Few Slow Ones
The test pyramid guides how to balance test types: lots of fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests, and a thin layer of slow end-to-end tests on top. Invert it (mostly E2E) and your suite is slow, flaky, and brittle — the dreaded "ice-cream cone."
LevelTestsTrait
Unit (many)One function/class in isolationFast, precise, cheap
Integration (some)Components together (DB, API)Slower, more realistic
E2E (few)The whole system as a userSlow, flaky, high-value paths only
TDD (Test-Driven Development) (write the test first) drives better design and guarantees coverage; BDD (Behavior-Driven Development) frames tests as behavior ("given/when/then"). Aim to test behavior, not implementation, so refactors don't break the suite.
💳 Technical Debt — Recognize & Pay It Down Craft ▶
Concept
Borrowing Speed Now Against Effort Later
Technical debt is the implied future cost of a quick-and-dirty choice. Like financial debt, a little is a useful tool (ship now, fix later); too much, unmanaged, and the "interest" — slower changes, more bugs — eventually consumes all your capacity.
TypeExample
Deliberate"We'll hardcode this to hit the deadline" (fine, if tracked)
AccidentalLearned a better design too late; code lagging behind understanding
Bit rotDependencies age, the world changes, code decays
Manage it: make it visible (a backlog, not tribal knowledge), pay it down opportunistically (Boy Scout Rule) plus dedicated time, and prioritize debt in code you touch often. Debt in a stable, untouched corner rarely matters.
📝 ADRs (Architecture Decision Record) & Design Docs Craft ▶
Reference
Write Down the Decision and the Why
Six months later, no one remembers why the team chose Postgres over Mongo, and the reasoning gets re-litigated. An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is a short doc capturing one decision: the context, the options, the choice, and the consequences. A design doc (or RFC) does the same before building something significant.
ArtifactPurpose
ADR1-page record of a single decision (context/options/decision/consequences)
Design doc / RFC (Request for Comments)Propose & get feedback before building; align the team
C4 modelDiagrams at 4 zoom levels: Context, Container, Component, Code
Keep them short and in the repo (version-controlled next to the code). The value is the trail of reasoning — it onboards new people and stops old debates from restarting.
🔌 Resilience Patterns — Circuit Breaker, Retry & Timeout Reliability ▶
Concept
Stop One Failure From Cascading
In a distributed system, one slow or dead dependency can drag down everything that calls it — threads pile up waiting, and the failure cascades. Resilience patterns contain that at every remote call.
PatternProtects against
TimeoutWaiting forever on a hung dependency
Retry + backoff + jitterTransient blips — but back off so you don't stampede
Circuit breakerA failing dependency — "trip open" and fail fast instead of hammering it
BulkheadOne overloaded feature sinking the rest (isolate resource pools)
FallbackDegrade gracefully — cached/default response over an error
Careful with retries: naive retries during an outage create a retry storm that keeps the dependency down. Always pair retries with backoff, jitter, and a circuit breaker; only retry idempotent operations.
💰 Distributed Transactions — Saga & Outbox Reliability ▶
Concept
Consistency Across Services Without 2PC
When a business action spans multiple services/databases (place order → charge card → reserve stock), you can't wrap it in one ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) transaction. Two-phase commit (2PC) technically can, but it's slow and fragile — so modern systems avoid it.
PatternHow
SagaA sequence of local transactions; on failure, run compensating actions to undo
OutboxWrite state + the "event to publish" in one local transaction, so the event can't be lost
2PCCoordinator locks all participants to commit atomically — avoided at scale (blocking, SPOF)
Sagas trade atomicity for availability: the system is briefly inconsistent, then converges (or compensates). "Charge failed → cancel the order" is a compensating transaction. Pair with idempotency (E3) so retried steps are safe.
🌊 Backpressure & Flow Control Reliability ▶
Concept
Don't Accept More Than You Can Handle
When work arrives faster than a system can process it, unbounded queues grow until memory runs out and everything crashes. Backpressure is the system signaling "slow down" upstream, so load is shed or throttled rather than silently piling up.
TechniqueDetail
Bounded queuesFixed size; reject/block when full instead of growing forever
Load sheddingDrop low-priority work under overload (protect the core)
Rate limitingCap intake at a sustainable rate (token bucket)
Reactive streamsConsumer signals demand to the producer (pull, not push)
The counter-intuitive lesson: a system that rejects excess load cleanly stays up; one that politely accepts everything falls over. Fail fast, shed early.
🎛️ Consistency in Practice — Quorums & Tunable Reads Reliability ▶
Concept
Dialing the CAP Trade-off Per Operation
The CAP theorem is abstract; in practice distributed databases give you knobs. With quorums, a value is written to/read from a majority of replicas — and by tuning how many must respond (W + R > N), you choose consistency vs latency per query.
TermMeaning
N / W / RReplicas / write acks required / read acks required
W + R > NGuarantees a read sees the latest write (strong)
Low W, low RFast + available, but reads may be stale (eventual)
Read repair / anti-entropyReplicas reconcile in the background
So a shopping-cart read can be fast-and-eventual (low R) while the final checkout uses a strong quorum — the same store, tuned per operation. This is how Dynamo-style systems make CAP practical (ties to the CAP Theorem topic).
🪜 The Engineering Ladder — Junior to Principal Career ▶
Reference
What Changes as You Level Up
Seniority isn't about writing more code — it's about the scope of impact and how much ambiguity you can absorb. The ladder describes a widening blast radius of responsibility.
LevelScope
JuniorCompletes well-defined tasks with guidance
MidOwns features end-to-end independently
SeniorOwns systems; mentors; handles ambiguity within a team
StaffImpact across multiple teams; sets technical direction
Principal+Org/company-wide technical strategy
The shift from senior → staff is the big one: from "I solve hard problems" to "I make other teams more effective" — via influence, not authority.
⭐ Staff+ Archetypes Career ▶
Reference
There's No Single "Staff Engineer"
Will Larson's Staff Engineer identifies four common shapes the role takes. Knowing them helps you play to your strengths and recognize the kind of senior leadership your org needs.
ArchetypeDoes
Tech LeadGuides a team's execution on a specific area
ArchitectOwns direction for a critical domain across teams
SolverParachutes into the gnarliest problems
Right HandExtends a senior leader's reach across the org
All four share the staff-level core: technical judgment, cross-team influence, and moving the org forward — not just shipping personal code.
🍴 Tech Lead vs Engineering Manager Career ▶
Concept
The Fork in the Senior Road
Around senior level, careers often fork into two tracks — both leadership, but different work. Good orgs value them equally; the mistake is assuming management is "up" and IC (Individual Contributor) is "stuck."
IC / Tech Lead trackManagement track
Leads throughTechnical influence & designPeople, process, delivery
Spends time onArchitecture, hard problems, mentoring1:1s, hiring, coordination, careers
Measured byTechnical outcomes & leverageTeam health & throughput
You can switch tracks (and back) — many do. Choose based on what energizes you: solving technical problems, or growing people and systems. Neither is superior.
📣 Influence Without Authority Career ▶
Concept
The Skill That Defines Senior+ Engineers
Past a certain level, your impact depends on getting other people and teams — whom you don't manage — to align on technical direction. That's done through credibility, clear writing, and trust, not org-chart power.
LeverDetail
Write it downAn RFC/design doc scales your idea & invites input
Build credibilityShip, help others, be right consistently
Frame in their termsTie your proposal to what stakeholders care about
Disagree & commitArgue hard, then support the decision fully
Give creditTrust compounds; hoarding credit destroys it
The best technical idea loses to a well-communicated mediocre one. Learning to write and persuade is as much a "senior engineering skill" as system design.
🎓 Cert Roadmaps — Choosing a Path Career ▶
Reference
A Study Order for the Big Tracks
Certs won't make you an engineer, but they structure learning and clear HR filters. Pick a track that matches your goal and work up it.
TrackPath
IT foundationsA+ → Network+ → Security+
Blue teamSecurity+ → CySA+ → (GCIH/GCIA) → CISSP (Certified Information Systems Security Professional)
Red teamSecurity+ → PenTest+ → OSCP (Offensive Security Certified Professional) → (OSEP/CRTO)
Cloud (AWS)Cloud Practitioner → Solutions Architect Assoc → Security Specialty
Cloud (GCP)Cloud Digital Leader → Associate Cloud Engineer → Professional Architect
ManagementPMP (Project Management Professional) / CISM (Certified Information Security Manager) for leadership tracks
The whole site maps to these — this reference domain (Red/Blue/Cloud/Engineering) is effectively a study companion for the tracks above.
☁️ Cloud-Native & Serverless Architecture Patterns Architecture ▶
Concept
Designing for the Platform, Not Just on It
Cloud-native architecture assumes elastic, disposable infrastructure and managed services. Serverless takes it further — you write functions and the platform handles scaling to zero and back. Both change how you decompose a system.
PatternDetail
Managed-service-firstPrefer a queue/DB/auth service over running your own
Event-driven / FaaSFunctions triggered by events; scale per-event
Strangler FigIncrementally replace a monolith by routing slices to new services
BFFBackend-for-frontend: a tailored API (Application Programming Interface) per client type
Cold starts / limitsServerless trade-offs: latency spikes, timeouts, statelessness
Trade-off: serverless minimizes ops and cost at low/spiky load but can get expensive and awkward at steady high volume (and vendor lock-in rises). Match the model to the traffic shape — ties to the "Choosing Compute" cloud card.
🗃️ Schema & Data Modeling Patterns Data Design ▶
Concept
Model the Data to Match the Access
How you shape data determines what's fast and what's painful. Relational normalization optimizes for integrity; denormalization and NoSQL optimize for read patterns. Good design starts from how the data is queried, not an abstract ideal.
ChoiceTrade-off
Normalization (3NF)No duplication, integrity — but more joins
DenormalizationFast reads, fewer joins — but update anomalies
NoSQL single-tableModel around access patterns (DynamoDB style)
Polyglot persistenceRight store per job: relational + doc + cache + search
Star / snowflakeDimensional modeling for analytics warehouses
Rule: normalize until it hurts, denormalize until it works. In NoSQL you design the table around queries up front — the opposite of relational's "model entities, query later."
📐 Estimation & Planning Career ▶
Concept
Why Software Estimates Are Always Wrong
Estimation is hard because building software is discovering the problem, not repeating a known task. Mature teams estimate relative effort and manage uncertainty rather than pretending to predict exact dates.
IdeaDetail
Story pointsRelative size (complexity/effort/uncertainty), not hours
VelocityPoints/sprint historically — forecast, don't commit to it
Planning pokerEstimate together to surface hidden complexity
Cone of uncertaintyEstimates tighten as you learn — re-estimate
Ranges & buffersGive "2–4 weeks", not "3 weeks"; account for the unknown
Senior move: break big work into small, independently shippable slices — small things estimate accurately, and you get feedback early. Padding a giant estimate just hides the risk.
🧑‍💻 Career Ladders & Interviews Career ▶
Reference
Leveling Up & Getting Through the Loop
A career ladder makes expectations explicit per level; interviews test whether you meet the bar. Preparing deliberately for each stage beats raw talent for both getting hired and getting promoted.
Interview stagePrep
CodingData structures & algorithms; think aloud, test your code (LeetCode-style)
System designUse the framework: requirements → estimate → API (Application Programming Interface) → data → scale → trade-offs
BehavioralSTAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) stories tied to the level's expectations (scope, impact)
Take-home / practicalClean, tested, documented — treat it like real work
For promotion: operate at the next level before the title — keep a brag doc of impact mapped to the ladder's criteria. The whole Engineering domain here is study material for the design & coding loops.
🧅 Coder vs Programmer vs Developer vs Architect JOB TITLES ▶
Scope Model
Same Keyboard, Different Blast Radius
These four titles are not four different skills — they are nested scopes. Each one contains the one inside it and adds a wider set of concerns. A coder is asked "write this." A programmer is asked "solve this." An architect is asked "how should this be built?" A developer is asked "should we build this at all, and what will it cost?" The further out you go, the more of the decision you own — and the fewer hours a day you spend typing code.
Developer — owns the outcome
RequirementsPlanning Business understandingBudget DeploymentStakeholders
Architect — owns the shape
Software designSystem architecture System integrationNon-functional requirements Trade-offs
Programmer — owns the solution
ProcessesAlgorithms Business logicPrioritization Data structures
Coder — owns the implementation
Coding
Software engineer ?
Why the last circle floats: "software engineer" is the one title that refuses to sit in the stack. In most companies it is simply the HR name for everyone above — the nesting model describes what someone does, while the title on the offer letter describes what the company calls it. Read the responsibilities, never the noun.
Reference
What Each Layer Adds
TitleAnswers the questionAdds on top of the layer insideFails when…
Coder "How do I express this in the language?" Syntax, idiom, working code against a clear spec The spec is vague — there is nothing to translate
Programmer "What is the right solution?" Algorithms, data structures, business logic, what to do first The solution is right but doesn't fit the surrounding systems
Architect "How should the whole thing be shaped?" Boundaries, integration, scalability, security, trade-offs The design is elegant but nobody asked for it or can pay for it
Developer "Are we solving the right problem?" Requirements, planning, budget, delivery, users The plan is sound but the implementation never lands
Career use: promotion is usually the act of growing one ring outward, not typing faster. If you want the next title, start answering the next question before anyone asks you to. See The Engineering Ladder and Staff+ Archetypes in this domain for how that maps to levels.
🗺️ The Wider IT Org — Roles Beyond Writing Code JOB TITLES ▶
Landscape
Who Owns What, In One Table
The nesting model above covers the people who build software. Most of IT does something else: it runs the machines that software lands on, the identities that reach it, the networks between them, and the rules around all of it. Titles vary wildly between companies — what does not vary is the thing the role is accountable for at 3 a.m. Read that column first.
RoleAccountable forTypical toolsEasily confused with
Software engineer / developer The application itself — features, correctness, its tests Language toolchain, Git, CI, IDE (Integrated Development Environment) Everyone below, by non-technical managers
DevOps engineer The path from commit to production, and the tooling on it CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery), Terraform, containers, Kubernetes SRE (Site Reliability Engineering), platform engineer, build engineer
Site reliability engineer Whether the service meets its SLOs (Service Level Objective), and the error budget Observability, incident tooling, automation DevOps — the difference is SLOs and on-call ownership
Platform engineer The internal product other engineers build on Kubernetes, internal developer portals, golden paths DevOps, infrastructure engineer
Systems administrator Servers and services staying up, patched and backed up Windows Server, Linux, Ansible, monitoring Infrastructure engineer, UEM (Unified Endpoint Management) engineer
Cloud engineer Cloud accounts, landing zones, cost and cloud services AWS (Amazon Web Services) / Azure / GCP (Google Cloud Platform), IaC (Infrastructure as Code), cloud IAM (Identity and Access Management) DevOps, cloud architect
Network engineer Packets getting where they should — and nowhere else Routers, switches, firewalls, SD-WAN (Software Defined Wide Area Network), VPN (Virtual Private Network) Network security engineer
UEM engineer Every end-user device: enrolled, configured, compliant, patched Intune, MECM (Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager), Jamf, Workspace ONE, Autopilot Sysadmin, desktop support, IAM engineer
IAM engineer Who can access what, and how that is proven Entra ID, Okta, SAML/OIDC, SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management), PAM (Privileged Access Management) tooling UEM engineer (device trust overlaps), security engineer
Service desk / desktop support The individual human who is blocked right now Ticketing, remote assistance, imaging, knowledge base UEM engineer — support consumes what UEM builds
Security engineer Controls that prevent and detect attacks EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), WAF (Web Application Firewall), hardening baselines SOC (Security Operations Center) analyst, security architect
SOC analyst Alerts triaged, incidents investigated and escalated SIEM, EDR, threat intel, playbooks Security engineer — analyst operates, engineer builds
Penetration tester Finding exploitable weaknesses before an attacker does Burp, nmap, C2 (Command and Control) frameworks, custom tooling Red teamer — scope and objective differ, not skill
GRC (Governance, Risk, and Compliance) analyst Evidence that controls exist and work, for auditors Policy, risk register, control frameworks, audits Security engineer — GRC proves, engineering builds
Data engineer Pipelines delivering trustworthy data on time SQL (Structured Query Language), Spark, orchestration, warehouses Data analyst, ML (Machine Learning) engineer, DBA
Database administrator The database staying fast, consistent and recoverable Query plans, backups, replication, tuning Data engineer, sysadmin
QA (Quality Assurance) / test engineer Whether the thing actually works before users find out Test frameworks, automation, exploratory testing SDET (Software Development Engineer in Test), release engineer
Two honest caveats. First, small companies collapse this whole table into two or three people — the roles still exist, they just share a chair. Second, the same title can mean opposite jobs at two employers; in interviews, ask "what would I be on call for?" rather than trusting the title.
🖥️ Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) Engineer JOB TITLES • Endpoint ▶
Role Definition
One Console for Every Device a Human Touches
A UEM engineer owns the fleet: laptops, desktops, phones, tablets, kiosks and increasingly virtual desktops — Windows, macOS, iOS, Android and Linux from a single management plane. Not "fixing laptops": designing the system that makes ten thousand laptops arrive configured, stay compliant, and update themselves without anyone touching them. The output of the job is policy, packaging and automation, not tickets closed.
TermWhat it covers
MDM (Mobile Device Management)Enrolment, configuration profiles, remote wipe — device-level control
MAM (Mobile Application Management)Policy applied to the app and its data, on devices you do not own (BYOD)
EMM (Enterprise Mobility Management)MDM + MAM + identity and content — the mobile-era bundle
UEMEMM merged with traditional desktop management, so mobile and PC are one estate
The lineage matters in interviews: UEM is what happened when the mobile-device world (MDM/EMM) and the domain-joined PC world (imaging, Group Policy, MECM) stopped being separate teams.
The Work
What Actually Lands in the Queue
AreaConcretely
Enrolment & provisioningAutopilot / ABM (Apple Business Manager) / Android Enterprise zero-touch, ESP (Enrollment Status Page), join type, naming
ConfigurationBaselines, CSP (Configuration Service Provider) and OMA-URI (Open Mobile Alliance Uniform Resource Identifier) policy, GPO-to-Intune migration, Wi-Fi/VPN/certificate profiles
Application deliveryWin32 packaging, MSI (Microsoft Installer), LOB (Line of Business) and store apps, dependencies, detection rules, uninstall paths
Patch & update ringsWUfB (Windows Update for Business), update rings, deferrals, macOS/iOS update policy, emergency out-of-band pushes
Compliance & device trustCompliance policies feeding Conditional Access, encryption, TPM/Secure Boot, attestation
HardeningCIS/STIG-aligned baselines, ASR (Attack Surface Reduction) rules, LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution), removable-media and firewall policy
AutomationPowerShell and shell remediation scripts, proactive remediations, Graph API (Application Programming Interface) reporting
LifecycleRefresh cycles, retire/wipe, stale-device cleanup, licence reclaim, offboarding
FirefightingWhy did this policy apply to 400 machines it shouldn't have — and how fast can it be pulled
The defining risk of the job: blast radius. A bad line of application code breaks a feature; a bad device policy bricks the fleet that everyone uses to report it. Ring-based deployment, a pilot group and a tested rollback are not bureaucracy here — they are the whole discipline.
Boundaries
How It Differs From the Roles Next Door
NeighbourWhere the line sits
Desktop support Support fixes this device for this person; UEM changes the policy so that class of problem stops happening. Support is the most common entry path into UEM.
Systems administrator Sysadmin owns servers and back-end services; UEM owns the end-user estate. They overlap on directory, certificates and patching.
IAM (Identity and Access Management) engineer IAM owns identity and Conditional Access policy; UEM owns the device signal those policies trust. Device compliance is the seam between them.
Security engineer Security defines the required control; UEM is usually the mechanism that actually delivers it to every endpoint — and reports which ones drifted.
DevOps engineer Same instincts — declarative config, staged rollout, automation — pointed at laptops instead of servers. The skills transfer in both directions.
Software engineer UEM writes glue code, not products: PowerShell, Bash, Graph API calls, packaging wrappers. Scripting is essential; software design is not.
Getting There
Skills, Tools and the Path In
BucketWhat to have
PlatformsMicrosoft Intune and MECM (Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager), Jamf Pro, Workspace ONE, Google Endpoint Management
IdentityEntra ID, Conditional Access, certificates and SCEP (Simple Certificate Enrollment Protocol), Kerberos and Group Policy fundamentals
ScriptingPowerShell first, then Bash and a little Python; Graph API for anything at scale
OS (Operating System) internalsWindows servicing and registry, macOS profiles and notarization, iOS/Android enterprise models
PackagingMSI/Win32 app authoring, detection and requirement rules, silent installs, PKG on macOS
CertsCompTIA (Computing Technology Industry Association) A+ as a base, then MD-102 (Microsoft Endpoint Administrator Associate) (Endpoint Administrator); Jamf Certified Tech for Apple estates
HabitsTest rings, documented rollback, change control, and reading the compliance report before declaring victory
Typical path: service desk → desktop support → endpoint/UEM engineer → senior or lead UEM, then a fork toward endpoint security, IAM, or workplace architect. The Endpoint Management domain in this reference is the technical companion to this role; the Blue Team domain covers the hardening side.
📊 Data & Databases
SQL DATA
SQL · DB Internals · NoSQL · Warehousing · DBA 40 topics · ~30 min ▾
⚙️ How a Database Actually Works Internals ▶
Concept
Pages, the Buffer Pool & the Write-Ahead Log
A database is not magic — it's a careful dance between disk and memory. Data lives on disk in fixed-size pages (commonly 8 KB); the engine caches hot pages in a memory buffer pool so most reads never touch disk. Durability comes from the write-ahead log (WAL).
ComponentJob
Storage engineReads/writes pages, manages indexes (InnoDB, Postgres heap)
Buffer poolIn-memory page cache — the #1 performance factor
WAL / redo logAppend every change before the data page — crash recovery
CheckpointFlush dirty pages to disk; trim the log
Why WAL: writing a tiny sequential log entry is fast and safe; the actual (random) page write can happen later. On crash, replay the log to recover committed work. This one idea gives you the "D" in ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) and underpins replication and point-in-time recovery.
🧮 The Relational Model — Keys & Integrity Foundations ▶
Concept
Tables, Keys & the NULL Gotcha
The relational model organizes data into relations (tables) of rows and typed columns, with relationships expressed by keys rather than pointers. Constraints let the database enforce correctness so your application doesn't have to.
TermMeaning
Primary keyUniquely identifies a row; not null
Foreign keyReferences a PK elsewhere — enforces referential integrity
Unique / CheckColumn-level rules the DB guarantees
Candidate / composite keyOther unique columns; keys spanning multiple columns
The NULL trap: NULL means "unknown," not zero or empty. It uses three-valued logic — NULL = NULL is not true but NULL, and WHERE x = NULL matches nothing (use IS NULL). NULLs silently break naive comparisons, joins, and aggregates — the single most common SQL (Structured Query Language) bug.
📐 Normalization — 1NF Through BCNF Design ▶
Concept
Eliminate Redundancy, Then Know When to Stop
Normalization structures tables so each fact is stored once, preventing update anomalies (change an address in one row, forget the other five). You progress through normal forms, each removing a specific kind of redundancy.
FormRule
1NFAtomic values — no repeating groups or lists in a cell
2NFNo partial dependency on part of a composite key
3NFNo transitive dependency (non-key → non-key)
BCNFEvery determinant is a candidate key (stricter 3NF)
Rule of thumb: normalize to 3NF for transactional (OLTP) systems — it keeps writes clean. Then denormalize deliberately for read-heavy or analytics workloads, trading duplication for fewer joins. Star schemas (analytics) are intentionally denormalized.
🔒 ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) & Transactions — Isolation Levels Foundations ▶
Concept
All-or-Nothing, and Who Sees What
A transaction groups statements so they succeed or fail as a unit. ACID is the guarantee: Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (constraints hold), Isolated (concurrent txns don't corrupt each other), Durable (committed = survives a crash).
Isolation levelPrevents
Read Uncommittednothing — can read dirty (uncommitted) data
Read Committeddirty reads (Postgres default)
Repeatable Read+ non-repeatable reads (MySQL default)
Serializable+ phantom reads — as if txns ran one at a time
The trade-off: stricter isolation = more correct but more locking/aborts and less concurrency. Know the three anomalies (dirty, non-repeatable, phantom) and pick the weakest level that's still safe for your workload.
🕸️ ER Modeling — Designing the Schema Design ▶
Reference
Entities, Relationships & Cardinality
Before writing DDL (Data Definition Language), you model the domain: what things exist (entities), their attributes, and how they relate. An entity-relationship diagram (crow's-foot notation) is the shared language between engineers and stakeholders.
RelationshipImplemented as
One-to-manyFK on the "many" side (most common)
Many-to-manyA junction/join table with two FKs
One-to-oneShared/unique FK — often a sign to merge tables
Crow's-foot marks each end with cardinality (one/many) and optionality (zero/one). Get the relationships right here and the tables, keys, and joins fall out naturally — this is the bridge from requirements to a normalized schema.
🔗 SQL (Structured Query Language) Joins — Every Type, and the NULL Traps SQL ▶
Reference
Combining Rows Across Tables
Joins match rows from two tables on a condition. The type decides what happens to rows that don't match — and that's where most bugs live. 
SELECT u.name, o.total
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;   -- keeps users with no orders
JoinReturns
INNEROnly rows that match in both tables
LEFT / RIGHTAll rows from one side; NULLs where no match
FULL OUTERAll rows from both; NULLs on either side
CROSSCartesian product (every combo) — usually a mistake
SELFA table joined to itself (hierarchies, pairs)
Traps: putting a filter on the outer table in WHERE silently turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN (put it in the ON instead); and joining on a nullable column drops rows because NULL = NULL isn't true. Watch for fan-out: a one-to-many join multiplies rows and inflates SUM().
🪟 Window Functions — Analytics Without Collapsing Rows SQL ▶
Reference
Rankings, Running Totals & Row-to-Row Math
GROUP BY collapses rows; window functions compute across a set of rows while keeping every row. The OVER() clause defines the "window" (partition + order). 
SELECT name, dept, salary,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,
  SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_total
FROM employees;
FunctionUse
ROW_NUMBER / RANK / DENSE_RANKOrdering & top-N per group
LAG / LEADCompare to the previous/next row (deltas, growth)
SUM/AVG OVERRunning totals & moving averages
NTILEBuckets/percentiles
Killer use: "top 3 earners per department" or "each order vs the customer's previous order" — one query, no self-joins. Window functions are the single biggest jump from beginner to intermediate SQL (Structured Query Language).
🧱 CTEs (Common Table Expression) & Recursion — Readable, Composable Queries SQL ▶
Reference
Name Your Steps With WITH
A Common Table Expression (WITH) names a subquery so you can build a complex query as readable, stacked steps instead of nested parentheses. Recursive CTEs traverse hierarchies and graphs. 
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC) rn
  FROM events
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;   -- latest event per user
Recursive form: an anchor query UNION ALL a step that references the CTE — perfect for org charts, category trees, or "all descendants of X." Readability tip: CTEs make a 60-line query reviewable; deeply nested subqueries don't. (Note: some engines materialize CTEs — check the plan if performance matters.)
Σ Aggregation — GROUP BY, HAVING & ROLLUP SQL ▶
Reference
Summarizing Rows Into Groups
Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN/MAX) collapse many rows into one per group. GROUP BY defines the groups; HAVING filters after aggregation (unlike WHERE, which filters before). 
SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(total) AS rev
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'          -- filter rows first
GROUP BY country
HAVING SUM(total) > 10000      -- filter groups after
ORDER BY rev DESC;
FeatureDoes
COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)All rows vs non-NULL values only
COUNT(DISTINCT …)Unique values
ROLLUP / CUBE / GROUPING SETSSubtotals & grand totals in one pass
FILTER (WHERE …)Conditional aggregates (Postgres)
Classic error: selecting a non-aggregated column that isn't in GROUP BY — either group by it or wrap it in an aggregate.
🎯 Subqueries, EXISTS & Set Operations SQL ▶
Reference
Queries Inside Queries
A subquery is a SELECT nested in another statement. It can return a scalar, a list (for IN), or a table. Correlated subqueries reference the outer row and run per-row. 
-- customers who have placed at least one order
SELECT name FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id);
ToolUse
IN / NOT INMembership — but NOT IN + NULLs = no rows (trap!)
EXISTS / NOT EXISTSExistence check — NULL-safe, often faster
UNION / UNION ALLStack result sets (ALL keeps duplicates & is faster)
INTERSECT / EXCEPTRows in both / in one but not the other
Prefer EXISTS over NOT IN whenever the inner column can be NULL — NOT IN (…NULL…) returns nothing, a famously silent bug. Many subqueries also rewrite cleanly as joins or CTEs (Common Table Expression); pick whichever reads clearest.
📇 Indexes Explained — B-tree, Hash & Covering Performance ▶
Concept
The Book's Index, for Your Data
An index is a sorted data structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table — the difference between O(log n) and O(n). The cost: every write must also update the index, and indexes take space.
TypeBest for
B-treeThe default — equality & range (=, <, BETWEEN, ORDER BY)
HashEquality only, very fast
GIN / GiSTFull-text, JSONB, arrays, geospatial (Postgres)
CompositeMulti-column — order matters (leftmost-prefix rule)
CoveringIncludes all columns a query needs → index-only scan
Composite key order: an index on (a, b) helps WHERE a=… and WHERE a=… AND b=…, but not WHERE b=… alone. Index the columns you filter/sort on; don't over-index — each one slows writes.
🔍 Reading Query Plans — EXPLAIN ANALYZE Performance ▶
Reference
Ask the Database What It's Doing
The optimizer turns your SQL (Structured Query Language) into a physical plan. EXPLAIN shows that plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs it and shows real timings and row counts. Reading plans is the core skill for fixing slow queries. 
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
SeeMeans
Seq ScanReading the whole table — often a missing index
Index Scan / Index-OnlyUsing an index (good)
Nested Loop / Hash / Merge JoinThe three join strategies
Rows estimated vs actualBig mismatch = stale statistics → bad plan
Workflow: find the node eating the most time, check if a Seq Scan should be an index, and compare estimated vs actual rows. A huge estimate error usually means ANALYZE (statistics) is out of date.
🚀 Query Optimization — Sargability & N+1 Performance ▶
Concept
Write Queries the Index Can Use
A query is sargable ("Search ARGument able") when it can use an index. Wrapping an indexed column in a function or leading a LIKE with a wildcard defeats the index and forces a scan. 
-- NOT sargable: function on the column
WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-01-01'
-- sargable: range on the raw column
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-02'
Anti-patternFix
func(col) = xRewrite as a range, or index the expression
LIKE '%foo'Leading wildcard can't use B-tree — use full-text
The N+1 query1 query + N per-row queries → JOIN or batch (IN)
SELECT *Fetch only needed columns → enables covering indexes
The N+1 problem is the #1 app-layer DB killer (ORMs love to cause it): loading a list, then firing one query per item. Fix by eager-loading with a join or a single WHERE id IN (…).
🚦 Locking & MVCC — Concurrency Without Chaos Internals ▶
Concept
How Readers and Writers Coexist
MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) is how Postgres/InnoDB let many transactions run at once: writers create new versions of rows instead of overwriting, so readers never block writers and writers never block readers. Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot.
ConceptDetail
Row versionsOld versions kept until no txn needs them
VACUUM (Postgres)Cleans up dead tuples — neglect it and the table bloats
Row vs table locksFOR UPDATE locks specific rows for a write
DeadlockTwo txns wait on each other — DB kills one; retry it
Avoiding deadlocks: acquire locks in a consistent order and keep transactions short. Explicit locking (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) is how you safely implement "decrement inventory" under concurrency.
🍰 Partitioning & Sharding — Scaling One Big Table Scale ▶
Concept
Split the Data When It Won't Fit
Partitioning splits one table into pieces within a single database (by range/list/hash) so queries scan less and old data is easy to drop. Sharding spreads data across multiple databases/servers to scale beyond one machine.
TechniqueDetail
Range partitionBy date — drop last month in one command (time-series)
Hash partitionEven spread by a key's hash
Shard keyChooses which server a row lives on — pick carefully
Cross-shard queries/joinsThe hard part — slow, complex; avoid by design
Order of escalation: optimize queries & indexes → add a read replica → partition → (only then) shard. Sharding adds real operational complexity; a bad shard key causes hotspots and painful re-sharding.
🐘 PostgreSQL — The Default Choice Postgres ▶
Reference
The Swiss-Army Relational Database
