PostgreSQL has become the default open-source RDBMS (Relational Database Management System): standards-compliant, extensible, rock-solid, and free. If you're starting a project and don't have a specific reason not to, reach for Postgres. 
# psql — the CLI you'll live in
psql -h localhost -U app -d mydb
\dt              # list tables
\d+ users        # describe a table
\di              # list indexes
\timing on       # show query durations
ConceptDetail
RolesUsers & groups are both "roles"; grant privileges
SchemasNamespaces within a database (public by default)
ExtensionsCREATE EXTENSION — pgvector, PostGIS, pg_stat_statements
MVCC + VACUUMAutovacuum reclaims dead rows; monitor bloat
🧰 Postgres Power Features — JSONB & Full-Text Postgres ▶
Reference
More Than Rows and Columns
Postgres blurs the line with NoSQL: store and index JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) documents, arrays, and run full-text search — often removing the need for a separate datastore. 
-- JSONB: query inside a document, indexed with GIN
SELECT data->>'email' FROM users
WHERE data @> '{"plan":"pro"}';

-- Full-text search
WHERE to_tsvector(body) @@ to_tsquery('postgres & index');
FeatureUse
JSONBSemi-structured data, indexed with GIN; @>, ->>
ArraysNative array columns & operators
Full-text searchtsvector/tsquery, ranking — no Elasticsearch needed for many apps
LISTEN/NOTIFYBuilt-in pub/sub for lightweight eventing
pgvectorStore embeddings & do similarity search (AI apps)
Rule: use JSONB for genuinely variable data, not as an excuse to skip schema design — relational columns are still faster and safer for structured fields.
🐬 MySQL / MariaDB — The Other Giant MySQL ▶
Reference
Powering LAMP and Half the Web
MySQL (and its community fork MariaDB) is ubiquitous — WordPress, countless web apps, and managed offerings everywhere. Very capable; a few behaviors differ from Postgres and catch people out.
Thing to knowDetail
InnoDB engineThe default — transactional, row-locking, FKs
Default isolationRepeatable Read (Postgres uses Read Committed)
Collation/charsetUse utf8mb4 — plain utf8 is a 3-byte trap
Looser SQL (Structured Query Language)Historically permissive; enable strict mode
Choosing: Postgres for richer features & strictness; MySQL where the ecosystem/hosting assumes it (WordPress) or the team knows it well. Both are excellent — the differences are smaller than the tribalism.
📦 SQLite — The Database That's Everywhere SQLite ▶
Reference
A Whole Database in One File
SQLite is an embedded, serverless database — the entire DB is a single file, no process to run. It's the most deployed database in the world: every phone, browser, and countless apps ship it.
Great forNot for
App/local storage, mobile, edgeHigh write concurrency (single-writer)
Tests & prototypesMultiple app servers sharing it
Analytics on a file (with extensions)Network access by many clients
Don't dismiss it: "SQLite is not a toy" — for read-heavy or single-node workloads it's blazing fast and zero-ops. Modern tools (Litestream, LiteFS, Turso) even give it replication. Know when not to reach for a server database.
🌊 Connection Pooling — Surviving Many Clients Ops ▶
Concept
Why Your DB Falls Over Under Load
Each database connection costs memory and a backend process. Open one per request and a traffic spike (or a serverless fleet) opens thousands, exhausting the server. A connection pool reuses a small, fixed set of connections.
LayerDetail
App-side poolHikariCP, pgx, SQLAlchemy — reuse connections per app
PgBouncerExternal pooler; transaction mode multiplexes many clients
ServerlessFunctions × requests = connection storm → use a pooler/proxy
Sizing: more connections isn't faster — past a point they just contend. A good pool is often just (cores × 2) + spindles, not hundreds. Connection exhaustion presents as timeouts under load; the fix is pooling, not a bigger max_connections.
🗂️ The NoSQL Landscape — Four Families NoSQL ▶
Concept
Not "No SQL (Structured Query Language)" — "Not Only SQL"
NoSQL databases relax the relational model to gain scale, flexibility, or a shape that fits a specific access pattern. They usually trade strong consistency and rich joins for horizontal scalability (the CAP trade-off).
FamilyModelExample
Key-ValueSimple map — fastest lookupsRedis, DynamoDB
DocumentJSON-like docs, flexible schemaMongoDB, Couchbase
Wide-ColumnRows with dynamic columns, huge scaleCassandra, Bigtable
GraphNodes & edges — relationships firstNeo4j
Choosing: pick NoSQL for a specific reason — massive scale, a document-shaped domain, or graph traversal — not to avoid SQL. Most apps are still best served by a relational database; "boring technology" wins more often than not.
🍃 MongoDB — Documents & the Aggregation Pipeline Document ▶
Reference
Store the Object, Not the Rows
MongoDB stores flexible JSON-like documents in collections. It shines when your data is naturally nested and your access pattern reads whole objects — no joins to reassemble them. 
// find + aggregate
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "paid" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$country", revenue: { $sum: "$total" } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } }
])
Schema design: model around access patterns — embed data you read together, reference data you read separately. Add indexes just like SQL (Structured Query Language). Modern Mongo has ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) multi-document transactions, but they signal you may have wanted relational.
Watch out: unbounded array growth, and treating it as schemaless forever — inconsistent documents become a nightmare. Enforce a schema at the app (or with schema validation).
⚡ Redis — The In-Memory Multi-Tool Key-Value ▶
Reference
Data Structures at Memory Speed
Redis keeps data in RAM (Random Access Memory), making it microsecond-fast. It's not just a cache — it offers real data structures and is the go-to for caching, sessions, rate limiting, queues, and leaderboards.
StructureUse
String / counterCache values, rate limits (INCR)
HashStore objects (session, user)
Sorted SetLeaderboards, time-ordered queues
List / StreamQueues & event logs
Pub/SubLightweight messaging
Caching patterns: cache-aside (check Redis, miss → DB → populate) is most common; always set a TTL (Time To Live) and plan for cache invalidation. Persistence (RDB snapshots / AOF) means it can survive restarts, but treat it as a fast layer, not the source of truth.
🏛️ Cassandra & DynamoDB — Wide-Column at Scale Wide-Column ▶
Concept
Design for the Query, Not the Entity
Cassandra and DynamoDB scale to enormous write volumes across many nodes with no single point of failure. The catch: you must model around your queries up front — there are no ad-hoc joins.
ConceptDetail
Partition keyDecides which node stores the row — even distribution is critical
Sort/clustering keyOrders rows within a partition
Single-table designDynamoDB: model many entities in one table by key design
Hot partitionA bad key funnels traffic to one node — throttling
Tunable consistency (quorums) lets you dial latency vs freshness per operation. These shine for known, high-volume access patterns (feeds, IoT, sessions) — and hurt when requirements need flexible querying. Choose the key like your scalability depends on it, because it does.
🕸️ Graph Databases — When Relationships Are the Data Graph ▶
Reference
Traversals Instead of Joins
A graph database stores nodes and relationships as first-class citizens. Questions that need many-hop joins in SQL (Structured Query Language) ("friends of friends who like X") become natural, fast traversals. 
// Neo4j Cypher: mutual connections
MATCH (me:Person {name:"Ann"})-[:KNOWS]->(f)-[:KNOWS]->(fof)
WHERE fof <> me
RETURN fof.name, count(*) ORDER BY count(*) DESC
Great forExample
NetworksSocial graphs, org charts
Recommendations"People who bought… also…"
Fraud / securityAttack-path & ring detection (cf. BloodHound)
The relationship is stored directly, so a traversal is a pointer-hop, not a join — performance stays flat as hops increase. Use a graph DB when connections are the primary query; otherwise a relational DB is simpler.
↔️ OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) vs OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) — Rows vs Columns Analytics ▶
Concept
Two Opposite Jobs, Two Storage Layouts
OLTP (transactional) handles many small reads/writes of whole rows — your app database. OLAP (analytical) scans huge numbers of rows over a few columns — your reporting warehouse. Their opposite needs drive opposite storage.
OLTP (row store)OLAP (column store)
AccessFew rows, all columnsMany rows, few columns
LayoutRows togetherColumns together
Wins atPoint lookups & writesAggregations & scans
ExamplePostgres, MySQLBigQuery, Snowflake, ClickHouse
Why columnar is fast for analytics: reading only the 3 columns a query touches (not all 50), plus massive compression on similar values. Don't run heavy analytics on your OLTP database — it competes with live traffic. Move it to a warehouse.
🧊 Columnar Engines — Parquet, DuckDB & ClickHouse Analytics ▶
Reference
The Fast Path for Big Scans
Columnar storage plus vectorized execution (processing batches of values at once) is what makes modern analytics fast. You'll meet it as a file format and as query engines.
ToolRole
ParquetColumnar file format — the lingua franca of data lakes
DuckDB"SQLite for analytics" — query Parquet/CSV locally, blazing fast
ClickHouseReal-time columnar DB for huge event volumes
Apache ArrowIn-memory columnar standard that ties them together
-- DuckDB: query a Parquet file directly, no loading
SELECT country, count(*) FROM 'events/*.parquet' GROUP BY 1;
Trend: DuckDB has made "big data" analytics possible on a laptop for datasets that once needed a cluster — reach for it before spinning up Spark.
🏞️ Warehouse vs Lake vs Lakehouse Analytics ▶
Concept
Where Analytical Data Lives
Three architectures for storing analytical data, each solving the previous one's limitation. The lakehouse is the current convergence.
ApproachWhat it is
Data WarehouseStructured, schema-on-write, SQL (Structured Query Language) — Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift
Data LakeRaw files (Parquet) in object storage, schema-on-read — cheap, flexible, messy
LakehouseLake storage + warehouse features (ACID, tables) via Delta/Iceberg/Hudi
Table formats (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake) are the key innovation — they add transactions, schema evolution, and time-travel on top of plain files, so one copy of data serves many engines. Warehouse = easy & governed; lake = cheap & open; lakehouse = both, at the cost of complexity.
📊 The Semantic Layer & Metrics Analytics ▶
Concept
One Definition of "Revenue," Everywhere
When every dashboard computes "active users" or "revenue" its own way, numbers disagree and trust evaporates. A semantic layer defines metrics once, centrally, so every tool and query returns the same answer.
PieceDetail
Metric definitionThe canonical formula for a KPI (Key Performance Indicator), version-controlled
DimensionsHow you slice it (time, region, plan)
GovernanceCertified vs experimental metrics
Toolsdbt Semantic Layer, Cube, LookML
The payoff: a single source of truth for business logic that BI (Business Intelligence) tools, notebooks, and APIs (Application Programming Interface) all consume — no more "whose number is right?" meetings. It's the analytics equivalent of DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).
✅ Data Quality & Observability Analytics ▶
Concept
Garbage In, Wrong Decisions Out
A pipeline that runs "successfully" can still deliver silently wrong data — a null spike, a duplicated load, a schema change upstream. Data quality makes correctness a tested, monitored property, not a hope.
DimensionCheck
FreshnessDid the data arrive on time?
VolumeRow count in the expected range?
SchemaDid columns/types change upstream?
DistributionNulls/values within normal bounds?
LineageWhat feeds this, and what breaks if it fails?
Tools: dbt tests & contracts, Great Expectations, Soda; observability platforms (Monte Carlo) auto-detect anomalies. Data contracts push the guarantee upstream to producers — the analytics equivalent of an API (Application Programming Interface) contract.
💾 Backups & Point-in-Time Recovery DBA ▶
Concept
A Backup You Haven't Restored Isn't a Backup
The database holds the business's most irreplaceable asset. Backups protect against hardware failure, bad deploys, and DELETE-without-WHERE. The goal is a tested path back to any moment before disaster.
TypeDetail
Logical dumppg_dump/mysqldump — portable, slow to restore, per-DB
Physical backupFile-level (pgBackRest, Percona) — fast, whole cluster
PITRBase backup + WAL (Write-Ahead Log) archive → restore to an exact second
SnapshotsCloud volume snapshots — fast but check consistency
RPO/RPO drive design: continuous WAL archiving gives near-zero data loss (RPO). But the only backup that counts is a restore you've actually tested — schedule restore drills, or you have Schrödinger's backup.
👯 Replication & High Availability DBA ▶
Concept
Copies for Scale and Survival
Replication streams changes from a primary to one or more replicas. It buys you read scaling, failover, and geographic locality — but introduces lag and failover complexity.
ConceptDetail
Async replicationFast writes, but replicas lag → possible stale reads/data loss on failover
Sync replicationNo data loss, higher write latency
Read replicasOffload reporting/read traffic
Automatic failoverPatroni/orchestrator promote a replica on primary death
Split-brainTwo primaries accept writes — data divergence; fencing prevents it
Replication lag means "read your own write" can fail — route critical reads to the primary. HA needs a leader-election mechanism; rolling your own failover is how you get split-brain.
🔀 Schema Migrations — Zero-Downtime Change DBA ▶
Concept
Changing the Schema While Live
Schema changes are code changes and must be versioned, reviewed, and reversible. The hard part is altering a big table without locking it or breaking the currently-running app version.
Tool / IdeaDetail
Migration toolsFlyway, Liquibase, Alembic, Rails — versioned, ordered scripts
Expand/contractAdd new → backfill → switch → remove old (multi-deploy)
Locking DDL (Data Definition Language)Some ALTERs rewrite/lock the table — check first
Online toolsgh-ost, pt-online-schema-change for big MySQL tables
Golden rule: every migration must be backward-compatible with the currently-deployed code, because during a rollout both versions run at once. "Add a nullable column, deploy, backfill, then enforce" beats a single locking change. Always have a rollback.
🛡️ Database Security — Least Privilege & RLS Security ▶
Reference
Protecting the Crown Jewels
The database is the highest-value target. Defense is layered: control who connects, what they can touch, and protect the data at rest and in transit. Ties directly to the security domain.
ControlDetail
Least-privilege rolesApp user ≠ superuser; separate read/write/migration roles
Row-Level SecurityPostgres RLS — rows filtered by policy (multi-tenant isolation)
EncryptionTLS (Transport Layer Security) in transit; TDE (Transparent Data Encryption) / disk encryption at rest
SecretsRotate credentials via Vault/IAM; never hardcode
AuditingLog privileged actions & access to sensitive tables
And of course: parameterized queries to stop SQL (Structured Query Language) injection (the app's job), and network isolation so the DB is never internet-facing. Column-level encryption/masking protects PII (Personally Identifiable Information) even from DB admins.
📟 Monitoring a Database — What to Watch DBA ▶
Reference
The Signals That Predict an Outage
Databases fail in fairly predictable ways. Watch the right handful of metrics and you catch trouble before users do — this is the ops side of the SRE (Site Reliability Engineering) golden signals, applied to data.
SignalWhy
Slow-query logFind the queries actually hurting — start here
Connections / saturationNearing max_connections → pool it
Cache hit ratioLow buffer-pool hits → more RAM (Random Access Memory) or better indexes
Replication lagRising lag → stale reads, failover risk
Bloat / vacuum (PG)Dead tuples piling up → autovacuum tuning
Disk & IOPS (Input/Output Operations Per Second)Running out of space is a hard outage
pg_stat_statements (Postgres) and the Performance Schema (MySQL) surface your worst queries — the single most useful place to look when the DB is slow.
🧑‍💼 Data Roles — Who Does What Career ▶
Reference
Analyst vs Engineer vs Scientist vs DBA (Database Administrator)
"Data" spans several distinct jobs that get conflated. Knowing the boundaries helps you pick a lane — and know who to hire.
RoleOwns
Data AnalystSQL (Structured Query Language) + BI (Business Intelligence) dashboards; answers business questions
Analytics Engineerdbt models & the semantic layer (analyst + SWE practices)
Data EngineerPipelines, ingestion, warehouses, infra (Kafka/Spark/Airflow)
Data ScientistStatistics, experiments, ML (Machine Learning) models
ML EngineerProductionizing models (MLOps)
DBARuns & tunes the operational databases
The modern stack blurred these: analytics engineering emerged from analysts adopting version control, testing, and CI. The common core is SQL — it's the one skill every data role shares.
🏗️ Designing a Schema From Requirements Craft ▶
Walkthrough
From "We Sell Stuff" to Tables
A repeatable process turns fuzzy requirements into a sound schema. Example: an e-commerce order system.
StepDo
1. Find nounsCustomer, Product, Order, OrderItem, Payment → entities
2. RelationshipsOrder has many OrderItems; OrderItem → one Product
3. Keys & typesPKs, FKs, pick types & constraints (money as decimal!)
4. Normalize to 3NFEach fact once; no update anomalies
5. Index for accessAdd indexes for the real queries
6. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) laterStar schema in the warehouse for reporting
Snapshot the price: an OrderItem stores the price at time of sale, not a live FK to Product.price — a classic modeling insight. Design OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) for correctness; derive OLAP from it.
⏱️ Time-Series & Event Data Craft ▶
Concept
When Time Is the Primary Axis
Metrics, logs, IoT (Internet of Things) readings, and financial ticks are append-heavy and queried by time window. Specialized handling keeps them fast and affordable as they grow without bound.
TechniqueDetail
Time partitioningChunk by day/week; drop old chunks instantly
Downsampling / rollupsKeep 1s data briefly, 1m/1h aggregates long-term
Retention policiesAuto-expire raw data past N days
ToolsTimescaleDB, InfluxDB, Prometheus, ClickHouse
The pattern that makes it sustainable: high-resolution recent + low-resolution history. You almost never need per-second data from last year, so roll it up and let raw data expire. Ties to the observability cards in ops.
🧭 Vector Databases — Embeddings & Similarity Search AI Bridge ▶
Concept
Searching by Meaning, Not Keywords
AI (Artificial Intelligence) models turn text/images into embeddings — vectors where similar meaning = nearby points. A vector database indexes these for fast nearest-neighbor search, the backbone of RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) and semantic search.
ConceptDetail
EmbeddingA model maps content → a high-dimensional vector
ANN (Artificial Neural Network) indexHNSW/IVF — approximate nearest-neighbor for speed
SimilarityCosine / dot product ranks "closeness"
Optionspgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus
Start simple: pgvector adds vector search to Postgres — often you don't need a separate vector DB at all. Hybrid search (vectors + keyword/filters) beats either alone. Direct bridge to the AI domain's RAG cards.
🎓 The Data Interview Career ▶
Reference
What They'll Actually Ask
Data interviews test a predictable set of skills. Prepare each and this whole domain becomes your study guide.
RoundPrep
SQL (Structured Query Language)Joins, window functions, group-by, "second highest salary"-style puzzles
Data modelingDesign a schema for X; normalize; star schema for analytics
Pipeline / system designIngest → store → transform → serve; batch vs streaming
WarehousingOLTP (Online Transaction Processing) vs OLAP (Online Analytical Processing), SCDs, dbt, incremental models
Case / product senseDefine a metric, debug a dashboard drop
Highest-leverage prep: window functions and the NULL/join traps — they separate mid from senior. Practice explaining why, not just writing the query. Every card in this domain maps to one of these rounds.
🌐 Web & Frontend Engineering
WEB JS
Browser · CSS · JS · Frameworks · Performance · A11y 35 topics · ~25 min ▾
🖼️ How the Browser Renders a Page Browser ▶
Concept
From Bytes to Pixels
Understanding the rendering pipeline is what separates people who "write CSS (Cascading Style Sheets)" from people who make fast sites. The browser turns your HTML/CSS into pixels through a fixed sequence of steps.
StepDoes
Parse → DOMHTML (HyperText Markup Language) becomes the Document Object Model tree
Parse → CSSOMCSS becomes the style tree
Render treeDOM + CSSOM combined (visible nodes only)
Layout (reflow)Compute geometry — where & how big everything is
PaintFill in pixels (text, colors, borders)
CompositeAssemble layers on the GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)
Render-blocking: CSS blocks rendering (the browser won't paint unstyled content); a plain <script> blocks parsing. Use defer/async and keep critical CSS small so the page paints fast.
🌀 Reflow, Repaint & What Causes Jank Performance ▶
Concept
Why Animations Stutter
To hit 60fps the browser has ~16ms per frame. Reflow (recomputing layout) is expensive; repaint is cheaper; compositing a transform is cheapest. Triggering layout every frame causes jank.
ChangeCost
width/height/top/leftReflow (layout) — avoid animating these
color/backgroundRepaint only
transform / opacityComposite only — GPU (Graphics Processing Unit), no layout (animate these!)
Layout thrashing: reading a layout property (like offsetHeight) right after writing one forces a synchronous reflow in a loop. Batch reads, then writes. Animate transform and opacity — they skip layout and paint entirely.
🌳 The DOM (Document Object Model) & Events — Bubbling & Delegation Browser ▶
Reference
How Clicks Travel Through the Page
The DOM is the live tree of the page that JavaScript manipulates. Events flow through it in phases — understanding this powers efficient event handling. 
// Event delegation: one listener for many children
list.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const item = e.target.closest('.item');
  if (item) select(item.dataset.id);
});
PhaseDetail
CaptureTop → target (rarely used)
TargetThe element clicked
BubbleTarget → top (default for listeners)
Delegation attaches one listener to a parent and uses bubbling to handle any child — essential for dynamic lists (no re-binding on add/remove). stopPropagation() halts bubbling; preventDefault() stops the browser's default action.
🗃️ Web Storage — Cookies, localStorage & IndexedDB Browser ▶
Reference
Where State Lives in the Browser
The browser offers several places to persist data, each with different size, lifetime, and security properties. Picking the wrong one causes bugs and vulnerabilities.
StoreUse / Note
CookiesSent with every request; use HttpOnly+Secure for auth tokens
localStorage~5MB, persists, sync API (Application Programming Interface) — readable by JS (JavaScript) (XSS risk)
sessionStoragePer-tab, cleared on close
IndexedDBLarge, async, structured — offline apps
Cache APIStore responses for service workers/PWAs
Security: never store auth tokens in localStorage — any XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) reads them. Prefer HttpOnly cookies (JS can't touch them). Ties to the web-security cards.
🛠️ DevTools Mastery Tooling ▶
Reference
Your Most-Used Debugging Tool
Browser DevTools (F12) are where frontend work actually happens. Fluency here is the fastest way to level up — most developers use 20% of them.
PanelUse
ElementsInspect/edit DOM (Document Object Model) & CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) live; check the box model
ConsoleLogs, run JS (JavaScript), $0 = selected element
NetworkRequests, timing, payloads, throttling
PerformanceRecord & find jank, long tasks, layout shifts
ApplicationStorage, cookies, service workers, manifest
LighthouseAudit performance, a11y (Accessibility), SEO (Search Engine Optimization), best practices
Pro moves: throttle to "Slow 3G" + 4× CPU (Central Processing Unit) to feel what users feel; use the Performance panel's flame chart to find the function eating your frame budget.
📏 Flexbox — One-Dimensional Layout CSS ▶
Reference
Aligning Things in a Row or Column
Flexbox lays out items along a single axis and is the go-to for components: navbars, toolbars, centering, card rows. Set display:flex on the parent, then control alignment and distribution. 
.bar {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;  /* main axis */
  align-items: center;             /* cross axis */
  gap: 1rem;
}
PropertyControls
flex-directionrow (default) or column — sets the main axis
justify-contentSpacing along the main axis
align-itemsAlignment on the cross axis
flex: 1Grow to fill; flex-wrap to wrap
gapSpace between items (no more margin hacks)
Centering, solved: display:flex; justify-content:center; align-items:center — the answer to a decade of "how do I center a div."
🔲 CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) Grid — Two-Dimensional Layout CSS ▶
Reference
Rows and Columns at the Same Time
Grid handles two dimensions at once — perfect for page layouts and any grid of cards. Where Flexbox is content-driven, Grid is layout-driven: you define the structure, items flow in. 
.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}
FeatureDetail
grid-template-columns/rowsDefine tracks; fr = fraction of free space
repeat() + minmax()Responsive columns without media queries
auto-fit / auto-fillWrap columns to fit the container
grid-template-areasName regions; lay out visually in CSS
Rule of thumb: Grid for the overall page/section layout, Flexbox for the components inside it. The auto-fit + minmax one-liner gives a fully responsive card grid with zero media queries.
📱 Responsive Design — Fluid, Mobile-First CSS ▶
Concept
One Site, Every Screen
Responsive design adapts the layout to the viewport. The modern approach is mobile-first (style the small screen, then add complexity up) and increasingly intrinsic (let the content size itself).
ToolUse
Media queriesBreakpoints by viewport width
Container queriesRespond to the parent's size — true component responsiveness
clamp()Fluid type/spacing: clamp(min, preferred, max)
rem / % / fr / vwRelative units over fixed px
<meta viewport>Required tag or mobile scales wrong
Container queries are the big recent shift: a card can restyle based on the space it has, so the same component works in a sidebar or full-width — impossible with media queries alone.
✨ Modern CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) — Custom Properties, :has() & Layers CSS ▶
Reference
CSS Got Genuinely Powerful
Recent CSS added features that used to need preprocessors or JavaScript. Worth knowing because they simplify code you may still be writing the old way. 
:root { --brand: #f97316; }
.btn { background: var(--brand); }
/* style a label only if it HAS an invalid input */
.field:has(input:invalid) { color: red; }
FeatureDoes
Custom propertiesReal variables — themeable, runtime-changeable
:has()The "parent selector" — style based on descendants
NestingNative nested rules (no Sass needed)
@layerCascade layers — tame specificity wars
clamp/min/maxMath in CSS for fluid design
Custom properties + prefers-color-scheme is how modern dark mode works — swap variable values, not whole stylesheets (exactly how this site themes itself).
🎨 Design Systems, Tokens & Tailwind CSS ▶
Concept
Styling That Scales Across a Team
At scale, ad-hoc CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) becomes unmaintainable. Design systems encode consistent spacing, color, and type as reusable tokens and components, so a large app stays coherent.
ApproachDetail
Design tokensNamed values (spacing-4, color-primary) — the source of truth
Utility-first (Tailwind)Compose small classes; consistency by constraint
Component librariesshadcn/ui, MUI, Radix — accessible building blocks
BEM / CSS ModulesNaming & scoping conventions
CSS-in-JSStyles colocated with components (styled-components)
The trade-off debate: Tailwind trades "ugly markup" for never leaving your HTML (HyperText Markup Language) and never fighting the cascade — hugely popular for that reason. Whatever the method, the win is constraints: a limited palette of choices keeps a big UI (User Interface) consistent.
🔒 Closures, Scope & this JavaScript ▶
Concept
The Interview Trio, Explained
Three JS concepts that confuse beginners and get asked in every interview. Get them and most "weird JavaScript" stops being weird. 
function counter() {
  let n = 0;                 // captured by the closure
  return () => ++n;         // remembers n after counter() returns
}
const c = counter(); c(); c();  // 1, 2
ConceptDetail
ScopeWhere a variable is visible; let/const are block-scoped
ClosureA function that remembers variables from where it was defined
thisDepends on how a function is called (not where defined)
Arrow functionsNo own this — inherit from the enclosing scope
this gotcha: a method passed as a callback loses its this. Arrow functions or .bind() fix it. Closures power data privacy, memoization, and every event handler that "remembers" state.
⏳ Async Deep — Promises, await & the Event Loop JavaScript ▶
Concept
How Single-Threaded JS Does Many Things
JavaScript runs on one thread but stays responsive via the event loop: long operations (network, timers) run elsewhere and their callbacks are queued back. Promises and async/await make this readable. 
async function load() {
  try {
    const [a, b] = await Promise.all([getA(), getB()]); // parallel
    return merge(a, b);
  } catch (e) { handle(e); }
}
ConceptDetail
PromiseA value that arrives later (pending → fulfilled/rejected)
async/awaitWrite async code that reads like sync
Microtask vs macrotaskPromises (micro) run before timers (macro)
Promise.all / race / allSettledCoordinate multiple promises
Parallel vs serial: await a; await b; runs one after the other; Promise.all([a,b]) runs them together — a common performance win. Never await in a loop when the iterations are independent.
🧬 Prototypes & Modern Classes JavaScript ▶
Concept
JavaScript's Real Inheritance Model
Under the class syntax, JS uses prototypal inheritance: objects delegate to a prototype object. Knowing this explains how method lookup and class actually work.
ConceptDetail
Prototype chainMiss a property → look up the chain until null
classSyntactic sugar over prototypes (constructor, methods)
extends / superInheritance & calling the parent
Static / #privateClass-level members; true private fields (#)
Modern advice: favor composition and plain objects /modules over deep class hierarchies. But you must understand prototypes to debug "why is this method undefined?" and to read library code.
📦 Modules & Bundlers — ESM (ECMAScript Modules), Vite & Tree-Shaking JavaScript ▶
Reference
From Many Files to Shipped Code
Modern JS (JavaScript) is written as ES modules (import/export) across many files, then a bundler optimizes them into what ships to the browser.
ConceptDetail
ESMStandard import/export (vs old CommonJS require)
BundlingCombine modules, resolve deps
Tree-shakingDrop unused exports → smaller bundles
Code-splittingLoad chunks on demand (per route)
Vite / esbuild / RollupFast modern tooling (webpack's successors)
Vite is the current default: instant dev server (native ESM, no bundling in dev) + optimized production builds. Tree-shaking is why import { thing } beats importing a whole library.
🔷 TypeScript — Types for JavaScript JavaScript ▶
Reference
Catch Bugs Before They Ship
TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript, caught at compile time. It's now the default for serious projects — the editor autocomplete and refactoring safety alone are worth it. 
type User = { id: number; name: string; email?: string };
function greet(u: User): string {
  return `Hi ${u.name}`;
}
FeatureDetail
Interfaces / typesDescribe object shapes
GenericsReusable, type-safe code (Array<T>)
NarrowingTypes refine via checks (unions, guards)
strict modeNull-safety & more — turn it on
Mental model: types are erased at build time — they guide the compiler and editor, then disappear. The payoff is fewer runtime undefined errors and fearless refactoring in large codebases.
⚛️ React — Components, Hooks & the Mental Model Frameworks ▶
Reference
UI (User Interface) as a Function of State
React's core idea: your UI is a function of state — UI = f(state). You describe what the screen should look like for the current data; React efficiently updates the DOM (Document Object Model) when state changes. 
function Counter() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>{n}</button>;
}
ConceptDetail
ComponentsReusable functions returning JSX (JavaScript XML)
PropsRead-only inputs passed down
useState / useReducerLocal state
useEffectSide effects (fetch, subscriptions) — has gotchas
KeysStable list identity — never use array index if items change
The rules of hooks: call them at the top level, same order every render. State updates are asynchronous and batched. "Lift state up" to the nearest common parent when siblings need to share it.
🪝 React Patterns & Pitfalls Frameworks ▶
Reference
Avoiding the Common Traps
Most React bugs come from a handful of misunderstandings around effects, re-renders, and stale state. Knowing them saves days.
TopicDetail
ContextShare data without prop-drilling (theme, auth)
useMemo / useCallbackMemoize expensive work / stable function identity
useEffect overuseDon't sync state you can derive during render
Stale closuresEffect captures old state — fix deps array
Unnecessary re-rendersNew object/array props break memoization
Modern guidance: "You Might Not Need an Effect" — derive values during render, handle events in handlers, and reserve useEffect for genuine external synchronization. Don't reach for memoization until you've measured a problem.
🟢 Vue & Svelte — Other Reactivity Models Frameworks ▶
Reference
Not Everything Is React
React isn't the only game. Vue and Svelte reach the same goal — reactive UI (User Interface) — with different (often simpler) models worth understanding.
FrameworkApproach
ReactRe-render on state change; virtual DOM (Document Object Model) diff; explicit
VueFine-grained reactivity + template syntax; gentle learning curve
SvelteCompiler — no virtual DOM; compiles away to tiny vanilla JS (JavaScript)
Solid / signalsFine-grained signals; the model many are converging on
The trend: signals. Fine-grained reactivity (Solid, Vue, Svelte 5, Angular signals) updates exactly what changed without re-running whole components — the industry direction. Learn React for jobs; learn signals to understand where things are going.
▲ Meta-Frameworks — Next.js & Rendering Modes Frameworks ▶
Concept
SSR (Server-Side Rendering), SSG (Static Site Generation), ISR & CSR (Certificate Signing Request) — When Each
Meta-frameworks (Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit) add routing, data fetching, and server rendering on top of the UI (User Interface) library. The key decision is where and when your HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is generated.
ModeHTML built…Best for
CSRIn the browserApp-like dashboards (behind login)
SSRPer request on the serverPersonalized, fresh pages
SSGAt build timeBlogs, docs, marketing (fastest)
ISRStatic + periodic rebuildLarge mostly-static sites
SSR/SSG win on first-load speed and SEO (Search Engine Optimization) (real HTML arrives immediately). React Server Components are the current frontier — render components on the server, ship less JS (JavaScript). Match the mode to the page: static where you can, dynamic where you must.
🗄️ State Management — When You Actually Need It Frameworks ▶
Concept
Don't Reach for Redux by Default
As apps grow, sharing state gets messy — but the answer usually isn't a big global store. Distinguish server state (data from an API) from client state (UI toggles); they need different tools.
NeedReach for
Server data (caching, refetch)React Query / SWR — not a global store
Simple shared UI (User Interface) stateContext, or lift state up
Complex global client stateZustand / Redux Toolkit / signals
URL (Uniform Resource Locator) as stateQuery params for filters/tabs (shareable)
Biggest insight: most "state management" pain is really server state (loading, caching, revalidation) — a data-fetching library like React Query solves it far better than Redux. Add global stores only for genuinely global client state.
🔌 Fetch, REST (Representational State Transfer) & CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) in Practice Backends ▶
Reference
How the Frontend Talks to APIs (Application Programming Interface)
The browser's fetch makes HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) requests. You'll spend real time on status codes, headers, and the one that trips everyone up: CORS. 
const res = await fetch('/api/users', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify(user),
});
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.status);   // fetch doesn't throw on 4xx/5xx!
ThingDetail
Status codes2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx client, 5xx server
CORSBrowser blocks cross-origin unless the server sends Access-Control-Allow-*
PreflightAn OPTIONS request before non-simple calls
fetch quirkOnly rejects on network error — check res.ok yourself
CORS is server-side: a CORS error means the API must allow your origin — you can't fix it from the browser. It's a browser security feature, not a bug in your code.
◈ GraphQL on the Backend — Schema, Resolvers & Caching Backends ▶
Reference
One Endpoint, Client-Shaped Responses
GraphQL exposes a typed schema through one endpoint; the client specifies exactly which fields it wants. It solves REST (Representational State Transfer)'s over- and under-fetching, at the cost of new complexity. 
query {
  user(id: 42) { name, orders { total } }   # exactly these fields
}
ConceptDetail
Schema & typesStrongly typed contract
Query / Mutation / SubscriptionRead / write / realtime
ResolversServer functions that fetch each field
N+1 resolversClassic pitfall — fix with DataLoader batching
When to use: many clients with different data needs, or deeply nested data. For simple CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete), REST is often simpler. Caching is harder than REST (one endpoint, POST) — weigh the trade-off.
🔴 Realtime — WebSockets, SSE (Server-Sent Events) & Polling Backends ▶
Reference
Pushing Data to the Browser
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is request/response — the server can't just push. For live features (chat, notifications, dashboards) you need a different transport. Pick the lightest one that fits.
OptionUse
WebSocketsFull-duplex, persistent — chat, games, collaboration
Server-Sent EventsServer→client stream over HTTP — feeds, notifications (simpler)
Long pollingFallback where sockets aren't available
Short pollingJust refetch on a timer — fine for low-frequency updates
Don't over-engineer: if data changes every few minutes, polling is simplest. Reserve WebSockets for genuinely bidirectional, high-frequency needs. SSE is the underrated middle ground for one-way streams.
🔑 Frontend Auth — Tokens, Cookies & OAuth (Open Authorization) Backends ▶
Concept
Logging Users In, Safely
Auth on the frontend is mostly about where you store the credential and how you attach it. Get this wrong and you ship an XSS-exploitable token. Ties directly to the security domain's OAuth/session cards.
ApproachDetail
HttpOnly cookieJS (JavaScript) can't read it → XSS-safe; pair with SameSite/CSRF protection
JWT (JSON Web Token) in localStorageConvenient but XSS-readable — widely discouraged
OAuth / OIDC (OpenID Connect) + PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange)"Sign in with…"; PKCE for public clients
Refresh flowShort-lived access token + refresh token rotation
Rule: prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies for session tokens. Never store long-lived secrets where JavaScript can read them. Auth is one place to use a battle-tested library, not roll your own.
🔄 Data Fetching Patterns — React Query & Caching Backends ▶
Reference
Server State Is Its Own Problem
Fetching data is easy; keeping it fresh, cached, and in sync across a UI (User Interface) is hard. Libraries like React Query (TanStack Query) and SWR handle the whole lifecycle so you don't reinvent it per component.
FeatureDoes
Caching & dedupSame query used twice → one request
Background refetchRevalidate stale data on focus/interval
Loading/error statesBuilt in — no manual flags
Optimistic updatesUpdate UI instantly, roll back on failure
Why it matters: hand-rolled useEffect + useState fetching leads to race conditions, duplicate requests, and stale UI. A query library turns all that into a hook — genuinely one of the biggest quality-of-life wins in modern frontend.
⚡ Web Performance — Core Web Vitals Performance ▶
Reference
The Metrics Google (and Users) Care About
Core Web Vitals are Google's user-centric performance metrics — they affect both experience and search ranking. Optimize these three and the site feels fast.
MetricMeasuresFix
LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)Largest content paint (load speed)Optimize images, server response, critical CSS (Cascading Style Sheets)
INP (Interaction to Next Paint)Interaction responsivenessBreak up long JS (JavaScript) tasks; less main-thread work
CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)Layout shift (visual stability)Set image/ad dimensions; reserve space
Big levers: ship less JavaScript (code-split, tree-shake), optimize & lazy-load images (modern formats, loading="lazy"), and cache aggressively. Measure with Lighthouse and real-user data (RUM) — lab and field can differ.
♿ Web Accessibility (a11y) — WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) & ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) A11y ▶
Concept
Usable by Everyone — and Often the Law
Accessibility means people using keyboards, screen readers, or with low vision can use your site. It's a legal requirement in many contexts (ADA, EAA) and simply good engineering — accessible sites are more robust for everyone.
Principle (POUR)Detail
Semantic HTML (HyperText Markup Language)Use real <button>/<nav>/<h1> — free a11y
KeyboardEverything operable without a mouse; visible focus
Contrast & text4.5:1 contrast; resizable text; alt text on images
ARIARoles/labels for custom widgets — only when HTML can't
First rule of ARIA: don't use ARIA — a native element beats a div with roles every time. Test by unplugging your mouse and by running a screen reader. WCAG AA is the common target. (This site follows these: keyboard nav, focus states, semantic structure.)
🧪 Frontend Testing — Unit, Component & E2E Quality ▶
Reference
Confidence Without Manual Clicking
Frontend tests catch regressions before users do. The test pyramid applies: lots of fast unit tests, fewer component tests, a handful of end-to-end tests for critical flows.
LevelToolTests
UnitVitest / JestPure functions, logic
ComponentTesting LibraryRender + interact like a user
E2EPlaywright / CypressReal browser, full flows (login → checkout)
Visual / a11yStorybook, axeRegression & accessibility checks
Testing Library philosophy: test behavior, not implementation — query by what a user sees (roles, text), not CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) classes. Then refactors don't break tests. A few reliable E2E tests on the money-path beat a hundred brittle ones.
🛡️ Frontend Security — XSS (Cross-Site Scripting), CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) & CSP (Content Security Policy) Security ▶
Concept
The Browser-Side Attack Surface
The frontend has its own security risks distinct from the server. The big three every web dev must know — directly bridging to the security domain's web cards.
AttackDefense
XSSInjected script runs in your page → escape output, avoid innerHTML/dangerouslySetInnerHTML, use CSP
CSRFForged request using the user's cookie → SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens
ClickjackingYour page iframed & tricked → X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors
CSPContent-Security-Policy limits what can load/run — big XSS mitigation
Frameworks help: React escapes by default (which is why dangerouslySetInnerHTML is named to scare you). Never build HTML (HyperText Markup Language) from untrusted strings; sanitize any rich content with a vetted library (DOMPurify).
🔍 SEO (Search Engine Optimization) & Metadata for Developers Quality ▶
Reference
Being Found & Shared Correctly
Technical SEO is the part developers own: making pages crawlable, fast, and correctly described. Modern SEO overlaps heavily with performance and semantic HTML (HyperText Markup Language).
ElementPurpose
Semantic HTML & headingsStructure crawlers understand
<title> & meta descriptionThe search-result snippet
Open Graph / Twitter cardsRich link previews when shared
Structured data (JSON-LD)Rich results (ratings, FAQs)
Sitemap & robots.txtGuide crawlers; canonical URLs (Uniform Resource Locator) avoid dupes
SSR/SSG helps SEO because crawlers get real HTML immediately. Core Web Vitals are a ranking factor too — so performance work doubles as SEO work.
📲 Progressive Web Apps — Offline & Installable Shipping ▶
Concept
Websites That Act Like Native Apps
A PWA (Progressive Web App) is a website with app-like superpowers: it can be installed to the home screen, work offline, and receive push notifications — all from the web platform. (This very site is installable — that's why the icon fix mattered.)
PieceRole
Web app manifestName, icons, theme → installability
Service workerA background proxy — caches responses, enables offline
Cache strategiesCache-first, network-first, stale-while-revalidate
Push / background syncNotifications & deferred actions
Service workers are powerful & sharp: they intercept every request, so a bad cache strategy can serve stale content forever. Test your update flow. For content sites, "offline + installable" is a big UX (User Experience) win for little cost.
🌍 Rendering at the Edge — CDNs (Content Delivery Network) & Edge Functions Shipping ▶
Concept
Compute Close to the User
A CDN caches static assets in hundreds of locations worldwide so users download from nearby. Edge functions push compute there too — run code milliseconds from the user.
ConceptDetail
CDN cachingStatic assets served from the nearest POP
Edge functionsLightweight compute at the edge (auth, redirects, A/B)
Image optimizationResize/format on the fly (WebP/AVIF) at the edge
Cache headersCache-Control, ETags, immutable hashed assets
Trade-off: edge runtimes are limited (no full Node APIs, short execution) — great for fast, small logic, not heavy work. Combined with hashed filenames + long cache TTLs (Time To Live), the edge makes global sites feel local.
🧩 WebAssembly — Native Speed in the Browser Platform ▶
Concept
When JavaScript Isn't Fast Enough
WebAssembly (Wasm) is a compact binary format that runs at near-native speed in the browser. Compile C/C++/Rust/Go to Wasm and call it from JS (JavaScript) for compute-heavy work.
Great forExample
Heavy computeImage/video editing, games, simulations
Porting native codeExisting C/C++ libraries to the web (FFmpeg, SQLite)
Beyond the browserWasm + WASI as a portable, sandboxed runtime (edge, plugins)
Not a JS replacement: Wasm can't touch the DOM (Document Object Model) directly and has call-overhead — reach for it for the hot compute path, not the whole app. Its bigger future may be server-side: a fast, secure, language-agnostic sandbox.
🚀 Frontend Build & Deploy — CI & Preview Deploys Shipping ▶
Reference
From Commit to Live
Modern frontend deploy is largely solved by platforms that build on every push and give each pull request its own preview URL (Uniform Resource Locator). Understand the pipeline so you can debug it — this static site uses exactly this flow (build script + CI + Netlify/Pages).
StageDetail
CI on pushInstall, build, test, lint on every commit/PR
Preview deploysEvery PR gets a live URL to review
Atomic deploys & rollbackInstant switch; revert to a prior build in one click
Env vars & secretsPer-environment config, never in the bundle
PlatformsNetlify, Vercel, Cloudflare/GitHub Pages
Client bundles are public: never put secrets in frontend env vars — anything shipped to the browser can be read. Keep secrets on the server/edge.
🔗 The Full-Stack Picture — How It All Connects Shipping ▶
Concept
Frontend + API (Application Programming Interface) + DB, End to End
Zooming out: a request flows through many layers you've now studied across the web, data, cloud, and ops domains. Seeing the whole path is what makes you full-stack. 
Browser (React) →  CDN/Edge  →  API (REST/GraphQL)
   →  Auth  →  Business logic  →  Cache (Redis)  →  Database
   →  back up the stack as JSON  →  React renders
LayerStudied in
UI (User Interface) & stateweb (frameworks, I4)
API & authweb (I5), sec (OAuth)
Data & cachedata (H*), ops (caching)
Deploy & observeops, cloud domains
The takeaway: no single layer is magic — each is a tractable piece you can learn. "Full-stack" is just fluency in how the request travels and where each concern lives. This domain, plus data, eng, ops, and cloud, is the whole map.
🖥️ Endpoint Management — Intune · MECM
MD-102 MEM
MECM · Entra · Intune · Autopilot · ESP · Co-management · Windows Admin · Troubleshooting 34 topics · ~1h 10m ▾
🏢 Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager (MECM) On-Prem ▶
Reference
ConfigMgr / SCCM (System Center Configuration Manager) — What It Is & Where It Fits
MECM (formerly SCCM, universally called ConfigMgr) is Microsoft's on-premises platform for managing Windows (and some Linux/macOS/servers) at scale: application deployment, patching, OS (Operating System) imaging, hardware/software inventory, and compliance. It ships in the Current Branch model — a new feature release roughly three times a year (e.g. 2403 = 2024, March), applied in-console.
StrengthWhy it still matters
Deep OS deploymentFull bare-metal imaging & task sequences Intune can't match
Bandwidth controlOn-prem DPs, peer caching for large/branch fleets
Granular software dist.Complex app models, supersedence, dependencies
Mature reportingSQL (Structured Query Language) Reporting Services, rich inventory
The direction of travel is cloud: most orgs now run co-management (ConfigMgr + Intune on the same device) and move workloads to Intune over time. ConfigMgr isn't dead — it's the on-prem anchor of a hybrid estate (see the Co-management card).
Architecture
Sites, the Database & Site System Roles
A ConfigMgr deployment is a hierarchy of sites, each identified by a 3-character site code (e.g. P01). Most orgs need only a single standalone primary site; very large or multi-geo estates add a CAS and/or secondary sites.
Site typePurpose
CAS (Central Admin Site)Top of a multi-primary hierarchy — reporting/admin only, no clients
Primary siteManages clients; holds the site database
Secondary siteControls content/upstream traffic for a remote location
Site system roleJob
Site database (SQL)Everything — config, inventory, status
SMS (Systems Management Server) ProviderWMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) layer the console talks through
Management Point (MP)Primary client ↔ site channel (policy, inventory)
Distribution Point (DP)Hosts & serves content
Software Update Point (SUP)Sits on WSUS (Windows Server Update Services); drives patching
Cloud Management Gateway (CMG)Manage internet-based clients via Azure (no VPN)
Reporting Services PointSSRS reports
Fallback Status Point (FSP)Collects client install/health state
The Client
Agent Install, Settings & Health
The ConfigMgr client (ccmsetup.exe → CcmExec service) runs policy, inventory, and deployments. It can be installed several ways; client behavior is governed by Client Settings (default + prioritized custom sets assigned to collections).
Install methodNotes
Client pushSite pushes to discovered devices (needs push account + firewall)
GPO (Group Policy Object) / logon scriptClassic mass deployment
Software update-basedClient delivered as an "update" via WSUS
Intune / co-mgmt (ccmsetup)Push the client as a Win32 app during Autopilot
Control Panel → Configuration Manager exposes actions like Machine Policy Retrieval, Hardware Inventory Cycle, and Software Updates Scan — the buttons you press when "it's not showing up yet." Client health is monitored by the built-in ccmeval scheduled task, which auto-remediates a broken client.
Content & Targeting
Boundaries, Boundary Groups & Distribution
Clients find their nearest servers via boundaries (IP subnet, AD site, IPv6 prefix, or IP range) grouped into boundary groups, which map to the MPs/DPs/SUPs a client should use — with fallback relationships and time delays.
ConceptDetail
Content librarySingle-instance store of all distributed content on a DP
Pull DPA DP that pulls content from another DP (scale-out)
Peer CacheClients serve content to peers on the same subnet
BranchCache / Delivery OptimizationPeer-to-peer to cut WAN (Wide Area Network) usage
Prestaged contentShip content on disk to a slow-link DP
#1 support ticket: "content won't download." Almost always a missing/overlapping boundary, content not distributed to the client's DP, or a boundary group with no fallback. Check LocationServices.log and ContentTransferManager.log.
Deploying Things
Applications, Updates & OS Deployment
Everything targets a collection (device or user; direct or query/WQL membership). The three big deployment workloads:
WorkloadKey pieces
ApplicationsDeployment types + detection method + requirement rules + supersedence; purpose Available (Software Center) or Required (enforced by deadline)
Software UpdatesSUP scan → deploy manually or via ADR (Automatic Deployment Rule) that grabs each Patch Tuesday into a deployment package
OS Deployment (OSD)Task sequence: boot image (WinPE) → partition → apply WIM (Windows Imaging Format) → drivers → join (AD/Entra) → apps
Detection method is the make-or-break of app deployment: it's how ConfigMgr decides "already installed?" (file version, registry, MSI product code, or script). Wrong detection = endless reinstall or false failure. Maintenance windows on a collection limit when Required installs/reboots may run — critical for servers.
Troubleshooting
Log Files & CMTrace
ConfigMgr troubleshooting is log reading. Open logs with CMTrace (ships in the client; live-tails and highlights errors). Client logs live in C:\Windows\CCM\Logs; during OSD (Operating System Deployment), in X:\Windows\Temp\SMSTSLog then C:\_SMSTaskSequence.
LogTells you
ccmsetup.logClient install
PolicyAgent.logPolicy download
AppEnforce.logApp install/uninstall & detection
AppDiscovery.logDetection method evaluation
WUAHandler.log / UpdatesDeployment.logPatching
smsts.logTask sequence (OSD) — the OSD bible
LocationServices.logBoundary/DP resolution
🪪 Azure AD (Active Directory) / Microsoft Entra ID — Endpoint Identity Identity ▶
Concept
The Identity Layer Everything Sits On
Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is the cloud directory behind Microsoft 365 and Intune. Every managed device gets a device object in Entra; how it obtains that identity (its join type) determines which management, SSO (Single Sign-On), and Conditional Access experiences are possible.
Join typeHow & when
Entra JoinedCloud-only. Set during OOBE/Autopilot or Settings. The modern default for corporate Windows
Entra Hybrid JoinedDomain-joined and synced to Entra (needs Entra Connect + SCP). For orgs still reliant on on-prem AD/GPO/apps
Entra RegisteredBYOD/personal — a work identity is added but the org doesn't own the device (Workplace Join)
Hybrid is heavier & more fragile (sync timing, SCP, network line-of-sight to a DC for the join). Microsoft's clear guidance: go cloud-native (Entra Joined) unless a hard dependency forces hybrid.
Internals
dsregcmd, the PRT (Primary Refresh Token) & Windows Hello for Business
The device's join/registration state is the first thing to check when SSO or enrollment misbehaves. dsregcmd /status is the definitive local tool. 
# Show device join & SSO state (run as the signed-in user)
dsregcmd /status
# Key fields:
#   AzureAdJoined : YES        -> Entra Joined
#   DomainJoined  : YES        -> (also) on-prem = Hybrid
#   AzureAdPrt    : YES        -> Primary Refresh Token present (SSO works)
#   MdmUrl / MdmEnrollmentUrl  -> auto-enrollment configured
TermMeaning
Primary Refresh Token (PRT)Issued at sign-in; grants seamless SSO to M365 apps & browsers
Windows Hello for BusinessPasswordless (PIN/biometric) bound to the device via asymmetric keys
Device objectThe Entra record CA & Intune reason about (compliant? managed? join type?)
Reference
MDM (Mobile Device Management) Authority & Automatic Enrollment
Entra is where devices are told to enroll. Under Entra → Mobility (MDM and MAM) → Microsoft Intune you set the MDM user scope (which users' devices auto-enroll on Entra join) and the MAM (Mobile Application Management) scope.
SettingEffect
MDM user scope = All / SomeDevices those users join auto-enroll into Intune
MAM user scopeApp-level (MAM) enrollment for BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) without full MDM
Dynamic device groupsMembership by rule (OS, ownership, enrollment profile) → drives targeting everywhere
Device categoriesAuto-place devices into groups at enrollment
Licensing gotcha: auto-enrollment and many CA features require the right licenses (Intune + Entra ID P1/P2, usually via M365 E3/E5). No license = "your device can't be enrolled" errors.
☁️ Microsoft Intune — Cloud MDM (Mobile Device Management) & MAM (Mobile Application Management) Cloud MDM ▶
Reference
The Cloud Endpoint-Management Service
Microsoft Intune (admin center intune.microsoft.com) manages devices (MDM) and apps (MAM) across Windows, macOS, iOS/iPadOS, Android, and Linux — no on-prem infrastructure. Admin scoping uses RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) roles + scope tags (limit which admins see which objects/devices).
ObjectDoes
Compliance policyDefines "healthy" (BitLocker on, min OS, Defender, not jailbroken) → feeds Conditional Access
Configuration profileSettings Catalog, ADMX (Administrative Template) templates (GPO-equivalent), custom OMA-URI (Open Mobile Alliance Uniform Resource Identifier)
AppsWin32, MSI/LOB, Store, web link, iOS/Android store & VPP (Volume Purchase Program)
App Protection Policy (APP/MAM)Protect data inside apps without enrolling the device
Endpoint securityAV, ASR (Attack Surface Reduction), disk encryption, firewall, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) onboarding
Enrollment
Getting Devices Under Management
The right enrollment path depends on platform and ownership. All assignment happens via Entra groups, optionally narrowed by filters (e.g. only Windows 11 24H2).
PlatformCorporateBYOD (Bring Your Own Device)
WindowsAutopilot / Entra join + auto-enroll / co-mgmtCompany Portal (Add work account)
iOS/iPadOSApple Business Manager (ADE) + enrollment profileCompany Portal + APP
AndroidAndroid Enterprise (fully managed / dedicated)Work profile
macOSABM (Apple Business Manager) / ADE, or Company PortalCompany Portal
Filters vs groups: use groups for who, filters for which devices — filters evaluate at assignment time and avoid proliferating dynamic groups.
Apps
Win32 Packaging, Detection & Assignment Intents
Real-world Windows apps ship as Win32 packages (.intunewin), built with the Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool. 
# Wrap a source folder + installer into .intunewin
IntuneWinAppUtil.exe -c "C:\Source" -s setup.exe -o "C:\Out"

# In Intune you then define:
#  Install:   setup.exe /silent
#  Uninstall: setup.exe /uninstall /silent
#  Detection: file/registry/MSI-code/script  (is it installed?)
#  Requirements: OS, architecture, disk, custom script
#  Dependencies & Supersedence: chain/replace other apps
IntentBehavior
RequiredInstalled automatically on assigned devices/users
AvailableOptional — appears in Company Portal
UninstallRemoves the app from targets
Detection rules are the #1 cause of app failures in Intune too (mirrors ConfigMgr). Supersedence lets a new version replace/upgrade an old one; dependencies install prerequisites first (e.g. VC++ runtime).
Policy & Security
Config Profiles, Compliance & Update Rings
AreaDetail
Settings CatalogThe modern way to configure almost anything — thousands of settings, per-setting search
ADMX-backed profilesBring familiar GPO (Group Policy Object) ADMX settings to MDM
Compliance policyHealth rules + actions for noncompliance (grace period, email, retire)
Update rings (WUfB)Windows Update for Business — deferrals, deadlines, active hours (ring 1 pilot → broad)
Feature update policyPin/roll a target Windows feature version
Endpoint security baselinesMicrosoft-recommended security config as a template
Conflict handling: if two profiles set the same setting differently the result is a conflict (neither applies) — the per-setting report shows which policies collided. Keep profiles small and single-purpose.
✈️ Windows Autopilot — Zero-Touch Provisioning Provisioning ▶
Concept
Ship a Sealed OEM Laptop Straight to the User
Windows Autopilot customizes the out-of-box experience (OOBE) so a factory device configures itself for your org — no imaging, no touching it in IT. The device's hardware identity is pre-registered to your tenant; at first boot it recognizes itself, Entra-joins, enrolls in Intune, and applies your apps/policies through the ESP (Enrollment Status Page).
Deployment modeUse case & behavior
User-drivenUser signs in during OOBE → device joins Entra as theirs. The standard mode
Pre-provisioning (White Glove)IT/OEM/partner runs the device phase first (apps, policies), reseals; user gets a short finish
Self-deployingNo user creds — kiosks, digital signage, shared/lab (requires TPM 2.0)
Existing devicesRe-provision an in-place PC via a ConfigMgr task sequence into Autopilot
Autopilot ResetWipe user data/apps but keep Entra join & enrollment — hand-off/refresh
Registration
Hardware Hash, Group Tags & Who Uploads It
A device becomes "an Autopilot device" when its hardware hash (a ~4KB device fingerprint) is uploaded to your tenant. Registration source matters for scale. 
# Capture the hash locally and register the device online
Install-Script Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo -Force
Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo -Online -GroupTag "Kiosk"
# -Online prompts Entra sign-in and uploads; -GroupTag stamps a
# tag used by dynamic groups to auto-assign a deployment profile.
Registration pathWhen
OEM / reseller (CSP)Best — vendor registers at purchase; you never touch it
Manual PowerShellExisting stock / pilots
ConfigMgr / Intune diagnosticsHarvest hashes from managed devices
Group Tag (a.k.a. OrderID) is the trick for targeting: a dynamic group with rule device.devicePhysicalIds -any (_ -eq "[OrderID]:Kiosk") auto-collects tagged devices and assigns the right profile.
Flow
Deployment Profile & the OOBE Sequence
A deployment profile (assigned to the device's group) defines the join type and OOBE behavior; the ESP then gates the desktop.
Profile settingControls
Join typeEntra joined vs Entra hybrid joined
OOBE togglesHide EULA/privacy, hide account-change, user account type (Std/Admin)
Naming templateAuto-name devices (e.g. AP-%SERIAL%)
Language/regionPre-set for self-deploying/pre-provisioning
Sequence: power on → network → OOBE fetches the Autopilot profile → branded Entra sign-in → Entra join → auto MDM (Mobile Device Management) enroll → ESP installs device- & user-targeted content → desktop. Requires internet + a supported Windows edition (Pro/Enterprise/Edu).
Troubleshooting
When Autopilot Doesn't Trigger
SymptomLikely cause
Normal OOBE (no branding)Device not registered, or profile not assigned yet (wait/sync)
"Something went wrong" (0x80180018 etc.)MDM auto-enroll/licensing not configured, or Entra join blocked
Stuck at ESPBlocking app failing / detection wrong / timeout too low (see ESP card)
ToolsShift+F10 for a console; Autopilot diagnostics page; Event Viewer → DeviceManagement-Enterprise-Diagnostics-Provider
⏳ Enrollment Status Page (ESP) Provisioning ▶
Concept
The Gate That Makes a Device Ready on Day One
The Enrollment Status Page is the full-screen progress screen during Autopilot/enrollment. Its purpose is to withhold the desktop until the device is genuinely ready — required apps installed, policies applied, certs delivered — so nobody lands on a half-configured machine and starts working before security settings arrive.
PhaseRunsTracks
Device preparationPre-sign-inTPM (Trusted Platform Module) attestation (self-deploy), Entra join, Intune enrollment
Device setupPre-sign-inDevice-targeted apps, policies, certificates, security
Account setupAfter user signs inUser-targeted apps & policies
Configured under Intune → Devices → Enrollment → Enrollment Status Page: a Default profile plus higher-priority profiles assigned to groups.
Settings
Every Knob and What It Does
SettingEffect
Show app/profile install progressMaster switch — turns the ESP on for the group
Block device use until all apps & profiles installHard gate — no desktop until success
Selected blocking appsExplicit list that must succeed before release
Show error when time exceeds (timeout)Default 60 min — raise for big app sets/slow links
Allow reset on failureUser can wipe & retry
Allow use of device on failureContinue to desktop if non-blocking items fail
Block until required apps installed if assignedChoose "all" vs a chosen subset
Allow log collection on failureUser can export diagnostics
Custom messagesBranded text at each phase
Reference
What Counts, Timeouts & Troubleshooting
ESP tracks only Required-assigned apps/policies that target the device/user in scope — Available apps are ignored. In the device phase it can only track device-targeted items (user isn't known yet), which is why heavy user-targeted apps belong in the account phase or pre-provisioning.
PitfallFix
Too many/large blocking apps → timeoutKeep blocking set minimal; raise timeout; use pre-provisioning
Wrong detection rule → waits foreverFix the app's detection method (it already installed)
User-targeted app tracked in device phaseAssign to devices, or move to account phase
Win32 app depends on another → orderModel dependencies so prerequisites finish first
Best practice: block only what a user truly needs on day one (security agent, VPN, core LOB app); set a realistic timeout; and front-load device-targeted apps via pre-provisioning so the end-user wait is minutes, not an hour. Logs: Event Viewer → DeviceManagement-Enterprise-Diagnostics-Provider and the Autopilot diagnostics page.
🔗 Co-management & Cloud Attach Hybrid ▶
Concept
ConfigMgr and Intune, on the Same Device
Co-management lets a Windows device be managed by both ConfigMgr and Intune at once. You migrate control gradually by moving workloads from ConfigMgr to Intune — one slider at a time — so there's no risky big-bang cutover.
Workload sliderWhen moved to Intune…
Compliance policiesIntune evaluates device health
Device configurationIntune profiles apply settings
Windows Update policiesWUfB (Windows Update for Business) rings drive patching
Endpoint ProtectionIntune manages Defender/ASR
Resource access / Office / Client appsIntune delivers profiles & apps
Each slider can point to Pilot (a chosen collection) or All — so you test on a ring before going wide.
Reference
Cloud Attach, Tenant Attach & the CMG (Cloud Management Gateway)
FeatureWhat it gives you
Tenant attachSurface ConfigMgr devices in the Intune admin center; run actions/scripts from the cloud (low effort, no client change)
Co-managementFull dual management + workload migration (client must be Entra-joined/registered + enrolled)
Cloud Management Gateway (CMG)Manage internet-based ConfigMgr clients through Azure — no VPN (Virtual Private Network), no inbound firewall
Cloud DP (in CMG)Serve content to remote clients from Azure
Recommended journey: start with tenant attach (fast win) → enable co-management → shift workloads to Intune ring-by-ring → new devices go cloud-native via Autopilot, retiring ConfigMgr for those. The CMG is what makes ConfigMgr work for a remote/hybrid workforce in the meantime.
🛂 Conditional Access & Device Compliance Zero Trust ▶
Concept
Tie Access to Device Health — the Zero-Trust Loop
The payoff of managing endpoints is being able to say "only healthy, managed devices reach corporate data." Conditional Access (Entra) is the policy engine; Intune compliance is the health signal it consumes. 
# The loop, end to end
Intune compliance policy  ──▶  device evaluated (encryption? Defender? min OS?)
        │                              │ writes result to…
        ▼                              ▼
Entra device object (compliant: true/false)
        │
        ▼
Conditional Access reads it  ──▶  Grant (compliant OR Entra-joined) / Block / require MFA
Reference
Building a CA Policy
A CA policy is if [assignments] then [controls]. Assignments = who + what they're accessing + conditions; controls = grant/block requirements.
PartExamples
Users/groupsAll users, exclude break-glass admins
Target resourcesOffice 365, a specific app, all cloud apps
ConditionsDevice platform, location, client app, sign-in risk (P2)
Grant controlsRequire MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), require compliant device, require Entra hybrid join, require app protection policy
Session controlsApp-enforced restrictions, sign-in frequency
Always keep a break-glass account excluded from CA (a CA misconfig can lock everyone — including you — out). Use report-only mode to preview impact before enforcing. Filters for devices let you scope by attributes (e.g. exclude kiosks). This is the concrete implementation of Zero Trust for endpoints.
🧰 Troubleshooting Toolkit & Log Reference Ops ▶
Reference
Where to Look When Enrollment/Policy Breaks
Most endpoint issues are diagnosable locally. These are the go-to commands, log paths, and Event Viewer channels for Intune/Autopilot/ESP. 
# Device identity / SSO / enrollment URLs
dsregcmd /status

# Force an Intune (MDM) policy sync from the device
# Settings ▸ Accounts ▸ Access work or school ▸ Info ▸ Sync, or:
Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName PushLaunch | Start-ScheduledTask

# Collect full MDM diagnostics into a CAB / folder
MdmDiagnosticsTool.exe -area "Autopilot;DeviceProvisioning;DeviceEnrollment" -cab C:\Temp\mdm.cab
SourceUse
Event Viewer → Apps & Services → Microsoft → Windows → DeviceManagement-Enterprise-Diagnostics-ProviderThe Intune/MDM log — enrollment, policy, app results
Registry HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\ProvisioningAutopilot profile & ESP (Enrollment Status Page) state
%ProgramData%\Microsoft\IntuneManagementExtension\LogsWin32 app & PowerShell-script (IME) logs
ConfigMgr C:\Windows\CCM\Logs + CMTraceCo-managed/ConfigMgr client
Intune admin center → Troubleshooting + ReportsPer-user/device view, policy & app status, device diagnostics upload
Common errors: 0x80180018 (MDM enrollment not allowed / licensing), 0x801c03ea (device cap / TPM), 80070774 (name resolution). First moves: confirm licensing, check dsregcmd /status, force a sync, then read the IME logs for Win32 app failures.
📖 Glossary — Acronyms, Logs & Task-Sequence Variables Reference ▶
Reference
Acronyms & Components You'll Keep Meeting
The alphabet soup of Microsoft endpoint management, decoded — the pieces that show up constantly in ConfigMgr/Intune/Autopilot work.
TermMeaning
WMIWindows Management Instrumentation — the local management data layer. ConfigMgr's console talks to the site through the SMS (Systems Management Server) Provider over WMI; the client stores state & inventory in the root\ccm and root\cimv2 namespaces (query with wbemtest / Get-CimInstance)
OSDOperating System Deployment — ConfigMgr's imaging feature: build & capture, then deploy Windows via a task sequence (WinPE boot image → apply WIM → drivers → join → apps)
CCMThe Configuration Manager client. Lives in C:\Windows\CCM, runs as the CcmExec service, WMI namespace root\ccm, cache at C:\Windows\ccmcache
MDMMobile Device Management — the cloud management channel (Intune) using the OMA-DM (Open Mobile Alliance Device Management) protocol over HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure); the modern alternative to the ConfigMgr agent
HKCUHKEY_CURRENT_USER — the registry hive for the signed-in user's settings (vs HKLM = machine-wide). Per-user policy, ADMX (Administrative Template) user settings, and app config live here
dsregcmdBuilt-in Windows tool for device registration state. dsregcmd /status shows AzureAdJoined, DomainJoined, the PRT (Primary Refresh Token), and MDM enrollment URLs (Uniform Resource Locator) — the first check for join/SSO/enrollment issues
Reference
Key Log Files (open with CMTrace)
ConfigMgr troubleshooting is log reading. Client logs live in C:\Windows\CCM\Logs; during OSD they start in X:\Windows\Temp\SMSTSLog (WinPE) and move to C:\_SMSTaskSequence\Logs then C:\Windows\CCM\Logs.
LogTells you
smsts.logThe task sequence engine — every OSD step, variable, and failure. The single most important OSD log
CAS.logContent Access Service — how the client locates content and whether it's already in the cache (cache hits/misses, requesting a DP list)
ContentTransferManager.logSchedules and tracks the actual content download jobs (via BITS or SMB) from a distribution point
DataTransferService.logThe BITS (Background Intelligent Transfer Service) transfer layer used for policy and content downloads — TLS/proxy/BITS errors surface here
Content-download triage order: CAS.log (is it cached / which DPs?) → ContentTransferManager.log (did a job start?) → DataTransferService.log (did BITS actually move the bytes?). During OSD, cross-reference all of it against smsts.log.
Reference
OSD Task-Sequence Variables Worth Knowing
Task-sequence variables tune how OSD downloads, caches, and stores content. Set them on a collection, in the deployment, or with a Set Task Sequence Variable step. TRUE/FALSE values are strings.
VariableWhat it does
SMSTSPreserveContentKeeps the TS's downloaded content in the ConfigMgr client cache (ccmcache) after the sequence finishes, instead of purging it — handy when the same content is needed again soon (TRUE)
SMSTSPersistContentPersists content in the task-sequence working cache (_SMSTaskSequence) for the duration of the sequence, so it survives reboots between steps
SMSTSDownloadRetryCountHow many times the client retries a failed content download (default 2) — raise it on flaky/slow links
SMSTSDownloadRetryDelaySeconds to wait between download retries (default 15) — pair with the count above for unreliable networks
SMSTSLocalDataDriveChooses the drive where the TS stores its temp working files & logs (the _SMSTaskSequence folder) — set it before content downloads to avoid X:\ (RAM) space issues in WinPE (Windows Preinstallation Environment)
SMSTSPeerDownloadEnables/allows the TS to pull content from peers (Windows PE Peer Cache / peer sources) rather than a DP — TRUE/FALSE
SMSTSDownloadProgramSpecifies an Alternate Content Provider (ACP) — a custom download program (e.g. third-party peer-to-peer like Nomad/Adaptiva) used instead of the built-in downloader
Common combos: on slow branch links, raise SMSTSDownloadRetryCount/Delay, set SMSTSLocalDataDrive=C early, and enable SMSTSPeerDownload so peers share content. Use SMSTSPreserveContent when a later phase (or a re-image retry) reuses the same packages. Verify all of it in smsts.log.
🩹 MECM (Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager) Client Health — Install, Repair & the Cycles MECM • Troubleshooting ▶
First Principles
A Silent Client Is Not the Same as a Broken Deployment
Before blaming a deployment, prove the client is alive: it is installed, it found a management point, it is downloading policy, and it is sending state back. Those four checks answer the majority of "the software never arrived" tickets, and each one has its own log.
CheckHowLog
Is the client installed and running?Get-Service CcmExec; Control Panel ▸ Configuration Managerccmsetup.log, CcmExec.log
Did it get a site code and a management point?Control Panel applet ▸ General tabLocationServices.log, ClientLocation.log
Is it receiving policy?Trigger a machine policy cycle and watchPolicyAgent.log, PolicyEvaluator.log
Is it reporting back?Compare the console's last-active timeStateMessage.log, InventoryAgent.log
 
# Trigger client actions from PowerShell — same as the Actions tab, scriptable
function Invoke-CMAction ($Id) {
  Invoke-CimMethod -Namespace root\ccm -ClassName SMS_Client `
    -MethodName TriggerSchedule -Arguments @{ sScheduleID = $Id }
}

Invoke-CMAction '{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000021}'   # Machine Policy Retrieval
Invoke-CMAction '{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000022}'   # Machine Policy Evaluation
Invoke-CMAction '{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001}'   # Hardware Inventory
Invoke-CMAction '{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000113}'   # Software Updates Scan
Invoke-CMAction '{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000121}'   # Application Deployment Evaluation
Invoke-CMAction '{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000108}'   # Software Update Deployment Evaluation

# Which site and management point does this client think it belongs to?
Get-CimInstance -Namespace root\ccm -ClassName SMS_Authority |
  Select-Object Name, CurrentManagementPoint
Repair Ladder
Escalate Slowly — Reinstalling Is Not Step One
StepDoWhen it helps
1Run the client actions and read the logsPolicy is simply stale
2ccmrepair.exe or the console's Client RepairAgent files or registrations are damaged
3Check WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation): winmgmt /verifyrepositoryInventory and policy both fail, applet is missing tabs
4Reinstall: ccmsetup.exe /uninstall, reboot, then reinstallRepair didn't take; clears a wedged install
5winmgmt /salvagerepository — last resortOnly when the repository is genuinely corrupt; it can break other agents
 
# A clean reinstall pointed at a specific MP and site
ccmsetup.exe /mp:mp01.contoso.com /forceinstall SMSSITECODE=P01 /logon

# ccmsetup writes to its own folder, NOT C:\Windows\CCM\Logs
#   C:\Windows\ccmsetup\Logs\ccmsetup.log

# Common ccmsetup exit codes
#   0        success
#   7        reboot required to finish
#   1603     generic MSI failure — read the MSI log beside it
#   0x87d00227  client could not download source from the MP (boundary/firewall/PKI)
The boundary trap: a client on an IP (Internet Protocol) with no boundary in a boundary group has no site assignment and no content source. It will look installed, log cheerfully in CcmExec.log, and never do anything useful. LocationServices.log is where that shows up.
📦 MECM (Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager) Deployment & Content Troubleshooting MECM • Troubleshooting ▶
Flow
Follow the Package Server-Side, Then Client-Side
An application reaches a device through a fixed chain: it is distributed to a distribution point, advertised in policy, located by the client, downloaded, then enforced. Find the first link that failed and stop reading logs from the wrong end.
StageWhereLog
Content sent to the DPSite serverdistmgr.log then PkgXferMgr.log
Content verified on the DPDistribution pointsmsdpmon.log, smsdpprov.log
Policy reaches the clientClientPolicyAgent.log, AppIntentEval.log
Client finds a sourceClientCAS.log — cached? which DP?
Bytes actually moveClientContentTransferManager.log, DataTransferService.log
Install runsClientAppEnforce.log (apps), execmgr.log (packages)
Result detectedClientAppDiscovery.log — the detection method's verdict
The single most common false failure: the installer ran fine, but the detection method looks for the wrong file, version or registry key — so MECM reports failure and retries forever. AppEnforce.log shows exit code 0 while AppDiscovery.log says "not detected". That combination always means the detection rule, never the installer.
Error Reference
Codes You Will See Weekly
CodeMeansFirst move
