0x87D00324Installed successfully but not detectedFix the detection method — check it by hand on the device
0x87D00269No content available at any distribution pointConfirm distribution finished; check boundary groups
0x80091007Content hash mismatchRedistribute the package; validate content on the DP
0x87D01106The install command line failedRun it manually as SYSTEM with PsExec to see the real error
1603Generic MSI (Microsoft Installer) failureRead the MSI verbose log; usually a prerequisite or a locked file
1618Another installation is already in progressWait and retry; check for a stuck msiexec
0x80070005Access deniedNetwork access account, share permissions, or running as the wrong context
Software Updates
When Patching Stops, Suspect WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) First
Software updates run on the software update point, which is WSUS wearing a MECM hat. Scan failures are almost always the WSUS side: a bloated database, an exhausted app pool, or a proxy in the way.
LogAnswers
wsyncmgr.logDid the catalogue sync from Microsoft, and what failed
WCM.log / WSUSCtrl.logIs MECM able to configure and reach WSUS at all
ruleengine.logAutomatic deployment rule runs
ScanAgent.logDid the client decide to scan, and against which SUP (Software Update Point)
WUAHandler.logWhat the Windows Update agent reported back
UpdatesDeployment.logDeployment enforcement, deadlines and reboots
0x80244010 — "exceeded max server round trips" — is the classic sign of an unmaintained WSUS: decline superseded updates and run the cleanup so the client can finish enumerating. 0x80072ee2 is a timeout, usually a proxy or firewall. And if the WSUS app pool keeps recycling, raise its private memory limit (0 = unlimited) before touching anything else.
🧬 MECM (Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager) OSD (Operating System Deployment) — Task Sequence Failure Triage MECM • Troubleshooting ▶
Method
Find smsts.log, Then Read Backwards
Every task sequence failure is in smsts.log. The hard part is knowing where it lives at the moment it failed — the file moves as the sequence progresses. Open it in CMTrace, jump to the end, and scroll up to the first red line: the error you see reported is usually the consequence, not the cause.
Phasesmsts.log lives at
In WinPE (Windows Preinstallation Environment), before the disk is formattedX:\Windows\Temp\SMSTSLog\smsts.log
In WinPE, after formattingX:\SMSTSLog\smsts.log then C:\_SMSTaskSequence\Logs
In the full OS (Operating System), before the client is installedC:\_SMSTaskSequence\Logs\SMSTSLog
In the full OS, client installedC:\Windows\CCM\Logs\SMSTSLog
After the sequence endsC:\Windows\CCM\Logs\smsts.log
 
# In WinPE: F8 needs to be enabled on the boot image (Enable command support)
# Keep the window open on failure so the log survives the reboot:
#   set the task sequence variable  SMSTSPostAction = cmd.exe /c pause
#   or copy the log out before it goes:
copy X:\Windows\Temp\SMSTSLog\smsts.log \\fileserver\logs\%COMPUTERNAME%-smsts.log

# Check the network stack from WinPE before blaming the sequence
ipconfig /all
ping mp01.contoso.com
net use \\dp01\SMSPKGD$ /user:CONTOSO\svc-osd
Error Reference
The Usual Suspects
CodeUsually meansCheck
0x80070002File not found — content missing or not distributedPackage distributed to a DP in this boundary group?
0x80070070Disk fullPartition size, or cache too small for the content
0x80072EE7Name resolution failed in WinPEDNS (Domain Name System) from PE, and whether the MP name resolves at all
0x80004005Generic failure — meaningless on its ownIgnore the code, read the lines above it
0x80220014Bad or missing task sequence variableA collection variable or Set Variable step that never ran
0x87D00267No task sequence deployment for this machineCollection membership, and whether the deployment is available to unknown computers
Missing NIC (Network Interface Card) or storage driverPE loads, then nothing worksDriver package injected into the boot image for the right architecture
Triage order that saves the most time: 1. Does the machine have a deployment at all — is it in the collection? 2. Can WinPE reach the network and resolve the MP? 3. Is the content on a DP this boundary group can reach? 4. Did a specific step fail, or did the sequence never start? Only then start reading step-level errors.
🏢 MECM (Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager) Site Health & Server Log Map MECM • Troubleshooting ▶
Reference
Which Server Log Owns Which Symptom
Client logs live in C:\Windows\CCM\Logs; site server logs live in <install>\Logs (commonly D:\Program Files\Microsoft Configuration Manager\Logs). When a symptom is fleet-wide rather than per-device, the answer is on the server.
SymptomLogComponent
Content stuck distributing to a DPdistmgr.log, PkgXferMgr.logDistribution Manager
Collections not updating membershipcolleval.logCollection Evaluator
Deployment status never changesstatesys.log, MP_StatusManagerState System
Inventory not arrivingdataldr.log, MP_HinvEndpointInventory Data Loader
Discovery not finding machinesadsysdis.log, ddm.logAD (Active Directory) System Discovery
Clients can't get policyMP_GetPolicy.log, MP_Location.logManagement Point
Console errors or slownessSMSProv.logSMS (Systems Management Server) Provider (WMI layer)
Site-to-site replication behindsender.log, despool.log, rcmctrl.logReplication
Site components in a warning statesitecomp.log, hman.logSite Component Manager
Before diving in, check Monitoring ▸ System Status ▸ Component Status and Site Status — MECM usually tells you which component is unhappy, which narrows the log list to one.
Real Time
CMPivot (Configuration Manager Pivot) — Ask the Fleet Instead of Waiting for Inventory
Hardware inventory is a scheduled snapshot; CMPivot queries live clients now, in a KQL-like syntax. It is the fastest way to answer "how many machines actually have this" during an incident — and it doubles as a hunting tool alongside the Blue Team domain. 
// Which machines still have the vulnerable version installed?
InstalledSoftware
| where ProductName contains 'Contoso Agent'
| summarize count() by ProductVersion

// Is the file present, and when was it last written?
File('C:\\Program Files\\Contoso\\agent.exe')
| project Device, Version, LastWriteTime

// Disk pressure across the fleet, worst first
LogicalDisk
| where DeviceID == 'C:'
| project Device, FreeGB = FreeSpace / 1024
| order by FreeGB asc
Two limits to keep in mind: CMPivot only reaches clients that are online and healthy — the broken ones you most want to see are exactly the ones that will not answer — and results are capped, so scope the query to a collection rather than the whole estate.
⚙️ Configuration Profiles — Settings Catalog, Templates & Custom Intune • Policy ▶
Choosing
Three Ways to Say the Same Thing, With Different Consequences
Every configuration profile ends up writing to a CSP (Configuration Service Provider) on the device. What differs is how you get there — and, more importantly, what you can see afterwards. Pick on reporting, not on which blade you found first.
Settings catalogTemplateCustom (OMA-URI)
What it is A searchable picker over the CSP surface A curated group of related settings The raw CSP path, typed by hand
Coverage Broad and growing; most new settings land here first Fixed — what the template author included Anything the device supports
Discoverability Search by name; the setting explains itself Grouped sensibly, but you must know the template None — you need the CSP documentation open
Reporting Per setting, per device Per setting, per device Profile-level only, with a raw error code
Fails like Named setting shows Error or Conflict Named setting shows Error or Conflict "Remediation failed" and a hex code, for the whole profile
Default to the settings catalog. Reach for a template when it groups something fiddly you would otherwise assemble by hand, and reach for custom OMA-URI (Open Mobile Alliance Uniform Resource Identifier) only when the setting genuinely is not surfaced anywhere else.
The trap: a custom OMA-URI profile reports at the profile level, not the setting level. One bad URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) in a profile of twenty makes the whole profile red on every device, and the console will not tell you which line it was. Keep custom profiles small and single-purpose — one setting per profile is not paranoid here, it is how you stay able to debug.
🥊 Policy Conflicts — Proving Which One Won Intune • Policy ▶
Concept
Nobody Wins a Conflict
The instinct from Group Policy is that the last writer, or the most restrictive value, wins. That is not how Intune configuration profiles behave. When two profiles set the same setting to different values, the usual outcome is a Conflict state and the setting is not applied at all — the device keeps whatever it had. A few CSP (Configuration Service Provider) areas do resolve to the more restrictive value, but relying on any tie-break is how you end up with a fleet that is neither configuration.
SituationWhat actually happens
Two Intune profiles, same setting, different valuesConflict — the setting is not applied
Two Intune profiles, same setting, same valueApplies cleanly; no conflict
Intune profile vs security baselineStill a conflict — a baseline is just another profile
Intune vs GPO (Group Policy Object) on a co-managed deviceDepends on the workload slider; whichever authority owns it wins
User-targeted vs device-targetedBoth apply to their own scope; a conflict only if the CSP is the same node
The fix is always the same: find the duplicate and delete one. There is no correct way to have two profiles arguing about one setting.
Diagnosis
Three Places to Look, In Order
#WhereWhat it tells you
1 Intune ▸ Devices ▸ the device ▸ Device configuration Per-profile state; drill into a profile for per-setting status including Conflict, and the name of the other policy involved
2 On the device — MDM (Mobile Device Management) diagnostics The full picture when the console disagrees with reality
3 Registry under PolicyManager The value the device actually holds right now, per area 
# Collect everything the MDM stack knows, into a folder you can read
MdmDiagnosticsTool.exe -area "DeviceEnrollment;DeviceProvisioning;Autopilot" -zip C:\Temp\mdm.zip

# The applied value, per policy area — this is the ground truth
Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\PolicyManager\current\device' |
  Select-Object -ExpandProperty PSChildName

# What a specific area currently holds (example: BitLocker)
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\PolicyManager\current\device\BitLocker'

# Which policies the device has been sent at all
Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Provisioning\NodeCache\CSP\Device\MS DM Server\Nodes'
Before you dig: confirm the device has actually checked in since you changed anything. Half of all "the policy is not applying" reports are a device that last synced yesterday. Force it from Settings ▸ Accounts ▸ Access work or school ▸ Info ▸ Sync, and give it a few minutes.
🛡️ Security Baselines Without Breaking the Fleet Intune • Policy ▶
Concept
A Baseline Is an Opinion, Not a Law
A security baseline is a large pre-built configuration profile carrying Microsoft's recommended values. It is genuinely useful and it is genuinely opinionated — it will turn things on that your users depend on being off. Treat it as a starting proposal to be reviewed setting by setting, not as a switch to flip.
OptionReach for it when
Security baselineYou want a defensible starting posture fast, and you can afford to review a few hundred settings
Settings catalog policyYou know the specific controls you need; you want per-setting reporting and no surprises
Baseline + targeted overridesTempting, and the main source of conflicts — every override is a future conflict report
CIS (Center for Internet Security) or STIG-derived policyAn external standard is the requirement; import it as a settings-catalog policy so it reports cleanly
Baselines are versioned. A new version does not apply itself — you review the changes and move the assignment to it. A baseline left on an old version quietly stops being the thing you think you deployed.
Rollout
Four Rings, and What to Hold Back on Day One
RingWhoSoakWhat you are watching for
0 — LabYour own devicesDaysDoes anything refuse to apply at all
1 — ITThe team, ~10 devices1 weekAdmin tooling, remote access, drivers
2 — PilotVolunteers across departments, ~5%2 weeksLine-of-business apps, printing, VPN (Virtual Private Network), peripherals
3 — BroadEveryone else—Ticket volume in the first 48 hours
Hold these back until ring 2 at the earliest: anything touching removable media, anything that blocks script execution, credential-delegation and remote-assistance restrictions, and the firewall profile. Each one is individually reasonable and each one has locked a fleet out of something it needed.
The rollback that actually works: remove the assignment, not the policy. Deleting a profile leaves settings behind on devices in many cases; unassigning triggers the tattoo-removal path where the CSP (Configuration Service Provider) supports it. Know before you deploy which of your settings will revert and which will stick.
📋 Administrative Templates & ADMX-Backed Policy Intune • Policy ▶
Reference
Group Policy's Vocabulary, Delivered Over MDM (Mobile Device Management)
Administrative Templates in Intune are ADMX-backed CSPs (Configuration Service Provider): the same setting names and the same explanatory text you know from the Group Policy editor, delivered through the MDM channel instead of SYSVOL (System Volume). It is a subset — a large one, but the gaps are what generate migration tickets.
Coming from GPO (Group Policy Object)In Intune
Most Windows, Office and Edge policiesPresent as Administrative Templates, same names
Third-party ADMX (Chrome, Adobe, your own)Supported by importing the .admx and its .adml, then referencing it in a custom profile
Preferences — drive maps, shortcuts, registry itemsNo equivalent; use a script or a remediation instead
Startup and logon scriptsUse platform scripts or the Intune Management Extension
Item-level targetingApproximated with filters and group assignment, not per-item
Loopback processingNo equivalent; rethink as device-scoped policy
The trap: Administrative Templates and the settings catalog are two different surfaces onto overlapping settings. A setting present in one is not guaranteed to be in the other, and configuring the same thing in both is a conflict waiting to happen. Pick one surface per setting and write down which.
Migration order that works: export your GPOs, run them through Group Policy analytics to see what has a direct MDM equivalent, port those first, and keep a deliberate list of the leftovers. The leftovers are the project — everything else is data entry.
🎯 Assignment Strategy — Users, Devices, Filters & Exclusions Intune • Policy ▶
Concept
Targeting Is Where Policy Goes Wrong
Most "the policy is assigned but not applying" tickets are not policy problems at all — they are targeting problems. Three rules cover nearly all of them.
RuleConsequence
Exclusion always beats inclusion A user in both an included and an excluded group is excluded. Nested groups count. This is the single most common cause.
Scope has to match the setting A device-scoped CSP (Configuration Service Provider) assigned to a user group applies to that user's devices; a user-scoped setting assigned to a device group may never apply at all.
A device with no primary user is invisible to user targeting Kiosks, shared and Autopilot pre-provisioned devices need device-group assignment.
Choosing
Groups, Filters, or Both
ToolReach for it whenCost
Static group Membership is a deliberate decision — pilot rings, exceptions Someone has to maintain it
Dynamic group Membership follows an attribute you trust — department, device type Rule evaluation is not instant; a new device is not in it immediately
Filter Narrowing one assignment by device property — OS (Operating System) version, ownership, model Evaluated at assignment time; no group sprawl, but invisible unless you open the assignment
All Users / All Devices Genuinely universal policy, plus a filter to narrow it Nothing to maintain, and nothing to stop it hitting a device you forgot about
The pattern worth standardising on: assign broadly to All Devices with a filter that expresses the real condition, and keep static groups only for exclusions and pilot rings. Group-per-policy is what produces a tenant with four hundred groups nobody can name.
Corporate-owned models change the answer: a COPE (Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled) device has a real primary user and user targeting works; a COBO (Corporate-Owned, Business Only) or kiosk device does not, and every policy for it must be device-assigned. Decide the ownership model before you design the group structure, not after.
📦 Win32 App Packaging — .intunewin End to End Intune • Apps ▶
Flow
Seven Steps, and Only One of Them Is the Installer
A Win32 app is a folder of source files wrapped into a single .intunewin container, uploaded once, then described to Intune well enough that it can decide — per device, forever — whether the app is present. Most packaging failures are in the describing, not the installing.
#StepWhere it goes wrong
1Stage a clean source folderExtra files bloat the package; missing dependencies fail only on clean devices
2Wrap with the content prep toolPointing at the wrong setup file — the wrapper records it inside the container
3Install commandNot silent; an installer that shows UI (User Interface) never completes under SYSTEM
4Uninstall commandLeft as a guess, then discovered during an emergency removal
5Detection ruleThe single biggest source of false failures — see the trap below
6RequirementsArchitecture and OS (Operating System) minimums too broad, so it attempts on devices it cannot work on
7Dependencies and supersedenceEvaluated per device at assignment; a cycle between two apps stalls both silently
 
# Wrap: -c source folder, -s the setup file inside it, -o output folder
IntuneWinAppUtil.exe -c C:\Pkg\ContosoAgent\Source -s ContosoAgent.msi -o C:\Pkg\Out

# Install / uninstall commands as Intune will run them (SYSTEM, no desktop)
msiexec /i "ContosoAgent.msi" /qn /norestart
msiexec /x "{PRODUCT-GUID-HERE}" /qn /norestart

# A wrapper script gives you logging and an exit code you control
powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\Install.ps1

# Test the exact command as SYSTEM before blaming Intune
PsExec64.exe -s -i cmd.exe
Supersedence is not an upgrade path by itself. It tells Intune the new app replaces the old one, optionally uninstalling it first. If the new installer already upgrades in place, adding an uninstall step removes user data on the way through. Decide which of the two is doing the upgrade, and only one of them.
👤 Install Contexts — System vs User Intune • Apps ▶
Comparison
Same Package, Two Completely Different Outcomes
Install context decides which account runs the installer, where it may write, and crucially where the detection rule looks. Getting it wrong produces an app that installs successfully and reports as failed, or one that reports success while being present for exactly one person.
System contextUser context
Runs asSYSTEM, no desktop, no user profileThe signed-in user, with their token
Installs forAll users of the deviceThat user only
Writes toProgram Files, HKLMAppData, HKCU
Detection looks inHKLM and machine pathsHKCU and the user's profile — per user
Needs a logged-in userNo — installs during provisioningYes — nothing happens until someone signs in
Good forAgents, drivers, anything sharedPer-user tools, anything that refuses to install machine-wide
The trap: a user-context app assigned to a device group installs for whoever happens to sign in first, and then reports success for the device. Every subsequent user sees a machine where the console says the app is installed and the Start menu disagrees. If the app must exist for everyone, it has to be system context — reassigning it later does not retroactively fix the devices.
Quick test: if the installer works from an elevated PsExec -s shell with no desktop, it will work in system context. If it needs a profile, a mapped drive or a UI (User Interface), it will not — and no amount of Intune configuration changes that.
🚚 Store, LOB (Line of Business) & Enterprise App Catalog Apps Intune • Apps ▶
Choosing
Five Vehicles, and Who Owns the Updates
The decisive question is not "how do I deploy this" — all five work. It is who updates it, and can you stop them.
VehicleUpdates owned byCan you pin a versionReach for it when
Win32 (.intunewin)YouYes You need control: a specific version, a custom install, a wrapper script
Microsoft Store appThe storeNo A common app where always-current is what you want anyway
Enterprise App CatalogMicrosoft packages it, you approveVersion-by-version Common third-party apps you would otherwise repackage every month
Line-of-business (MSI)YouYes A plain MSI (Microsoft Installer) with no wrapper needed — simpler than Win32, and less capable
Web linkNobody — it is a shortcutn/a A web app you want on the Start menu and in Company Portal
Store apps update themselves. That is usually a feature and occasionally an incident — when a vendor ships a breaking release to your whole fleet on a Tuesday. If a version must be pinned for a compliance or compatibility reason, Win32 is the only honest answer.
Required vs Available matters more than people expect: Required installs without asking; Available puts it in Company Portal for the user to choose. Making everything required is how you end up pushing 4 GB of design software to laptops that will never open it.
🧴 App Protection Policies — MAM (Mobile Application Management) Without Enrolment Intune • Apps ▶
Reference
Protecting the Data on a Device You Do Not Own
App protection policies apply controls to the app and its data rather than to the device. That is what makes BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) workable: the user keeps their phone unmanaged, and company data inside supported apps still obeys your rules.
ControlWhat it does
Data transferRestricts save-as, copy/paste and open-in to other policy-managed apps
EncryptionEncrypts company data at rest inside the app's sandbox
Access requirementsPIN or biometric on the app itself, independent of the device lock
Conditional launchBlocks or wipes on jailbreak, minimum OS (Operating System), minimum app version, offline grace period
Selective wipeRemoves company data from the app and leaves everything personal alone
The boundary is the app, and only the app. Protection applies to apps that are policy-aware. A document opened in an unmanaged PDF (Portable Document Format) viewer, forwarded from an unmanaged mail client, or synced by a personal cloud client has left the boundary — and the policy has no view of it. The controls are real, but they are a fence around a set of apps, not around the data itself.
Pair it with Conditional Access. App protection decides what happens to data once the app has it; Conditional Access decides whether the app gets it at all. Requiring an approved client app plus an app protection policy is the combination that makes unenrolled BYOD defensible.
🔎 Application Troubleshooting — Reading the IME (Intune Management Extension) Log Intune • Apps ▶
Artifact Map
Where the Answer Lives
Win32 apps and PowerShell scripts are delivered by the Intune Management Extension, which keeps its own logs on the device. Read them in this order; the console is a summary of what these files already said.
LogAnswers
IntuneManagementExtension.logDid the app arrive, what did detection decide, what was the exit code
AgentExecutor.logWhat the PowerShell script actually did, and its output
ClientHealth.logWhether the extension itself is healthy and checking in
Win32 app cacheWhether content downloaded at all — under C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Intune Management Extension\Content
Intune ▸ Apps ▸ the app ▸ Device install statusThe fleet view, and the error code to search for
 
# The logs live here — open with CMTrace, they are CMTrace-formatted
C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\IntuneManagementExtension\Logs\

# Follow an install in near real time
Get-Content 'C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\IntuneManagementExtension\Logs\IntuneManagementExtension.log' -Tail 50 -Wait

# Force the extension to re-check for app assignments
Restart-Service IntuneManagementExtension
Error Reference
The Codes That Come Up Weekly
CodeMeansFirst move
0x87D00324Installed, but the detection rule says it is not thereRun the detection check by hand on the device — the installer is fine
0x87D00325Detection found it when it should not haveUsually a leftover key or file from a previous version
0x87D300Content download failedProxy, TLS (Transport Layer Security) inspection, or the device cannot reach the CDN (Content Delivery Network)
1603Generic MSI (Microsoft Installer) failureRead the MSI verbose log; usually a prerequisite or a file in use
1618Another install is already runningWait; check for a stuck msiexec or a competing deployment
3010Success, reboot requiredNot a failure — map it as a soft-reboot return code in the app
The one worth memorising, again: exit code 0 in the log with "not detected" in the console is always the detection rule and never the installer. It is the same failure as its MECM (Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager) counterpart — see MECM Deployment & Content Troubleshooting in this domain, which describes the identical trap in the other console.
🔄 Windows Update for Business — Rings, Deferrals & Deadlines Intune • Servicing ▶
Flow
Four Rings, and the Setting Everyone Forgets
Update rings are a deferral policy, not a deployment. Windows fetches updates itself; the ring decides how long it waits, when it stops waiting, and how much warning the user gets before a reboot happens anyway.
RingWhoQuality deferralDeadlineGrace
0 — CanaryIT, a handful of devices0 days2 days1 day
1 — EarlyVolunteers, ~5%2 days3 days2 days
2 — BroadMost of the fleet5 days5 days2 days
3 — CriticalExecutives, clinical, production floor9 days7 days3 days
The grace period is the whole user experience. A deadline with no grace period reboots someone mid-meeting, and you will hear about it for a year. The deadline says "you can no longer defer"; the grace period says "and you have this long to pick your moment". Set both, always.
Deferral and deadline are measured from different points: deferral counts from the day the update was published, deadline counts from the day it became applicable to that device. A machine that was off for a fortnight starts its deadline clock when it comes back, not retroactively — which is why "everyone is patched by day 7" is a claim about machines that were switched on.
🧩 Feature vs Quality vs Driver Updates Intune • Servicing ▶
Comparison
Three Pipelines, Three Risk Profiles, Three Sets of Controls
FeatureQualityDriver
What it isA new Windows versionMonthly cumulative fixesHardware and firmware from vendors
CadenceAnnualSecond Tuesday, plus out-of-bandContinuous, vendor-driven
RiskHigh — app compatibilityModerate — regressions happenUnderrated — a bad driver is a brick
Rollback10 days by defaultUninstall the LCU (Latest Cumulative Update), not the SSU (Servicing Stack Update)Roll back in Device Manager, or block the update
Controlled byTarget version, deferralDeferral, deadline, pauseSeparate driver policy — or Autopatch
They are independent. Pausing quality updates does not pause drivers, and a feature-update deferral says nothing about either. The commonest version of this mistake is an incident where someone "paused updates" and a driver shipped anyway.
SSU and LCU travel together and do not come apart. Since they were combined into one package, the servicing stack update cannot be uninstalled — only the cumulative part can. "We will just roll it back" is a plan that works for the LCU and not for the SSU underneath it.
🤖 Windows Autopatch — What It Takes Over Intune • Servicing ▶
Choosing
Handing the Rings to Microsoft
Autopatch runs the update rings for you: it builds the ring population, progresses deployments, watches the signals, and halts a rollout that is going wrong. The trade is real and worth stating plainly — you gain a service that does the babysitting, and you lose your rings as the source of truth.
ConcernAutopatch ownsStill yours
Ring membershipBuilds and balances itWhich devices are registered at all
ProgressionAdvances and halts automaticallyDeciding to pause the whole thing
Quality updatesYes—
Feature updatesTarget version and cadenceApp compatibility testing
Drivers & firmwareOptional, per policyVendor-specific exceptions
Third-party appsNoAll of it
ExceptionsLimitedAnything genuinely bespoke
Have the exit path before you enrol. Coming back out means rebuilding rings, deferrals and deadlines by hand — the policies you used to have are not waiting for you. Export the current ring configuration first; it costs ten minutes and it is the difference between a decision and a one-way door.
Good fit: a fleet of reasonably standard devices where update babysitting is eating a person. Poor fit: heavily regulated change windows, machines pinned to a validated OS (Operating System) build, or anywhere "we patch when the plant is down" is a real constraint.
📊 Update Compliance Reporting — Where the Truth Lives Intune • Servicing ▶
Artifact Map
Four Sources, and What Each One Actually Knows
SourceKnowsDoes not know
Intune ▸ Reports ▸ Windows updatesRing assignment and per-device update stateAnything about a device that has not checked in
Windows Update for Business reportsDeployment progress and failure reasons at fleet scaleDevices not sending diagnostic data
The device's own update historyThe ground truth for that one machineEverything else
Defender / vulnerability managementWhether the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) is actually still exploitable hereWhy the patch did not apply
 
# Ground truth on a single device — what is installed, and when
Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 10

# The full update history including failures, which Get-HotFix hides
Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient/Operational' -MaxEvents 40 |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message

# Build number and revision — "patched" is a revision, not a version
Get-ComputerInfo -Property OsName, OsVersion, OsBuildNumber, WindowsVersion
"Not applicable" and "unknown" are not compliant. Most dashboards blur three different states into one green number: patched, not-applicable (the update never targeted this device), and unknown (nobody has heard from it). Report them separately or the figure you give leadership is higher than the truth — and the unknown bucket is exactly where the compromised machine lives.
🚨 Emergency Patching — Advisory to Verified Intune • Servicing ▶
Flow
Six Steps, Starting Before You Touch a Console
#StepThe question it answers
1Triage the advisoryDoes it affect us — the product, the version, the configuration? Is it on CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency)'s exploited list?
2Count the exposureHow many devices, and are any of them internet-facing or high-value?
3Pick the vehicleExpedited quality update, a Win32 app, a remediation script, or a configuration change as a stopgap
4Decide about ringsSkip to broad only if exploitation is active and the patch is low-risk. Otherwise canary first, even now
5Deploy and watchFailure rate in the first hour, and one named person watching it
6VerifyQuery the fleet for the actual build or file version — not the deployment's success percentage
 
# Verification is a query about the device, not about the deployment.
# CMPivot, or the same idea via a proactive remediation:
OperatingSystem
| summarize count() by Version

# Or check the specific patched binary, which survives version ambiguity
File('C:\\Windows\\System32\\example.dll')
| summarize count() by Version
Skipping rings in a real emergency is defensible. Skipping verification never is. A deployment reporting 98% success is a claim about what the agent believes it did. The only statement worth putting in the incident record is a query result showing what the devices actually run.
Write the comms before the deployment, not during. Who is told, what they are told, when the reboot lands, and who they contact if it breaks something. Two paragraphs, drafted while you are calm, saves the hour you will not have later.
Beginner Windows Administration Fundamentals
Core Concept
The Windows Admin Toolkit
Enterprise Windows administration revolves around a handful of tools. Learn these early — they show up in every IT job that involves Windows:

GUI (Graphical User Interface) Tools (MMC Snap-ins):
• dsa.msc — Active Directory Users & Computers (ADUC).
• gpmc.msc — Group Policy Management Console.
• compmgmt.msc — Computer Management (local users, disks, services).
• eventvwr.msc — Event Viewer (logs for everything).
• services.msc — Start/stop/configure Windows services.

Command-line:
• cmd.exe — the classic command prompt (legacy but everywhere).
• powershell.exe / pwsh.exe — the modern admin shell.
• wmic / winrm — remote management from CLI (Command Line Interface).
User Management
Managing Users in Active Directory
Common day-one helpdesk tasks in Active Directory Users & Computers (ADUC):
-- Open ADUC: Win+R → dsa.msc -- Or via PowerShell (if RSAT tools installed): # Create a new AD user New-ADUser ` -Name "Bob Jones" ` -SamAccountName "bjones" ` -UserPrincipalName "bjones@corp.example.com" ` -AccountPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString "TempP@ss1" -AsPlainText -Force) ` -ChangePasswordAtLogon $true ` -Enabled $true ` -Path "OU=Finance,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com" # Unlock a locked-out account Unlock-ADAccount -Identity bjones # Reset a password Set-ADAccountPassword bjones ` -NewPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString "NewP@ss99" -AsPlainText -Force) ` -Reset # Disable an account (departing employee) Disable-ADAccount -Identity bjones # Find all disabled accounts in an OU Search-ADAccount -SearchBase "OU=Finance,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com" ` -AccountDisabled | Select Name, SamAccountName
Group Policy
Group Policy Objects (GPOs) Explained
A GPO is a collection of settings pushed from the domain controller to computers and users automatically. Examples of what GPOs control:

• Password complexity requirements.
• Screen lock after N minutes of inactivity.
• Mapped drives (e.g. H: = home folder on file server).
• Software deployment (install apps on logon).
• Firewall rules, browser settings, USB (Universal Serial Bus) restrictions.

GPOs apply in order: Local → Site → Domain → OU (LSDOU). Later policies win unless "Enforced" is set. Use gpresult /r on a PC to see which GPOs actually applied.

You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — GPOs don't stop a determined user completely, but they raise the barrier and give you an audit trail when something goes wrong.
Remote Access
Remote Desktop & PowerShell Remoting
Two primary ways to manage remote Windows machines:
# ── Remote Desktop (RDP) ── # From Linux: install freerdp2 xfreerdp /v:workstation01.corp.example.com /u:alice /d:CORP # From Windows: mstsc.exe mstsc /v:workstation01.corp.example.com # ── PowerShell Remoting (WinRM) ── # Enable on the target machine (run as admin once): Enable-PSRemoting -Force # Connect to a remote session Enter-PSSession -ComputerName workstation01 -Credential CORPlice # Run a command on multiple machines at once Invoke-Command -ComputerName srv01, srv02, srv03 ` -ScriptBlock { Get-Service -Name Spooler | Select Name, Status } # Copy a file to a remote machine $s = New-PSSession -ComputerName srv01 -Credential CORPlice Copy-Item -Path C:\patch.msi -Destination C:\Temp\ -ToSession $s Remove-PSSession $s
🔐 BitLocker at Scale — Silent Enablement, Key Escrow & Recovery Endpoint • Security ▶
Concept
The Only Question That Matters Is "Can You Get the Key Back"
Encrypting the fleet is easy; a policy does it in an afternoon. The part that ends careers is a device that has gone into recovery and a recovery key that was never escrowed anywhere. At scale, BitLocker is a key-management problem wearing an encryption costume — design the escrow first, then turn on encryption, never the other way round.
PieceWhat it is
TPM (Trusted Platform Module)The chip that seals the key to a known-good boot state; unlocks transparently at boot
Recovery keyThe 48-digit fallback when the TPM refuses — the thing you must have escrowed
Escrow locationEntra ID for cloud-joined devices, AD (Active Directory) for hybrid; MECM (Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager) keeps its own recovery store too
Encryption methodXTS-AES 128 or 256; used space only vs full disk on first encryption
Flow
Silent Enablement, and the Order It Must Happen In
Silent enablement means the user never sees a prompt — the disk encrypts and the key escrows without interaction. It only works if the prerequisites are already true when the policy lands, and the classic failure is a device that reports "encrypted" with a key that reached nowhere.
StepMust be true
1 PrerequisitesTPM present and ready, UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface), Secure Boot on, no third-party encryption already resident
2 Policy appliesDisk-encryption profile assigned; "allow standard users to enable" set for non-admin devices
3 EncryptKicks off silently; used-space-only is faster on a fresh device
4 EscrowThe one to verify — confirm the key is visible in Entra/AD before you call it done
A device can be encrypted and unrecoverable at the same time. Report on escrowed keys, not on encryption status. The two diverge exactly on the devices you will most need to recover.
Troubleshooting
Why a Device Drops Into Recovery
Recovery is the TPM doing its job — something in the measured boot path changed, so it refused to release the key. Most are benign and self-inflicted, which is why users should never see the recovery screen as a crisis.
TriggerUsually
Firmware/BIOS updateChanged PCRs; expected — suspend BitLocker before flashing firmware
Secure Boot / boot-order changeSomeone changed a UEFI setting
Docking / hardware changeSome configs measure it; re-seal or adjust the PCR profile
Repeated recovery on one modelA driver or firmware bug — a real fleet issue, not a user one
🛡️ Defender for Endpoint & Intune — Onboarding, ASR (Attack Surface Reduction) Rules & Tamper Protection Endpoint • Security ▶
Concept
Two Products, One Connector
Defender for Endpoint is the EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) platform; Intune is how you configure it on managed devices. The seam between them is the service-to-service connector — turn it on once, and Intune can onboard devices, ship Defender policy, and consume the device risk score for Conditional Access. Half of "Defender isn't working" tickets are that connector being off or the onboarding blob never landing.
Flow
Onboarding, and How to Know It Worked
StepDetail
1 ConnectEnable the Intune ↔ Defender connector in both consoles
2 OnboardEDR policy pushes the onboarding package; device registers with the service
3 VerifyDevice appears in the Defender portal and the detection test script alerts
4 Risk flowsDevice risk level becomes a Conditional Access signal
Reference
ASR Rules — Audit Before You Block, Always
Attack Surface Reduction rules block whole classes of behaviour malware relies on — Office spawning child processes, credential theft from LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service), script-launched executables. They are high value and high blast radius, because legitimate software does some of these things too. Every ASR rule has an audit mode that logs what it would have blocked; run there first and read the reports, or you will block a line-of-business app on day one.
ModeUse
AuditLog only — the mandatory first phase; mine it for false positives
BlockEnforce, once audit is clean for that rule
WarnUser can bypass — a middle ground for rules with legitimate edge cases
Per-rule exclusionsScalpel, not the off switch — exclude the one path, keep the rule
Tamper protection stops malware — and local admins, and your own scripts — from disabling Defender. Leave it on; when it blocks a legitimate change, make that change through policy, which is the supported path through it.
🧑‍💼 Local Admin Rights — Removing Them, and Endpoint Privilege Management Endpoint • Security ▶
Concept
Standing Local Admin Is the Single Biggest Endpoint Risk You Control
A user who is a local administrator turns every phishing click and every malicious installer into a full device compromise, and defeats most of the controls on the rest of this page. Removing standing admin is the highest-leverage endpoint hardening there is — and the reason it survives everywhere is that removing it naively generates a wall of "I can't do my job" tickets. The work is not deleting the right; it is replacing what people legitimately used it for.
Choosing
What Replaces the Right
They used admin to…Replace with
Install approved softwareCompany Portal self-service; deploy as system-context apps
Run one app that demands elevationEndpoint Privilege Management — elevate the app, not the user
Change a setting IT lockedA settings-catalog policy exposing exactly that control
Genuine developer / IT needA time-boxed, audited elevation, or a separate admin account — never their daily login
Reference
Endpoint Privilege Management — Elevate the Task, Not the Person
EPM lets a standard user run a specific, approved action with admin rights while staying a standard user for everything else. The unit of trust moves from the person to the task, which is the whole point.
ModelHow it works
Automatic ruleA named, hash-verified app always elevates, silently — for known-good tools
User-confirmedUser clicks through a justification prompt; logged
Support-approvedRequest routes to IT for one-time approval — for the long tail
Full audit trailEvery elevation recorded — the evidence that makes admin removal defensible
Rule on the file's hash or signature, not its name. A rule that elevates anything called setup.exe is a privilege-escalation primitive you built and handed to an attacker.
🗝️ Windows LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) — Local Admin Password Rotation in Entra and AD (Active Directory) Endpoint • Security ▶
Concept
The Built-In Admin Account Is Still There — LAPS Makes It Safe
Even after you remove user admin rights, every Windows device has a built-in local administrator account, and the historic sin was giving it one shared password across the whole fleet. One machine compromised, that password dumped, and it unlocks every other machine — the textbook lateral-movement path. LAPS sets a unique, random password per device, rotates it on a schedule, and escrows it centrally so support can still get in.
Reference
Windows LAPS vs the Legacy One, and Where the Password Lives
"Windows LAPS" is the modern built-in feature, distinct from the old downloadable Microsoft LAPS. It stores the password in the directory the device is joined to, and retrieval is a permission you grant deliberately and audit.
AspectDetail
Backup targetEntra ID for cloud-joined, on-prem AD for hybrid — chosen by policy
ConfigurationAn Intune policy or GPO (Group Policy Object); no agent to deploy on current Windows
RetrievalScoped directory permission; every read is logged
RotationOn a schedule, and automatically right after a password is used
Password encryptionEncrypted in the directory (AD path); readable only by the accounts you authorize
LAPS and admin-rights removal are a pair. Removing standing user admin closes the front door; LAPS makes sure the emergency key under the mat is different for every house. Deploy them together, not years apart.
🚫 Firewall & Removable Media Policy — The Two Controls Auditors Ask About Endpoint • Security ▶
Concept
Two Small Policies With Outsized Audit Weight
The host firewall and USB (Universal Serial Bus) storage control are unglamorous, and they are on nearly every compliance checklist because they map directly to a breach story: malware beaconing out, and data walking out on a thumb drive. Both are a single policy to deploy and both have one classic way to lock a fleet out of something it needed — which is why they belong in a late rollout ring, not ring zero.
Reference
Host Firewall — Default Deny Inbound, Log Everything
SettingSensible default
ProfilesDomain, Private, Public — all three enabled; Public is the strictest
InboundDefault deny; allow by explicit rule only
OutboundUsually allow, but log; outbound-deny is high-maintenance — reserve for high-security fleets
Rule mergingDecide whether local admin rules merge with policy — "off" is safer and a common surprise
LoggingOn, for dropped packets — the evidence you need when an app breaks
The trap is rule merging: turn it off and every locally-created allow rule vanishes, which is correct for security and will break the one legacy app whose installer added a rule nobody documented. Audit first.
Reference
Removable Media — Block, or Allow Read-Only, or Require Encryption
PostureWhat it means
Block allNo USB storage at all — cleanest to defend, hardest on legitimate needs
Read-onlyData can come in, nothing walks out — the common compromise
Require BitLocker To GoWritable only to encrypted media; the removable-drive counterpart to disk encryption
Allow by device IDApproved hardware only — for hardware tokens and specific peripherals
Scope by storage, not all USB — a policy that blocks "USB devices" rather than "USB mass storage" also kills keyboards, mice and the webcam, and that ticket arrives within the hour.
🏢 Windows Server & Infrastructure
AZ-800 Server
Server foundations · AD DS · Group Policy · Domain controllers · FSMO · SYSVOL 28 topics · ~1h 00m ▾
🧾 Windows Server Editions & Licensing — What You Are Actually Buying Server • Licensing ▶
The decision
Standard vs Datacenter Is a Virtualisation Question, Not a Feature Question
People assume Datacenter is "the one with the good features". For almost every role that matters — AD DS (Active Directory Domain Services), DNS (Domain Name System), DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), file services — the two editions are identical. What you are buying is how many Windows virtual machines that hardware may run. Choose on VM density, then check the handful of features that genuinely differ.
StandardDatacenter
Virtual instances per licensed host 2 Unlimited
AD DS, DNS, DHCP, file, print Yes Yes
Storage Spaces Direct No Yes
Software-defined networking No Yes
Typical fit Physical box, or a host running one or two VMs A virtualisation host, or anything hyper-converged
The verdict: if a host will ever run more than about four Windows VMs, Datacenter usually costs less than stacking Standard licences — and you stop having to count. Below that, Standard. Get this wrong in the direction of Standard and you are not merely under-licensed, you are under-licensed retroactively, which is how licensing turns into an audit finding.
Core counting
Licensing Follows Cores, and There Is a Floor
Windows Server is licensed per physical core, with minimums that catch people out: you license every physical core in the host, at least 8 per processor and at least 16 per server, regardless of how few you use. A 2× 6-core host is still billed as 16 cores. Licences are sold in 2-core packs, so the arithmetic is always even.
The trap is hardware refresh. Moving a workload from an 8-core box to a 32-core box does not carry the licence with it — the new host needs double the core licences before the first VM boots. Price the licence alongside the tin, not after it.
The forgotten half
CALs (Client Access License) — Licensing the Connection, Not the Server
Core licences let the server run. CALs let something connect to it. They are bought separately, they are frequently forgotten, and they are the single most common finding in a Microsoft licensing review.
ModelBuy one perCheaper when
User CALNamed person, any number of devicesPeople have a laptop, a phone and a desktop
Device CALNamed device, any number of usersShift workers share a terminal or a shop-floor PC
External connectorServer, for unlimited external usersAnonymous or public-facing access
The verdict: count your CALs by whichever number is smaller — people or devices — and remember that Remote Desktop Services needs its own CAL on top of the Windows Server CAL. Two separate purchases for one session.
Failure mode
Evaluation Media That Quietly Expires
Evaluation installs run for 180 days and then begin shutting down hourly. It is a reliable source of a mystifying outage roughly six months after someone stood up a "temporary" server. Check what you are running before it tells you: 
# Which edition and how many days are left?
slmgr /dlv

# Evaluation to full: list targets, then convert (needs a reboot)
DISM /Online /Get-TargetEditions
DISM /Online /Set-Edition:ServerStandard /ProductKey:XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX /AcceptEula
A domain controller cannot be edition-converted in place. If the expiring server is a DC, you promote a replacement, transfer the roles, and demote the old one — which is a far longer evening than the one you were planning.
⬛ Server Core — Why You Would Remove the GUI (Graphical User Interface), and How You Manage It Anyway Server • Installation ▶
The trade
A Smaller Server Is a Smaller Target and a Shorter Patch Queue
Server Core is Windows Server without the desktop shell, Explorer, Edge, or most of the management consoles. The argument for it is not disk space. It is that code you did not install cannot be exploited and does not need patching — fewer components means fewer monthly reboots and a materially smaller attack surface.
Server CoreDesktop Experience
Local managementCommand line, sconfigFull GUI
Attack surfaceSmallerLarger
Patch/reboot frequencyLowerHigher
Vendor agent supportCheck first — some installers need a GUIAssumed
Good fitDC (Domain Controller), DNS (Domain Name System), DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), file, Hyper-V hostAnything with a vendor GUI console
The verdict: infrastructure roles that you administer remotely anyway are the easy yes. The blocker is almost never Windows — it is a third-party agent, backup client or line-of-business installer that assumes a desktop. Test the agents before committing the estate.
One-way door
You Cannot Switch Between Them After Installation
In Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 you could add and remove the GUI at will. That was removed in 2016 and has not returned. On any currently supported release, choosing Core or Desktop Experience at install time is permanent — changing your mind means a rebuild.
This is worth treating as a genuine one-way door: decide per role, write the decision into the build documentation, and default to Desktop Experience only where an agent actually requires it.
Local admin
sconfig, and the Handful of Commands Worth Memorising
A freshly built Core box needs enough local configuration to become remotely manageable — then you never sign in locally again. sconfig is a menu that covers most of it. 
# The menu that covers naming, domain join, networking, updates, remote management
sconfig

# Or do it directly in PowerShell
Rename-Computer -NewName DC03 -Restart
Add-Computer -DomainName corp.example.com -Restart
Enable-PSRemoting -Force

# Lost the command prompt entirely? This brings it back.
# (Task Manager -> File -> Run new task -> cmd)
The last one is not a joke. Closing the only console window on a Core box leaves you staring at a blank blue screen with no way in, and it is the first thing that happens to everyone exactly once.
Remote by default
Manage It From Somewhere Else — That Was Always the Point
Server Core is not "harder to manage". It is a server you manage the way you should have been managing the others: remotely, from an administrative workstation, over PowerShell remoting or with the graphical consoles pointed at it. 
# Interactive session on the remote server
Enter-PSSession -ComputerName DC03

# Fan out one command across many servers at once
Invoke-Command -ComputerName DC01,DC02,DC03 -ScriptBlock {
    Get-Service ADWS | Select-Object PSComputerName, Status
}
Once every server is administered this way, the presence or absence of a local GUI stops being a meaningful distinction — which is the actual argument for Core, and the reason it reads as difficult only to teams still signing in at the console.
🛠️ Server Manager, RSAT (Remote Server Administration Tools) & Windows Admin Center — Which Console Wins Server • Tooling ▶
Choosing
Three Overlapping Tools, Each Best at One Thing
These are not generations of the same product, and the newest does not replace the others. They overlap awkwardly, and knowing which to reach for saves more time than knowing any one of them deeply.
Server ManagerRSATWindows Admin Center
What it is Built-in role and server dashboard The classic MMC (Microsoft Management Console) snap-ins, installed on your workstation Browser-based gateway to many servers
Best at Adding roles; a quick health glance Deep object work — AD (Active Directory) users, DNS (Domain Name System) zones, GPOs (Group Policy Object) Day-to-day ops across a fleet; managing Core
Weak at Anything at scale Fleet views; needs a domain-joined workstation Niche AD tasks the classic snap-ins still own
Runs on The server, or your workstation Your workstation only A gateway server or your workstation
The verdict: install RSAT on your admin workstation and use it for AD, DNS and Group Policy work — the snap-ins remain the most complete tools for those objects. Use Windows Admin Center for everything fleet-shaped: patching status, certificates, event logs, remote PowerShell, and anything on Server Core. Use Server Manager to install a role and then close it.
Getting RSAT
RSAT Ships With Windows Now — Stop Downloading It
RSAT used to be a separate download matched to your exact Windows build. Since Windows 10 1809 it is a Feature on Demand built into the OS (Operating System), which means no download, no version mismatch, and one command. 
# See what is available and what is already installed
Get-WindowsCapability -Name RSAT* -Online | Select-Object Name, State

# The three most people actually want
Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name Rsat.ActiveDirectory.DS-LDS.Tools~~~~0.0.1.0
Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name Rsat.GroupPolicy.Management.Tools~~~~0.0.1.0
Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name Rsat.Dns.Tools~~~~0.0.1.0
In a managed estate this is frequently blocked, because Features on Demand are pulled from Windows Update and the policy points at an internal update server that does not carry them. If the command fails with an 0x800f0954, that is the cause — the fix is a policy exception, not a download.
Failure mode
The Admin Workstation Is the Real Attack Surface
Every one of these tools concentrates domain-wide authority onto whatever machine you installed it on. A workstation that reads email, browses the web and holds Domain Admin tooling is the single most valuable target in the estate, and compromising it skips every other step of an intrusion.
The standard mitigation is a privileged access workstation: a separate, hardened machine with no mail client and no general browsing, used only for administration. Where that is not affordable, the minimum is a separate admin account that never signs in to a daily-driver machine — the smallest useful version of the tiered-administration model.
🧩 Roles & Features — What Installing a Role Actually Changes Server • Configuration ▶
The distinction
A Role Is a Job; a Feature Is a Capability
A role is what the server is for — domain controller, DNS (Domain Name System) server, file server. A feature supports a role or the administrator: failover clustering, .NET, the management tools. The practical difference is that roles usually open ports and start listening, and features usually do not.
Adding a role is therefore never only a software install. It typically creates service accounts, opens firewall rules, registers service principal names, writes new event log channels, and may add a scheduled task. That is why "just add the role to see" is a poor instinct on a production box — removing it afterwards does not reliably undo all of it.
Doing it
Install It in PowerShell So It Is Repeatable
# What is installed, and what could be?
Get-WindowsFeature | Where-Object Installed

# Install a role with its management tools (omit the switch on a server
# you manage remotely — the tools belong on your workstation, not here)
Install-WindowsFeature -Name AD-Domain-Services -IncludeManagementTools

# Capture a known-good server's feature set, then reproduce it elsewhere
Get-WindowsFeature | Where-Object Installed | Export-Clixml .\baseline.xml
Install-WindowsFeature -ConfigurationFilePath .\baseline.xml
The GUI (Graphical User Interface) and the cmdlet do the same work, but only one of them leaves a record you can diff, review and re-run. Build servers from a script even when you build them once — the second server always arrives eventually.
Failure mode
Role Creep, and the Server Nobody Dares Reboot
Servers accumulate roles because adding one to an existing box is faster than building a new one. The result is the machine that is somehow a domain controller, a file server, a print server and a licensing server — and therefore cannot be patched without scheduling four separate teams.
Keep domain controllers doing one job. A DC holds every password hash in the domain; every additional role on it is another way in, and every additional service is another reason someone objects to the reboot. If a server needs an explanation of what it does, it has too many roles.
🛡️ Server Hardening Baseline — The Short List That Removes Most Risk Server • Hardening ▶
Priorities
Six Things, Roughly in Order of Return
Hardening guides run to hundreds of settings and are mostly ignored because of it. This is the short list — the items that remove the most attacker options per hour spent. Do these before opening a benchmark document.
Do thisBecause
Deploy LAPS Randomises the local administrator password per machine. Kills lateral movement by reused local credentials, which is the most common way one compromised host becomes all of them
Never browse or read mail from a server Free, and removes the two most common initial-access paths in one decision
Install only the roles the server needs Every role is listening code and another patch dependency
Turn on an audit policy that logs something useful Default auditing will not tell you what happened. Logon events, account management, and process creation with command line are the minimum
Separate admin accounts from daily-driver accounts Stops a phished user session from being a domain-admin session
Patch on a schedule you actually keep A predictable monthly window beats an ambitious weekly one that slips
The verdict: LAPS first. It is the cheapest single control here and it breaks the technique that turns one workstation into the whole domain.
Baselines
Do Not Write Your Own — Start From a Published One
Microsoft's Security Compliance Toolkit and the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Benchmarks both publish server baselines as importable GPO (Group Policy Object) backups. Starting from one and documenting your exceptions is far better than assembling settings by hand, because the exceptions become the thing you review rather than the whole configuration.
Apply a baseline to a pilot OU first. Baselines routinely break older line-of-business applications by disabling legacy protocols and weak ciphers — which is the point of them, and also why they need a controlled rollout rather than a domain-wide link on a Friday.
Failure mode
Hardening That Was Never Verified
A baseline linked at the domain root is not evidence that it applied. Group Policy can be blocked, filtered out by a missing security group, or beaten by a more specific GPO — and none of that reports itself. Verify on a real machine: 
# What did this machine actually receive? Read the "Denied" reasons, not just Applied.
gpresult /h C:\rsop.html /f

# Is auditing on where you think it is?
auditpol /get /category:*

# Is LAPS actually storing a password for this computer object?
Get-LapsADPassword -Identity SRV01 -AsPlainText
This is the same lesson as any other control: the configuration you intended and the configuration in force are different claims, and only the second one protects anything.
🧱 AD DS (Active Directory Domain Services) Boundaries — When to Add an OU, a Domain, or a Forest AD DS • Design ▶
Orientation
The Objects Are Covered Elsewhere; This Is the Decision
What a forest, domain and OU are — and how they are attacked — is in Active Directory — Structure, Objects & Attacks in the Security domain. This card answers the question that actually lands on an administrator: something needs to be separated, so which boundary do you reach for? Almost always the answer is the cheapest one, and almost always people pick a more expensive one than they need.
BoundaryWhat it actually separatesCost to run
Organisational unit Policy targets and delegated administration Free — make as many as you need
Domain Replication scope, password policy scope, some legacy defaults Its own DCs (Domain Controller), its own trusts, its own backups
Forest Security. This is the only real security boundary A parallel directory in every respect
The verdict: a domain is not a security boundary — a Domain Admin in any domain of a forest can reach every other domain in that forest. If the requirement is "these administrators must never be able to touch that", the answer is a separate forest, and nothing cheaper will do. If the requirement is "different policy" or "different people administer it", the answer is an OU.
Design
Structure the Directory for Delegation and Policy, Not the Org Chart
The most common OU design mirrors the company's departments, and it is the wrong one, because reorganisations then force directory work that has no technical reason to happen. Structure instead by what you do to objects: the two things an OU exists for are attaching Group Policy and delegating rights.
A structure that survives reorganisation usually separates by object type first (workstations, servers, users, service accounts), then by whatever genuinely drives different policy — region, build standard, or regulatory scope. Keep it shallow. Deep nesting makes precedence hard to reason about and gains nothing that a well-named security group could not do.
Failure mode
The Default Containers Are Not OUs
CN=Users and CN=Computers are containers, not organisational units, and Group Policy cannot be linked to them. Anything created without a specified location lands there — which is where every new machine goes when someone joins it to the domain in a hurry.
The result is a machine that silently receives none of your workstation policy. Redirect the defaults once, at build time, and the problem stops existing: 
# Point the default containers at real OUs you control
redircmp "OU=Workstations,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com"
redirusr "OU=Staff,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com"

# Find the machines already stranded in the default container
Get-ADComputer -SearchBase "CN=Computers,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com" -Filter * |
    Select-Object Name, Created
👑 FSMO (Flexible Single Master Operations) Roles — The Five Jobs That Cannot Be Done by Everyone AD DS • Operations ▶
Why they exist
Multi-Master Replication Has Five Exceptions
Active Directory is multi-master: change an object on any domain controller and the change replicates outward. That model breaks for operations where two simultaneous answers would corrupt the directory — handing out the same identifier twice, or two DCs disagreeing about the schema. Those five operations are pinned to a single holder.
RoleScopeDoes whatIf it is down
Schema masterForest Owns schema changes Nothing, until you extend the schema
Domain naming masterForest Adds and removes domains Nothing, until you add a domain
RID (Relative Identifier) masterDomain Issues pools of identifiers for new objects New object creation stops once DCs exhaust their pool
PDC (Primary Domain Controller) emulatorDomain Time authority, password-change target, lockout processing, GPO (Group Policy Object) edit target Noticed within the hour — this is the one that hurts
Infrastructure masterDomain Fixes cross-domain object references Stale names in cross-domain group memberships
The verdict: four of the five can be offline for days without anyone noticing. The PDC emulator cannot — it anchors domain time, and Kerberos rejects tickets once clocks drift past the tolerance. When someone reports "nobody can log in", check the PDC emulator and check time.
The one that matters
Transfer Is Routine; Seize Is a Decision You Cannot Undo
Transfer is a graceful handover between two running DCs — use it for maintenance and decommissioning, and it is entirely routine. Seizing is for a holder that is never coming back. It tells the forest a role has moved without the old holder's agreement.
The rule after a seizure is absolute: the old holder must never be brought back online. Two DCs believing they hold the same role produces divergence that is far worse than the outage you were fixing. Wipe it, do not boot it. 
# Who holds what, right now
netdom query fsmo
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object PDCEmulator, RIDMaster, InfrastructureMaster
Get-ADForest | Select-Object SchemaMaster, DomainNamingMaster

# Graceful transfer
Move-ADDirectoryServerOperationMasterRole -Identity DC02 -OperationMasterRole PDCEmulator

# Seizure — only when the old holder is gone for good
Move-ADDirectoryServerOperationMasterRole -Identity DC02 -OperationMasterRole PDCEmulator -Force
Note that the same cmdlet does both, and the only difference is -Force. Read the command twice before running it.
Placement
Where to Put Them, and the RID Pool Nobody Watches
For most organisations the defaults are fine: leave the roles where the first DC put them, keep the two forest roles together, and put the PDC emulator on a well-connected DC in the main site. Complexity here buys very little.
The one number worth monitoring is the RID pool. Each domain has a finite supply of relative identifiers, and while exhaustion is rare, it is unrecoverable in the sense that the fix is a domain migration. Scripted account creation that runs in a loop is the usual cause of a sudden jump. 
# How much of the RID space has been issued?
dcdiag /test:ridmanager /v | Select-String "Available RID Pool"
🔄 AD (Active Directory) Replication — How Changes Travel, and Triage When They Stop AD DS • Troubleshooting ▶
The model
Nothing Is Pushed Immediately, and That Is by Design
Each DC (Domain Controller) tracks a monotonic update sequence number per partition. A partner asks "what has changed since the number I last saw from you?", and receives only that delta. This makes replication cheap, and it means a change is never instantly everywhere.
WhereNormal delayPlanned by
Within a siteSeconds — change notification, no scheduleThe KCC (Knowledge Consistency Checker), automatically
Between sites15 minutes by default, and compressedSite links you configure
Urgent changesImmediate, regardless of scheduleAccount lockout, password changes to the PDC (Primary Domain Controller)
The verdict: "the change has not appeared yet" is usually correct behaviour rather than a fault. Before troubleshooting, confirm enough time has passed for the path involved — and remember a user's password change reaches the PDC emulator immediately even when everything else waits.
Triage
Three Commands, in This Order
Replication problems produce vague symptoms — a group membership that will not take, a password that works on one site and not another. Start broad and narrow: 
# 1. One-line summary of every partner link. Look at the failure columns first.
repadmin /replsummary

# 2. Which partition is failing, between which pair, and with what error?
repadmin /showrepl * /csv > repl.csv

# 3. Broad DC health — DNS, services, roles, the SYSVOL share
dcdiag /v /c /e

# Force a sync when you have fixed the cause and want to confirm
repadmin /syncall /AdeP
In practice the root cause is DNS (Domain Name System) far more often than replication itself. A DC that cannot resolve its partners' service records cannot replicate with them, and the error it reports describes the symptom rather than the cause.
Failure mode
The Tombstone Lifetime, and the DC You Left Switched Off
Deletions replicate as tombstones — markers that persist for a fixed lifetime, 180 days on any modern domain. A DC that is offline longer than that has missed the window in which it could learn about those deletions, and Active Directory will refuse to replicate with it rather than resurrect deleted objects.
There is no supported way to talk it round. A DC offline past the tombstone lifetime must be forcibly demoted, its metadata cleaned from the directory, and the server rebuilt and re-promoted. The practical rule: a domain controller is either in service or decommissioned. "Powered off for a while" is not a state AD supports, and the lab DC someone shut down in spring is the usual victim.
🤝 Trusts — Direction, Transitivity & Why They Are Backwards AD DS • Identity ▶
The confusing part
Trust Direction Is the Opposite of Access Direction
This trips up nearly everyone, including people who have configured trusts before. If domain A trusts B, then users in B can access resources in A. Access flows against the arrow. The trusting side is the one giving something up.
Read it as a sentence about credentials rather than a diagram: "A is willing to accept that B has authenticated someone." Whenever a trust seems to be working the wrong way round, it is almost always working correctly and being read backwards.
Types
Four You Will Meet, and What Each Is For
TypeBetweenTransitiveReach for it when
Parent–childDomains in one forestYes, automaticNever — it is created for you
ForestTwo forest rootsYesA merger, or a permanent partnership
ExternalTwo specific domainsNoOne domain needs access, and only that one
ShortcutTwo domains in one forestYesAuthentication is slow across a long referral path
The verdict: prefer external and one-way whenever the requirement allows it. A forest trust is transitive and two-way by default, which means it grants far more than most projects actually asked for — and trusts are rarely revisited once the project that needed them is closed.
Failure mode
SID Filtering Is the Control That Keeps a Trust Survivable
A Kerberos ticket carries the account's security identifiers, including a history field used during migrations. Without filtering, a compromised administrator in a trusted domain can inject an identifier belonging to a privileged group in your domain, and your DCs (Domain Controller) will honour it. That turns a trust into a full privilege path between organisations.
SID filtering discards identifiers that did not originate in the trusted domain, and it is enabled by default on external and forest trusts. It gets disabled during migrations, because SID history is exactly what migrations rely on — and then not re-enabled, which is the failure worth checking for. 
# List trusts and their properties
Get-ADTrust -Filter * | Select-Object Name, Direction, ForestTransitive, SIDFilteringQuarantined

# Inspect and re-enable filtering (quarantine) on a named trust
netdom trust corp.example.com /domain:partner.example.net /quarantine
netdom trust corp.example.com /domain:partner.example.net /quarantine:yes
Audit trusts on a schedule. They outlive the projects that created them, nobody owns them afterwards, and each one is a path into your directory that your own controls do not govern.
🗺️ Sites & Subnets — Why Clients Authenticate Against the Wrong DC (Domain Controller) AD DS • Topology ▶
The mechanism
A Site Is a Subnet List, and That Is How Clients Find a Nearby DC
Active Directory has no map of your network. It knows only what you told it: a site is a named object, and subnets are associated with sites. When a client starts up it looks up its own address, learns which site it is in, and asks for a domain controller in that site.
Sites drive three things: which DC a client authenticates against, how replication is scheduled between locations, and which distributed file system targets a client prefers. All three degrade the same way when the subnet list is wrong.
Failure mode
A Missing Subnet Sends Branch Offices Across the Country
If a client's address matches no defined subnet, AD (Active Directory) cannot place it in a site — so it hands back any domain controller. A new branch office whose subnet nobody added will authenticate against a DC on another continent, and the symptom is not an error but slow logons, slow group policy, and file shares that mysteriously prefer the wrong server.
This is self-diagnosing if you know where to look. Every unmatched client is logged on the domain controller that served it: 
# Clients whose subnet is not defined — NETLOGON logs every one
Get-Content C:\Windows\debug
etlogon.log | Select-String "NO_CLIENT_SITE"

# Which site does this machine think it is in?
nltest /dsgetsite
dcdiag /test:DCGetDcName

# Add the missing subnet
New-ADReplicationSubnet -Name "10.30.7.0/24" -Site "Branch-Leeds"
Make the NETLOGON check routine. It is the cheapest health check in Active Directory, it costs nothing to run, and it silently accumulates every network change nobody told the directory about.
Design
Site Links Describe Cost, Not Bandwidth
A site link says which sites replicate with each other, how often, and at what cost — an arbitrary number where lower means more preferred. It is not measured in anything; it exists so you can express "prefer this path" when more than one route exists. Consistency matters more than the values.
Keep the topology as simple as the network allows. The Knowledge Consistency Checker builds and repairs the replication topology automatically, and hand-crafted connection objects stop it doing that — so they survive as fossils long after the link they were working around was upgraded.
📜 Group Policy Architecture — Where the Settings Actually Live Group Policy • Internals ▶
Two halves
A GPO Is a Directory Object Plus a Folder, and They Can Disagree
What looks like one object in the management console is stored in two places. The container lives in Active Directory and holds the metadata — version numbers, status, which client-side extensions are involved. The template is a folder in SYSVOL (System Volume) holding the actual settings files.
Group Policy containerGroup Policy template
Lives inThe AD (Active Directory) databaseThe SYSVOL share, named by GUID (Globally Unique Identifier)
HoldsVersion, status, extension listRegistry.pol, scripts, preferences XML (eXtensible Markup Language)
Replicated byAD replicationDFSR (Distributed File System Replication)
Fails asMissing GPO in the consoleGPO applies inconsistently by site
The verdict: these replicate over two independent mechanisms, so they can fall out of step. A policy that works in one office and not another, with no error anywhere, is the signature of SYSVOL replication being behind — not of a policy problem. Check DFSR before re-reading the GPO.
What it writes
Most of Group Policy Is Just Registry Keys With Rules About Them
Administrative template settings compile down to registry values in Registry.pol. What makes them policy rather than configuration is where they land: the four policy branches of the registry, which ordinary applications and users cannot write to, and which are re-applied on a schedule.
This is exactly why a true policy setting cannot be permanently changed by the user — the next refresh puts it back — and why a preference can. It is also why an .admx file is only a description of a setting: it tells the console what to show and which key to write, and installing one changes nothing on its own. 
# The central store — one copy of the templates for the whole domain,
# so every admin console shows the same settings
\\corp.example.com\SYSVOL\corp.example.com\Policies\PolicyDefinitions\

# Without it, each console uses its own local C:\Windows\PolicyDefinitions,
# and settings appear or vanish depending on who opened the editor
Create the central store early. Its absence produces one of the most confusing symptoms in Group Policy: a colleague cannot find the setting you just configured, because their console does not know it exists.
🔢 Processing Order & Precedence — LSDOU (Local, Site, Domain, Organisational Unit), Enforcement & Loopback Group Policy • Precedence ▶
The order
Last Writer Wins, and the Order Is LSDOU
Policies apply in a fixed sequence — Local, Site, Domain, OU — and each pass overwrites conflicting settings from the one before. The nearest OU therefore wins by default, which matches the instinct that specific beats general. Multiple GPOs (Group Policy Object) linked to the same container are applied by link order, lowest number last, so link order 1 wins.
ModifierEffectBeats
Enforced (on a link)Cannot be overridden by anything more specificEverything below it, and Block Inheritance
Block Inheritance (on an OU)Stops policies from above reaching this OUEverything above — except Enforced links
Link orderOrders GPOs on one containerOnly its peers on that container
Link disabledThe GPO exists but does nothing here—
The verdict: Enforced and Block Inheritance are both escape hatches that make precedence hard to reason about, and they interact — Enforced wins over a block. Use them sparingly and document each one, because the person debugging the resulting behaviour in two years will not guess why they are there.
Two halves again
Computer Settings and User Settings Follow Different Objects
Every GPO has a computer half and a user half, and they are evaluated against different objects in different places. The computer half applies based on where the computer account sits; the user half based on where the user account sits. Linking a GPO with user settings to an OU full of computers does exactly nothing, and reports no error.
Timing differs too: computer policy applies at startup, user policy at sign-in, and both refresh in the background roughly every 90 minutes with a random offset so that an estate does not stampede a DC (Domain Controller). Some settings — drive maps, folder redirection, software installation — only take effect at the full startup or logon event, which is why a change sometimes needs a reboot rather than a refresh.
Loopback
The Setting for "This Machine, Whoever Signs In"
Sometimes user settings should depend on the machine rather than the person: a kiosk, a shared clinical workstation, a terminal server. Loopback processing tells the computer to apply the user half of the GPOs linked to the computer's OU.
ModeWhat the user getsUse when
MergeTheir own user policy, then the machine's user policy on topMostly normal machine, a few local overrides
ReplaceOnly the machine's user policy; theirs is discardedKiosk or locked-down shared terminal
Loopback is the correct tool for a real requirement and a common cause of "why did this user's settings vanish on that one machine". If a user behaves differently on a particular device and nowhere else, check the device's OU for loopback before anything else.
🧪 Filtering — Security Groups, WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) & Item-Level Targeting Group Policy • Scoping ▶
Three tools
Narrowing a GPO (Group Policy Object) Below the OU It Is Linked To
A link scopes a policy to a container. When that is still too broad, there are three ways to narrow it — and they differ enormously in cost, because two are evaluated on every single client at every refresh.
