Security filteringWMI filteringItem-level targeting
GranularityWhole GPOWhole GPOA single preference item
CostEffectively freeA WMI query per client, per refreshCheap
Works forUsers and computers by groupAnything WMI can expressPreferences only
DebuggabilityObvious in the consoleInvisible until you test the queryBuried in item properties
The verdict: reach for security filtering first — it is free, visible, and understood by everyone. Use item-level targeting when only one drive map or shortcut needs the condition. Treat WMI filtering as a last resort: it is the standard answer to "apply only to laptops", and it is also a per-client query on every refresh that slows logons across the estate.
Failure mode
The Security Filtering Change That Broke Everything in 2016
For a GPO to apply to a user or computer, that object needs both Read and Apply Group Policy. Removing Authenticated Users from security filtering and adding a specific group used to be the standard technique — until a security update made computers require Read access via the computer account itself.
The result: policies that had worked for years silently stopped applying. The fix is to leave Authenticated Users with Read on the delegation tab while restricting Apply to the target group. It looks redundant and it is load-bearing. 
# Check what a GPO is actually scoped to
Get-GPPermission -Name "Laptop Power Settings" -All |
    Select-Object @{n='Who';e={$_.Trustee.Name}}, Permission

# Restore the Read that the 2016 change made mandatory
Set-GPPermission -Name "Laptop Power Settings" -TargetName "Authenticated Users" `
    -TargetType Group -PermissionLevel GpoRead
🎛️ Group Policy Preferences — The Half People Forget Exists Group Policy • Preferences ▶
The distinction
Policies Are Enforced; Preferences Are Set and Let Go
A policy setting is re-applied on every refresh and the interface for it is greyed out. A preference writes an ordinary value that the user can then change — and, depending on the action you chose, it may never be written again.
ActionBehaviourUse for
CreateWrite only if absent; never touch againA default the user may override
ReplaceDelete and recreate every refreshSettings you need to stay correct
UpdateCreate if absent, amend if presentThe usual choice
DeleteRemove itCleaning up a previous mistake
The verdict: "the drive map is not updating" is nearly always Create where Update or Replace was meant. Create fires once and then stays silent forever, which looks exactly like a broken policy.
Security
Never Set Passwords Through Preferences — MS14-025
Preferences could once set local account passwords. The password was stored in the preferences XML (eXtensible Markup Language) in SYSVOL (System Volume), encrypted with a key Microsoft published in its own documentation — so any domain user who could read SYSVOL, which is every domain user, could decrypt it.
Microsoft removed the ability to create these in 2014, but did not remove existing ones. They persist in SYSVOL until someone deletes them, and finding them is a standard early step in an intrusion. Check now; it takes one command: 
# Any cpassword left in SYSVOL is a live credential leak to every domain user
Get-ChildItem -Path "\\corp.example.com\SYSVOL" -Recurse -Include *.xml -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern "cpassword" | Select-Object Path, LineNumber
If that returns anything: treat those credentials as compromised, rotate them, and delete the preference. Use LAPS for local administrator passwords — that is the control this anti-pattern was replaced by.
🔍 GPO (Group Policy Object) Troubleshooting — Proving What a Machine Actually Received Group Policy • Troubleshooting ▶
Method
Ask the Client, Not the Console
The management console shows what you configured. Only the client can tell you what it received, and the gap between those two is where every Group Policy problem lives. Start at the machine, and read the denied entries rather than the applied ones — the reason a GPO was filtered out is the answer. 
# The single most useful command: a full report with denied GPOs and reasons
gpresult /h C:\rsop.html /f

# Another user's result, from your own session
gpresult /scope:user /user corp\jdoe /r

# Force a refresh; add /boot or /logoff if the extension needs it
gpupdate /force

# The operational log — timings, slow extensions, real errors
Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-GroupPolicy/Operational" -MaxEvents 40 |
    Format-Table TimeCreated, Id, Message -Wrap
gpupdate /force is not a diagnosis. It re-applies everything and often masks the problem for one cycle, which is why the fault returns tomorrow. Read the report first.
Checklist
Why a GPO Did Not Apply, in the Order Worth Checking
CheckSymptom when this is the cause
Is the object in the OU the GPO is linked to?Object was moved, or landed in the default container
Right half of the GPO for the object type?User settings linked to a computer OU — no error, no effect
Security filtering — Read and Apply?Applied until 2016, then stopped for no visible reason
WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) filter actually true on this client?Applies to some hardware and not others
Block Inheritance or a more specific GPO?Correct in the console, absent on the machine
Has the client refreshed since the change?Works after a reboot, not before
Is SYSVOL (System Volume) replicating?Works in one site, not another
Slow link detection?Fails only on VPN (Virtual Private Network) or a branch link
The verdict: work down this list rather than re-reading the policy. Six of these eight produce no error message anywhere — the policy is simply absent — so the absence of an error tells you nothing about which one you are looking at.
👥 Group Nesting Strategy — AGDLP, and Why Nested Groups Become a Mess AD DS • Identity ▶
The convention
AGDLP — Accounts, Global, Domain Local, Permissions
Put Accounts into Global groups by who people are ("Finance Staff"), put those global groups into Domain Local groups by what is being accessed ("Ledger Share — Modify"), and grant Permissions only to the domain local group.
The payoff is that the two things change independently. People move between roles constantly; resources change permissions rarely. One membership edit moves a person's entire access, and no access control list is ever touched.
The rule that makes it work: never grant a permission to a user, and never to a global group. The moment someone shortcuts it, the resource stops describing its own access and you can no longer answer "who can read this?" from the group model.
Failure mode
Token Bloat — When Group Membership Breaks Logon
Every group a user belongs to adds a security identifier to their Kerberos ticket. Past roughly 1,000 groups the ticket exceeds default buffer sizes and authentication fails — often as an HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) 400 from a web application rather than anything mentioning Kerberos, which makes it a genuinely difficult diagnosis.
Deep nesting is the usual cause, because membership is transitive and nobody counts the indirect ones. Check the effective total, not the direct list: 
# Transitive group count — the number that matters
(Get-ADUser jdoe -Properties TokenGroups).TokenGroups.Count

# Users closest to the limit, worst first
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties TokenGroups |
    Select-Object Name, @{n='Groups';e={$_.TokenGroups.Count}} |
    Sort-Object Groups -Descending | Select-Object -First 20
Keep nesting to two levels — the depth AGDLP implies and no more. Every extra level makes membership harder to audit and pushes users toward a limit whose symptom does not name its cause.
🤖 Service Accounts — gMSA (group Managed Service Account) and Retiring the Shared Password AD DS • Identity ▶
The problem
A Password Nobody Can Change Is a Password Nobody Controls
The classic service account has a password set years ago, typed into several servers, recorded in a spreadsheet, and never rotated because nobody knows everything that uses it. It usually has more privilege than it needs, and it never expires — which is exactly the profile of the account an intruder wants.
OptionPassword managed byWorks across servers
User account as a serviceA human, in theoryYes
Managed service accountActive DirectoryOne host only
Group managed service accountActive DirectoryYes — clusters and farms
Built-in virtual accountsNothing to manageLocal only
The verdict: gMSA is the default answer for a domain service. AD (Active Directory) generates a 240-character password, rotates it every 30 days, and the servers authorised to use it retrieve it themselves. Nobody ever knows it, so nobody can leak it.
Doing it
One-Time Forest Setup, Then One Object Per Service
# Once per forest — creates the root key. Wait 10 hours, or force
# the effective time backwards in a lab that has a single DC.
Add-KdsRootKey -EffectiveImmediately

# Per service: who may retrieve the password
New-ADServiceAccount -Name svc-webapp -DNSHostName svc-webapp.corp.example.com `
    -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword "WebFarm-Servers"

# On each server that runs it
Install-ADServiceAccount -Identity svc-webapp
Test-ADServiceAccount -Identity svc-webapp

# In services.msc the account is CORP\svc-webapp$ with a BLANK password
The trailing $ and the empty password field are correct and are the two things people undo when they assume it is broken. If the service will not start, check that the server is in the retrieval group and reboot it — group membership on a computer account needs a new ticket.
🎫 Kerberos in Operations — SPNs (Service Principal Name), Delegation & Clock Skew AD DS • Troubleshooting ▶
Orientation
The Flow Is Covered; These Are the Three Things That Break It
Kerberos Authentication Flow in the Security domain explains the ticket exchange, and Kerberos Attacks — Rubeus & Kerbrute in Red Team covers abuse. Operationally, almost every Kerberos incident is one of three causes: a service principal name that is missing or duplicated, delegation configured too broadly, or clocks that have drifted.
SPNs
A Duplicate SPN Breaks Authentication for Everyone
A service principal name maps a service on a host to the account running it. If it is missing, clients silently fall back to NTLM (NT LAN Manager) — which usually still works, so the symptom is "Kerberos is not being used" found during an audit rather than an outage. If it is duplicated across two accounts, the domain controller cannot decide which key to encrypt with and authentication fails outright. 
# Duplicates across the whole forest — run this before blaming the app
setspn -X

# What is registered for a given account, and adding one
setspn -L CORP\svc-webapp
setspn -S HTTP/app.corp.example.com CORP\svc-webapp
Use -S rather than -A: it refuses to create a duplicate. -A adds blindly and is how most duplicate-SPN outages are created, usually by someone fixing a different problem.
Failure mode
Five Minutes of Drift and Nobody Logs In
Kerberos timestamps tickets to prevent replay, and rejects anything outside a tolerance of five minutes by default. Beyond that, authentication fails across the estate at once, and the error text does not mention time.
The domain's time hierarchy is strict: every member syncs from a DC (Domain Controller), every DC from the PDC (Primary Domain Controller) emulator, and the PDC emulator from an external source. The classic incident is a virtualised PDC emulator syncing from its hypervisor host and an external source, and oscillating between them. 
w32tm /query /status              # what am I syncing from?
w32tm /monitor                    # offsets across all DCs
w32tm /stripchart /computer:dc01 /samples:5 /dataonly
Disable host time sync on a virtualised PDC emulator. One authority only. Two sources of truth for time is the same class of mistake as two sources of truth for data, and it fails more visibly.
☁️ Entra Connect & Hybrid Identity — Choosing How Passwords Are Checked Identity • Hybrid ▶
The decision
Three Ways to Authenticate a Synced User
Directory synchronisation copies objects to the cloud. Authentication is a separate choice, and it is the one with operational consequences — it decides what happens to cloud sign-in when the on-premises directory is unreachable.
Password hash syncPass-through authFederation
Where the password is checkedCloudOn-premises, via an agentOn-premises, by AD FS (Active Directory Federation Services)
Survives a site outageYesNoNo
Infrastructure to runNoneLightweight agentsA farm, plus certificates
Leaked-credential detectionYesNoNo
The verdict: password hash sync unless a written requirement forbids it. It is the only option that keeps people working when the on-premises environment is down — which is precisely when they most need email. It syncs a hash of a hash, not the password, and it is what makes leaked-credential reporting possible at all.
Failure mode
The Sync Account and the Deletion Threshold
Sync runs as a highly privileged account that can write to both directories, and it is frequently excluded from the tiering model on the grounds that it is "just sync". It is a full path from the on-premises directory into the tenant, and should be treated as tier 0.
The related operational risk is an accidental mass deletion — someone moves an OU out of sync scope and the objects are deleted in the cloud. Accidental deletion prevention stops this by default at 500 objects per run; know the threshold exists before you meet it. 
Get-ADSyncExportDeletionThreshold
Get-ADSyncScheduler                 # is sync even running?
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta
🧹 Cleaning Up a Legacy Directory — Stale Objects & Over-Permissive ACLs (Access Control List) AD DS • Hygiene ▶
Method
Disable, Wait, Then Delete — Never Delete First
Every inherited directory contains accounts for people who left years ago and computers that were decommissioned. Each is a credential nobody is watching. The cleanup is easy; doing it safely is the part that needs a method, because deleting an account that turns out to run a nightly job is a worse outcome than leaving it.
Disable, move to a quarantine OU, and wait a full business cycle — a quarter, so that anything quarterly has had its chance to fail loudly. Then delete. The disable is instantly reversible; the delete is not. 
# Accounts unused for 90 days, still enabled
Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00 -UsersOnly |
    Where-Object Enabled | Select-Object Name, LastLogonDate

# Computers the same, then disable and park them
Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00 -ComputersOnly |
    Disable-ADAccount -PassThru |
    Move-ADObject -TargetPath "OU=Quarantine,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com"
LastLogonDate derives from a replicated attribute that is deliberately imprecise — it can lag by up to two weeks. That is fine for a 90-day threshold and wrong for a 7-day one. Do not tighten the window without switching to a per-DC attribute.
The bigger risk
Permissions Nobody Granted Deliberately
Stale accounts are the visible debt. The dangerous debt is delegation: rights granted on an OU during a project a decade ago, still held by a group that now contains the whole service desk. These do not appear in any account review, because no account looks unusual — the permission does.
Look forWhy it matters
Non-admins with Reset Password on an OUTake over any account in it
Write to member on a privileged groupSelf-service Domain Admin
GenericAll or WriteDACL anywhereEffectively ownership
Unconstrained delegation on a non-DCCompromise the host, capture any ticket sent to it
Accounts with adminCount=1 no longer privilegedInheritance stays broken after removal
Enumerate this with the attacker's tooling. BloodHound — see BloodHound & SharpHound — Attack-Path Graphing in Red Team — computes exactly these paths and is the fastest honest answer to "who can become Domain Admin?". Running it against your own directory before someone else does is ordinary defensive work.
🧭 Windows DNS (Domain Name System) Administration — Zones, Scavenging & Forwarders Infra • Name Resolution ▶
Orientation
The Protocol Is Covered; This Is the Service AD (Active Directory) Cannot Live Without
DNS Deep Dive — Records, Resolution & Security in the Networking domain covers records, resolution and DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions). This card is about running Microsoft's DNS as the directory's locator service — because in an AD environment, DNS is not a supporting service. It is how every client finds a domain controller, and almost every "Active Directory is broken" incident is DNS.
Domain controllers register service records announcing which DCs serve which site and role. Clients query those records to find one. Break DNS and nothing authenticates, no policy applies, and replication stops — all reporting errors that describe symptoms rather than the cause.
Zone storage
AD-Integrated Zones Replicate Themselves
AD-integratedStandard primary/secondary
Stored inThe directoryA text file on one server
ReplicationAD multi-master — any DC accepts writesZone transfer from one master
Secure dynamic updatesAvailableNot available
Single point of failureNoneThe primary
Use AD-integrated zones with secure-only dynamic updates. Non-secure updates let any host on the network overwrite any record — including a domain controller's — which is a straightforward path to intercepting authentication.
Failure mode
Scavenging: Off Means Stale Records, On Wrongly Means Deleted Ones
Dynamic registration creates records; nothing removes them when a machine leaves. Over years the zone fills with stale entries and clients connect to addresses now belonging to something else. Scavenging deletes records that have not refreshed — and it is the single most dangerous switch in Windows DNS, because enabling it wrongly deletes live records.
Two intervals govern it. During no-refresh a record cannot update its timestamp; during refresh it can; after both elapse without a refresh it becomes eligible. Both default to seven days, so a record survives at least 14 days of silence. The trap is a static record with a timestamp — it will be scavenged. 
# Check before enabling anything
Get-DnsServerScavenging -ComputerName dc01

# Static records must have NO timestamp, or scavenging eats them
Get-DnsServerResourceRecord -ZoneName corp.example.com -RRType A |
    Where-Object { $_.Timestamp -ne $null -and $_.HostName -match '^(vpn|printer|nas)' }
Enable it on one zone, leave it a month, and read what it removed before enabling it everywhere. An aggressive interval on a site whose laptops are away for three weeks is an outage waiting for the holidays.
Resolution path
Conditional Forwarders Beat Stub Zones for Partner Domains
A forwarder sends everything unresolved to an upstream server. A conditional forwarder sends only queries for a named domain, which is the right tool for resolving a partner or acquisition domain across a trust. Root hints are the fallback when no forwarder answers.
Never point a domain controller's own client DNS settings at a public resolver. It must resolve the directory's records first — pointing it at 8.8.8.8 as a "backup" produces intermittent, extremely confusing replication failures, because sometimes the public server answers first and knows nothing about your domain.
📮 DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) Administration — Scopes, Reservations, Failover & Relay Infra • Addressing ▶
Design
Lease Length Is the Only Setting With Real Consequences
Most DHCP configuration is mechanical. Lease duration is the judgement call, and it trades address availability against churn: too long and a guest network exhausts its pool, too short and clients renew constantly and a server outage bites within hours.
NetworkTypical leaseReason
Wired office8 daysStable devices; renewal traffic is wasted work
Wireless corporate1 dayDevices come and go; addresses must return
Guest or conference2–4 hoursHigh churn, small pool
VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) handsetsLong, or reserveAddress changes disrupt call routing
Clients renew at half the lease, so an 8-day lease means a server can be down for four days before anyone notices. That is resilience, and also why nobody discovers DHCP has been broken until the following week.
Resilience
Failover Modes, and the Relay Everyone Forgets
Built-in failover replaces the old trick of splitting a scope 80/20 across two servers. Load balance shares requests between two servers in one site; hot standby keeps one passive for a remote site. Both replicate lease state, so a client keeps its address through a failure.
DHCP discovery is a broadcast and does not cross a router. Every subnet without a local server needs an IP (Internet Protocol) helper on its gateway pointing at the servers — and this is the thing forgotten when a new VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) is created, producing "the new subnet does not work" with everything on the Windows side configured correctly. 
Add-DhcpServerv4Failover -ComputerName dhcp01 -PartnerServer dhcp02 `
    -Name "Site-A" -ScopeId 10.10.0.0 -LoadBalancePercent 50

Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -ComputerName dhcp01   # pool exhaustion
Get-DhcpServerInDC                                       # authorised servers
Authorisation is a real control worth knowing. A Windows DHCP server refuses to serve leases until authorised in AD (Active Directory), which prevents a lab server from handing out addresses on production. It does nothing about a non-Windows rogue server — that needs DHCP snooping on the switches.
📁 File Services — Share vs NTFS (New Technology File System) Permissions, DFS (Distributed File System) & Quotas Infra • Storage ▶
The classic confusion
Two Permission Sets, and the Effective Right Is the Lesser
A file reached over the network passes two checks: the share permission and the NTFS permission. The effective access is the more restrictive of the two. Reached locally, only NTFS applies — which is why a permission problem can vanish when you test by signing in to the server.
The convention that removes the confusion entirely: set the share to Everyone — Full Control, and do all real work in NTFS. One place to look, one place to audit. Share permissions predate NTFS having any, and maintaining both is a way to create a puzzle for your successor.
DFS
Namespaces Buy You the Right to Move Data Later
A DFS namespace gives users a stable path — \\corp\shares\finance — that points at whichever server actually holds the data. Migrate the data, repoint the target, and no mapped drive, script or shortcut anywhere needs changing.
DFS replication is separate and keeps copies in sync. The pairing is powerful and has one sharp edge: DFSR (Distributed File System Replication) resolves a conflicting edit as last-writer-wins, moving the loser to a hidden ConflictAndDeleted folder. It is not a multi-master file system, and using it for a shared working folder across sites will lose someone's work.
Deploy the namespace even for a single file server. It costs almost nothing now and is the difference between a weekend migration and a transparent one.
Failure mode
The Share That Filled the System Drive
Without quotas, one user's export fills the volume, and if the share lives on the system drive the server stops — event logs cannot write, and the failure cascades well beyond the share. Two separate mechanisms exist and people configure the wrong one: NTFS quotas are per user per volume; File Server Resource Manager quotas are per folder and are the useful ones. 
# Soft quota — warn at 80%, do not block. Start here.
New-FsrmQuota -Path "E:\Shares\Finance" -Size 100GB -SoftLimit `
    -Threshold (New-FsrmQuotaThreshold -Percentage 80)

# And keep shares off the system volume in the first place
Start with soft quotas and reporting. A hard limit imposed without warning produces a support queue and a workaround culture — people start saving to their desktops, which is worse than the disk usage you were managing.
📜 AD CS (Active Directory Certificate Services) Design — Offline Roots, Issuing CAs (Certificate Authority) & Publishing Infra • PKI ▶
Orientation
The Theory Is Covered; This Is the Deployment You Have to Live With
PKI & Certificate Lifecycle in the Security domain covers chains of trust, certificates and revocation as concepts. This card is about the internal certificate authority you actually run — a system whose design decisions are effectively permanent, because rebuilding a root means re-issuing every certificate it ever signed.
Structure
Two Tiers, and the Root Stays Switched Off
The standard design is a standalone offline root that signs one thing — the issuing CA's certificate — and is then powered off and stored securely. An enterprise issuing CA, domain-joined, does all day-to-day work.
Offline rootIssuing CA
Domain-joinedNo — standalone, deliberatelyYes, for templates and auto-enrolment
Powered onOnly to sign or re-publish a CRL (Certificate Revocation List)Always
Compromise meansRebuild the entire PKI (Public Key Infrastructure)Revoke its certificate, stand up a new one
The verdict: the offline root exists so that the worst realistic incident is recoverable. A single online enterprise root is simpler to build and turns one compromised server into a full trust rebuild across every device — which is why the two-tier design is worth the extra afternoon.
Failure mode
The Offline Root's CRL Expires, and Everything Stops
A certificate revocation list has a validity period. When a client cannot fetch a current CRL for any CA in the chain, strict validation fails — so an offline root whose CRL quietly expired invalidates every certificate beneath it. The root is switched off, so nothing warns you, and the failure arrives all at once.
Set the offline root's CRL validity long — a year or more — publish it to a location that stays reachable, and put the renewal in a calendar owned by a team rather than a person. Check that the published locations resolve from a normal client, not from the CA: 
# Validate the whole chain and every revocation URL a client would use
certutil -verify -urlfetch cert.cer

# What the CA publishes, and when the current CRL expires
certutil -getreg CA\CRLPublicationURLs
certutil -CRL                       # force a fresh CRL now
The distribution points are baked into every certificate at issuance. Changing the URL (Uniform Resource Locator) later does not fix already-issued certificates — they carry the old address until they expire. Get the publishing addresses right before issuing anything.
🧾 Certificate Templates — The Settings That Matter, and the Ones That Get You Owned Infra • PKI ▶
What a template is
A Template Is a Standing Offer to Issue Certificates
A template defines what a certificate will contain, who may request one, and whether a human approves it. Publishing a template to a CA (Certificate Authority) is not configuration — it is an authorisation decision, standing until revoked, and it is the part people treat casually.
SettingSafeDangerous
Subject nameBuilt from AD (Active Directory)Supplied in the request
Enrolment rightsA specific groupDomain Users / Domain Computers
Manager approvalRequired for anything privilegedDisabled everywhere
Extended key usageNarrow — server auth onlyClient authentication, or Any Purpose
The right-hand column is one finding, not four. A template that lets the requester choose the subject, allows client authentication, and can be enrolled by any domain user is a request for a certificate that authenticates as anyone — including a Domain Admin. That is ESC1, and it is a configuration mistake rather than a software vulnerability.
Defender's view
ESC1–ESC8 Are Your Audit Checklist
ADCS Abuse — Certipy & the ESC Techniques in the Red Team domain covers exploitation. The defensive point is that these are named, enumerable misconfigurations — so the same tooling that finds them for an attacker finds them for you, faster than reading template properties by hand. 
# Enumerate templates and CA settings, flagging the known ESC patterns.
# Run this against your own PKI as routine defensive work.
certipy find -u user@corp.example.com -p '...' -dc-ip 10.0.0.10 -vulnerable

# Native equivalents for spot checks
certutil -TCAInfo
Get-CATemplate
Two settings deserve a standing audit: any template where the requester supplies the subject, and EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 on the CA itself — the latter lets any request specify an alternative name, which turns every template into an impersonation primitive.
🔄 Certificate Lifecycle — Auto-Enrolment and the Expiry Nobody Scheduled Infra • PKI ▶
Auto-enrolment
Getting Certificates Onto Devices Without Touching Them
Auto-enrolment issues and renews certificates automatically for accounts that have the rights. It needs three things aligned: Autoenroll permission on the template, the template published to an issuing CA (Certificate Authority), and a Group Policy setting enabling auto-enrolment for the computer or user.
All three, or nothing happens and nothing complains. That silence is the whole troubleshooting difficulty — check the three in order rather than re-reading the template, and confirm on a client with certutil -pulse followed by the CertificateServicesClient operational log.
Failure mode
Expiry Is the Outage That Is Fully Predictable and Still Happens
Every certificate carries the date it will break. Expiry outages are therefore unique: entirely foreseeable, scheduled by you, and still among the most common causes of self-inflicted downtime. They happen because nobody owns the inventory — the certificate was installed during a project, by someone who has moved on. 
# Everything the CA issued that expires in the next 60 days
certutil -view -restrict "NotAfter<=now+60:00:00,Disposition=20" `
    -out "CommonName,NotAfter,RequesterName"

# Local store on a server
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My |
    Where-Object NotAfter -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(60) |
    Select-Object Subject, NotAfter, Thumbprint
Monitor expiry from outside, on the live endpoint. A CA report misses every certificate not issued by that CA — the public ones, the appliance ones, the one a vendor installed. The check that catches all of them connects to the port and reads what is actually being served.
🚑 Domain Controller Recovery — Authoritative vs Non-Authoritative Restore AD DS • Recovery ▶
The distinction
Two Restores That Look Identical and Do Opposite Things
Restoring a domain controller is not like restoring a file server, because the data is replicated and the other copies are still running. The question is whether the restored data should win.
Non-authoritativeAuthoritative
After restoreCatches up from its partnersOverwrites its partners
Use forA failed DC (Domain Controller) — almost always this oneRecovering objects deleted everywhere
RiskLowReintroduces everything else from that backup too
Reach for the Recycle Bin before either. If the AD (Active Directory) Recycle Bin is enabled, deleted objects are restorable in place with their group memberships intact — no backup, no downtime, no restore. Enable it now if it is not on; it is a one-way switch and costs nothing. 
# Is it on? If not, turn it on — irreversible, and you want it
Get-ADOptionalFeature -Filter 'name -like "Recycle Bin*"'

# Restore a deleted user, memberships intact
Get-ADObject -Filter 'Name -like "*jdoe*"' -IncludeDeletedObjects |
    Restore-ADObject
Failure mode
USN Rollback — Why You Never Snapshot a Domain Controller
Reverting a DC to a virtual machine snapshot rewinds its update sequence numbers. Partners have already seen higher numbers from it, so they ignore everything it sends — the DC believes it is replicating and is silently isolated, diverging from the domain until someone notices weeks later.
Modern Windows and hypervisors support VM-GenerationID, which detects the rollback and recovers safely. Do not rely on it: restore a DC with a supported system-state backup, or demote and rebuild. Rebuilding a DC is genuinely routine — promote a new one, let it replicate, remove the old.
Test the restore, not the backup. A backup job reporting success proves a file was written. The forest recovery procedure is long, involves seizing FSMO (Flexible Single Master Operations) roles and resetting the KRBTGT (Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket account) account twice, and reading it for the first time during an incident is how a bad day becomes a bad month.
🗑️ Decommissioning a Server Properly — The Checklist That Prevents Next Year's Outage Infra • Lifecycle ▶
Method
Power Off Is Not Decommissioned
A server switched off and left in the rack is the origin of a specific recurring incident: eighteen months later someone reclaims the address or the name, and something nobody knew depended on it breaks. The fix is a sequence with a waiting period, not a single action.
StepWhy this order
Find what still talks to itFirewall logs and DNS (Domain Name System) query logs, not the documentation
Lower the DNS record's time-to-liveSo the later removal propagates in minutes, not a day
Stop the services, leave the host upFailures now name the server; after a shutdown they do not
Wait a full business cycleA quarter, so quarterly jobs get their chance to fail
Power off, keep the record and the objectStill trivially reversible
After another cycle: remove DNS, AD (Active Directory) object, monitoring, backup job, licenceThe list nobody finishes
Stopping the services while the host stays up is the step that earns the most. A dependency that fails against a running server produces a connection refused naming the host. The same dependency after a shutdown produces a timeout somewhere else entirely, and nobody connects it to the decommissioning.
Failure mode
Domain Controllers and File Servers Do Not Just Get Switched Off
A domain controller must be demoted, which removes its metadata, transfers any FSMO (Flexible Single Master Operations) roles it holds and cleans up its service records. Powering one off instead leaves records advertising a DC that no longer answers, and clients will keep trying it — producing slow logons that survive every other fix.
If the DC is already gone and cannot be demoted, clean the metadata explicitly. Do not leave it: replication partners keep attempting it, and the errors mask real faults. 
# Graceful, on the DC itself
Uninstall-ADDSDomainController -DemoteOperationMasterRole -ForceRemoval:$false

# The DC is gone for good — remove it from the directory
ntdsutil "metadata cleanup" "remove selected server DC03" quit quit
Get-ADObject -Filter 'objectClass -eq "computer"' -SearchBase `
    "OU=Domain Controllers,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com"
The same applies to a file server behind a DFS (Distributed File System) namespace: remove the folder target first and let clients move, then decommission. Reversing those two steps is a user-visible outage instead of a silent migration.
📐 Mathematics — Calculus
Calculus
Limits · Derivatives · Integrals · Series · Differential Equations · Cheat Sheet 16 topics · ~55 min ▾
📐 Calculus Cheat Sheet — Everything on One Page MATH • Cheat Sheet ▶
Derivatives

Rules

Powerd/dx xⁿ = n·xn−1
Product(fg)′ = f′g + fg′
Quotient(f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′) / g² — "low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared"
Chaind/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) · g′(x)
ImplicitDifferentiate both sides in x, write dy/dx whenever you differentiate a y, then solve for dy/dx

The ones to know cold

Pattern worth noticing: every co-function derivative (cos, csc, cot) carries a minus sign. That one observation halves what you have to memorise.

Antiderivatives — every one gets + C

Integrals

The Fundamental Theorem, and the three techniques

NameStatement / method
FTC Part 1d/dx ∫ax f(t) dt = f(x) — differentiation undoes integration
FTC Part 2∫ab f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F′ = f
u-substitutionReverse chain rule. Pick u = the inside function; you need its derivative present (up to a constant). Change the limits when the integral is definite, or convert back before evaluating
By parts∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. Choose u by LIATE: Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential — earliest in the list becomes u
Partial fractionsFor a rational function with the degree of the numerator lower than the denominator: factor the denominator, split into simpler fractions, integrate each. If the degree is not lower, do polynomial long division first
Applications

Area, volume, length, average

QuantityFormula
Area between curves∫ab (top − bottom) dx
Volume — diskV = π ∫ab [R(x)]² dx
Volume — washerV = π ∫ab ([R(x)]² − [r(x)]²) dx — outer squared minus inner squared, not the difference squared
Volume — shellV = 2π ∫ab x · h(x) dx
Arc lengthL = ∫ab √(1 + [f′(x)]²) dx
Average valuefavg = 1/(b−a) · ∫ab f(x) dx
Series

Convergence tests and the four Maclaurin series

TestVerdict
nth-term (divergence)If lim an ≠ 0, it diverges. If the limit is 0, this test says nothing
Geometric Σ a·rⁿConverges iff |r| < 1, to a/(1 − r)
p-series Σ 1/npConverges iff p > 1. So Σ1/n diverges, Σ1/n² converges
Ratio testL = lim |an+1/an|. L < 1 converges, L > 1 diverges, L = 1 inconclusive
Alternating seriesConverges if terms decrease in magnitude and tend to 0
SeriesExpansion
eˣΣ xⁿ/n! = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + …
sin xx − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − … (odd powers)
cos x1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − … (even powers)
1/(1 − x)1 + x + x² + x³ + … for |x| < 1

Taylor series about a: f(x) = Σ f(n)(a)·(x − a)ⁿ / n!. A Maclaurin series is just the case a = 0.

Foundations

Trig identities and limits you will keep needing

Identity
Pythagoreansin²θ + cos²θ = 1  |  1 + tan²θ = sec²θ  |  1 + cot²θ = csc²θ
Double anglesin 2θ = 2 sinθ cosθ  |  cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 2cos²θ − 1 = 1 − 2sin²θ
Special limitslimx→0 (sin x)/x = 1  |  limx→0 (1 − cos x)/x = 0
L'Hôpital (L'Hopital)Only for 0/0 or ∞/∞: then lim f/g = lim f′/g′. Check the form every time before applying it
Continuity at aAll three: f(a) exists, limx→a f(x) exists, and the two are equal
1️⃣ Unit 1 — Foundations: Functions, Continuity, Vectors & Trig MATH • Ch 1–5 ▶
Ch 1–2

Functions, graphs and continuity

IdeaWhat to hold onto
Transformations of f(x)f(x) + k up · f(x + k) left · a·f(x) vertical stretch · f(ax) horizontal compression by 1/a. Inside the parentheses does the opposite of what it looks like
Domain killersDivision by zero, even roots of negatives, logs of non-positives. Almost every "find the domain" question is one of those three
ContinuityValue exists, limit exists, they match. A removable discontinuity is a hole; a jump is one-sided limits disagreeing; an infinite one is a vertical asymptote
AsymptotesVertical where the denominator is 0 and the numerator is not. Horizontal from comparing degrees: bottom-heavy → y = 0, equal → ratio of leading coefficients, top-heavy → none (slant instead)
Ch 3

Vectors

OperationFormula
Magnitude|v| = √(v₁² + v₂² + v₃²)
Unit vectorv̂ = v / |v|
Dot producta·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ = |a||b| cos θ — a scalar. Zero means perpendicular
Angle betweencos θ = (a·b) / (|a||b|)
Cross producta × b — a vector, perpendicular to both. |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ. Zero means parallel

The one that gets missed on tests: dot gives a number, cross gives a vector. If your answer has the wrong type, you used the wrong product.

Ch 4–5

Trig values, and the calculator trap

θ0π/6 (30°)π/4 (45°)π/3 (60°)π/2 (90°)
sin01/2√2/2√3/21
cos1√3/2√2/21/20
tan0√3/31√3undefined

Degrees versus radians is the single most common avoidable error in a calculus course. Calculus is done in radians. If your calculator is in degree mode, sin(π) returns about 0.0548 instead of 0. Check the mode indicator before every test — this costs one second and has ended many otherwise-correct attempts.

Two more calculator habits worth building: parenthesise the whole denominator (1/(2+3), never 1/2+3), and remember that −2² is −4 while (−2)² is 4 — the minus sign is not part of the base unless you make it so.

2️⃣ Unit 2 — Derivatives: Limits, Rules, Graphing & Applications MATH • Ch 6–10 ▶
Ch 6

Evaluating a limit — try these in order

#TryWhen
1Substitute. If you get a number, you are doneAlways first. Most limits are this easy
2Factor and cancelSubstitution gave 0/0 and it is a polynomial or a simple rational
3Multiply by the conjugate0/0 with a square root in it
4Divide by the highest power of x in the denominatorx → ±∞ on a rational function
5L'Hôpital / L'HopitalConfirmed 0/0 or ∞/∞ and the above did not help

A nonzero number over zero is not indeterminate — it is infinite (check the sign from each side). Only the seven forms 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞−∞, 1∞, 00, ∞0 are indeterminate.

Ch 7–8

What a derivative means, before what it computes

A derivative is a rate of change and, geometrically, the slope of the tangent line. Everything in this unit is one of those two readings: f′(a) is the instantaneous rate at a, and the tangent line there is y − f(a) = f′(a)(x − a).

Position → velocity → acceleration is the same fact applied twice: v = s′, a = v′ = s″. Speed is |v|, which is why an object can have negative velocity and increasing speed at the same time.

Ch 9

Reading a graph off the derivatives

If…Then f is…
f′ > 0increasing
f′ < 0decreasing
f′ = 0 or undefinedat a critical point — a candidate for a max or min, not a guarantee
f″ > 0concave up (holds water)
f″ < 0concave down
f″ changes signinflection point — the sign must actually change, not merely reach zero

Second derivative test: at a critical point, f″ > 0 means local minimum, f″ < 0 means local maximum, and f″ = 0 tells you nothing — fall back to the first derivative sign chart.

Ch 10

Optimisation and related rates — the same four steps

# OPTIMISATION
1. Draw it. Label what varies with letters.
2. Write the quantity to optimise as an equation.
3. Use a CONSTRAINT to reduce it to ONE variable.
4. Differentiate, set = 0, solve, then test the critical
   points AND the endpoints of the domain.

# RELATED RATES - the difference is step 3
1. Draw it. Label what varies with letters, not numbers.
2. Write an equation relating the quantities.
3. Differentiate BOTH SIDES with respect to TIME (implicitly).
   Every variable produces a d/dt term via the chain rule.
4. NOW substitute the numbers for the instant asked about,
   and solve for the rate you want.

# The classic mistake in related rates is substituting the
# numbers at step 2. Do that and the varying quantity becomes
# a constant, whose derivative is zero, and the problem
# collapses. Numbers go in LAST.
3️⃣ Unit 3 — Integrals: Series, Area, Techniques & Differential Equations MATH • Ch 11–15 ▶
Ch 11

Picking a convergence test

If the series has…Reach for
Terms that clearly do not go to 0nth-term test — done, it diverges
The form Σ a·rⁿGeometric: converges iff |r| < 1
The form Σ 1/npp-series: converges iff p > 1
Factorials or n-th powersRatio test — factorials cancel beautifully in a ratio
(−1)ⁿAlternating series test

Always run the nth-term test first. It is one line, and when it applies it ends the problem immediately. Remember it can only prove divergence — a limit of 0 does not prove convergence, which is exactly why Σ1/n diverges.

Ch 12–13

Choosing an integration technique

The integrand looks like…Try
A function and (a multiple of) its own derivativeu-substitution
A product of two unrelated types — x·eˣ, x·sin x, ln xBy parts, choosing u by LIATE
A rational function with a factorable denominatorPartial fractions
√(a² − x²), √(a² + x²), √(x² − a²)Trig substitution
Nothing obviousAlgebra first — expand, split the fraction, or use an identity. Many "hard" integrals are easy once rewritten

Two habits that catch most errors: after any indefinite integral, differentiate your answer and check you get the integrand back — it takes ten seconds and is a complete verification. And when you substitute in a definite integral, either change the limits to u-values or convert back to x before evaluating. Mixing the two is the most common wrong answer in this chapter.

Ch 15

Differential equations

TypeMethod
Separable dy/dx = g(x)·h(y)Separate: dy/h(y) = g(x) dx, integrate both sides, + C on one side only, then solve for y
Initial value problemFind the general solution first, then use the initial condition to pin down C. Not the other way round
Exponential growth / decay dy/dt = k·yy = y₀·ekt. Positive k grows, negative k decays. Half-life and doubling-time questions are this equation
Slope fieldsAt each point, the segment's slope is dy/dx evaluated there. A solution curve follows the segments — you are reading a picture, not computing

Verification works here too, and is even easier: substitute your solution back into the original equation. If both sides match, you are right, regardless of how you got there.

✅ Chapter Tests & the Final — Where the Marks Actually Go MATH • Exam Strategy ▶
The trap

Most lost marks are not conceptual

ErrorGuard
Calculator in degree modeCheck before question 1. sin(π) should read 0
Dropping + CWrite it as you write the integral sign, not afterwards
Forgetting the chain rule's inner derivativeUnderline the inside function before differentiating
Sign slips on cos, csc, cot derivativesCo-functions are negative. Say it once per test
u-sub limits not changedDecide up front: change the limits, or convert back. Never half of each
Substituting numbers too early in related ratesDifferentiate first, numbers last
Answering the wrong questionThe question asks for the value, the rate, or the x where it happens. Re-read the last line before submitting
In practice

Using this site on this course

Every card here is a flashcard and a quiz option automatically. Pick the 📐 Math deck rather than All domains, and star (★) the cards for the chapter whose test is next so they land in your study list.

The techniques in the Productivity domain apply directly: The Memory Palace is well suited to the derivative and integral tables, which are exactly the ordered arbitrary lists it is for. Hansei after each practice set — what broke, what would have caught it — turns a wrong answer into a countermeasure rather than a bad mood. And Sleep matters more here than for most subjects, because a calculation error rate is one of the first things sleep loss moves.

A note on the scores so far: an honest way to read a 73% is that roughly one question in four is going wrong, and the error table above is where those usually live. It is worth spending one practice set doing nothing but checking your own work — differentiate every antiderivative, substitute every solution back — before assuming the gap is conceptual.

🔢 Logarithms & Exponents — Rules and How to Solve MATH • Formulas ▶
Core Concept

A log is an exponent — that is the whole idea

logb(x) = y means exactly by = x. "What power do I raise b to, to get x?" Every log rule below is an exponent rule wearing a different hat, which is why the two columns mirror each other line for line.

Reference

The mirror

Exponent ruleLog rule
bm · bn = bm+nlog(MN) = log M + log N
bm / bn = bm−nlog(M/N) = log M − log N
(bm)n = bmnlog(Mp) = p · log M
b0 = 1logb(1) = 0
b1 = blogb(b) = 1
b−n = 1/bnlog(1/M) = −log M
b1/n = n√blog(n√M) = (1/n) · log M

Change of base: logb(x) = ln x / ln b = log x / log b. This is how you compute log7(200) on a calculator that only offers ln and log.

ln is loge, and log with no base written usually means log10. In calculus assume natural log unless told otherwise — e is the base that makes the derivative clean.

The trap

The three rules that do not exist

WrongRight
log(M + N) = log M + log NNo such rule. A log of a sum does not split. log M + log N = log(MN) — the sum is on the outside
log M / log N = log(M − N)No. log M − log N = log(M/N). A quotient of logs is a change of base, not a subtraction
(log M)p = p · log MOnly log(Mp) = p · log M. The exponent must be inside the log

And the one that costs marks quietly: a log of a negative number or of zero is undefined, so after solving any log equation you must check every solution in the original. Extraneous roots are normal here, not evidence you made a mistake.

Hands-on

The two shapes, and how each is solved

# VARIABLE IN THE EXPONENT -> take a log of both sides
   3^(2x) = 50
   ln(3^(2x)) = ln 50
   2x · ln 3 = ln 50          # the power rule pulls it down
   x = ln 50 / (2 · ln 3) ≈ 1.78

# VARIABLE INSIDE A LOG -> condense to ONE log, then exponentiate
   log(x) + log(x − 3) = 1
   log(x(x − 3)) = 1          # product rule condenses
   x(x − 3) = 10^1            # base 10 implied by "log"
   x² − 3x − 10 = 0
   (x − 5)(x + 2) = 0  ->  x = 5 or x = −2

   CHECK: x = −2 would need log(−2). Undefined. Reject.
   Answer: x = 5 only.
📊 Trigonometry — The Unit Circle, Identities & Inverses MATH • Formulas ▶
Diagram

The unit circle — every value you are asked to know

Each point is (cos θ, sin θ). Reading it beats recalling a table: the x-coordinate is the cosine, the y-coordinate is the sine, and the tangent is their ratio. Where the x-coordinate is 0 — at π/2 and 3π/2 — the tangent is undefined, which is exactly where tan has its vertical asymptotes.

Only the first quadrant needs memorising. Everything else is those values with signs from ASTC: All positive in QI, only Sine in QII, only Tangent in QIII, only Cosine in QIV.

Reference

Identities worth knowing by heart

FamilyIdentities
Reciprocalcsc θ = 1/sin θ  |  sec θ = 1/cos θ  |  cot θ = cos θ/sin θ
Pythagoreansin²θ + cos²θ = 1  |  1 + tan²θ = sec²θ  |  1 + cot²θ = csc²θ
Even / oddcos(−θ) = cos θ (even)  |  sin(−θ) = −sin θ and tan(−θ) = −tan θ (odd)
Sumsin(A ± B) = sinA cosB ± cosA sinB
cos(A ± B) = cosA cosB ∓ sinA sinB — the sign flips
Double anglesin 2θ = 2 sinθ cosθ
cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 2cos²θ − 1 = 1 − 2sin²θ
Power reductionsin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2  |  cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2 — the ones that make ∫ sin²x dx doable

The second and third Pythagorean identities are just the first divided through by cos²θ and by sin²θ. Derive them in ten seconds instead of memorising three separate facts.

And the first one is the Pythagorean theorem itself. On the unit circle the legs are cos θ and sin θ and the hypotenuse is 1, so a² + b² = c² becomes cos²θ + sin²θ = 1. That is why the family is named after him — it is one theorem in trigonometric clothing.

Reference

Inverse trig, and the two laws

InverseRange — the principal values
arcsin x[−π/2, π/2] — QIV and QI
arccos x[0, π] — QI and QII
arctan x(−π/2, π/2) — QIV and QI, never reaching the ends

Those ranges are why arcsin(sin(3π/4)) is π/4, not 3π/4 — the answer has to land inside the range. It is a favourite exam question precisely because the obvious answer is wrong.

LawFormulaUse when
Sines — the law of sinesa/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin CYou have an angle paired with the side opposite it
Cosines — the law of cosinesc² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos CThree sides, or two sides and the angle between them
📈 The Two Pictures — Derivative as Slope, Integral as Area MATH • Diagrams ▶
Diagram

The derivative is a limit of slopes

Take two points on the curve. The line through them — the secant — has slope Δy/Δx = [f(x+h) − f(x)] / h, the average rate of change across that interval. Now slide the second point toward the first. The secant pivots, and in the limit as h → 0 it becomes the tangent, whose slope is f′(x) — the instantaneous rate.

That is the whole definition, and it is worth being able to sketch, because it turns several memorised rules into obvious consequences: f′ = 0 at a peak because the tangent is flat there; a corner has no derivative because the secants approach different slopes from each side; and a vertical tangent means f′ is undefined rather than zero.

Diagram

The integral is a limit of sums

Slice the region under the curve into rectangles and add their areas — that is a Riemann sum, and it is an approximation. More, thinner rectangles give a better one; the definite integral is what those sums converge to. The elongated S of ∫ is literally an S, for "sum".

Which is what makes the Fundamental Theorem surprising rather than merely true. These two pictures — slopes of tangents, areas under curves — look unrelated, and the theorem says each undoes the other. Area is found by reversing slope. That is the biggest single idea in the course; almost everything in Units 2 and 3 follows from it.

One consequence to carry into the tests: a definite integral is a signed area. Region below the axis counts as negative, which is why ∫02π sin x dx = 0 even though the curve plainly encloses area. If a question asks for total area rather than for the integral, split at the zeros and take absolute values.

📏 Algebra & Geometry Formulas — The Prerequisites MATH • Formulas ▶

NameFormula

Discriminantb² − 4ac — positive gives two real roots, zero gives one, negative gives none real
Pythagorean theorema² + b² = c² — legs a, b, hypotenuse c. Only for right triangles; otherwise use the law of cosines, which is its generalisation
Difference of squaresa² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)
Perfect square(a ± b)² = a² ± 2ab + b²
Sum / difference of cubesa³ ± b³ = (a ± b)(a² ∓ ab + b²)
Slopem = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)
Point-slope formy − y₁ = m(x − x₁) — the form every tangent-line answer takes
Distanced = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)

Circle (centre h,k)(x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²; the unit circle is x² + y² = 1
